lessons.title: Start here — Service applicability, legal obligations and controlled documents
lessons.body:
# L05: Service applicability, legal obligations and controlled documents

Keep each Vendor assessed against actual work and current procedures. This course teaches the decisions needed to implement that purpose in field operations. It covers service/exposure register; jurisdiction review; document control; approved exclusions. The examples involve fictional oilfield crews and companies; none is a real incident record or evidence of a company's implementation.

Read six substantive lessons, answer each attached knowledge check, then study two applied cases and answer the twenty final questions. Every question has three choices and one correct answer. The course records the first answer separately from any correction. Completion requires all 26 answered correctly or acknowledged remediation, including reading the specific explanation for each correction. A remediated result must never replace the original score. There is no speed requirement: take the time needed to explain the decision in your own words.

The audience includes workers who recognize gaps, supervisors who coordinate work and program owners who maintain the system. Each has a different decision boundary. An observer may report an uncertain safeguard without personally being qualified to repair it. A supervisor may coordinate a hold without being the person authorized to clear a technical prerequisite. Learn both the action and the limit on that action.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Map services to exposures
lessons.body:
## Map services to exposures

A service profile describes the actual work sold and performed, including subcontracted work, locations, assets and people. Service names alone may hide different exposures: gate support differs from fuel delivery even when one company supplies both. Identify what changes when a service is added. Requirements follow the real exposure rather than the company's preferred category. Unknown scope must be clarified before approving an exclusion.

### Deeper application

Build the exposure profile by asking what the service requires workers to do, not merely what the marketing description calls it. A gate company might provide office administration only, direct traffic or also operate vehicles; those are different task combinations. Include temporary and subcontracted delivery arrangements so outsourcing does not make an exposure disappear on paper. Keep active and proposed scope distinct. A proposed service can create readiness tasks before it becomes an authorized operational offering.

### Worked oilfield example

A gate-support company adds fuel delivery but requests driving requirements remain excluded because it historically owned no trucks. The decision is to update the service and exposure profile and assess transport prerequisites before accepting delivery work.

Applicability follows current work. A historical exclusion cannot cover a newly introduced exposure. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A revised scope profile identifying delivery assets, drivers, cargo and transport obligations. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the revised profile omits fuel delivery subcontracted to another company. The appropriate correction is to include the subcontracted exposure and bridge the performing company's relevant requirements. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

An implementation record and a later effectiveness check answer different questions. The first shows whether the required action occurred within the stated scope. The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. In this example, the follow-up should return to the actual gap described above, rather than simply asking whether the file now looks complete. A genuine unknown must remain visible until resolved by appropriate evidence.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Identify obligations through competent review
lessons.body:
## Identify obligations through competent review

Legal, client and manufacturer requirements have different sources and scopes. Assign a competent owner to identify jurisdiction and activity applicability, capture the current source and explain how it translates into practice. An internet summary or another customer's procedure is not automatically governing. Where interpretation is uncertain, seek appropriate expertise rather than making a universal claim. Record the decision and the limits of the review.

### Deeper application

For each obligation, retain the source, revision or retrieval basis, jurisdiction, affected activity and responsible interpreter. A law, manufacturer instruction and client condition can all apply, but they do not have identical legal status. Do not call a client's contractual condition a universal regulation. Where sources conflict or applicability is uncertain, record the question and obtain suitable advice. The operational procedure should translate the resolved requirements into usable steps without pretending the register itself performs the work.

### Worked oilfield example

A manager applies a neighboring state's driver rule without checking the routes and jurisdiction actually used. The decision is to have the competent transport owner verify applicable requirements for the actual operation.

Similar work can fall under different requirements; a traceable applicability decision is needed. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: An obligation register linking jurisdiction, service, source, responsible owner and applicability decision. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the register lists an outdated source without a current applicability review. The appropriate correction is to verify the current governing source and assess any resulting changes to the affected work. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

An implementation record and a later effectiveness check answer different questions. The first shows whether the required action occurred within the stated scope. The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. In this example, the follow-up should return to the actual gap described above, rather than simply asking whether the file now looks complete. A genuine unknown must remain visible until resolved by appropriate evidence.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Control document versions
lessons.body:
## Control document versions

A controlled procedure has an identity, approved revision, scope, owner and effective date. Workers need access to the version applying to their work, including offline conditions. Remove obsolete copies from operational use while preserving historical records. A printed page is not inherently invalid, but its version and controlled distribution must be clear. Do not alter past job records to make them appear to have used a later revision.

### Deeper application

A controlled document lifecycle includes drafting, competent review where needed, approval, issue, access, revision and withdrawal from use. Archive the superseded version with its effective period so a historical job can still be understood. Withdrawal from use is different from deleting history. For offline copies, define who supplies updates and how users recognize the applicable revision. A current master document in the office does not prevent an obsolete field copy from directing actual work.

### Worked oilfield example

A supervisor's truck contains an old isolation instruction that conflicts with the approved current work pack. The decision is to hold the conflicting activity and obtain the applicable controlled instruction and competent resolution.

Version control protects the method used, not merely the label on a page. Conflicting instructions require resolution. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A controlled distribution record and confirmation the obsolete operational copy was withdrawn. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the obsolete page was archived correctly but remains in an active field binder. The appropriate correction is to remove it from operational use and verify the crew has the applicable replacement. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

An implementation record and a later effectiveness check answer different questions. The first shows whether the required action occurred within the stated scope. The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Evaluate change before expanding work
lessons.body:
## Evaluate change before expanding work

New equipment, jurisdictions, roles, subcontractors or services can change the required controls. Evaluate the change before mobilization, identify added prerequisites and reuse existing evidence only where its scope remains valid. A change review should show who assessed technical implications and what remains unready. Commercial urgency cannot make an unmatched credential or procedure applicable. Changed work must reach dispatch and site personnel, not only the document register.

### Deeper application

A change review can be proportional: identify what is different, which earlier evidence still matches and which requirements are newly triggered. Reusing valid evidence avoids unnecessary repetition, but scope must be checked explicitly. A new attachment may leave first-aid training unchanged while changing equipment assessment and operator authorization. Record pending prerequisites in allocation systems. Adding a service in a catalogue should not silently change the operational status to ready before its people, equipment and interfaces are verified.

### Worked oilfield example

A maintenance company introduces a new lifting attachment but relies on an assessment for its previous configuration. The decision is to review equipment suitability and matching competence before releasing the changed operation.

A changed configuration can alter both equipment suitability and the operator's assessed task scope. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A change review linking the attachment, manufacturer information, task assessment and authorization limits. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the change was approved in the office but not communicated to dispatch. The appropriate correction is to update dispatch restrictions and confirm the changed authorization is understood before allocation. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

An implementation record and a later effectiveness check answer different questions. The first shows whether the required action occurred within the stated scope. The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. In this example, the follow-up should return to the actual gap described above, rather than simply asking whether the file now looks complete. A genuine unknown must remain visible until resolved by appropriate evidence.

lessons.title: Lesson 5 — Decide and preserve exclusions
lessons.body:
## Decide and preserve exclusions

An N/A request needs a bounded reason and authorized review. Exclusion is not a way to gain full credit or hide missing evidence. Removing a service from the catalogue does not erase active job obligations or historical assessments. Distinguish no current exposure from unknown exposure. If an entire category appears inapplicable, follow the approved review rules rather than inventing a reweighting method.

### Deeper application

A good exclusion reason identifies an exposure that is genuinely absent within a stated scope. No trucks owned is inadequate if the company dispatches subcontracted fuel deliveries. Explain what evidence supports the request and who reviewed it. The decision should show its effective scope and change triggers. N/A neither earns full points nor removes historical events. When work is removed, check active jobs and obligations before changing applicability; deleting a catalogue label cannot cancel an existing operational commitment.

### Worked oilfield example

A vendor removes a service listing while an accepted job using that service remains active. The decision is to preserve the job obligations and have the exclusion reviewed against actual continuing work.

Applicability is a reviewed scope judgment, not deletion of an inconvenient requirement or event history. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A reviewed exclusion decision with scope, rationale, active-job check and preserved history. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the exclusion rationale says no exposure but no one checked active assignments. The appropriate correction is to verify active work and correct the applicability decision before relying on the exclusion. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

An implementation record and a later effectiveness check answer different questions. The first shows whether the required action occurred within the stated scope. The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. In this example, the follow-up should return to the actual gap described above, rather than simply asking whether the file now looks complete. A genuine unknown must remain visible until resolved by appropriate evidence.

lessons.title: Lesson 6 — Audit access and real use
lessons.body:
## Audit access and real use

A complete register is useful only if people use current instructions in relevant conditions. Sample jobs, versions and worker understanding across representative shifts and services. Compare the procedure required with the one actually available. An auditor should distinguish an inaccessible document from an obsolete one and from an unclear instruction; each needs a different correction. A favorable sample is bounded evidence, not proof of universal compliance.

### Deeper application

Document assurance should sample retrieval as well as content. Ask a field user to obtain the instruction they would actually use, identify its revision and explain the relevant decision. If connectivity fails, inspect the authorized fallback. If the user finds two conflicting versions, resolve which governs before relying on either. Capture whether the problem was access, obsolete distribution or unclear instruction so the corrective action addresses the real failure instead of merely adding another document.

### Worked oilfield example

A remote crew cannot retrieve the controlled procedure because the only approved copy requires unavailable connectivity. The decision is to provide an approved accessible arrangement and confirm the crew has the applicable instructions before dependent work.

Distribution must support actual conditions of use; an inaccessible current procedure does not guide the crew. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A field access check identifying revision, offline arrangement and worker comprehension. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the offline copy is available but no process updates it after revision. The appropriate correction is to establish controlled updating and verify obsolete offline versions are withdrawn from use. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

An implementation record and a later effectiveness check answer different questions. The first shows whether the required action occurred within the stated scope. The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. In this example, the follow-up should return to the actual gap described above, rather than simply asking whether the file now looks complete. A genuine unknown must remain visible until resolved by appropriate evidence.

lessons.title: Two applied scenarios and fully worked solutions
lessons.body:
## Applied scenario 1: an incomplete decision chain

A gate-support company adds fuel delivery but requests driving requirements remain excluded because it historically owned no trucks. At the handover, a second issue is identified: The register lists an outdated source without a current applicability review. The receiving supervisor has the earlier record but does not yet have evidence that the new issue was resolved. A colleague proposes the following shortcut: Use the truck copy because it is familiar. Work is due to begin on the next shift, so the supervisor needs a defensible decision that protects people and preserves a clear history.

### Worked solution — immediate decision

The first response is: Update the service and exposure profile and assess transport prerequisites before accepting delivery work. The reason is specific: Applicability follows current work. A historical exclusion cannot cover a newly introduced exposure. Determine which assignment depends on that unresolved condition. Tell the affected people the restriction and who is coordinating resolution. If there is an immediate exposure, move to a safe position and use the established warning or emergency route rather than completing records first. The supervisor must not use a favorable overall company score as a substitute for this missing decision.

### Worked solution — resolve the additional issue

For the handover finding, the next action is: Verify the current governing source and assess any resulting changes to the affected work. The supporting record should show: An obligation register linking jurisdiction, service, source, responsible owner and applicability decision. This is important because similar work can fall under different requirements; a traceable applicability decision is needed. The receiving shift needs the actual status, not an assurance that someone intends to finish the check later. Identify the responsible role and obtain acknowledgment of the restriction. If the required authority or expertise is unavailable, the affected assignment remains unready; unrelated authorized work may be considered only after its interfaces are checked.

### Worked solution — reject the shortcut and verify the result

The proposed shortcut fails because version control protects the method used, not merely the label on a page. Conflicting instructions require resolution. The suitable decision is: Hold the conflicting activity and obtain the applicable controlled instruction and competent resolution. Evidence for review would include: A controlled distribution record and confirmation the obsolete operational copy was withdrawn. Separate correction of the immediate problem from confirmation that the change works in later comparable conditions. A reviewer should check the actual control used and the scope represented by the evidence. If the same weakness recurs, reopen the issue and retain both the original decision and the new observation.

### What can be concluded

This solution establishes a bounded route from an identified gap to evidence and responsible acceptance. It does not establish that an assessment, clinical decision, technical test or employer authorization actually happened in a real company. The fictional case teaches how to decide and what to verify. Actual release remains with the designated employer/site authority after the applicable prerequisites are met.

## Applied scenario 2: an incomplete decision chain

A maintenance company introduces a new lifting attachment but relies on an assessment for its previous configuration. At the handover, a second issue is identified: The exclusion rationale says no exposure but no one checked active assignments. The receiving supervisor has the earlier record but does not yet have evidence that the new issue was resolved. A colleague proposes the following shortcut: Treat online publication as proof every crew can use it. Work is due to begin on the next shift, so the supervisor needs a defensible decision that protects people and preserves a clear history.

### Worked solution — immediate decision

The first response is: Review equipment suitability and matching competence before releasing the changed operation. The reason is specific: A changed configuration can alter both equipment suitability and the operator's assessed task scope. Determine which assignment depends on that unresolved condition. Tell the affected people the restriction and who is coordinating resolution. If there is an immediate exposure, move to a safe position and use the established warning or emergency route rather than completing records first. The supervisor must not use a favorable overall company score as a substitute for this missing decision.

### Worked solution — resolve the additional issue

For the handover finding, the next action is: Verify active work and correct the applicability decision before relying on the exclusion. The supporting record should show: A reviewed exclusion decision with scope, rationale, active-job check and preserved history. This is important because applicability is a reviewed scope judgment, not deletion of an inconvenient requirement or event history. The receiving shift needs the actual status, not an assurance that someone intends to finish the check later. Identify the responsible role and obtain acknowledgment of the restriction. If the required authority or expertise is unavailable, the affected assignment remains unready; unrelated authorized work may be considered only after its interfaces are checked.

### Worked solution — reject the shortcut and verify the result

The proposed shortcut fails because distribution must support actual conditions of use; an inaccessible current procedure does not guide the crew. The suitable decision is: Provide an approved accessible arrangement and confirm the crew has the applicable instructions before dependent work. Evidence for review would include: A field access check identifying revision, offline arrangement and worker comprehension. Separate correction of the immediate problem from confirmation that the change works in later comparable conditions. A reviewer should check the actual control used and the scope represented by the evidence. If the same weakness recurs, reopen the issue and retain both the original decision and the new observation.

### What can be concluded

This solution establishes a bounded route from an identified gap to evidence and responsible acceptance. It does not establish that an assessment, clinical decision, technical test or employer authorization actually happened in a real company. The fictional case teaches how to decide and what to verify. Actual release remains with the designated employer/site authority after the applicable prerequisites are met.

lessons.title: Final assessment — twenty questions
lessons.body: Answer each question individually. Apply the taught decisions to the facts given. Your first choices are retained. If an answer is wrong, read the specific explanation and explicitly acknowledge the corrected answer. A corrected score records learning after feedback; it does not overwrite the first-answer result. All twenty final questions and all six lesson checks must be completed.

lessons.title: Finish — separate practical qualification
lessons.body:
## Written completion and what it proves

Completion requires all 26 answered correctly or acknowledged remediation. Both first-answer and remediated scores remain separate. Completing the guided course is evidence that you worked through its knowledge and decision questions; it is not an observed practical performance result, a legal license, a provider certification or an employer authorization. Training evidence contributes to review within its scope and validity, rather than automatically establishing the whole company program.

## What needs separate assessment

The assessment should test recognition of an abnormal condition as well as routine performance. A person who can repeat a procedure but cannot identify when to stop has not demonstrated the whole task. Employer authorization should state the person, tasks, equipment or site limits, required supervision and the basis for the decision. Applicable legal, issuer, client and change-trigger requirements govern validity; this course invents no universal renewal period.

## Before actual work

Confirm current local instructions, reporting routes, emergency arrangements and the person who can resolve an operating hold. If assigned work exceeds your assessed scope, say so before accepting it. The Partner's job/site readiness decision remains separate from the company's evidence review. Preserve real records through the authorized process and protect personal information. The fictional examples in this course must never be submitted as evidence that your company performed the actions described.

courses.title: H01 — Task risk assessment and JSA/JHA
courses.purpose: Identify energy sources and effective controls before routine and nonroutine work.

content.title: H01 — Task risk assessment and JSA/JHA
content.description: Complete guided H01 training: six taught lessons, two worked scenarios, six checks and a 20-question final. Separate first-answer and remediated scores; wrong answers require explicit correction acknowledgment.

explanations.H01_check1: A broad task label cannot reveal where exposure occurs or what controls are needed. The analysis must represent the actual work and location before it can support a safe plan.
explanations.H01_final_1_1: Hazards can arise before the main activity or during restoration and cleanup. An analysis that omits these stages can leave unplanned exposure despite describing the central task accurately.
explanations.H01_final_1_2: Step detail should support decisions. Overly broad steps conceal hazards, while excessive fragmentation makes the analysis hard to brief and use; group actions by meaningful changes in exposure.
explanations.H01_final_1_3: Worker participation supplies task knowledge that a generic form may lack. It does not remove the need for competent technical review or operating authorization when the hazards require them.
explanations.H01_check2: A useful description names the source, exposure pathway and people. It gives the team something specific to control and verify rather than a broad warning that each person interprets differently.
explanations.H01_final_2_1: Energy paths and releases do not follow company boundaries. Helpers, other contractors, drivers and bystanders may need separation, coordination or information even when they are not performing the step.
explanations.H01_final_2_2: Uncertainty about a serious hazard is a planning gap, not evidence that the hazard is small. Resolve it through suitable expertise and information before exposing people to find out.
explanations.H01_final_2_3: Controls must account for credible departures such as a jam or lost signal. Planning these responses prevents workers from improvising inside the hazard when the normal sequence fails.
explanations.H01_check3: Gloves do not stop a crushing movement. The team should change the exposure through an approved handling or separation arrangement and then assess any remaining protective equipment needs.
explanations.H01_final_3_1: A suitable remote method can remove a person from the harm pathway. Its own limitations still need assessment, but it changes exposure more directly than a reminder alone.
explanations.H01_final_3_2: PPE must match the specific exposure and user. It may be necessary alongside stronger controls, but it does not automatically justify leaving a preventable energy or release hazard uncontrolled.
explanations.H01_final_3_3: The hierarchy does not authorize improvised modifications. Technical changes can create new failure modes and must pass the applicable design, change and operating review processes.
explanations.H01_check4: Control ownership and evidence make the plan executable. An unassigned statement can be assumed complete by everyone while no one establishes or verifies it.
explanations.H01_final_4_1: A useful record allows another reviewer to understand what was established and when. Predicting success or using vague labels obscures failures and can falsely imply current readiness.
explanations.H01_final_4_2: A critical safeguard is not optional because other controls passed. The failure must be resolved through the responsible process; arithmetic and favorable labels do not replace the missing barrier.
explanations.H01_final_4_3: Evidence has scope and currency. A photograph can document a condition but may not demonstrate current performance or the whole boundary; verification must match the control being claimed.
explanations.H01_check5: Separate analyses do not resolve shared exposure. The interaction needs an agreed control, ownership and communication that both crews and the site authority understand.
explanations.H01_final_5_1: A comprehension check tests whether the instruction can guide behavior. Attendance and experience may support training history but cannot show that the current job and changed controls are understood.
explanations.H01_final_5_2: The new worker can change communication and coordination needs. They must understand the actual scope, controls and role limits before participating, rather than learning them while exposed.
explanations.H01_final_5_3: Coordination follows credible interaction, not employer identity. Shared energy, access and operating states can affect a job even when another company owns the adjacent task.
explanations.H01_check6: The analysis must match the work actually performed. A changed exposure invalidates assumptions even if the administrative job number remains the same.
explanations.H01_final_6_1: A favorable outcome can occur despite missing controls. Effectiveness review examines implementation and performance, including near misses and interventions, within the sampled work scope.
explanations.H01_final_6_2: Completion of a task does not automatically establish readiness for operation. Handback communicates the actual state and unresolved restrictions to the designated operating authority.
explanations.H01_final_6_3: A standard analysis is a starting resource. Its scope and assumptions must be checked against the present job; reuse without field confirmation can carry obsolete controls into a different exposure.
explanations.H01_final_scenario1: The new activity changes the first crew’s exposure and escape assumptions. Both affected plans need coordination; separate employer responsibility does not isolate the physical hazards.
explanations.H01_final_scenario2: The physical control must match the plan before people rely on it. Neither administrative completion nor a risk label compensates for an exposed pedestrian route.

lessons.title: Start here: learning, scores and role boundaries
lessons.body:
# H01: Task risk assessment and JSA/JHA

This original VNDRLY course teaches decisions for common; detail follows tasks. Its purpose is to identify energy sources and effective controls before routine and nonroutine work. The six lessons explain the hazard, planning decisions, controls, checks, changing conditions and handback. Worked examples and two fictional scenarios show how those decisions fit together. Read the teaching before answering; no live hazardous activity is needed to complete this course.

There are six lesson knowledge checks and a 20-question final assessment. Submit each answer before viewing its feedback. Your first answer remains in the original score. If an answer is wrong, read the specific explanation and explicitly acknowledge the correction; acknowledged corrections contribute to a separate remediated score. Completion requires all sections and all 26 questions correct or explicitly acknowledged after remediation. A later corrected answer never erases the first-answer record.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Describe the real task in usable steps
lessons.body:
A JSA or JHA is a job safety or hazard analysis: a way to examine how a task can harm people and choose controls before exposure. It is not a list of reassuring words. Begin with the actual job, equipment identity, location, people and work limits. Walk the location with the people who perform the work; they often know handling difficulties, access restrictions and informal workarounds that a desk description misses. Include setup, normal execution, interruptions, cleanup and handback.

Break the job into steps detailed enough to reveal a changing hazard but not so detailed that every hand movement becomes an unreadable line. For replacing a pump guard, useful steps might cover obtaining authorization, establishing the required safe energy state, removing and storing the guard, performing the authorized work, and controlled reinstatement. The analysis does not itself authorize isolation or maintenance.

Worked example: “service pump” hides access, lifting and stored-energy exposure. “Remove the identified guard after authorized isolation verification” shows both the activity and the prerequisite. If the proposed job later includes opening a process connection, that is a different exposure needing assessment, not an unrecorded extra step.

### Applying the mechanism

A useful step is an observable part of the job with a clear beginning and end. If the team cannot tell when the exposure changes, combine or split the step until it supports a specific control decision. Reusing a template is efficient only after that comparison with the real task.

### Decision principles

Hazards can arise before the main activity or during restoration and cleanup. An analysis that omits these stages can leave unplanned exposure despite describing the central task accurately.

Step detail should support decisions. Overly broad steps conceal hazards, while excessive fragmentation makes the analysis hard to brief and use; group actions by meaningful changes in exposure.

Worker participation supplies task knowledge that a generic form may lack. It does not remove the need for competent technical review or operating authorization when the hazards require them.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Explain the harm pathway, not just the hazard label
lessons.body:
For each step, identify the source of harm, how it can reach a person and who can be exposed. “Pressure” is a category; “a trapped section can release liquid toward the person loosening the connection” describes a pathway. Consider electrical, mechanical, hydraulic, pneumatic, chemical, thermal and gravitational energy, movement of vehicles and loads, airborne exposure, noise, weather and ergonomics. Look beyond the person holding the tool to helpers, gate staff, adjacent crews and the public.

Ask what can go wrong during both intended and foreseeable abnormal conditions: a stuck component, dropped tool, loss of communication, failed restraint or unexpected restart. This is not an invitation to speculate without bounds. Use the equipment, material, operating state and site interactions to identify credible events, and seek specialist review when the team cannot establish them.

Worked example: a hose crosses a shared walkway. The crew identifies tripping, but also asks whether a vehicle could damage the hose and expose a nearby worker to the released contents. One object can create several harm pathways requiring different controls.

### Applying the mechanism

Describe the event in physical terms: what releases, moves, contacts or exposes whom. “Injury” describes a consequence but not its cause. Naming the pathway helps the crew choose a control that interrupts it and helps an observer check whether that control actually protects the intended people.

### Decision principles

Energy paths and releases do not follow company boundaries. Helpers, other contractors, drivers and bystanders may need separation, coordination or information even when they are not performing the step.

Uncertainty about a serious hazard is a planning gap, not evidence that the hazard is small. Resolve it through suitable expertise and information before exposing people to find out.

Controls must account for credible departures such as a jam or lost signal. Planning these responses prevents workers from improvising inside the hazard when the normal sequence fails.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Choose controls that change exposure
lessons.body:
Control selection begins by asking whether the hazardous activity or exposure can be removed. If not, consider a safer method or material, then engineered separation or containment, supported by procedures, access control, training and suitable PPE.

A statement such as “stay alert” relies on continuous human performance and does not create a physical separation. A correctly designed guard, controlled route or remote method can reduce dependence on attention. PPE can be essential, but it has selection, fit, compatibility and use limitations and does not eliminate the release or moving equipment.

Worked example: a worker is asked to steady a heavy part by hand in a pinch point. The team first examines an approved handling arrangement that removes the hand from the crushing zone. Gloves may still protect against minor contact hazards, but gloves do not make a hand safe between moving steel surfaces.

### Applying the mechanism

Ask how the proposed safeguard changes the pathway. A barrier that only marks a boundary may depend on access discipline; an engineered enclosure may physically contain movement. Both can have roles, but they have different failure modes and need different verification. Avoid calling every warning an engineering control.

### Decision principles

A suitable remote method can remove a person from the harm pathway. Its own limitations still need assessment, but it changes exposure more directly than a reminder alone.

PPE must match the specific exposure and user. It may be necessary alongside stronger controls, but it does not automatically justify leaving a preventable energy or release hazard uncontrolled.

The hierarchy does not authorize improvised modifications. Technical changes can create new failure modes and must pass the applicable design, change and operating review processes.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Make each safeguard observable and owned
lessons.body:
An analysis becomes usable when each control has an owner and a way to verify it. “Area secure” is ambiguous. A better instruction identifies which access points are controlled, what barrier or separation arrangement is required, who establishes it, and who confirms it before the relevant exposure. For technical controls, the approved procedure defines the method and acceptance criteria; the JSA should link to it rather than inventing a test.

The person checking a control needs suitable competence and a view of the actual condition. A prior signature or photograph can support a record but may not establish current function. Record failed and uncertain checks honestly and hold the affected work until they are resolved. A risk score summarizes an assessment; it does not energize a missing safeguard.

Worked example: the JSA requires an exclusion boundary before a pressure activity. The supervisor walks the boundary and finds a side access left open. The correct result is a failed readiness check followed by correction and re-verification. Checking the box because most of the barrier is installed would hide the very gap the check is meant to find.

### Applying the mechanism

Assign ownership at the point where the safeguard must exist. The person ordering a barrier and the person verifying its installed boundary may be different. Make both duties explicit so a purchasing milestone is not mistaken for field readiness. Record actual failed checks as useful findings.

### Decision principles

A useful record allows another reviewer to understand what was established and when. Predicting success or using vague labels obscures failures and can falsely imply current readiness.

A critical safeguard is not optional because other controls passed. The failure must be resolved through the responsible process; arithmetic and favorable labels do not replace the missing barrier.

Evidence has scope and currency. A photograph can document a condition but may not demonstrate current performance or the whole boundary; verification must match the control being claimed.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Brief for understanding and coordinate interfaces
lessons.body:
The briefing is a shared operating conversation. Explain the job steps, serious harm pathways, assigned controls, stop triggers, communication method and emergency arrangements. Ask workers to describe their own part and the boundary they must not cross. A signature can record participation, but a person who cannot understand the language or explain the instruction is not ready merely because their name is on the sheet.

Coordinate with the site authority and other crews when work shares equipment, access, utilities, atmosphere, lifting routes or emergency resources. One team’s safe sequence can conflict with another team’s restart or movement. Resolve those interfaces before work; do not expect two separate JSAs to coordinate themselves.

Worked example: a maintenance crew briefs a pump task while another crew plans to move a load through the same access. The supervisors and site authority agree separation in time or another approved arrangement, update both briefings and identify who releases each stage. Telling each crew to “watch out” leaves the conflict unresolved.

### Applying the mechanism

Use a short teach-back: ask a worker what they will do if the adjacent crew starts its equipment or the planned escape route becomes blocked. The response reveals whether the briefing taught the interaction and stop trigger, rather than merely presenting a list of hazards.

### Decision principles

A comprehension check tests whether the instruction can guide behavior. Attendance and experience may support training history but cannot show that the current job and changed controls are understood.

The new worker can change communication and coordination needs. They must understand the actual scope, controls and role limits before participating, rather than learning them while exposed.

Coordination follows credible interaction, not employer identity. Shared energy, access and operating states can affect a job even when another company owns the adjacent task.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Reassess changes and learn from completed work
lessons.body:
A JSA is bounded by its assumptions. Stop and reassess when scope, equipment, method, crew, weather, operating state, nearby activity or a critical control changes. First protect people from the affected exposure; then involve the right operating and technical roles, revise the analysis and any linked authorization, verify controls and rebrief. Editing the form while work continues through an uncontrolled condition defeats the purpose.

At completion, account for equipment, temporary controls, remaining defects and handback responsibilities. Record what actually happened, including interventions, not an idealized version of the original plan. The program owner can compare later observations against the analysis to identify recurring gaps and improve planning. “No injury” is useful outcome information but does not prove that every control was present.

Worked example: wind moves an airborne contaminant toward a nearby crew. The team stops affected work and coordinates a revised exposure arrangement. Later review checks whether the monitoring and briefing system detected the changing pathway promptly, rather than declaring the original JSA effective because everyone escaped injury.

### Applying the mechanism

A post-job review should compare the predicted steps with the sequence actually used. If workers needed an unplanned workaround, examine why the approved method was impractical and whether a technical change is needed. Do not simply add the unsafe workaround to tomorrow’s template as accepted practice.

### Decision principles

A favorable outcome can occur despite missing controls. Effectiveness review examines implementation and performance, including near misses and interventions, within the sampled work scope.

Completion of a task does not automatically establish readiness for operation. Handback communicates the actual state and unresolved restrictions to the designated operating authority.

A standard analysis is a starting resource. Its scope and assumptions must be checked against the present job; reuse without field confirmation can carry obsolete controls into a different exposure.

lessons.title: Two applied scenarios and worked decisions
lessons.body:
## Applied scenarios: complete worked decisions

### Scenario 1: A second crew arrives

A pump-maintenance JSA was briefed in the morning. At noon another contractor begins opening an adjacent process line and uses the maintenance crew’s escape route for materials.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** The maintenance supervisor pauses the affected work and establishes a safe waiting condition. Both crews and the site authority examine shared releases, access, isolation interfaces and emergency routes. They agree a controlled sequence or other approved separation, assign owners and verify the actual safeguards. The JSA and related permits are revised as required, and both crews are rebriefed before the authorized restart. The original signed sheet remains part of the history rather than being silently replaced.

### Scenario 2: A completed form and a missing barrier

A supervisor has a signed JSA showing a controlled vehicle route. During the pre-start walk, a worker finds an open crossing used by pedestrians. Dispatch is pressing for the first vehicle movement.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** The worker reports the failed control and the affected movement remains held. The responsible supervisor resolves the crossing through the approved traffic arrangement and checks that pedestrians and drivers understand it. A suitable verifier checks the full route, including side access, before the authorized movement. The record identifies the failure and correction. The team learns that signatures are evidence of discussion, not proof that the route was physically controlled.

lessons.title: Final assessment: 20 individual decisions
lessons.body: Answer the 20 questions individually using the taught principles. Each submission preserves your first answer. Review feedback after submitting. When an answer is incorrect, explicitly acknowledge the correct decision and explanation before moving on. The result must show both the first-answer score and the remediated score across all 26 questions. Do not attempt a live hazardous task to obtain an answer; the assessment is a knowledge and judgment exercise.

lessons.title: Completion and separately assessed practical competence
lessons.body:
## What this completion means

The course is complete only after every section and all 26 questions have been accomplished, through correct responses or explicit acknowledgment of the supplied correction. Preserve the original and remediated results separately. Acknowledgment is a learning action, not evidence that the learner has performed the task safely in the field.

questions.prompt: A reused analysis says only “service equipment.” What should happen before work?

options.label: Define the specific equipment and meaningful task steps with the crew.
Sign it because the title is familiar.
Add more PPE names without visiting the job.

questions.prompt: Which stages belong in a task analysis?

options.label: Only the main production movement.
Only activities after someone reports an injury.
Setup, work, interruptions, cleanup and handback as applicable.

questions.prompt: How much step detail is useful?

options.label: A separate line for every finger movement.
Enough to identify changing hazards and controls without losing readability.
One line for an entire maintenance campaign.

questions.prompt: Why involve the people who perform the task?

options.label: They can identify practical access, handling and sequencing hazards.
Their signatures replace technical review.
Only supervisors can observe hazards accurately.

questions.prompt: Which hazard description is most useful?

options.label: Be careful around vehicles.
General safety risk.
A moving vehicle can strike workers entering the shared loading route.

questions.prompt: Who should be considered as potentially exposed?

options.label: Only employees of the company preparing the form.
Workers performing the step and others affected by its energy or movement.
Only the person signing the analysis.

questions.prompt: What should happen when a technical hazard is uncertain?

options.label: Hold the affected step and obtain competent technical assessment.
Assign a low risk score to keep moving.
Let the newest worker test it in practice.

questions.prompt: Why consider abnormal conditions?

options.label: Only successful operation matters.
Abnormal conditions can always be left to emergency responders.
A foreseeable failure can change the exposure and required controls.

questions.prompt: A glove is proposed as the only control for a crushing pinch point. What is the better planning response?

options.label: Write “experienced worker” as the control.
Remove or separate the hand from the crushing exposure using an approved method.
Use thicker gloves and leave the method unchanged.

questions.prompt: Which proposal most directly reduces exposure?

options.label: Perform the approved inspection remotely instead of placing a person in the release path.
Add the phrase “use caution.”
Require the worker to remember last year’s briefing.

questions.prompt: What role can PPE have?

options.label: Proof that every uncontrolled hazard is acceptable.
Replacement for isolation on every maintenance job.
Protection against assessed residual hazards within its limitations.

questions.prompt: Who approves a technical change to equipment controls?

options.label: The training platform after a passing score.
The designated competent technical and operating authorities.
Any crew member who prefers a different guard.

questions.prompt: A critical control is listed but no one owns its verification. What is missing?

options.label: A named responsible role and an observable acceptance check.
A more attractive form layout.
Another signature from someone not at the site.

questions.prompt: What should a verification record describe?

options.label: Only the word “safe.”
A predicted result entered before the check.
The control actually checked, result, responsible person, time and relevant conditions.

questions.prompt: What should happen after a failed critical-control check?

options.label: Proceed if the overall risk score is green.
Hold affected work, correct the gap and verify before authorization to proceed.
Average it with successful checks.

questions.prompt: Why might an old photograph be insufficient?

options.label: It may show a different time, configuration or incomplete view of the safeguard.
Photographs can never be evidence.
A photograph automatically proves every control’s function.

questions.prompt: Two crews share an access route and their plans conflict. What is required?

options.label: Let the larger crew take priority informally.
Keep separate signed JSAs and assume that is enough.
Coordinate a defined arrangement and brief both crews before affected work.

questions.prompt: What best checks briefing understanding?

options.label: Assuming experience makes explanation unnecessary.
Workers explain their assigned actions and stop conditions in an understandable language.
Counting signatures alone.

questions.prompt: What should a newly arriving worker receive?

options.label: A task-specific briefing and verification of applicable prerequisites before joining exposure.
Only a copy of the attendance sheet.
Permission to learn by following others inside the boundary.

questions.prompt: Which interface belongs in coordination?

options.label: Only activities on the same payroll.
Only issues discovered after both jobs finish.
A nearby crew’s restart that can affect the shared equipment or area.

questions.prompt: The method changes mid-job and creates a new exposure. What happens next?

options.label: Continue because the original job title is unchanged.
Pause affected work, reassess, verify revised controls and rebrief before authorized restart.
Add the new method after the shift.

questions.prompt: What does a job without injury prove?

options.label: Only that no injury was observed or reported in that outcome.
That every listed safeguard existed.
That the analysis is suitable for all future tasks.

questions.prompt: What belongs in handback?

options.label: Only the time the crew leaves.
Automatic permission for anyone to restart equipment.
Remaining defects, temporary arrangements, equipment state and responsible acceptance.

questions.prompt: When should a standard JSA be reused?

options.label: Only after deleting old failure records.
After confirming it fits the actual task and updating changed conditions and controls.
Whenever its title is similar.

questions.prompt: What is the central failure in the second-crew scenario?

options.label: The original analysis no longer represents shared exposure and access conditions.
The first crew used too many task steps.
Only the second employer needs to know about the conflict.

questions.prompt: What permits the affected movement to be reconsidered?

options.label: The existing signatures without a field check.
A low calculated risk score despite the open crossing.
Verified correction of the route control through the responsible site process.

content.description: Complete guided H02 training: six taught lessons, two worked scenarios, six checks and a 20-question final. Separate first-answer and remediated scores; wrong answers require explicit correction acknowledgment.
