content.title: H05 — Confined-space entry
content.description: Complete guided H05 training: six taught lessons, two worked scenarios, six checks and a 20-question final. Separate first-answer and remediated scores; wrong answers require explicit correction acknowledgment.

explanations.H05_check1: Appearance cannot establish atmosphere, engulfment or other serious hazards. Classification must consider the configuration and actual work under the applicable program.
explanations.H05_final_1_1: Permit classification follows defined hazards and configuration, not a visual shorthand. Atmospheric, engulfment, trapping and other serious hazards need competent assessment.
explanations.H05_final_1_2: Ventilation and gas behavior depend on the actual conditions. An opening alone does not demonstrate acceptable conditions at the worker’s breathing location.
explanations.H05_final_1_3: The proposed activity can consume oxygen, release contaminants or introduce ignition and mechanical hazards. The entry plan must address these task-created exposures.
explanations.H05_check2: The attendant is an entry safeguard with specific duties. Leaving without a valid relief or suspension removes that safeguard even if communication equipment remains available.
explanations.H05_final_2_1: Entry authorization is a defined operational role supported by verified conditions. Written awareness completion does not grant that authority.
explanations.H05_final_2_2: Attendant duties include summoning the planned response and preventing unauthorized entry. Entering without rescue training and protection can create another casualty.
explanations.H05_final_2_3: Connected processes and concurrent work can change entry conditions. Exchanging information and coordinating responsibilities closes gaps between employers’ assumptions.
explanations.H05_check3: Entry readiness requires the complete protective system. Acceptable atmosphere readings do not control the risk of material or energy entering through an unisolated connection.
explanations.H05_final_3_1: Testing needs hazard knowledge, instrument suitability and sampling competence. A detector alone does not establish the ability to characterize the space safely.
explanations.H05_final_3_2: Ventilation addresses a defined atmospheric control function. Other hazards require their own assessment and safeguards and cannot be dismissed because air is moving.
explanations.H05_final_3_3: A measurement is bounded by place, time and method. The entry authority must know that the relevant conditions still exist when people rely on the result.
explanations.H05_check4: A contact number is not evidence of capability, access, equipment or response arrangements. Rescue readiness must be established before entry, not improvised after an emergency.
explanations.H05_final_4_1: Rescue limitations can make an otherwise planned entry unacceptable. They must be resolved before exposure so an emergency does not become the first test of the method.
explanations.H05_final_4_2: Improvised retrieval can fail or injure the entrant. A suitable plan must address routing, attachments, equipment and obstructions under competent review.
explanations.H05_final_4_3: An unknown atmosphere or other serious hazard can incapacitate a would-be rescuer. Only the designated qualified response undertakes rescue under the plan.
explanations.H05_check5: Loss of a required control invalidates the entry basis. Waiting for symptoms or a later alarm exposes the entrant while the protective system is uncertain.
explanations.H05_final_5_1: Communication is part of the entry system. Its loss can prevent warnings and accountability, so the defined failure response must be followed rather than improvised inside.
explanations.H05_final_5_2: Authorization is conditional. Changed atmosphere, process state or control performance can require evacuation and revalidation before the permit’s nominal end time.
explanations.H05_final_5_3: A space interacts with its surroundings and connected systems. The entry arrangement must address credible external sources and concurrent operations.
explanations.H05_check6: Replacing one device addresses only part of the failed safeguard. The authority must establish current entry conditions and the applicable re-entry authorization.
explanations.H05_final_6_1: Closeout must communicate what is actually complete and what remains restricted. Entry completion is not equivalent to operating readiness.
explanations.H05_final_6_2: A complete chronology supports investigation and learning. Later success does not erase an earlier failed control or explain how it was resolved.
explanations.H05_final_6_3: Each role requires task-specific skills, practical evaluation and employer designation. The written course establishes awareness and assessed knowledge only.
explanations.H05_final_scenario1: Task duration and informal labels do not determine the hazards or entry boundary. The actual exposure must be assessed under the entry program.
explanations.H05_final_scenario2: The required role must remain effective throughout entry. Equipment left behind does not perform the attendant’s observation, communication and response duties.

lessons.title: Start here: learning, scores and role boundaries
lessons.body:
# H05: Confined-space entry

This original VNDRLY course teaches decisions for service-specific: tanks, pits, vessels, sewers and similar spaces. Its purpose is to control atmosphere, engulfment, access and rescue risks. The six lessons explain the hazard, planning decisions, controls, checks, changing conditions and handback. Worked examples and two fictional scenarios show how those decisions fit together. Read the teaching before answering; no live hazardous activity is needed to complete this course.

There are six lesson knowledge checks and a 20-question final assessment. Submit each answer before viewing its feedback. Your first answer remains in the original score. If an answer is wrong, read the specific explanation and explicitly acknowledge the correction; acknowledged corrections contribute to a separate remediated score. Completion requires all sections and all 26 questions correct or explicitly acknowledged after remediation. A later corrected answer never erases the first-answer record.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Recognize a space and assess its hazards
lessons.body:
A confined-space assessment begins with the space’s configuration and intended work, not its everyday name. A space large enough for bodily entry, with limited or restricted entry or exit and not designed for continuous occupancy can meet the general-industry definition. Permit-required classification then considers hazardous atmosphere, engulfment, trapping configuration or other serious hazards. Applicable construction or other sector rules must be determined separately.

A tank can remain hazardous after it appears empty. Residues can release contaminants, cleaning can change the atmosphere, and connected systems can introduce material. A shallow or open-topped space can still present serious atmospheric or access hazards. No single reassuring feature replaces assessment.

Worked example: a worker plans to lean through a vessel opening to retrieve a part. The task is referred to the site entry program before any part of the body crosses the boundary; calling it retrieval does not avoid entry controls.

### Applying the mechanism

Entry classification and task planning should consider the space as a system. Connected lines, internal moving parts, residues, sloping surfaces and access restrictions can each affect the worker. A space that was acceptable for one task may become hazardous when cleaning chemicals, welding or coatings are introduced. The assessment must also consider whether a worker can exit unaided if conditions deteriorate. Do not use size or depth alone as a shortcut. The employer determines the applicable entry rules and competent assessment. If a worker is unsure whether leaning through an opening crosses the entry boundary, resolve that question before any body part is placed through it.

### Decision principles

Permit classification follows defined hazards and configuration, not a visual shorthand. Atmospheric, engulfment, trapping and other serious hazards need competent assessment.

Ventilation and gas behavior depend on the actual conditions. An opening alone does not demonstrate acceptable conditions at the worker’s breathing location.

The proposed activity can consume oxygen, release contaminants or introduce ignition and mechanical hazards. The entry plan must address these task-created exposures.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Separate entry roles and their responsibilities
lessons.body:
The entry supervisor verifies the required conditions and authorization under the program. Authorized entrants understand the hazards, equipment, communication and exit duties. The attendant remains assigned outside, maintains required awareness and communication, monitors conditions and summons the planned response. Exact staffing and duties follow the applicable program; roles cannot be combined when the combination prevents safe performance.

An attendant is not a spare laborer to leave for deliveries. Their presence also does not make them an entry rescuer. Contractors and host operations must exchange hazard information and coordinate entry activities and other work that can affect the space.

Worked example: the attendant is asked to fetch a tool from another building. The task cannot simply continue unattended. Entry pauses or the program’s proper relief arrangement is established before the attendant leaves.

### Applying the mechanism

Each entry role needs enough capacity to perform its actual duties. An attendant distracted by unrelated deliveries may miss an entrant’s condition or a change outside the space. A supervisor who cannot establish rescue readiness has not completed the authorization decision merely by signing the permit. An entrant needs to recognize alarms, communication failures and other exit triggers without waiting for a personal negotiation. When staffing changes, use the program’s controlled relief and briefing process.

### Decision principles

Entry authorization is a defined operational role supported by verified conditions. Written awareness completion does not grant that authority.

Attendant duties include summoning the planned response and preventing unauthorized entry. Entering without rescue training and protection can create another casualty.

Connected processes and concurrent work can change entry conditions. Exchanging information and coordinating responsibilities closes gaps between employers’ assumptions.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Establish isolation and acceptable entry conditions
lessons.body:
Before authorization, the entry plan addresses connected energy and materials, atmosphere, mechanical hazards, access, lighting, communications, equipment and other task risks. Isolation must match the actual connections and required safe state. Ventilation can help control atmosphere but is not a substitute for eliminating or isolating another serious hazard.

Qualified personnel establish the atmospheric assessment and testing method, suitable instrument, locations, response time, sequence and monitoring needed. Measurements must represent the relevant space and work conditions. A test outside the opening or from an earlier configuration does not automatically clear every location inside.

Worked example: a vessel has acceptable initial atmosphere readings but a connected feed remains uncontrolled. Entry is not ready. The missing process isolation must be resolved and all entry conditions verified; one passing category does not compensate for another failed safeguard.

### Applying the mechanism

Acceptable atmosphere is only one part of entry readiness. Isolation must prevent credible inflow or movement, and the work method must control hazards it introduces. Ventilation needs a suitable source, delivery and exhaust arrangement; moving air without understanding its path may not control the relevant location. A sampling method must allow the target atmosphere to reach the sensors and account for spatial differences and response time. The qualified entry program establishes how testing and ongoing monitoring fit the task. General learners should recognize these prerequisites and request competent resolution, rather than inventing acceptable concentrations or declaring a space safe from one convenient reading.

### Decision principles

Testing needs hazard knowledge, instrument suitability and sampling competence. A detector alone does not establish the ability to characterize the space safely.

Ventilation addresses a defined atmospheric control function. Other hazards require their own assessment and safeguards and cannot be dismissed because air is moving.

A measurement is bounded by place, time and method. The entry authority must know that the relevant conditions still exist when people rely on the result.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Plan feasible rescue before entry
lessons.body:
A rescue plan must be workable for the actual space, hazards and access. It identifies the capable service, how it is summoned, expected response arrangements, equipment and any non-entry retrieval method that is appropriate and required. Listing an emergency telephone number does not demonstrate that a team can reach and remove an entrant in the needed conditions.

Rescue personnel require appropriate training, equipment and practice for the space and hazards. Retrieval systems must be assessed for the entrant, route and entanglement or configuration constraints. Do not attach improvised ropes and assume rescue is solved. The entry program determines the method and duties.

Worked example: a vessel has an internal obstruction that prevents the proposed retrieval path. The plan is corrected and verified before entry rather than discovering the problem with an incapacitated worker inside.

### Applying the mechanism

Rescue feasibility should be examined against the same access and internal geometry the entrant will use. A narrow opening, ladder, internal obstruction or casualty position can prevent a planned removal method from working. The rescue service must be capable of the relevant hazards and available through the agreed arrangement. Non-entry retrieval, where suitable and required, still needs a technical assessment of attachments, route and entanglement risk. Practice should use safe simulations that reveal these constraints before exposure. Do not call a general emergency number and assume a team has the equipment or knowledge for the space. The entry authority needs actual evidence of a workable response.

### Decision principles

Rescue limitations can make an otherwise planned entry unacceptable. They must be resolved before exposure so an emergency does not become the first test of the method.

Improvised retrieval can fail or injure the entrant. A suitable plan must address routing, attachments, equipment and obstructions under competent review.

An unknown atmosphere or other serious hazard can incapacitate a would-be rescuer. Only the designated qualified response undertakes rescue under the plan.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Monitor conditions and evacuate on loss of safeguards
lessons.body:
Entry conditions must remain acceptable for the work. Follow the specified monitoring, communication and observation arrangements throughout. Entrants leave when an alarm, prohibited condition, symptoms, evacuation instruction or other program trigger occurs. The attendant initiates the required response and maintains accountability. Do not troubleshoot a failed monitor inside the space while exposure continues.

Changing weather, nearby exhaust, process operation, ventilation failure or the task itself can alter conditions. A permit duration is not a guarantee that those conditions will persist. If a critical safeguard is lost, exit first through the approved response, then reassess from safety.

Worked example: the ventilation supply stops while an entrant is working. The entrant follows the evacuation instruction instead of waiting for a gas alarm to confirm deterioration. The responsible roles investigate and re-establish conditions before considering re-entry.

### Applying the mechanism

The entrant and attendant should know what changes invalidate the entry basis. A ventilation failure, alarm, new release, communication loss or unexpected behavior may require immediate exit under the program even before symptoms occur. This avoids using the entrant’s body as a warning device. After evacuation, account for everyone and preserve the observations. A later acceptable reading does not automatically reactivate the entry; the responsible roles establish the cause, restored controls and current authorization. If the task changes, such as adding a solvent or hot-work tool, reassess the new hazard rather than treating it as a minor convenience within the old permit.

### Decision principles

Communication is part of the entry system. Its loss can prevent warnings and accountability, so the defined failure response must be followed rather than improvised inside.

Authorization is conditional. Changed atmosphere, process state or control performance can require evacuation and revalidation before the permit’s nominal end time.

A space interacts with its surroundings and connected systems. The entry arrangement must address credible external sources and concurrent operations.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Close, hand back and preserve role limits
lessons.body:
After exit, account for entrants, tools, materials and temporary arrangements. The designated roles close or cancel the entry authorization and communicate the actual equipment state to operations. Restoring process connections or equipment follows its own controlled process; an empty space is not automatically ready for service.

Record the conditions, monitoring, interruptions and problems so the program can improve. Preserve a failed-entry event even when a later attempt succeeds. A written course supports understanding but does not create an entry team.

Worked example: a crew exits after a monitor fault. A tested replacement is later provided. Re-entry still requires the responsible authority to reassess and reauthorize the conditions; swapping the instrument alone does not silently reactivate the prior entry.

### Applying the mechanism

Closeout transfers the actual equipment state, not merely the fact that people left. Account for temporary ventilation, lighting, tools, blanks and other arrangements through the applicable systems. Operations needs to know whether the vessel remains isolated, open, restricted or ready for a separate restoration stage. A cancelled entry can leave equipment in a different state from a completed task, and the record must show that difference. Program review then asks whether the space assessment, communications, monitoring and rescue arrangements worked as intended. Record specific deficiencies and corrective actions without claiming that one successful entry proves the method suitable for every space.

### Decision principles

Closeout must communicate what is actually complete and what remains restricted. Entry completion is not equivalent to operating readiness.

A complete chronology supports investigation and learning. Later success does not erase an earlier failed control or explain how it was resolved.

The written course establishes awareness and assessed knowledge only.

lessons.title: Two applied scenarios and worked decisions
lessons.body:
## Applied scenarios: complete worked decisions

### Scenario 1: The quick retrieval

A worker drops a tool inside a vessel and proposes leaning through the opening while a coworker watches. No space assessment or entry plan has been established.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** The retrieval remains held. The site entry program assesses the boundary, space and actual task, including atmosphere, isolation and rescue. Watching from outside is not a substitute for the full required entry system. If the item can be retrieved using an approved non-entry method, that alternative is assessed without exposing a person through the opening. Any entry requires its own verified prerequisites and authorized roles.

### Scenario 2: A busy attendant

During entry, the attendant is asked to unload a delivery outside communication range. The entrant says they can finish in five minutes.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** The attendant does not abandon the assigned function. The responsible entry supervisor establishes proper relief under the program or suspends entry and accounts for the entrant before the attendant leaves. Delivery pressure does not change the need for monitoring, communication and response. The interruption is recorded and any restart follows the entry system.

lessons.title: Final assessment: 20 individual decisions
lessons.body: Answer the 20 questions individually using the taught principles. Each submission preserves your first answer. Review feedback after submitting. When an answer is incorrect, explicitly acknowledge the correct decision and explanation before moving on. The result must show both the first-answer score and the remediated score across all 26 questions. Do not attempt a live hazardous task to obtain an answer; the assessment is a knowledge and judgment exercise.

lessons.title: Completion and separately assessed practical competence
lessons.body:
## What this completion means

The course is complete only after every section and all 26 questions have been accomplished, through correct responses or explicit acknowledgment of the supplied correction. Preserve the original and remediated results separately. Acknowledgment is a learning action, not evidence that the learner has performed the task safely in the field.

## Legal requirements for the named work role
These apply only when you perform the work described below. They are not additional steps for completing this online course.

29 CFR 1910.146(k)(2)(iv) — Employer-designated employees performing covered permit-space rescue: Practice the assigned permit-space rescues at least every 12 months using the specified actual or representative spaces, subject to the real-rescue exception. This is a rescue-team duty, not a practical test required of every awareness-course learner. Source: https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.146

Its clean appearance.
A worker’s willingness to enter.

Only a space deeper than a worker’s height.

No; hazardous atmospheres can exist despite an open top.

options.label: Cleaning, coatings, tools and connected operations can introduce new hazards.

options.label: The equipment supplier’s delivery driver.

Any worker with a recent online score.

options.label: No; rescue is a separately planned qualified capability.
Yes, whenever an entrant collapses.

options.label: Only the entrant’s employer knows anything relevant.

options.label: Yes, if the entrant moves quickly.
No; all required entry conditions, including isolation, must be established.

options.label: Personnel qualified and authorized for that task and program.

options.label: That every serious hazard is eliminated.
That no permit conditions are needed.

options.label: Only the permit number matters.
Changed connections or tasks can change atmosphere and release conditions.

options.label: A capable, available and feasible rescue arrangement for the actual space.
Nothing; the number proves rescue readiness.

options.label: After the first entrant is inside.
Only after a failed rescue.
Before entry authorization and when relevant conditions change.

questions.prompt: Can any rope arrangement be treated as a retrieval system?

options.label: Yes, if two coworkers can pull it.
No; the method must suit the space, person and assessed constraints.
Yes, if the rope is new.

questions.prompt: What should an unqualified coworker do if an entrant collapses?

options.label: Summon the designated response and avoid unprotected entry.
Enter immediately while holding a breath.
Use a monitor as breathing protection.

questions.prompt: A required ventilation safeguard fails during entry. What is the response?

options.label: Continue until symptoms appear.
Assume the initial readings remain valid.
Follow the entry program’s evacuation and reassessment process.

questions.prompt: What should happen on required communication failure?

options.label: Ask the entrant to shout occasionally and ignore the failure.
Follow the program’s exit and response arrangements.
Continue because the permit has time remaining.

questions.prompt: Does a valid permit guarantee continuing safe conditions?

options.label: No; conditions and safeguards must remain verified as required.
Yes, until the printed end time.
Yes, if the entrant has experience.

questions.prompt: Why monitor nearby activities?

options.label: Only work inside the space can change its atmosphere.
Another employer’s activity is outside the entry assessment.
Exhaust, releases or operating changes can affect the space.

questions.prompt: A failed monitor is replaced after evacuation. Does entry automatically resume?

options.label: Yes, if the original permit has not expired.
No; the responsible entry process must verify conditions and authorize re-entry.
Yes, because the replacement turns on.

questions.prompt: What belongs in entry closeout?

options.label: Personnel accounting, equipment state, unresolved issues and controlled handback.
Only a finish time.
Automatic process restart.

questions.prompt: What should happen to records of interrupted entry?

options.label: Delete them once re-entry succeeds.
Replace them with the final acceptable reading.
Preserve the interruption, cause, response and later authorization distinctly.

questions.prompt: Which practical role is granted by this written course alone?

options.label: Atmospheric rescue team member.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with calling the vessel task “quick retrieval”?

options.label: The label does not remove entry exposure or its required assessment.

questions.prompt: Which arrangement resolves the attendant conflict?

options.label: Entrant self-monitoring until the delivery ends.

lessons.title: Start here: learning, scores and role boundaries
lessons.body:
# H06: Hot work and fire watch

This original VNDRLY course teaches decisions for service-specific: welding, cutting, grinding and ignition-producing tasks. Its purpose is to prevent fire/explosion during work around flammable materials. The six lessons explain the hazard, planning decisions, controls, checks, changing conditions and handback. Worked examples and two fictional scenarios show how those decisions fit together. Read the teaching before answering; no live hazardous activity is needed to complete this course.

There are six lesson knowledge checks and a 20-question final assessment. Submit each answer before viewing its feedback. Your first answer remains in the original score. If an answer is wrong, read the specific explanation and explicitly acknowledge the correction; acknowledged corrections contribute to a separate remediated score. Completion requires all sections and all 26 questions correct or explicitly acknowledged after remediation. A later corrected answer never erases the first-answer record.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Identify ignition sources and safer alternatives
lessons.body:
Hot work includes activities capable of producing ignition energy, such as welding, cutting and many grinding operations. The hazard is not limited to a visible flame. Sparks, hot surfaces and heat conducted through metal can ignite materials away from the immediate tool. First ask whether the work can be avoided, performed by an approved non-ignition method or relocated to a suitably controlled area.

Changing to a battery-powered tool does not automatically make an activity cold work. The actual mechanism, equipment suitability and atmosphere determine the hazard. The site authority classifies and authorizes the task under its rules.

Worked example: a crew proposes grinding a bracket beside process drains. The task is assessed as an ignition source; familiarity with the bracket does not establish the drains are free of flammable material.

### Applying the mechanism

Ignition assessment follows energy and material paths. A spark can travel through a gap, while heat can conduct through metal into an area the operator cannot see. Flammable material may come from the equipment being worked on or from a separate process, drain or nearby activity. That is why classifying only the tool is insufficient. The authority assesses the task in its surroundings and considers alternatives that avoid introducing ignition. A cold-cutting proposal also needs technical assessment; changing the method can introduce mechanical or chemical hazards. The goal is a suitable controlled task, not replacing one familiar label with another and assuming the risks disappeared.

### Decision principles

Eliminating or relocating the ignition task can reduce exposure more directly than adding precautions around a process hazard, provided the alternative is technically assessed.

The assessment must consider heat transfer and hidden combustibles, not just the tool’s immediate location. Adjacent spaces may need protection and observation.

Classification is an operating-control decision. A convenient job label or familiar tool does not remove the requirement to assess ignition and surrounding hazards.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Prepare the area and connected interfaces
lessons.body:
The permit and assessment identify the work location, equipment, time and conditions. Remove combustibles where practicable or provide the approved protection. Examine openings, drains, ducts, wall penetrations, lower levels and opposite sides through which sparks, heat or flammable material can travel. Process systems and vessels need their own preparation and isolation; never weld or cut a container merely because it appears empty.

Coordinate with operations and nearby crews. A separate transfer or venting activity can introduce flammable material after the area was prepared. Barriers and signs control access but do not make the atmosphere safe.

Worked example: a floor opening leads to an occupied lower level with stored packaging. The plan addresses that level before hot work starts; a screen beside the welder alone does not control the opening.

### Applying the mechanism

Walk the area beyond the operator’s immediate position. Examine where hot material can fall or travel and what lies on the other side of surfaces receiving heat. Stored packaging, oily deposits and hidden voids can create delayed ignition. The preparation plan identifies what is removed, protected or isolated and who verifies each part. It also defines how the arrangement remains effective as materials and people move. If a screen is shifted for access, the crew reassesses the exposed path rather than assuming the original preparation still applies. Nearby operations must know the ignition task is active so they do not introduce a release into the protected area.

### Decision principles

Container preparation requires the approved technical assessment and methods. Visual appearance cannot establish the absence of hazardous residues or connected sources.

Hot work interacts with process operations and adjacent work. Physical releases and spark paths do not follow employer or paperwork boundaries.

Screens can control particular light or spark exposures, but they do not remove flammable gases or establish process isolation.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Verify atmosphere and authorization prerequisites
lessons.body:
Where required, qualified personnel establish gas testing, instrument suitability, locations, frequency and acceptance criteria under the site procedure. A measurement is bounded by the actual atmosphere and sampling method. The course does not invent a universal acceptable gas number or permit duration. The authorized issuer and performing lead confirm the required safeguards before the task starts.

A detector that powers on is not necessarily fit for the target hazards. Failed required checks or monitoring remove the safeguard from reliance. The crew must not use a favorable older reading to override a present alarm or changed process condition.

Worked example: the area passed an initial test before a nearby transfer began. The transfer changes the assessment assumptions, so the authority reassesses and revalidates the work rather than relying on the earlier result.

### Applying the mechanism

Atmospheric testing must support the actual hot-work decision. The qualified tester selects suitable sensors and locations and follows the specified timing and monitoring requirements. A reading from an accessible point may not represent a drain, enclosed pocket or changing process release. The authority establishes the applicable criteria; workers do not convert a detector alarm setting into a universal hot-work allowance. If the instrument is unsuitable or its required checks fail, the safeguard is missing. The task remains held until a verified arrangement is restored. A signed permit can record authorization but cannot make an inadequate measurement method representative of the work area.

### Decision principles

Instrument possession does not establish sampling and interpretation competence.

Readings cannot predict every future condition. The monitoring arrangement and change triggers must maintain the basis for safe work.

A failed monitoring control invalidates reliance on that safeguard. Workers must not expose themselves while troubleshooting or guessing the atmosphere.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Understand the fire watch function
lessons.body:
A fire watch is a trained assigned role with suitable extinguishing equipment, communication and a clear view of the areas being protected. The watch looks for ignition, unsafe change and spread, and has authority to stop the work and raise the alarm. Work assignments must not distract from those duties. A watch may need coverage of more than one level or side where the assessment identifies hidden spark or heat pathways.

The watch acts only within training and safe response limits. The priority is alerting, evacuation and the site emergency system when a fire cannot be safely managed by the assigned initial response. A portable extinguisher is not permission to enter smoke or a hazardous atmosphere.

Worked example: the watch is asked to help carry materials out of view. The required coverage is maintained by proper relief or hot work stops; the welder does not become their own effective watch by glancing around.

### Applying the mechanism

The fire watch must understand the assigned coverage and the response limits. Observation should include the identified spark and heat pathways, not merely watching the operator. The watch needs a way to stop the work promptly and summon help without leaving the protected area unobserved. Where several levels or sides require coverage, the plan establishes suitable staffing or another approved arrangement. The watch does not accept unrelated work that prevents those duties. Extinguisher readiness includes the person’s training and a safe escape, not just a cylinder on the floor. A developing fire beyond safe initial response requires the emergency system and evacuation rather than a heroic attempt to protect the equipment.

### Decision principles

The role is bounded by the plan, training and safe response conditions. It does not replace the emergency response system or authorize hazardous entry.

Coverage must match the identified ignition pathways. Hidden or lower areas can require additional arrangements rather than assuming one viewpoint is sufficient.

Initial response must preserve the responder’s safety and escape. Training and the emergency plan determine limits; equipment availability does not justify uncontrolled exposure.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Stop when conditions change
lessons.body:
Stop hot work when a required control fails, a gas alarm occurs, the fire watch is unavailable, conditions change or the site issues an emergency instruction. Secure the activity only as the approved response allows without delaying escape or creating exposure. Notify the responsible authority from safety. Do not reset the alarm and relight the torch as an informal restart.

Changes include new combustibles, shifted screens, blocked access, process release, weather affecting sparks or ventilation, and a different work method. The authority determines whether the existing authorization can be revalidated or a new one is needed.

Worked example: wind begins carrying sparks beyond the protected area. The crew stops and reassesses the actual path and protection. The original briefing is not a guarantee that the area remains controlled.

### Applying the mechanism

Stop triggers should be discussed before work so they do not become debates under pressure. The operator and watch should know what to do on alarm, failed monitoring, loss of coverage, new combustibles or changed wind. The response must not require a person to remain exposed simply to make the work look tidy. After the stop, the authority reviews both the initiating change and any unfinished task state. An incomplete cut or hot component may require a controlled follow-up method, but it does not justify relighting without clearance. Rebriefing should explain what changed and what has been verified, not merely announce that the permit is still within its time window.

### Decision principles

Protective response comes before fault investigation. A suspected false alarm cannot be treated as atmospheric clearance.

A changed method can introduce a new ignition source and controls. The administrative job title does not authorize every technique.

Restart is conditional on restored safeguards and site authorization. Silencing a warning or production urgency does not establish readiness.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Complete post-work monitoring and handback
lessons.body:
Ignition can occur or become visible after the tool stops. Maintain the watch and inspections for the period required by the applicable rules and approved permit, including any additional monitoring identified by the assessment. Do not invent a shorter universal interval or assume departure is allowed because no flame is visible.

Closeout confirms the work area and affected adjacent spaces, equipment state, temporary protection, remaining restrictions and responsible acceptance. Preserve records of stops, alarms and corrective actions. The operating authority controls return to service; the welder’s completion does not clear a process system.

Worked example: the weld is complete, but hot material remains near a protected penetration. The watch completes the specified post-work duties and the authority accepts handback only after the required checks, rather than treating tool shutdown as job clearance.

### Applying the mechanism

Delayed ignition is a reason for defined post-work duties. Heat can remain in material or conceal smoldering beyond the operator’s direct view. The applicable rules and permit establish the watch and inspection period, and the task assessment may require additional coverage. Do not substitute a number remembered from another site. Closeout checks the affected adjacent areas and records unresolved conditions before handback. If an area cannot be inspected as required, that gap remains visible to the authority. The operating owner accepts the actual final state and any continuing restriction; stopping the tool and collecting the permit do not themselves establish that every ignition pathway is clear.

### Decision principles

Requirements depend on applicable law and site controls. This course does not replace them with an invented duration.

Handback must inform the operating authority of readiness and remaining limits. Craft completion and process restoration are distinct decisions.

A quiz cannot demonstrate those field skills.

lessons.title: Two applied scenarios and worked decisions
lessons.body:
## Applied scenarios: complete worked decisions

### Scenario 1: Hidden ignition path

A welder has a prepared area upstairs. Sparks can pass through a cable penetration to packaging below, where no watch or protection is assigned.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** Hot work remains held. The lead and site authority assess the complete spark and heat paths, remove or protect affected materials using approved methods, establish required coverage and verify access and response. The lower area is included in the briefing and closeout. A screen upstairs and a signed permit do not control an unassessed space below.

### Scenario 2: Alarm near the finish

A crew is nearly finished when a gas alarm sounds. The operator wants thirty seconds to complete the cut and avoid rework.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** The crew follows the prescribed stop and emergency response without bargaining for completion time. The watch raises the appropriate notification, and people move through the site plan. Qualified investigation establishes the cause and the authority verifies conditions before any restart. The unfinished cut is treated as a task state needing controlled reassessment, not as a reason to remain exposed.

lessons.title: Final assessment: 20 individual decisions
lessons.body: Answer the 20 questions individually using the taught principles. Each submission preserves your first answer. Review feedback after submitting. When an answer is incorrect, explicitly acknowledge the correct decision and explanation before moving on. The result must show both the first-answer score and the remediated score across all 26 questions. Do not attempt a live hazardous task to obtain an answer; the assessment is a knowledge and judgment exercise.

lessons.title: Completion and separately assessed practical competence
lessons.body:
## What this completion means

The course is complete only after every section and all 26 questions have been accomplished, through correct responses or explicit acknowledgment of the supplied correction. Preserve the original and remediated results separately. Acknowledgment is a learning action, not evidence that the learner has performed the task safely in the field.

questions.prompt: A battery grinder is proposed beside process drains. What is the correct classification approach?

options.label: Assess its actual ignition potential and site hot-work requirements.
Treat all battery tools as cold work.
Assume no flame means no ignition hazard.

questions.prompt: What should be considered before selecting hot work?

options.label: Only how quickly the permit can be signed.
Only the welder’s preferred tool.
An approved safer method or relocation that avoids the ignition exposure.

questions.prompt: Can heat create a hazard on the opposite side of a metal wall?

options.label: Only if the wall is transparent.
Yes; conducted heat can affect hidden or adjacent materials.
No; only visible sparks matter.

questions.prompt: Who decides whether the site requires hot-work authorization?

options.label: The designated site authority using the actual task and rules.
Any worker who calls the task minor.
The tool’s owner automatically.

questions.prompt: Sparks can fall through an opening to a lower level. What must be addressed?

options.label: Only the welder’s immediate floor area.
Only a sign at the tool.
The complete spark path, affected materials and people below.

questions.prompt: Why is an apparently empty container not automatically safe to cut?

options.label: A clean exterior proves internal preparation.
Residue or connected material can create fire, explosion or toxic hazards.
Empty containers cannot contain vapor.

questions.prompt: What should coordination include?

options.label: Nearby transfers, venting, access and work that can change ignition or exposure conditions.
Only people employed by the welder’s company.
Only tasks using the same permit number.

questions.prompt: Does a welding screen establish a safe atmosphere?

lessons.title: Start here: learning, scores and role boundaries
lessons.body:
# H07: Lifting, rigging and suspended loads

This original VNDRLY course teaches decisions for service-specific: crane, hoist and rigging work. Its purpose is to avoid dropped loads, overturning and line-of-fire exposure. The six lessons explain the hazard, planning decisions, controls, checks, changing conditions and handback. Worked examples and two fictional scenarios show how those decisions fit together. Read the teaching before answering; no live hazardous activity is needed to complete this course.

There are six lesson knowledge checks and a 20-question final assessment. Submit each answer before viewing its feedback. Your first answer remains in the original score. If an answer is wrong, read the specific explanation and explicitly acknowledge the correction; acknowledged corrections contribute to a separate remediated score. Completion requires all sections and all 26 questions correct or explicitly acknowledged after remediation. A later corrected answer never erases the first-answer record.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Define the lift and assign qualified roles
lessons.body:
A lift plan describes the actual load, equipment, configuration, route, landing area and operating conditions. The competent planner classifies the lift under the employer and site system and identifies required review. A familiar-looking lift can become different when the radius, ground, load center, rigging or nearby operation changes.

Roles include the lifting lead, qualified operator, riggers and signal persons as applicable. Their qualifications must match the equipment and task. One person may perform more than one role only where allowed and where duties remain effective. A general awareness learner does not acquire these roles through a quiz.

Worked example: a crew reuses yesterday’s plan but the crane must now stand farther away. The changed radius can alter capacity and geometry, so the competent plan is reviewed before setup or lifting.

### Applying the mechanism

Planning must connect the load information with the equipment’s actual setup. A crane’s apparent size or maximum advertised capacity does not establish capacity at the intended radius and configuration. The plan also considers how the load will be controlled, where people stand and what happens if conditions change. Classification under the site system identifies the required technical review; workers should not downgrade a lift by calling it routine. If the work is repeated, compare the actual setup each time. A moved crane, different attachment or changed ground can make a repeated lift materially different. The competent planner resolves those differences before the team relies on the earlier plan.

### Decision principles

The lift is a system of load, support, equipment and people. A plan must define the arrangement that is being assessed and authorized.

Classification determines planning and approval needs and must follow the actual risks and site criteria, not an informal label.

Rigging competence includes selecting, attaching and controlling loads in real configurations. Written awareness alone cannot establish those skills.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Establish load and center-of-gravity information
lessons.body:
The plan needs a defensible load weight and relevant center-of-gravity information. Include attachments, contents, retained liquid and lifting accessories as required by the capacity calculation. An unverified estimate from appearance is not a suitable basis for a consequential lift. Use approved drawings, weighing or other competent methods.

The center of gravity affects balance and sling forces. A load can rotate or tip when lifted even if its total weight is within capacity. Lifting points must be suitable for the intended direction and load, not merely convenient holes or protrusions.

Worked example: a vessel marked with an empty weight still contains residue and attached piping. The planner resolves the actual lifted weight and attachments before selecting the system; the marking is useful information but not the whole load.

### Applying the mechanism

Weight and balance information should have a stated basis. Drawings may describe an empty component while field attachments, retained liquid or modifications change the actual load. A center of gravity away from the expected position can cause rotation when support changes. Lifting points must suit the load and direction imposed by the arrangement. Do not use the first trial lift to discover an unknown weight or unverified attachment. The plan may include controlled checks as part of a qualified method, but that is different from guessing and hoping the equipment can carry it. Where information is missing, the safe planning outcome is a hold and competent resolution.

### Decision principles

Load balance must be understood before lifting. Unexpected rotation can overload components or move the load into people or structures.

A point’s appearance or accessibility does not demonstrate strength or approved loading direction. Competent technical information must support its use.

The lifting system supports more than the named component. Omitted contents or accessories can invalidate capacity and balance assumptions.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Match equipment, rigging and support conditions
lessons.body:
Capacity depends on the actual equipment configuration, radius, boom or attachment arrangement and manufacturer limits. Rigging selection considers rated capacity, hitch, sling angles, edge protection, compatibility and condition. Do not calculate or alter these from memory when the task requires a competent plan.

Ground and support must withstand the imposed loads in the proposed setup. Underground services, voids, slopes, recent disturbance and nearby excavations can matter. Outriggers and mats do not automatically solve unknown ground conditions. Weather and wind limits follow the equipment and plan.

Worked example: a crane is positioned beside a recent trench. The planner obtains the required support assessment and approved setup. A flat-looking surface is not proof that it can carry the crane’s reactions.

### Applying the mechanism

Rigging geometry affects the forces carried by individual components. An acceptable sling in one hitch or angle may not support the same load in another configuration. Edges, heat, chemicals and attachments can further limit use. The qualified rigger and planner use the applicable rated information and inspect the actual items. Ground support is equally part of the system: crane reactions can be concentrated and affected by voids, trenches or weak surfaces. Mats and outriggers need the approved setup, not an improvised appearance of stability. A user should be able to identify the required configuration and report discrepancies without attempting to calculate a new lift from memory.

### Decision principles

A connected assembly can still be overloaded or unsuitable. The rated performance must apply to the actual hitch, geometry and service conditions.

Nominal capacity is not a universal rating at every radius or setup. The plan must use applicable configuration information and support conditions.

Unknown rating or damage defeats the basis for selection. Informal labeling cannot restore traceability or establish load-bearing condition.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Control the route, landing and exclusion area
lessons.body:
Plan the full movement, not just the pick. The load path and landing area must account for structures, utilities, vehicles, workers and adjacent operations. Keep people outside the assessed fall, swing and crushing areas. Never place a person under a suspended load to guide it by hand.

Tag lines or other control methods are used only where suitable under the plan; they can create entanglement or pull a worker into danger if improvised. The landing arrangement must support the load and allow rigging to be removed without an uncontrolled pinch exposure.

Worked example: the pick area is clear but the landing point requires a helper to reach beneath the load to position blocking. The plan is revised before lifting so support and access can be established without that exposure.

### Applying the mechanism

The route plan includes the space occupied by the load and equipment during swing, travel and landing, not only a line between two points. A load can rotate or deflect, and workers can be trapped against nearby structures. Separate people from those paths and control all approaches. The landing arrangement should be ready before lifting so helpers do not reach beneath the load to insert supports. Material and rigging removal must be possible after stability is established. If the planned destination is blocked, stop and review the change rather than choosing a convenient spot while the load is suspended. The revised location needs its own support and exposure assessment.

### Decision principles

A lift can fail or expose people at any stage. Landing and de-rigging often introduce pinch and stability hazards that must be addressed in advance.

A tag line can introduce entanglement or pulling hazards. Its use must fit the load, environment and worker positioning under the approved method.

The lifting envelope includes equipment and load movement. Utility clearances and controls require qualified planning under applicable rules and site arrangements.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Communicate and stop on deviation
lessons.body:
Agree the signal system, designated signal role, operator communication and response to loss of signal before the lift. Everyone must know how to raise an emergency stop through the site arrangement. Stop if a person enters the exclusion area, the load behaves unexpectedly, weather exceeds limits or the setup differs from the plan.

Do not chase a swinging load or use a body to arrest its movement. The operator and lifting lead establish the controlled state according to the plan. A plan change requires the appropriate competent review and rebriefing, not an improvised discussion while people remain exposed.

Worked example: radio contact fails with the load suspended. The operator follows the agreed stop and safe-state procedure rather than interpreting distant hand movements from unassigned observers.

### Applying the mechanism

Signals should be unambiguous and matched to the actual visibility and noise. The operator must know the designated signal arrangement and the response to conflicting or lost instructions. Workers need a clear emergency-stop channel without everyone improvising movement directions. A helper who sees danger reports the stop rather than running into the path to correct it physically. During a hold, the operator and lifting lead establish the safe condition under the plan. Do not treat a suspended load as a meeting room while a new method is discussed. People remain clear until a controlled plan and any required technical review establish the next stage.

### Decision principles

The plan’s approval applies to its assumptions. A changed load, configuration or environment can invalidate that basis and requires competent reassessment.

Trying to physically stop a load can place the helper in a severe crushing path. The lifting system and approved method must control movement.

Workers need a clear way to report imminent danger. The specific controlled response follows the lifting plan and operator duties.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Land, inspect and close the lift
lessons.body:
A landed load must be stable and supported before rigging is released. Follow the planned sequence so removing a sling or restraint does not initiate rolling, tipping or pinch exposure. The competent roles confirm the final state and clear the work area before returning access to others.

Inspect and control any rigging or equipment affected by abnormal loading, impact or damage. Record deviations, stops and changes, including why the final arrangement was accepted. A lift without injury is not proof that a damaged sling or unstable support was acceptable.

Worked example: a load lands unevenly and remains supported partly by the crane. The rigger does not release the assembly to hurry closeout. The lifting lead establishes the approved stable condition first.

### Applying the mechanism

Landing transfers support from the lifting system to the destination. Confirm that the load is stable under the planned support before releasing rigging. A partly supported or uneven load can move when tension changes, exposing the rigger during removal. Follow the approved sequence and keep hands out of pinch gaps. Afterward, inspect or control equipment affected by impact, abnormal loading or damage. Record the actual deviation and disposition so the next lift does not inherit an unknown item. A successful landing is an outcome, but it does not retrospectively prove that the earlier rigging or separation was adequate. Review the controls as well as the result.

### Decision principles

Abnormal loading can impair future strength without obvious external failure. Traceable equipment control prevents unverified gear from reaching the next lift.

Records should explain the work actually performed and remaining equipment restrictions. The approval remains bounded to that lift and configuration.

Awareness supports recognition but cannot replace role-specific demonstration and authorization.

lessons.title: Two applied scenarios and worked decisions
lessons.body:
## Applied scenarios: complete worked decisions

### Scenario 1: Uncertain load

A skid has a catalog weight, but field modifications and retained fluid are not documented. A supervisor suggests using the catalog figure because the crane appears large.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** The lift remains held while the competent planner establishes the actual load and balance, equipment configuration, rigging and support requirements. The plan records the defensible weight basis and any approved technical assumptions. The operator does not discover adequacy by beginning to lift. Equipment appearance and slow movement cannot replace capacity verification.

### Scenario 2: Changed landing

The original landing area is blocked. A helper proposes another spot beside an occupied walkway and will hold the load away from pedestrians.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** The lifting lead stops the change and obtains competent review of the new path, support, exclusion and de-rigging arrangement. Pedestrians are controlled through the site system and workers are rebriefed. A helper’s body is not a load-control barrier. The lift resumes only when the revised plan and required authorization are established.

lessons.title: Final assessment: 20 individual decisions
lessons.body: Answer the 20 questions individually using the taught principles. Each submission preserves your first answer. Review feedback after submitting. When an answer is incorrect, explicitly acknowledge the correct decision and explanation before moving on. The result must show both the first-answer score and the remediated score across all 26 questions. Do not attempt a live hazardous task to obtain an answer; the assessment is a knowledge and judgment exercise.

lessons.title: Completion and separately assessed practical competence
lessons.body:
## What this completion means

The course is complete only after every section and all 26 questions have been accomplished, through correct responses or explicit acknowledgment of the supplied correction. Preserve the original and remediated results separately. Acknowledgment is a learning action, not evidence that the learner has performed the task safely in the field.

## Legal requirements for the named work role
These apply only when you perform the work described below. They are not additional steps for completing this online course.

29 CFR 1910.178(l)(2), (4), (6) — Operators of powered industrial trucks covered by this standard: Formal instruction, practical training and workplace performance evaluation are required before independent operation, with employer certification and applicable refresher/evaluation duties. A trainer/evaluator needs the knowledge, training and experience specified in (l)(2)(iii); an outside assessor is not universally required. Source: https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.178

29 CFR 1926.1427(a), (f) — Operators of construction cranes/equipment covered by Subpart CC, subject to the stated exceptions: Meet the applicable operator training/certification or licensing provisions and employer evaluation requirements for the equipment and assigned work. Do not apply this crane rule to every lifting worker or every piece of mobile equipment. Source: https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1926/1926.1427

29 CFR 1926.1428(a), (c)(5) — Construction crane signal persons covered by Subpart CC: Demonstrate the specified knowledge through an oral or written test and a practical test. The standard permits a qualified third-party evaluator or the employer's qualified evaluator, with the stated documentation and portability limits. Source: https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1926/1926.1428

questions.prompt: The crane location changes and the load is farther away. What is required?

options.label: Competent review of the actual configuration and plan.
Reuse yesterday’s capacity assumption.
Lift slowly to compensate.

questions.prompt: What should a lift plan identify?

options.label: Only the destination.
Only the operator’s name.
The actual load, equipment, configuration, route, conditions and responsible roles.

questions.prompt: Who classifies the lift and required review?

options.label: The training administrator.
The designated competent lifting planner under the applicable system.
Any bystander who calls it routine.

questions.prompt: Does this course qualify someone as a rigger?

options.label: No; task-specific practical evaluation and designation are separate.
Yes, for any sling with a readable tag.
Yes, if they have watched previous lifts.

questions.prompt: A vessel’s marking gives empty weight but contents remain uncertain. What is required?

options.label: Use the empty weight without adjustment.
Add an arbitrary small percentage.
Resolve the actual lifted weight and load condition through a competent method.

questions.prompt: Why does center of gravity matter?

options.label: It matters only after the load is airborne.
It affects balance, rotation and forces in the lifting arrangement.
Only total weight matters.

questions.prompt: Can any convenient hole be used as a lifting point?

options.label: No; suitability must be established for the intended load and direction.
Yes, if a hook fits.
Yes, for a brief lift.

questions.prompt: What can be part of the total lifted load?

options.label: Only the bare item’s catalog weight.
Only items visible from ground level.
Relevant attachments, retained material and lifting accessories.

questions.prompt: The planned crane setup is beside a recent trench. What is needed?

options.label: Faster lifting to reduce ground exposure.
Competent assessment of ground and support for the actual setup.
A visual guess that the surface is flat.

questions.prompt: What determines rigging suitability?

options.label: Rating, configuration, angles, compatibility, condition and the approved plan.
Only sling color.
Only whether the hardware connects.

questions.prompt: Does a higher crane nominal capacity prove every configuration is safe?

options.label: Yes, if the load is light by appearance.
Yes, if outriggers are visible.
No; the actual configuration and manufacturer limits govern.

questions.prompt: What should happen to damaged or unidentified rigging?

options.label: Recreate its tag by guessing.
Remove it from reliance and follow the equipment control process.
Use it for the easiest portion only.

questions.prompt: The landing plan requires a helper beneath the suspended load. What is the decision?

options.label: Revise the approved method to prevent that exposure before lifting.
Allow it if the helper is quick.
Require a harder helmet.

questions.prompt: Which part of the movement needs planning?

options.label: Only the moment the load leaves the ground.
Only the crane’s parking position.
Pick, travel, swing, landing and safe release of rigging.

questions.prompt: Are tag lines automatically safe for every lift?

options.label: Yes, regardless of nearby equipment.
No; their suitability and safe use must be assessed.
Yes, because they keep hands away from the load.

questions.prompt: Why coordinate overhead and nearby utilities?

options.label: Contact or proximity can create serious hazards beyond the load itself.
Only the load weight matters.
Utility ownership prevents crane interaction.

questions.prompt: The agreed signal is lost during movement. What happens?

options.label: Continue toward the expected destination.
Accept signals from whoever waves first.
Stop under the plan and restore controlled communication.

questions.prompt: What if actual conditions differ materially from the plan?

options.label: Let the nearest worker improvise.
Stop and obtain the required review before changing the lift.
Continue because the plan is signed.

questions.prompt: What should a helper do with a swinging load?

options.label: Stay clear and use the approved stop and control arrangement.
Catch it with their body.
Stand between it and a structure.

questions.prompt: What should everyone know about emergency stopping?

options.label: Only the signal person may ever report danger.
A stop can wait until the load is landed regardless of exposure.
How to communicate a stop through the agreed system.

questions.prompt: A load is touching down but is not stable. May rigging be released?

options.label: Yes, if the operator holds the brake.
No; establish the planned stable support before release.
Yes, because contact with ground means landed.

questions.prompt: What should happen after abnormal rigging loading or damage?

options.label: Control the item and obtain the required competent inspection or disposition.
Return it to the common bin immediately.
Erase the event if the load landed.

questions.prompt: What does lift closeout record?

options.label: Only a successful outcome label.
A guarantee for every future lift.
Actual configuration, deviations, condition and accepted final state.

questions.prompt: Who grants practical lifting role competence?

options.label: Any person who attended the briefing.
The employer’s qualified assessment and designation process for the actual role.
This written course alone.

questions.prompt: Why is the catalog figure insufficient here?

options.label: It does not establish the modified skid’s actual lifted weight and balance.
Catalogs are never useful for any lift.
A large crane eliminates weight uncertainty.

questions.prompt: What is required before using the alternate landing area?

options.label: Only verbal confidence from the helper.
A faster landing to shorten exposure.

courses.purpose: Prevent falls and falling-object injuries.
courses.practicalBoundary: 29 CFR 1910.132(f)(2), (g) — Employees using the eye/face, head, foot, hand or personal fall protection covered by paragraph (g): Before that work, demonstrate understanding of the PPE training and ability to use the PPE properly.
