lessons.title: Start here: learning, scores and role boundaries
lessons.body:
# H11: Breaking containment and process handback

This original VNDRLY course teaches decisions for service-specific: piping, vessels, maintenance and production. Its purpose is to prevent hydrocarbon/chemical release on opening equipment. The six lessons explain the hazard, planning decisions, controls, checks, changing conditions and handback. Worked examples and two fictional scenarios show how those decisions fit together. Read the teaching before answering; no live hazardous activity is needed to complete this course.

There are six lesson knowledge checks and a 20-question final assessment. Submit each answer before viewing its feedback. Your first answer remains in the original score. If an answer is wrong, read the specific explanation and explicitly acknowledge the correction; acknowledged corrections contribute to a separate remediated score. Completion requires all sections and all 26 questions correct or explicitly acknowledged after remediation. A later corrected answer never erases the first-answer record.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Recognize the containment boundary and actual contents
lessons.body:
Breaking containment means opening equipment or connections that can release process contents or energy. It includes lines, filters, drains, hoses and vessels, not only large pipework. Establish the correct equipment identity, contents, operating history and connected sources before planning the opening. Residues can remain after normal operation stops.

Consider pressure, temperature, toxic or flammable material, corrosive contents and oxygen displacement, along with gravity and connected energy. An apparently empty line can hold liquid in low points or gas in isolated sections. Unknown contents are a hold requiring competent resolution.

Worked example: a worker calls a small filter change routine. The assessment still identifies its actual process connection and retained contents. Small component size does not eliminate a release toward the worker.

### Applying the mechanism

The containment boundary must be described at the point where the worker will intervene. Equipment can have multiple connections, low points, dead legs or trapped sections that are not obvious from the exterior. Contents may differ from the normal process after cleaning, upset or maintenance. A label describing the routine fluid is useful but may not establish the current residue or temperature. Operations and technical personnel use controlled information and the actual configuration to define the hazards. The performing crew confirms the identified work point and reports contradictions. The aim is a shared, bounded statement of what can be released and what preparation is required, rather than a general claim that a whole skid is safe because one process is stopped.

### Decision principles

Filters, drains and hoses can create the same release pathway as larger equipment. The actual boundary and contents determine the controls.

Recent service and abnormal operation can change residues and energy. History informs the assessment but does not substitute for verifying current conditions.

Unknown material can create severe exposure. Identification must use the approved information and safe technical process, not direct sensory exposure.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Coordinate isolation, draining and depressurization
lessons.body:
The operations owner and authorized isolation personnel establish the required boundary, energy control, draining, depressurization and verification. The work crew confirms what conditions have actually been established and what remains restricted. Closing one valve is not automatically sufficient for every process or hazard.

Drain and vent paths must be suitable and controlled so making equipment safe does not expose another worker or release material to an unsuitable location. Blockages, trapped pockets and connected sources require competent assessment. Do not assume a zero local indicator describes the entire section.

Worked example: a drain produces no flow, but it may be blocked. The crew does not treat “nothing came out” as proof of empty equipment. The responsible authority verifies the condition through the prescribed method.

### Applying the mechanism

Preparation must address where retained contents go. Draining a hazardous liquid into an open container can create splash, vapor, ignition or overflow exposure outside the original equipment. Venting a gas can affect another crew or an intake. The approved plan therefore treats draining and depressurization as tasks with their own controls, not invisible administrative prerequisites. Isolation must also consider whether a source can leak through or reintroduce material. Where the method requires particular physical separation or verification, a convenient closed valve is not an automatic equivalent. Workers should understand the verified boundary and any ongoing monitoring, but they must not redesign the isolation or select a drain destination beyond their authority.

### Decision principles

Preparation affects operating systems and exposed workers. The designated roles must establish and communicate the boundary and verified state.

Making one item safe must not create another uncontrolled exposure. Release destination and containment are part of the preparation plan.

Isolation adequacy depends on the system and consequences. A universal valve-count assumption cannot replace the competent procedure.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Choose a controlled opening method
lessons.body:
The competent task plan establishes the opening sequence, position, tools, containment, protection and emergency response. The method must keep people out of the credible discharge path and account for residual contents. This awareness course does not provide a universal flange-loosening technique or authorize a worker to improvise one.

PPE selection follows the assessed material, temperature and release mechanism and must be compatible and usable. PPE does not replace verified preparation. Establish access and a route to withdraw without crossing a release. Keep unneeded people away and coordinate nearby ignition sources.

Worked example: an opening is directly above a walkway. The plan addresses collection, separation and the actual release path before work; a bucket below is not automatically adequate containment.

### Applying the mechanism

Safe positioning begins before the tool is applied. The approved method considers the credible direction and reach of residual discharge, the worker’s body position, nearby people, access and withdrawal. Protection may include containment, shields or remote arrangements selected for the material and geometry, but none replaces the verified preparation. A shield that blocks splash toward the operator could redirect it toward a helper if the whole path is not assessed. Tools and fasteners also need a controlled handling plan so the worker does not reach into the potential release path to catch a part. The competent procedure establishes the actual sequence; this course deliberately does not offer a universal loosening technique that could be unsafe on a different connection.

### Decision principles

Opening methods depend on equipment, contents and energy.

PPE is one layer in the control system. It cannot establish a safe energy state or make uncontrolled discharge acceptable.

A usable route reduces the chance of being trapped or moving through the discharge. It must exist before exposure, not be discovered during an event.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Verify readiness at the work point
lessons.body:
Before the first break, match the equipment identity, scope and preparation records to the actual work point. Confirm required permits, isolation verification, atmosphere controls, containment, communications and roles. A record for the adjacent line is not clearance for the intended one. The crew must understand the verified state and what observations require stopping.

Technical testing and process verification require qualified personnel. If a required condition is missing or ambiguous, hold the affected opening. Do not use the first loosened connection as the verification method unless that is specifically part of an approved qualified procedure.

Worked example: the permit identifies a different filter housing. The crew resolves identity and protection with operations before touching the fasteners.

### Applying the mechanism

At the work point, compare the permit, equipment identity and isolation or preparation references with the physical item. Ask the responsible authority to resolve any mismatch before touching it. A record may be genuine and still apply to the wrong housing or branch. The crew should be able to explain the expected condition and the stop response without claiming technical knowledge they do not possess. If a safeguard depends on a test, identify who performed it and what scope it establishes. Do not silently broaden an external atmosphere result to a vessel interior or a zero pressure at one point to every branch. Readiness is the combined set of verified prerequisites for this opening, not the existence of several unrelated signed forms.

### Decision principles

A broad administrative match cannot establish the specific containment boundary. The verified conditions must apply to the equipment being opened.

Atmosphere and isolation address different hazards. One completed record cannot stand in for a missing required technical safeguard.

Improvised opening can expose workers to retained pressure or material. Verification must follow the task-specific safe method and role limits.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Stop on unexpected contents or response
lessons.body:
Unexpected pressure, temperature, material, odor, leakage or equipment movement invalidates the expected opening condition. Stop through the prescribed response, withdraw from the exposure and notify the responsible authority. Do not keep opening to see whether the flow will finish. A suspected hazardous atmosphere requires the site emergency and escape actions, not a closer sensory check.

The authority reassesses isolation, trapped sections, contents and the method before any further intervention. Keep nearby people away through safe communication. Preserve the actual observation in the record even if later testing finds an acceptable condition.

Worked example: a supposedly drained line releases hot liquid. The crew withdraws and raises the response. The event is investigated before the opening is continued; a later empty drain does not erase the failed preparation.

### Applying the mechanism

Unexpected material is information that the preparation basis may be wrong. Even a small release can indicate a larger trapped volume or connected source. The worker should not assume it will stop harmlessly or try to diagnose the system while standing in the discharge. Follow the planned stop and withdrawal actions, communicate observed facts and keep others clear from safety. The technical and operating roles investigate the source and establish the next safe condition. Preserve what was actually seen, including time and equipment identity; avoid inventing pressure or concentration values. If exposure occurred, activate the appropriate emergency and medical interface. Resuming after the visible release diminishes requires the approved reassessment, not a personal judgment that the worst is over.

### Decision principles

The discrepancy can reflect trapped or connected energy. The task must return to its controlled preparation and verification process.

Clear factual reporting helps the responsible team identify the failed assumption. Unsupported conclusions can misdirect the response.

A changing release does not establish that the remaining system is safe. Restart depends on the approved technical and operating process.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Reinstate and hand back the actual system
lessons.body:
Reassembly requires the specified components, condition, assembly method and any inspection or testing. Account for blanks, temporary hoses, drains, vents, tools and removed parts through the approved system. The operations owner accepts the final configuration before controlled restoration. Do not silently leave a temporary arrangement in service.

Record what was opened, findings, replacements, checks, remaining restrictions and acceptance. A repair invoice alone cannot establish correct reinstatement. If the configuration changes, use the technical change process and refresh affected evidence.

Worked example: a temporary drain remains connected after the filter is reassembled. Handback identifies and resolves its disposition before operation rather than assuming someone else will remove it.

### Applying the mechanism

Reinstatement is more than closing the opening. Correct parts, orientation, assembly, cleanliness and required inspection or tests support containment integrity. Temporary blinds, caps, hoses and instruments must be accounted for through the applicable system so their removal or retention is deliberate. The operating authority needs the actual state before restoring energy or process contents. A crew might finish its craft work while another required inspection remains outstanding; the handback must preserve that restriction. When a seal or fitting differs from the approved specification, technical review decides whether it is acceptable and what verification is needed. A tidy exterior or successful static appearance does not establish compatibility under operating temperature, pressure and chemistry.

### Decision principles

Integrity depends on the actual assembly and required verification. Administrative completion cannot establish technical readiness.

The operating owner must understand the final state and restrictions before restoration. Craft completion does not automatically grant operating clearance.

Written understanding supports, but does not replace, those decisions.

lessons.title: Two applied scenarios and worked decisions
lessons.body:
## Applied scenarios: complete worked decisions

### Scenario 1: No drain flow

A filter is scheduled for opening. The drain gives no flow, but the service is known to leave deposits and blockage has not been ruled out.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** The opening remains held. Authorized operations and isolation personnel verify the actual contents and energy state using the approved method, including any trapped sections. The crew reviews the equipment identity, containment and opening plan after preparation is established. The record distinguishes no observed drain flow from verified absence of retained pressure or material.

### Scenario 2: Wrong replacement seal

The housing is ready for reinstatement, but the available replacement seal looks similar and lacks verified material compatibility.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** The crew does not assemble it as an informal substitute. The technical authority establishes the correct component and any required change approval, then verifies assembly and testing under the procedure. Operations receives the accepted final state and restrictions. A visually similar part can fail in the actual fluid or temperature service.

lessons.title: Final assessment: 20 individual decisions
lessons.body: Answer the 20 questions individually using the taught principles. Each submission preserves your first answer. Review feedback after submitting. When an answer is incorrect, explicitly acknowledge the correct decision and explanation before moving on. The result must show both the first-answer score and the remediated score across all 26 questions. Do not attempt a live hazardous task to obtain an answer; the assessment is a knowledge and judgment exercise.

lessons.title: Completion and separately assessed practical competence
lessons.body:
## What this completion means

The course is complete only after every section and all 26 questions have been accomplished, through correct responses or explicit acknowledgment of the supplied correction. Preserve the original and remediated results separately. Acknowledgment is a learning action, not evidence that the learner has performed the task safely in the field.

questions.prompt: A small filter is called routine but its contents are uncertain. What happens?

options.label: Hold opening until contents and hazards are established.
Open slowly to identify the contents.
Assume small size means low risk.

questions.prompt: What counts as breaking containment?

options.label: Only cutting a large pipeline.
Only opening a vessel marked hazardous.
Opening a connection or item that can release process contents or energy.

questions.prompt: Why check operating history?

options.label: Only the equipment age matters.
It can reveal retained material, temperature or unusual conditions.
History replaces current verification.

questions.prompt: What should unknown contents trigger?

options.label: A hold and competent identification and assessment.
A guess based on pipe color.
A quick sniff at the opening.

questions.prompt: A drain shows no flow but blockage is possible. What is established?

options.label: The equipment is certainly safe.
Every connected pocket has drained.
The absence of flow alone does not prove the equipment is empty or depressurized.

questions.prompt: Who coordinates process isolation and preparation?

options.label: The course administrator.
The authorized operations and isolation roles with the performing crew.
Any worker who finds a convenient valve.

questions.prompt: Why assess drain and vent destinations?

options.label: Preparation can transfer hazardous material or energy to another location.
Any discharge point is acceptable during maintenance.
Only the final opening matters.

questions.prompt: Does closing one valve always establish adequate isolation?

options.label: Yes, for every liquid system.
Yes, if the handle is difficult to move.
No; the approved task-specific isolation method governs.

questions.prompt: The proposed opening can discharge onto a walkway. What is needed?

options.label: A warning after the first release.
A task-specific controlled method, containment and separation arrangement.
Only a bucket placed below.

questions.prompt: Who defines the safe opening technique?

options.label: The competent approved task procedure and responsible roles.
A universal technique invented by this quiz.
Whoever has the largest wrench.

questions.prompt: What is PPE’s role in containment opening?

options.label: Permission to skip depressurization.
Proof that any release can be tolerated.
Protection against assessed residual exposure within its limitations.

questions.prompt: Why plan withdrawal access?

options.label: Experienced workers can always jump away.
A release can require immediate safe separation.
Only material delivery needs access planning.

questions.prompt: The preparation record names an adjacent housing. What happens?

options.label: Hold and resolve identity and protection before opening.
Use it because both housings are similar.
Change the label on the record without verification.

questions.prompt: What should pre-opening verification match?

options.label: Only the general site name.
Only the crew’s attendance list.
The actual work point, scope, contents and required safeguards.

questions.prompt: What if a required atmospheric check is missing?

options.label: Proceed because isolation paperwork exists.
Hold the affected activity and obtain the qualified check.
Substitute smell.

questions.prompt: Can the first release always be used to verify preparation?

options.label: No; only the approved qualified procedure can define any such controlled step.
Yes, loosen anything slowly.
Yes, if a coworker watches.

questions.prompt: Unexpected hot liquid appears during opening. What is required?

options.label: Continue until the line empties.
Tighten while standing in the discharge.
Stop, withdraw through the approved response and obtain reassessment.

questions.prompt: What does unexpected pressure indicate?

options.label: Permission to vent through the worker’s opening.
The assumed safe state is not established and must be reassessed.
Only that the gauge needs a new label.

questions.prompt: What should workers report?

options.label: Actual observations, location, equipment and uncertainties from safety.
Invented concentrations.
Only a claim that the line is safe now.

questions.prompt: When may the opening resume?

options.label: When the visible flow slows.
When the crew needs to finish.
After required reassessment, verified safeguards and authorized restart.

questions.prompt: A temporary drain remains at handback. What is required?

options.label: Leave it for the next shift without notification.
Resolve and record its approved final disposition before restoration.
Ignore it because the housing is closed.

questions.prompt: What supports safe reinstatement?

options.label: Correct components and assembly, required checks and responsible acceptance.
Only a completed invoice.
Only the absence of visible leakage at rest.

questions.prompt: Who accepts return to service?

options.label: Any worker leaving the area.
The course platform.
The designated operations authority through the controlled handback.

questions.prompt: What qualification does this course not provide?

options.label: Knowledge of reporting duties.
Authority to isolate, break containment or approve process reinstatement.
Awareness of stop conditions.

questions.prompt: Why is no drain flow insufficient here?

options.label: A blocked drain can conceal retained contents and pressure.
No flow always means empty.
Deposits make verification unnecessary.

questions.prompt: What establishes the replacement seal’s suitability?

options.label: Similar appearance.
The fact that it fits the groove.
Verified technical compatibility and approved acceptance for the actual service.

content.title: H12 — Electrical work and arc-flash controls
content.description: Complete guided H12 training: six taught lessons, two worked scenarios, six checks and a 20-question final. Separate first-answer and remediated scores; wrong answers require explicit correction acknowledgment.

explanations.H12_check1: An indicator can fail or represent only part of a system. Electrical safe-state verification must use the qualified approved method, not a display assumption.
explanations.H12_final_1_1: Electrical energy can produce several harm pathways. The assessment must address actual equipment and task conditions rather than only direct contact.
explanations.H12_final_1_2: Damage can expose energized parts and arc hazards. Unqualified intervention can create contact or fault conditions; the electrical authority must assess it.
explanations.H12_final_1_3: Different protective functions and performance are involved. Selection must follow the qualified assessment and applicable electrical program.
explanations.H12_check2: Electrical competence is bounded by demonstrated knowledge and skills for the task. Different equipment, energy and methods can require additional evaluation and authorization.
explanations.H12_final_2_1: Deenergizing and verifying removes exposure where required. Energized work is subject to specific justified conditions and controls, not convenience.
explanations.H12_final_2_2: Boundaries depend on the equipment and electrical hazards. Awareness workers respect established limits rather than inventing them.
explanations.H12_final_2_3: Duration and material do not remove the electrical exposure. Access must follow the qualified control arrangement and role limits.
explanations.H12_check3: The observed discrepancy means the assumed safe state is not established. The qualified process must resolve sources, identity and instrument behavior before exposure.
explanations.H12_final_3_1: Testing requires task-specific skill and suitable equipment because the conductors may still be energized during verification.
explanations.H12_final_3_2: The measurement is only reliable within the instrument’s condition and method. Required function checks help prevent a false safe-state conclusion.
explanations.H12_final_3_3: A control response is bounded and can fail for many reasons. Qualified electrical verification must address the actual conductors and sources.
explanations.H12_check4: Energized work is governed by specific conditions and safeguards. Convenience alone does not establish that those conditions are met.
explanations.H12_final_4_1: Protective performance must match the exposure and work method. Generic issue or appearance does not establish adequacy.
explanations.H12_final_4_2: Protective equipment does not supply the knowledge and skill needed to avoid faults and contact. Qualified execution is still required.
explanations.H12_final_4_3: Damage can defeat protective performance. The applicable inspection and replacement process must restore the safeguard before reliance.
explanations.H12_check5: The rescuer can become part of the circuit. Safe electrical control precedes contact and first aid; the designated response handles the energized hazard.
explanations.H12_final_5_1: Function does not prove insulation integrity. Damage can expose users to shock or faults and must pass the approved repair or replacement process.
explanations.H12_final_5_2: Pulling equipment by its cord can damage insulation and connections. Handling must preserve the electrical protective condition.
explanations.H12_final_5_3: Equipment ratings and protection must match the environment. A device that works in one location may create unacceptable risk in another.
explanations.H12_check6: Restoration must establish the actual safe operating and access condition. Craft completion alone does not restore enclosure protection or clear people from exposure.
explanations.H12_final_6_1: People may still rely on the previous isolated state. Clear communication prevents inadvertent contact or conflicting work after energization.
explanations.H12_final_6_2: Traceability links verification to the actual system and condition. Vague or predicted records cannot establish the work performed.
explanations.H12_final_6_3: Written awareness cannot establish hands-on electrical testing, repair or rescue skills. The employer and applicable licensing system determine those qualifications.
explanations.H12_final_scenario1: Conflicting identity information can leave a worker on a live source despite following the wrong label. Qualified resolution and verification are necessary.
explanations.H12_final_scenario2: Protective equipment is one safeguard within a qualified program. It cannot replace the technical basis and practical competence for hazardous electrical work.

lessons.title: Start here: learning, scores and role boundaries
lessons.body:
# H12: Electrical work and arc-flash controls

This original VNDRLY course teaches decisions for service-specific: electrical/instrumentation; basic awareness for exposed workers. Its purpose is to prevent shock, arc flash and ignition. The six lessons explain the hazard, planning decisions, controls, checks, changing conditions and handback. Worked examples and two fictional scenarios show how those decisions fit together. Read the teaching before answering; no live hazardous activity is needed to complete this course.

There are six lesson knowledge checks and a 20-question final assessment. Submit each answer before viewing its feedback. Your first answer remains in the original score. If an answer is wrong, read the specific explanation and explicitly acknowledge the correction; acknowledged corrections contribute to a separate remediated score. Completion requires all sections and all 26 questions correct or explicitly acknowledged after remediation. A later corrected answer never erases the first-answer record.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Recognize shock, arc and unexpected energy hazards
lessons.body:
Electricity can injure through contact, arc energy, fire and unexpected equipment movement. A circuit can remain hazardous after a control switch is off, and alternate supplies or stored energy can defeat an assumed boundary. Damaged cords, open enclosures, moisture and unidentified equipment require a hold and reporting, not informal repair by an unqualified worker.

Shock and arc-flash hazards are related but different. Insulating protection for one exposure is not automatically adequate for another. The competent electrical assessment establishes the actual hazards and controls. A general worker’s role is to respect boundaries, recognize defects and contact the designated electrical authority.

Worked example: a panel display is dark. That does not establish that conductors are deenergized; a failed display can coexist with live supply.

### Applying the mechanism

A person can encounter an electrical hazard without intending electrical work. Moving a long object near exposed parts, opening a damaged enclosure or handling wet equipment can create contact or a fault. The electrical assessment also considers stored energy and alternate sources that may remain after a normal supply is disconnected. For an unqualified worker, the useful skill is recognizing the boundary of knowledge: do not infer voltage absence from silence, a switch position or a dark lamp. Report the specific equipment and condition and keep clear through the site arrangement. Protective clothing and confidence cannot convert an unknown circuit into an acceptable work area. The qualified electrical authority establishes the technical condition and access restrictions.

### Decision principles

Electrical energy can produce several harm pathways. The assessment must address actual equipment and task conditions rather than only direct contact.

Damage can expose energized parts and arc hazards. Unqualified intervention can create contact or fault conditions; the electrical authority must assess it.

Different protective functions and performance are involved. Selection must follow the qualified assessment and applicable electrical program.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Plan deenergized work and qualified boundaries
lessons.body:
Plan to establish a verified electrically safe condition wherever required and feasible under the applicable rules. Only qualified and employer-authorized people perform electrical tasks within their assessed scope. Qualification is task-specific: experience with one voltage or equipment type does not grant unlimited electrical authority.

The responsible electrical plan identifies sources, isolation, verification, boundaries, tools, protection and restoration. Other workers remain outside the defined limits and do not cross them to deliver material. The course does not invent universal approach distances or incident-energy values.

Worked example: a mechanic needs access near electrical equipment but is not qualified for exposed electrical work. The electrical authority establishes the safe arrangement and access limits before the mechanical task begins.

### Applying the mechanism

Qualification should be recorded by task rather than as a broad title. A person trained to operate equipment may not be qualified to expose conductors, select a tester or interpret an electrical fault. A technician competent on one system may need additional assessment for another voltage, configuration or hazard. The work plan identifies the qualified roles and how other trades interact with them. Mechanical crews may need a safe electrical state established before their own work, but that does not make them the electrical testers. Similarly, a site supervisor can coordinate the job without having technical authority to approve energized repair. Clear role boundaries allow people to ask for the right capability instead of using hierarchy as a substitute for electrical competence.

### Decision principles

Deenergizing and verifying removes exposure where required. Energized work is subject to specific justified conditions and controls, not convenience.

Boundaries depend on the equipment and electrical hazards. Awareness workers respect established limits rather than inventing them.

Duration and material do not remove the electrical exposure. Access must follow the qualified control arrangement and role limits.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Verify absence of voltage using suitable methods
lessons.body:
Opening a disconnect and applying protection are necessary parts of some safe-state procedures, but they do not alone prove absence of voltage. A qualified person uses suitable rated test equipment and the prescribed verification process, including checks of instrument function as required. Alternate supplies, induced or stored energy and incorrect circuit identification must be addressed.

Testing can itself occur near energized parts, so it requires the relevant protection and technique. A noncontact indicator or a failed start is not a universal substitute for the specified absence-of-voltage test. The exact method belongs to the qualified electrical procedure.

Worked example: a tester gives an unexpected result. The worker stops and resolves the circuit and instrument condition rather than selecting the reading that agrees with the isolation sheet.

### Applying the mechanism

A suitable test instrument must match the circuit and environment, including its rating, leads, condition and intended measurement. Damaged leads or an unsuitable instrument can create a fault or produce misleading results. The qualified procedure addresses how the instrument’s function is established before and after the relevant test, and how the worker is protected while the condition may still be energized. Do not use a general awareness explanation as a step-by-step testing instruction. The learner’s decision is to require the qualified method and recognize that an unexpected result keeps the work held. Selecting the favorable value, changing the record or assuming the meter is wrong defeats the verification that protects everyone who later relies on the safe state.

### Decision principles

Testing requires task-specific skill and suitable equipment because the conductors may still be energized during verification.

The measurement is only reliable within the instrument’s condition and method. Required function checks help prevent a false safe-state conclusion.

A control response is bounded and can fail for many reasons. Qualified electrical verification must address the actual conductors and sources.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Treat energized work as a controlled exception
lessons.body:
Where energized work is permitted under applicable rules, it requires its specific technical basis, assessment, authorization and protective arrangement. Avoiding production delay is not by itself a technical justification. The qualified authority determines whether the proposed task meets the governing conditions and what safeguards are necessary.

Tools, test instruments, insulating equipment and arc-rated protection must match the actual assessment and be in suitable condition. PPE is not permission for an unqualified worker to perform energized work. Keep nonessential people away and plan emergency response and access.

Worked example: a supervisor requests live repair to avoid a shutdown. The electrical authority reviews the request against the applicable criteria. The supervisor’s schedule preference does not create an energized-work authorization.

### Applying the mechanism

Energized-work controls must be established before a person enters exposure. The technical basis and governing requirements determine whether the task is permitted in that state, and the assessment defines suitable tools, barriers, approach limits and protective equipment. These controls are not selected by matching a suit to a cabinet’s appearance. Equipment condition and the specific work can affect the hazard. If the job changes from observation to adjustment or repair, the authority reassesses rather than allowing the worker to expand the task informally. Production pressure can be communicated as a scheduling issue, but it is not evidence of technical necessity. The qualified process decides the allowable method and the worker remains within that assessed scope.

### Decision principles

Protective performance must match the exposure and work method. Generic issue or appearance does not establish adequacy.

Protective equipment does not supply the knowledge and skill needed to avoid faults and contact. Qualified execution is still required.

Damage can defeat protective performance. The applicable inspection and replacement process must restore the safeguard before reliance.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Control portable equipment and respond safely
lessons.body:
Inspect portable electrical equipment and cords under applicable requirements before use. Damaged insulation, missing pins, crushed cords or evidence of internal damage require removal from reliance and competent disposition. Do not use a cord to lift equipment or create makeshift repairs. Wet or hazardous locations can impose additional suitability requirements.

If a person is in contact with electricity, do not touch them or conductive equipment while the source may remain live. Activate the emergency system and follow the trained safe isolation and rescue arrangements. First aid is performed only after the scene is safe and within the responder’s training.

Worked example: a worker sees a damaged extension cord near water. The equipment is not used; the site’s safe isolation and defect-control process is followed rather than moving the live damaged section by hand.

### Applying the mechanism

Portable equipment can carry damage from transport and handling into a new location. Inspect the actual cord, plug, enclosure and visible condition using the applicable criteria, and route cords so vehicles, sharp edges and doors do not damage them. Keep connections suitable for moisture and the environment under the approved system. A device that ran successfully yesterday may have been crushed or contaminated since then. If protection trips or the equipment behaves abnormally, follow the defect process rather than repeatedly resetting it to finish the task. Repeated operation is not a diagnostic method for an unqualified user. The owner arranges competent assessment and prevents the item returning to service without the required verification.

### Decision principles

Function does not prove insulation integrity. Damage can expose users to shock or faults and must pass the approved repair or replacement process.

Pulling equipment by its cord can damage insulation and connections. Handling must preserve the electrical protective condition.

Equipment ratings and protection must match the environment. A device that works in one location may create unacceptable risk in another.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Restore, communicate and retain practical limits
lessons.body:
Restoration follows the qualified procedure: account for people and tools, restore covers and protection, handle isolation devices under their rules, communicate the changed state and energize only through the authorized process. A completed repair does not automatically mean the system is ready for power.

Record circuit identity, work, tests, defects, changes and acceptance. Any later configuration change can require new review.

Worked example: testing is complete but a cover is still removed for cleanup. The authorized restoration process resolves the exposed condition before returning the equipment to normal access.

### Applying the mechanism

Restoration changes the assumptions of everyone working around the system. The qualified procedure accounts for tools, temporary grounds or protection where applicable, covers, people and isolation devices before energization. Communication must reach affected workers who may still believe the system is deenergized. If testing requires a temporary energized stage followed by more exposed work, the plan explicitly controls both transitions and re-establishes the required safe state before access resumes. Record the actual tests and configuration so a later worker can understand what was accepted. Do not use a general “repair complete” message as permission for every subsequent activity. Electrical maintenance, operating readiness and access authorization remain distinct controlled decisions.

### Decision principles

People may still rely on the previous isolated state. Clear communication prevents inadvertent contact or conflicting work after energization.

Traceability links verification to the actual system and condition. Vague or predicted records cannot establish the work performed.

Written awareness cannot establish hands-on electrical testing, repair or rescue skills. The employer and applicable licensing system determine those qualifications.

lessons.title: Two applied scenarios and worked decisions
lessons.body:
## Applied scenarios: complete worked decisions

### Scenario 1: Wrong circuit identity

A panel label and drawing disagree. The worker has opened the labeled disconnect but has not resolved the circuit identity.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** The task remains held. The qualified electrical authority resolves the actual sources and circuit, establishes the required isolation and verification, and updates controlled information. The worker does not choose the label that makes the job easiest or expose a conductor to test assumptions informally. A safe state must apply to the actual work point.

### Scenario 2: Live repair for convenience

A supervisor asks an unqualified mechanic to tighten a connection inside an energized cabinet to avoid stopping production. A protective suit is available.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** The mechanic does not enter the electrical task. The designated electrical authority evaluates the work, plans the required safe condition and determines any lawful energized-work exception and controls. Qualified personnel perform only within their assessed scope. The suit does not create qualification, technical justification or work authorization.

lessons.title: Final assessment: 20 individual decisions
lessons.body: Answer the 20 questions individually using the taught principles. Each submission preserves your first answer. Review feedback after submitting. When an answer is incorrect, explicitly acknowledge the correct decision and explanation before moving on. The result must show both the first-answer score and the remediated score across all 26 questions. Do not attempt a live hazardous task to obtain an answer; the assessment is a knowledge and judgment exercise.

lessons.title: Completion and separately assessed practical competence
lessons.body:
## What this completion means

The course is complete only after every section and all 26 questions have been accomplished, through correct responses or explicit acknowledgment of the supplied correction. Preserve the original and remediated results separately. Acknowledgment is a learning action, not evidence that the learner has performed the task safely in the field.

## Legal requirements for the named work role
These apply only when you perform the work described below. They are not additional steps for completing this online course.

29 CFR 1910.269(a)(2)(viii) — Employees doing covered electric-power generation, transmission or distribution work: Demonstrate proficiency in the applicable work practices before the training required by this paragraph is treated as complete. This does not impose the power-industry rule on every employee taking electrical awareness. Source: https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.269

lessons.title: Start here: learning, scores and role boundaries
lessons.body:
# H13: H2S and hazardous-atmosphere awareness

This original VNDRLY course teaches decisions for service-specific: sour gas, production, tanks and affected support staff. Its purpose is to recognize gas danger and escape without unplanned rescue. The six lessons explain the hazard, planning decisions, controls, checks, changing conditions and handback. Worked examples and two fictional scenarios show how those decisions fit together. Read the teaching before answering; no live hazardous activity is needed to complete this course.

There are six lesson knowledge checks and a 20-question final assessment. Submit each answer before viewing its feedback. Your first answer remains in the original score. If an answer is wrong, read the specific explanation and explicitly acknowledge the correction; acknowledged corrections contribute to a separate remediated score. Completion requires all sections and all 26 questions correct or explicitly acknowledged after remediation. A later corrected answer never erases the first-answer record.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Recognize exposure without relying on your senses
lessons.body:
Hydrogen sulfide, or H2S, can be present in production fluids, sour gas, tanks, pits and other affected systems. Breathing it can injure or kill. A release can occur during sampling, opening equipment, draining or disturbing liquids, even when the routine job title sounds harmless. The risk assessment must consider what the worker will actually do and what nearby equipment can release. A gate attendant near an affected process may need awareness and escape instruction even though the attendant never opens a valve.

H2S may have a rotten-egg odor, but smell is an unreliable warning. The sense of smell can stop detecting it, and a worker must not interpret disappearing odor as improving air. Irritated eyes, headache or dizziness can be warning signs, but symptoms are neither a detector nor a safe clearance test. High exposure can incapacitate rapidly. Other gases can displace oxygen or introduce fire and toxicity hazards without an H2S reading. Treat an unknown atmosphere as unknown, rather than assuming a familiar location is safe.

Worked example: a driver smells an unusual odor while waiting beside a tank battery. The driver follows the site escape and notification procedure from a safe location. The driver does not walk toward the tank to identify the smell or wait for symptoms. The task and location are reassessed by the designated site authority.

### Decision principles

Exposure follows the material and release mechanism, not the worker’s title. Sampling, draining, opening and nearby releases can expose support workers as well as process personnel.

A sensor reports its own target and limitations. Oxygen deficiency, flammable gas and other toxic contaminants require their own assessed detection and control arrangements.

Symptoms can have several causes and may indicate a serious exposure. The priority is escape and emergency notification; investigating or self-diagnosing inside the affected area adds exposure.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Understand detectors, sensors and their limits
lessons.body:
A personal monitor is part of a protective system, not a permission slip. The employer selects sensors, range, hazardous-location suitability and sampling arrangements for the assessed hazards. Before reliance, an authorized user checks device identity, assigned sensors, battery, inlets, physical condition, status messages and required manufacturer checks. A monitor worn inside a sealed bag or obstructed by clothing may not sample the air the worker breathes. Position it as specified by the approved instruction and manufacturer.

A functional challenge or bump test exposes the instrument to known test gas to confirm response and alarms. Calibration establishes or adjusts measurement response against a known reference. A startup self-test or fresh-air zero does not replace the specified gas challenge. A device can turn on and still have a failed, poisoned, obstructed or unsuitable sensor. Failed checks, unexplained readings or an overdue required service remove the device from reliance.

Worked example: an assigned monitor starts normally but its required functional test fails. The worker obtains an approved tested replacement through the equipment system. The worker does not silence the warning, record a pass or borrow a device whose sensors cannot be identified.

### Decision principles

A bump test is a functional challenge of the instrument. It is not a substitute for calibration when required, assessment of the workplace, or checking that the sensors match the hazards.

Different instruments and sensor combinations detect different substances and ranges. The task assessment and manufacturer information must support selection; the number of display channels alone is insufficient.

Personal monitoring is intended to represent the wearer’s exposure within the method’s limitations. Obstruction or remote placement can delay or prevent detection of the air reaching the worker.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Separate readings, limits and clearance decisions
lessons.body:
A displayed concentration is a measurement for a particular device, place and time. It is not a prediction of conditions at a hatch, behind a barrier, at another elevation or later in the shift. A qualified assessment determines where and how to sample, how long to allow for instrument and sample-line response, and what continuous or repeated monitoring is needed. Remote sampling is not performed by putting an unprotected person into the hazard to carry the instrument.

Occupational exposure limits, instrument alarm settings, entry criteria and emergency action levels serve different purposes. Their legal scope and averaging periods can differ. This awareness course does not assign a universal alarm number, safe exposure duration, evacuation threshold or re-entry criterion. The approved program must identify applicable requirements and conservative site actions before the worker is exposed. An alarm setting is not permission to remain below that number indefinitely.

Worked example: a tank was tested earlier, but an agitator starts and the hatch configuration changes. The previous measurement does not clear the changed task. The authorized tester and operating authority reassess the release and monitoring method before affected work resumes.

### Decision principles

Exposure limits may use particular averaging periods and jurisdictional rules. Alarm settings trigger protective actions within a defined program; neither should be casually converted into an operating permission.

Sampling requires knowledge of atmosphere behavior, target hazards, instrument limitations, locations and response time. Written awareness completion does not demonstrate those field testing skills.

A zero reading must be interpreted within sensor range, condition, method and location. It does not prove future safety or rule out contaminants the instrument cannot detect.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Prepare an escape before entering the exposure area
lessons.body:
Before entering an affected area, know the alarm signals, escape routes, wind indicators, communications, primary muster and alternatives. Routes must be practicable from the actual work position, including darkness, obstacles and changing operations. Wind can help determine a route but is not a guarantee that an area is gas-free; terrain, structures and changing releases complicate dispersion. Follow the site plan for moving away from the release and toward the designated safe area, adapting only through the emergency instructions when the planned route is compromised.

Escape equipment, where required, must be selected for the assessed atmosphere and escape duration by the responsible qualified program. An escape-only unit is not equipment for investigation, continued work, re-entry or rescue. A dust mask does not protect against H2S, and an air-purifying device is not a supply of oxygen.

Worked example: a service worker can describe the alarm but cannot locate the alternate muster or use the assigned escape unit. The missing readiness is resolved with the supervisor and competent trainer before exposure. A completed online module does not fill either practical gap.

### Decision principles

Escape-only protection has a bounded emergency purpose. Its presence does not authorize entry, rescue or continued work, and its limitations must be taught for the exact device.

An escape plan must fit current access, obstructions, wind information and site instructions. A memorized route can become unsafe when equipment, operations or conditions change.

Particulate filtering and gas or oxygen-deficiency protection are different functions. Respiratory selection must be made by the qualified program; improvising with available masks is unsafe.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Respond to alarms without creating a second casualty
lessons.body:
On an alarm, suspected release or emergency instruction, stop the affected activity and leave by the approved escape procedure. Do not delay evacuation to finish paperwork, close a convenient valve, silence a detector or investigate a suspected sensor fault. From a safe location, communicate the location, alarm or symptoms, people potentially affected and any missing persons. Follow the site accountability process so responders do not have to guess who is still inside.

A collapsed person can trigger a strong rescue impulse. Entering an unknown or hazardous atmosphere without the designated rescue capability can rapidly create multiple casualties. Call the emergency response system and keep others from entering when this can be done safely. Only the designated trained, equipped and authorized team undertakes atmospheric rescue under its plan. A nearby coworker with a personal monitor is not thereby a rescue team.

Worked example: a worker sees a colleague down beyond a gas alarm point. The worker stays outside the affected area, summons the rescue response, gives the last known location and reports their own safe location. The worker does not run in holding a breath or follow an unprotected supervisor.

### Decision principles

A suspected instrument fault is not atmospheric clearance. Protective response comes first; qualified investigation occurs from a safe, controlled arrangement without exposing workers to prove the alarm wrong.

Accurate accountability helps the designated response team direct resources. Uncoordinated searching exposes more people and can make the missing-person count less reliable.

Report observations and uncertainties distinctly. Responders need location and exposure clues, but fabricated readings or unsupported clearance claims can misdirect the rescue plan.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Control re-entry, investigation and evidence
lessons.body:
An alarm ending, a reset display or a worker feeling better does not authorize re-entry. The designated operating/site authority coordinates technical assessment of the cause, current atmosphere, affected equipment and safeguards. Re-entry or restart follows the approved authorization process after its conditions have been verified. Workers remain in the designated safe area unless directed through that process; they do not treat a production deadline as a change in atmospheric conditions.

Keep an accurate record of the event and response: location, time, activity, device identity if known, observed alarm, evacuation and accountability, notifications, technical findings and who authorized the next stage. Do not overwrite an alarm log with a later acceptable reading. Both can be true and both matter. Review whether the release mechanism, detection placement, escape route or communication needs improvement.

Worked example: after a tank alarm, operations identifies a changed vent path. A qualified review corrects the control arrangement, tests the relevant conditions and briefs the affected crews. The revised task can be considered for authorization. The training administrator merely records course evidence; that administrator does not clear the tank.

### Decision principles

Measurements and events form a chronology. Later acceptable conditions do not erase the earlier exposure warning; preserving both supports cause analysis and defensible authorization.

A written score cannot establish hazardous field performance.

An event without injury may still reveal failed or fragile controls. Review observable conditions and decisions, assign improvements and verify effectiveness rather than treating the outcome as proof of safety.

lessons.title: Two applied scenarios and worked decisions
lessons.body:
## Applied scenarios: complete worked decisions

### Scenario 1: Gate alarm during a delivery

A delivery driver waits at an affected production gate. A fixed gas alarm activates. A coworker says the sensor often misbehaves and suggests finishing the delivery. The driver has a personal monitor but has not been assigned a gas-testing role.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** The driver follows the site evacuation and accountability instructions, warns others without entering the affected area, and reports the alarm from safety. The delivery pauses. The driver does not approach the fixed sensor with the personal monitor to adjudicate which instrument is correct. The site authority arranges qualified investigation, verifies the conditions and controls, and communicates any authorized re-entry. The record preserves the initial alarm, action taken and later technical findings. A delivery schedule cannot substitute for that clearance.

### Scenario 2: Tank task after a configuration change

A crew has an earlier gas-test record for an external tank task. The planned work now includes opening a hatch after circulation starts. One worker argues that the old reading and their recent course completion make another review unnecessary.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** The supervisor pauses the changed work and confirms the new scope with operations. Opening the hatch and changing circulation can alter release pathways, so a qualified person reassesses the atmosphere and monitoring plan, together with isolation, exposure, escape and any permit requirements. If the work could constitute entry, confined-space assessment is also required; it is not cleared by an external reading. The crew receives the revised briefing only after the responsible authorities establish the actual safeguards. The written course supports recognition of the change, not approval to test or open the tank.

When an answer is incorrect, explicitly acknowledge the correct decision and explanation before moving on. The result must show both the first-answer score and the remediated score across all 26 questions. Do not attempt a live hazardous task to obtain an answer; the assessment is a knowledge and judgment exercise.

These apply only when you perform the work described below. They are not additional steps for completing this online course.

questions.prompt: A worker no longer notices the odor after several minutes. What does that establish?

options.label: Nothing about atmospheric safety; follow the approved response and detection system.
The release has stopped.
The worker has adapted and can remain.

questions.prompt: Which activity can create H2S exposure?

options.label: Only entering a vessel marked sour.
Only work performed by a gas tester.
Opening or disturbing affected process equipment or liquids.

questions.prompt: What does an H2S sensor alone establish about oxygen?

options.label: It measures every atmospheric hazard indirectly.
It does not establish oxygen concentration.

questions.prompt: What should a worker do with possible exposure symptoms?

options.label: Leave according to the emergency plan and obtain emergency help from a safe location.
Remain to compare symptoms with a chart.

options.label: Use it because its display works.

options.label: Permanent accuracy regardless of later damage.

A complete exposure survey of the work area.

options.label: A detector may lack the sensor or range needed for the actual contaminant.

options.label: Inside a sealed pocket to protect it from dust.
On a vehicle left far from the worker.

options.label: Any nearby confined-space entry.

options.label: They serve different functions and require program-specific interpretation.

options.label: Any worker who completed this online awareness course.

options.label: The equipment cannot release gas later.

options.label: Task-specific practical instruction and verification before exposure.

options.label: Returning to retrieve tools.
Continuing a short production task.
Leaving the hazardous area within its approved limitations.

options.label: The nearest low spot is automatically safest.

options.label: It does not provide the required gas and atmosphere protection.

options.label: Rush in while holding your breath.
Enter with a normal personal monitor as protection.

questions.prompt: An alarm is dismissed as probably faulty. What should an affected worker do?

options.label: Remove the battery so the sound does not distract.

options.label: Promptly through the emergency and muster system from a safe location.

After every worker independently searches the process area.

options.label: An invented gas concentration to speed dispatch.
A claim that a familiar tank is certainly safe.
Last known location, observed alarm or symptoms, people affected and safe contact point.

options.label: The course administrator after checking quiz scores.

The first worker who hears silence.

questions.prompt: What should happen to the initial alarm record after a later acceptable test?

options.label: Preserve both records with their times and conditions.

Delete the alarm because it may look bad.

questions.prompt: Which qualification is established by this written course alone?

options.label: Qualified field gas tester for every instrument.
Atmospheric rescue specialist.
Awareness learning and assessed written judgment only.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of reviewing an alarm response?

options.label: Reclassify the release as safe because no injury occurred.
Identify whether detection, escape, communication and process controls worked and correct gaps.
Prove that every worker was to blame.

questions.prompt: In the gate scenario, which action exceeds the driver’s awareness role?

options.label: Entering the affected area to test whether the fixed alarm is genuine.
Reporting from the designated safe area.
Following muster accountability instructions.

questions.prompt: Why is the earlier tank reading insufficient for the changed task?

options.label: All readings expire at an invented universal interval.
A higher quiz score would make the reading valid.
The release conditions and scope have changed, requiring qualified reassessment.
