lessons.title: Start here: Lone work, workplace violence and remote check-ins
lessons.body:
# Lone work, workplace violence and remote check-ins

This original VNDRLY course teaches decisions within the company safety program. Work through six lessons, their six checks, two worked scenarios and a 20-question final. All cases are fictional. No equipment operation is required to complete the online learning.

Each of the 26 questions requires a recorded answer. Completion requires a correct answer or explicit acknowledgment of the explanation and corrected answer after an error. Preserve the first-attempt score separately from the remediated score; a correction never rewrites what was first understood. Read the explanation, return to the relevant lesson and resolve uncertainty with the responsible supervisor. The course does not substitute for a site assessment, permit or employer authorization.

The linked references support the subject and identify source context. Client procedures are examples of client requirements, not universal law or endorsement of this course. Apply the governing jurisdiction and actual site procedure; no numerical technical limits or universal renewal interval are invented here.

## Primary reference context

[OSHA Workplace violence](https://www.osha.gov/workplace-violence). Read the reference within its stated scope. Company examples are not universal technical rules; regulatory applicability must be determined for the actual task and jurisdiction.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 - Decide whether the task may be done alone
lessons.body:
Lone work means help may not be immediately available when a person is injured, threatened or unable to communicate. It can occur in a gatehouse, a remote pump station, a yard after other workers leave or a room where a person is isolated from the rest of the crew. Being on a busy site does not guarantee someone will notice distress. A delivery driver passing the gate is not a designated responder.

Assess the actual task, location, time and foreseeable failure. Consider traffic exposure, illness, slips, violence, communications coverage, access for help and tasks that could incapacitate the person. Ask how the worker could raise the alarm after the credible event, not just before it. A worker pinned by a vehicle or unconscious from illness may be unable to make a phone call. The assessment must address that limitation rather than assuming the phone solves it.

Some activities require another trained person or a specialist team under the applicable procedure. The lone-work assessment cannot waive those requirements. Do not turn a required attendant, standby person, rescue team or traffic spotter into a remote telephone contact. Where risks cannot be adequately controlled, change the staffing, method or schedule, or do not perform the task alone.

Distinguish planned duty from scope creep. A gate worker authorized to monitor admissions may be asked to inspect a remote drainage pit after dark. That is a new task with different exposure and rescue access. Report the request and obtain assessment before leaving the agreed location. An urgent request from a client does not automatically amend the employer's lone-work boundary.

The worker should know the exact permitted area, tasks, communications, withdrawal conditions and responsible monitor before starting. 'Call if you need anything' is an offer of help, not a complete arrangement. A practical pre-start discussion should expose uncertainty before the worker becomes isolated.

## Worked field example

A lone gate attendant is asked to leave the booth and inspect an unlit remote pit.

The safe decision is to hold the additional task until the employer assesses its lone-work suitability and establishes the required controls. Approval for gate duty does not cover a different remote task or its rescue limitations.

A useful field record is specific: A task-specific assessment showing permitted activities, location limits and available response arrangements. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 - Make check-ins an active response system
lessons.body:
A check-in arrangement needs a sender, a receiver and a defined action when the expected contact does not occur. Agree the worker's location, task, expected contacts, method, risk-based timing, backup method and escalation before the shift. Do not invent a universal interval. The interval and response stages must reflect how rapidly harm could develop, communications reliability, travel time and the available response.

The receiver must be a named, available person or a monitored service with a defined duty. A message sent to an unattended group chat may look documented while nobody is responsible for reading it. Confirm the receiver accepts the assignment and knows when the next contact is due. A worker saying 'all good' is useful only if the message can be linked to the right person, location and task.

Plan what happens if the primary receiver becomes unavailable. A supervisor attending a meeting, going off shift or losing their phone must transfer monitoring to the designated backup. That handover includes last successful contact, next expected contact, known hazards, current location and escalation status. Do not leave a gap while assuming the other person is watching.

Check-ins should confirm the agreed information without encouraging unsafe phone use. A driver must not type while moving, and a worker handling equipment should first make the task safe. Arrange the method and work timing so the communication can occur safely. If the contact method repeatedly conflicts with the task, redesign the arrangement.

The check-in record must be usable during an emergency. Include a location description that another person can act on, not just 'north gate.' Distinguish scheduled contacts from occasional friendly messages. An informal message earlier in the shift does not automatically reset the next due contact or close an unresolved alarm.

## Worked field example

A lone gate worker sends scheduled messages to a group chat after the assigned supervisor goes off duty.

The safe decision is to restore a named available receiver and transfer the live monitoring information to the backup. A sent message does not establish that anyone accepted responsibility to act on a missed contact.

A useful field record is specific: A confirmed receiver handover recording last contact, next due contact, location and escalation duty. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 - Test devices, coverage and duress routes
lessons.body:
Test communication where the worker will actually work. A phone that works at the office may fail behind steel tanks or in a remote gatehouse. Consider battery life, charging, weather protection, network coverage, radio interoperability and the worker's ability to use the device while wearing required clothing. Follow site restrictions on electronic equipment in hazardous areas; this awareness course does not approve a device for an explosive atmosphere.

A test must include the receiving and response side. Verify the correct person receives the alarm, recognizes the location and can start the required escalation. A successful outgoing call proves only part of that chain. A duress device that sends an alert to an unmonitored address is not an effective control. Know how accidental alerts are handled without teaching people to ignore them.

A duress arrangement should allow a person to seek help when an overt call could worsen a threat. Use only the employer's agreed method, code or device; do not improvise a secret phrase that the receiver does not understand. Keep sensitive details within the approved access controls. Training must make the worker's action clear while preserving the security of the arrangement.

Discuss incapacitation. Some assessed systems may include monitored devices or automatic alerts, but no technology removes the need to assess coverage and response. A device can fail, be left on a desk or be unable to describe a changing location. The worker should know the fallback and the point at which the lone activity must pause because the control is unavailable.

When a test fails, stop relying on the affected arrangement. Report the failure, obtain a verified alternative or change the work so isolation is removed. Do not keep working alone while treating 'battery low' as a maintenance note for tomorrow. The failure changes today's readiness.

## Worked field example

A duress test sends an alert, but the monitoring contact receives no location and cannot identify the gate.

The safe decision is to hold reliance on the arrangement until the alert and actionable location reach the responsible receiver. An alarm is useful only when the receiver can interpret it and initiate an effective response.

A useful field record is specific: A documented end-to-end test from the actual work location to the assigned receiving and escalation roles. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 - Manage threats without escalating the encounter
lessons.body:
Violence can include threats, intimidation, assault and behavior that creates a credible safety concern. Gate workers can face conflict over denied access, delays, alcohol or drugs, employment disputes and personal grievances. The job is to apply the authorized access process from a safe position, not to win an argument or physically enforce every refusal.

Know the safe retreat route and the site's duress and emergency contacts before an encounter. Arrange the work area so the worker can withdraw rather than becoming trapped behind a visitor or a locked barrier. Use physical separation and access design where the assessment calls for it. Do not publicly disclose personal details, shift patterns or sensitive security information while trying to calm someone.

Communicate briefly and calmly. Explain the decision and the authorized contact who can review it, without insults, threats or a promise outside your authority. Keep distance and avoid touching the person or reaching into a vehicle. If behavior becomes threatening, disengage and seek help through the agreed procedure. You do not need to remain at the counter to preserve a perfect entry record.

An aggressive driver may try to force a gate or follow another vehicle. Do not stand in front of the vehicle or hold the barrier with your body. Withdraw, activate the site response and give location, direction of travel and a factual description from a safe place. Protect other workers by using the approved notification route; do not chase the vehicle.

After the immediate danger, support the affected worker and record observable behavior, exact threats where appropriate, actions taken and witnesses. Avoid speculative diagnoses or blame. The employer should review the controls, staffing and support needs before resuming the same arrangement. A worker asking for help is reporting a safety issue, not failing a customer-service test.

## Worked field example

A refused driver threatens the attendant and moves the truck toward the closed barrier.

The safe decision is to withdraw to the designated safe position and activate the agreed duress or emergency response. The attendant’s access role does not authorize physical confrontation or standing in a vehicle path.

A useful field record is specific: A factual incident account and review of retreat, separation, response and staffing arrangements. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

lessons.title: Lesson 5 - Act on missed contact and uncertain welfare
lessons.body:
A missed check-in is information requiring the agreed response. It is not proof of injury, but it is also not proof that everything is fine. The plan should define the initial contact attempt, backup method, escalation responsibility and conditions requiring emergency services. Apply those instructions promptly rather than inventing a new waiting period because the worker is usually reliable.

Use the last known location, task and hazards to guide escalation. A call going to voicemail could mean poor coverage, a flat battery or incapacity. Try the approved alternatives while the designated role assesses the situation. Where information indicates immediate danger, activate the emergency route without delaying for routine paperwork or repeated administrative calls.

Do not send an unbriefed coworker alone into an unknown hazard to 'have a look.' The checking response must itself be safe. A gate welfare check may require controlled vehicle access; a remote industrial area may require isolation, atmospheric assessment or trained responders. The lone-work plan should identify how a safe verification can occur within the site's emergency system.

Preserve the timeline. Record when contact was due, attempts made, information received, escalation started and responsibility transferred. Distinguish an actual successful welfare confirmation from a message that merely shows the phone is online. If the worker makes contact during an escalation, tell the response coordinator so resources are not left searching. Confirm the worker's condition, location and ability to continue before closing the event.

A missed contact that turns out to be a device failure is still useful learning. Restore effective monitoring before more lone work, investigate the failure and determine whether the risk-based arrangement needs revision. Do not silently disable alerts to avoid future inconvenience.

## Worked field example

A worker misses a planned check-in; calls go unanswered and the last task was beside an active delivery lane.

The safe decision is to activate the agreed missed-contact escalation and arrange a safe welfare verification through the responsible roles. Uncertain welfare beside a known hazard requires the planned response rather than an improvised delay.

A useful field record is specific: A timeline of due contact, attempts, escalation, safe welfare confirmation and restored monitoring. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

lessons.title: Lesson 6 - Review readiness and hand over the whole arrangement
lessons.body:
Lone-work controls must survive shift changes, holidays, staffing shortages and device faults. Before accepting a lone assignment, confirm that the task is within the assessment, the location is known, the receiver is available, the device works and the response resources can reach the worker. If one element is missing, raise the gap before the isolation begins.

Review events and near misses with the people who perform the work. Repeated late check-ins may reveal a poor schedule, inaccessible device, excessive task load or unclear receiver duty. Repeated threats may indicate a need for revised access design, staffing, escort or security support. Training the same worker again will not repair a physical trap or an unmonitored phone.

Assess performance through safe simulation. A worker can demonstrate a check-in, a communication failure, withdrawal from a fictional threatening encounter and the escalation information without being exposed to an aggressive person or live traffic. The receiving role should demonstrate its own actions; testing only the worker misses half the control.

Records should distinguish understanding from readiness. A course result shows answers to learning questions. A shift confirmation shows the actual monitoring and response resources were available. These are related but different kinds of evidence. None should be used to conceal the absence of another.

Close an improvement only after the revised arrangement has been checked. If a backup receiver is named but has never accepted the duty or received access to the contact information, the action is not implemented. Keep sensitive threat and health records restricted while giving operational staff the information they need. Reassess when the worker's task, location, schedule or foreseeable response changes.

## Worked field example

A new backup monitor is listed on the roster but has not been briefed or accepted the duty.

The safe decision is to confirm the backup’s capability and acceptance before relying on that person for lone-work monitoring. A name on a roster does not establish an available and competent response function.

A useful field record is specific: A safe end-to-end exercise and confirmed acceptance of the monitoring and escalation role. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

lessons.title: Two applied scenarios and worked solutions
lessons.body:
## Scenario 1

A fictional remote gate is staffed by Sam alone overnight. The assessment permits admission checks from the protected booth but excludes remote yard inspections. At midnight the supervisor hands the monitoring phone to a relief supervisor without discussing current contacts. Sam's next check-in is missed. The relief supervisor sees an old message saying 'all quiet' and assumes no action is needed. A caller then reports a truck standing oddly near the gate. Sam's radio does not answer.

Work through the response without assuming Sam is injured, safe, or merely forgetful. Identify what information the receiving supervisor needs and what must be restored before the next lone shift.

### Worked solution

The relief supervisor activates the agreed missed-contact response using the actual due contact and known hazards. The old message does not confirm Sam's present welfare or reset the schedule. The report about the truck adds relevant information; it should be passed to the response coordinator, not treated as a reason to walk into the vehicle area alone.

The receiver establishes Sam's last confirmed location, assigned task, expected contact method, due time and any live restrictions. Approved alternative contact attempts can continue while the responsible role arranges safe welfare verification. If the available information indicates immediate danger, emergency assistance is requested through the site route without waiting for routine reporting. The verification method must address vehicle and access hazards and remain within the responder's competence.

The supervisor records times and actions accurately and gives responders usable directions to the actual entrance. Nobody assumes Sam entered the remote yard simply because a call is unanswered. If Sam is found safe with a failed radio, the response coordinator is told, his condition and location are confirmed, and the event is closed through the agreed process. If medical help is needed, the site emergency arrangement governs it.

Before further lone work, effective monitoring is restored and tested. The handover failure is reviewed: the relief role needs explicit acceptance, current location and task, last contact, next due contact, backup and escalation instructions. The employer checks why the old message was mistaken for a current confirmation and whether the monitoring system makes due contacts visible. A completed incident form does not by itself restore a functioning receiver.

The learning is about both sides of the arrangement. Sam's obligation to check in does not excuse an unassigned monitoring role. The supervisor's missed handover does not justify unsafe spontaneous rescue. The company must provide an arrangement that detects uncertainty and produces a safe response.

## Scenario 2

At a fictional equipment yard, Amina handles the late gate shift alone. A driver denied entry becomes verbally threatening and says he knows when her shift ends. The driver's truck is stopped beside the booth exit. Amina has a duress button, but the last test only confirmed a light on the device; nobody verified receipt. The regular monitor has left early. A manager tells Amina to keep the driver talking while he finishes another call and suggests she take a photo of the driver's licence at the cab.

Identify immediate safe actions and the changes needed before the same lone arrangement is used again. Do not assume Amina is a security officer or has authority to detain the driver.

### Worked solution

Amina prioritizes withdrawal and assistance through the available safe route. She does not approach the cab, take a photograph in the conflict area or attempt to detain the driver. The threat and blocked exit are information for the emergency contact. She uses the agreed duress or emergency method that can summon help and, from safety, provides the gate location, observable behavior and vehicle position. If one method fails, she uses the approved alternative or emergency route; she does not remain exposed to prove the button is faulty.

The manager treats this as a safety response, rather than asking Amina to prolong the encounter. The responsible site roles manage access, security and any emergency-service involvement. Other workers are warned through the authorized route. The driver is not physically confronted by an untrained coworker sent to protect the gate record.

After the immediate event, Amina receives appropriate support and the employer reviews the threat, escape access, booth layout, monitoring gap and duress failure. The threat about her shift is recorded factually and handled with appropriate confidentiality. The review considers whether lone staffing remains suitable and whether separation, changed access procedures or additional support is necessary.

Before any approved resumption, the communications test must cover the whole chain from Amina's actual position to a named receiver with actionable location and escalation duty. The receiver and backup must accept monitoring. A safe exercise demonstrates withdrawal, alarm receipt and response coordination without exposing Amina to a real confrontation.

The fact that the device illuminated is insufficient: it proves a local indication, not receipt or response. The fact that the driver eventually leaves is also insufficient: it does not show that the lone-work arrangement was effective. The company must verify the controls it plans to rely on and record the scope of that verification.

lessons.title: Start here: Manual handling and ergonomics
lessons.body:
# Manual handling and ergonomics

This original VNDRLY course teaches decisions within the company safety program. Work through six lessons, their six checks, two worked scenarios and a 20-question final. All cases are fictional. No equipment operation is required to complete the online learning.

Each of the 26 questions requires a recorded answer. Completion requires a correct answer or explicit acknowledgment of the explanation and corrected answer after an error. Preserve the first-attempt score separately from the remediated score; a correction never rewrites what was first understood. Read the explanation, return to the relevant lesson and resolve uncertainty with the responsible supervisor. The course does not substitute for a site assessment, permit or employer authorization.

The linked references support the subject and identify source context. Client procedures are examples of client requirements, not universal law or endorsement of this course. Apply the governing jurisdiction and actual site procedure; no numerical technical limits or universal renewal interval are invented here.

## Primary reference context

[OSHA Ergonomics](https://www.osha.gov/ergonomics). Read the reference within its stated scope. Company examples are not universal technical rules; regulatory applicability must be determined for the actual task and jurisdiction.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 - Assess the entire handling task
lessons.body:
Manual handling includes lifting, lowering, carrying, pushing, pulling and holding. Assess the load, grip, reach, posture, repetition, frequency, duration, route and environment with the people doing the work. Weight alone does not describe risk. A lighter awkward item handled repeatedly from the floor can still create substantial exposure.

Observe the real task, including the beginning and end of the shift. Ask where discomfort occurs and what workers do when the normal arrangement fails. Do not assume a strong or experienced worker is protected from strain.

Use competent input for complex or persistent problems. This course provides no universal safe lifting weight or medical diagnosis.

## Worked field example

A worker repeatedly lifts awkward valve boxes from floor level and reports increasing discomfort.

The safe decision is to pause the aggravating task and review load, reach, repetition and the work arrangement with the worker. Handling risk depends on the whole task rather than weight or worker strength alone.

A useful field record is specific: A task observation and worker input identifying the actual handling exposures. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

## Detailed field application

A handling assessment should observe the worker, load and workplace together. Consider a box that is easy to lift at a waist-height demonstration bench but normally arrives on a low pallet behind other stock. The real task includes reaching over the pallet, turning with the box and setting it onto a surface occupied by tools. Teaching only the demonstration lift leaves most of the exposure unexamined.

Ask workers how the process varies. A delivery surge, damaged packaging or a different product size may make the normal method unusable. The assessment should state the conditions it covers and the action when they change. Do not blame a worker for failing to follow a method that cannot be performed in the available space.

Also review pushing and pulling. Wheel condition, floor surface, gradient, visibility and stopping control affect a loaded trolley. A label giving nominal capacity does not establish manageable force or stability along the actual route. Competent advice is needed when the forces or task complexities cannot be adequately evaluated through the ordinary process.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 - Redesign before relying on technique
lessons.body:
Look first for elimination of handling, improved delivery placement, smaller units, suitable working height or mechanical assistance. A lift table can reduce low-level handling, but its suitability and pinch hazards must be assessed. The best change removes the awkward action rather than teaching people to tolerate it.

Lifting technique is a supporting skill, not a substitute for redesign. Telling a worker to bend their knees does not solve a load with no usable grip or a repeated long reach across a bench.

Check that the new method works for receiving, storage and final placement. A device that helps lift onto a trolley but leaves an uncontrolled final lift has solved only part of the task.

## Worked field example

A manager proposes another lifting video instead of fixing repeated floor-to-bench handling.

The safe decision is to review task redesign and suitable assistance before relying on technique training. Technique alone cannot remove the force, reach and repetition built into the task.

A useful field record is specific: A redesigned handling sequence verified from receipt through final placement. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

## Detailed field application

Redesign should begin early enough to affect procurement and delivery. Ask whether a supplier can deliver at a suitable height, provide usable handling points or divide the load without creating another hazard. A smaller package can reduce one lift while increasing repetition; review the complete shift rather than one favorable feature.

At a shop bench, the worker should be able to position the item without a long reach or twist. Suitable fixtures can support the work and reduce sustained holding, but their clamping and release need assessment. The method should also account for removing the completed item and dealing with rejects.

Use a trial with appropriate safe conditions to understand the proposed arrangement. Do not ask a worker with discomfort to prove that a design is acceptable by enduring the old load. The assessor chooses a suitable demonstration, records limitations and uses worker feedback to refine the method. A prototype's apparent convenience does not eliminate the need to check its new pinch or stability hazards.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 - Use suitable aids and routes
lessons.body:
Select handling aids for the actual load, surface, gradient, space and task. Check capacity and condition through the approved method and ensure the worker is trained for the aid. Do not turn a trolley into a personnel platform or use it with an unstable load.

Inspect the route before movement. Thresholds, hoses, potholes and tight corners can increase force or destabilize a load. Clear the route or choose a reviewed alternative. Keep hands and feet out of pinch and crush points during loading, movement and placement.

A mechanical aid does not make every movement safe. Powered equipment may require separate authorization, and the final placement still needs a controlled method.

## Worked field example

A loaded trolley must cross a hose and broken threshold to reach the bench.

The safe decision is to correct or change the route and verify a stable controlled movement before transport. A handling aid can still create high force and instability on an unsuitable route.

A useful field record is specific: A pre-move route check and observation of the suitable aid with the actual load. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

## Detailed field application

Before using an aid, confirm its intended purpose and the actual load configuration. A trolley rated for a distributed load may behave differently with a tall, off-center component. Secure or support the item through the approved method, keep the view and route adequate and use the designated means of control.

Inspect wheels, handles, brakes and other relevant components according to the device. A worker should report a stiff wheel rather than compensate by pulling harder. Remove defective equipment from use when required and provide a suitable alternative or hold the task.

The route review includes the destination. A clear corridor is not enough if the final doorway is too narrow or the unloading position traps hands. Check where the worker can stand, how the load is stopped and how the aid is withdrawn. Powered equipment introduces its own operator, pedestrian and energy controls; completing this ergonomics lesson does not grant that authorization.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 - Coordinate team handling
lessons.body:
Team handling needs a planned method, suitable people, a clear route and agreed communication. Assign coordination and confirm when to lift, move, stop and lower. Do not assume adding another person divides risk evenly or compensates for an awkward unstable load.

Workers need room to hold the item without trapping hands against a doorway or stepping backward into hazards. If one person loses grip or cannot continue, use the agreed safe response rather than expecting the others to catch a falling load.

Where coordination or geometry cannot be made suitable, change the method or use appropriate mechanical assistance. Team handling is an assessed option, not the automatic fallback when an aid is missing.

## Worked field example

Two workers plan to carry a long pump part through a narrow doorway without a lowering or stop instruction.

The safe decision is to plan the route, positions and coordinated stop/lower method or select a suitable alternative. Uncoordinated team handling can create trapping and sudden load transfer.

A useful field record is specific: A briefing and safe demonstration of coordinated movement and placement. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

## Detailed field application

Team handling needs more than a verbal count to three. Confirm each person's position, visibility, grip, path and ability to use the agreed stop signal. A person walking backward cannot assume the route stays clear. Another worker should not be placed where the load can trap them against a fixed object.

Discuss what to do if the item cannot be placed as planned. A suitable supported intermediate position may be necessary through the reviewed method. Do not expect the team to hold an awkward load indefinitely while someone clears the destination.

Changes in team composition also matter. A new worker may not know the signals or route. Brief and assess them within the task rather than relying on the previous team's experience. Record any limits, including conditions under which team handling is not permitted. If the arrangement needs an improvised catch or an exposed hand beneath the load, return to redesign.

lessons.title: Lesson 5 - Review repetition and workstation exposure
lessons.body:
Ergonomics includes repeated hand actions, sustained posture, awkward viewing and prolonged static work. A gate desk, packing bench or tool station can create exposure even when no heavy lift occurs. Adjust the work to the person and task through a reviewed arrangement.

Task rotation helps only if it changes the exposure. Rotating between two jobs that use the same reach, grip and posture may not provide meaningful recovery. Review work pace and the ability to vary position rather than treating rotation as proof of control.

Workers should report discomfort early through the appropriate process. The employer reviews the task and any health restrictions while keeping clinical details confidential.

## Worked field example

A worker rotates between two packing stations that both require the same repeated overhead reach.

The safe decision is to review and redesign the exposure rather than assuming rotation provides recovery. Changing station does not remove risk if the same loading pattern continues.

A useful field record is specific: An exposure comparison and verified workstation change reducing the repeated awkward reach. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

## Detailed field application

For repeated desk or bench work, observe where information and controls are placed. A scanner outside comfortable reach may create a repeated shoulder movement, while a poorly positioned screen can create sustained neck posture. Move or adjust the work through a reviewed arrangement that preserves visibility, emergency access and other important functions.

Allow suitable opportunities to vary posture and task where the assessment calls for them. Rotation is meaningful only if the alternative changes the loading pattern. A schedule that alternates two near-identical reaches should not be reported as exposure reduction without evidence.

Workers should have an accessible way to report discomfort and limitations. The supervisor can discuss task conditions without asking for detailed clinical history. Medical concerns follow the appropriate health process, and any work restrictions are communicated through the authorized route. Early reporting should lead to review, not a challenge to prove an injury.

lessons.title: Lesson 6 - Verify improvement in real use
lessons.body:
After changing a task, observe whether the intended method is used and whether new problems appear. A lift table stored behind pallets is not an available control. A better bench height that creates a long sideways reach may need further adjustment.

Use worker feedback alongside task observation and appropriate competent review. Distinguish immediate comfort from longer-term effectiveness and avoid promising that one change prevents all injuries.

Do not ask a worker to attempt an unsuitable load to prove strength. Record limits and any unassessed element and resolve gaps before assignment.

## Worked field example

A purchased lift aid remains blocked by storage while workers continue lifting from the floor.

The safe decision is to restore usable access and verify the redesigned method in the actual task. A purchased device does not control exposure when workers cannot use it.

A useful field record is specific: An observed complete task using the accessible aid with worker feedback. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

## Detailed field application

Verification should follow the complete work cycle after the change has become routine. An aid can be accessible during training but blocked during receiving. A new bench can work for one product size while forcing an awkward reach for another. State what products, shifts and conditions the observation represents.

Ask whether the new method is practical under normal workload. If workers bypass it, investigate access, time, fit and instruction rather than assuming unwillingness. Correct the actual obstacle and recheck use. Keep the original concern and the subsequent decisions in the record.

They identify what was not tested, including unfamiliar powered devices or loads. A successful safe demonstration supports a bounded assignment, not unlimited handling capacity. Future changes in load, route, frequency or worker restrictions should trigger the appropriate review.

At handover, tell the receiving worker which load sizes, aid and route the reviewed method covers. A different package or blocked route needs the appropriate reassessment before handling.

lessons.title: Two applied scenarios and worked solutions
lessons.body:
## Scenario 1

A fictional shop receives awkward pump components on floor pallets. Workers lift them onto a high bench many times per shift. One reports discomfort. A lift table is available but the receiving route is blocked, and the supervisor suggests a two-person lift for every item.

### Worked solution

The aggravating task is paused and the actual receiving-to-bench sequence reviewed with workers. The assessment includes force, reach, grip, repetition, route and placement. The team-lift suggestion is evaluated rather than treated as an automatic solution. A suitable aid and work-height arrangement are selected, with the route cleared and pinch hazards controlled. Workers safely demonstrate the complete method. Any health concern follows the proper confidential process. The company checks use after implementation and asks whether discomfort and awkward handling persist. Buying equipment or issuing a technique reminder alone does not establish that the exposure changed.

## Scenario 2

A fictional gate attendant enters vehicle details at a high counter for long periods and repeatedly reaches sideways for a scanner. A proposed rotation moves the worker to another identical counter. Explain how to evaluate the proposal.

### Worked solution

The review observes the real posture, reach, viewing, pace and opportunities to vary position. The second station is compared with the first; if the same loading pattern continues, rotation has not materially changed the exposure. The employer considers layout and equipment positioning, suitable work height and work organization. The attendant tests the revised arrangement safely and provides feedback. The assessor checks for new issues such as obstructed visibility or a compromised retreat route. The record identifies what changed and what was observed, with follow-up to confirm continued use.

lessons.title: Start here: Machine guarding, hand tools and housekeeping
lessons.body:
# Machine guarding, hand tools and housekeeping

This original VNDRLY course teaches decisions within the company safety program. Work through six lessons, their six checks, two worked scenarios and a 20-question final. All cases are fictional. No equipment operation is required to complete the online learning.

Each of the 26 questions requires a recorded answer. Completion requires a correct answer or explicit acknowledgment of the explanation and corrected answer after an error. Preserve the first-attempt score separately from the remediated score; a correction never rewrites what was first understood. Read the explanation, return to the relevant lesson and resolve uncertainty with the responsible supervisor. The course does not substitute for a site assessment, permit or employer authorization.

The linked references support the subject and identify source context. Client procedures are examples of client requirements, not universal law or endorsement of this course. Apply the governing jurisdiction and actual site procedure; no numerical technical limits or universal renewal interval are invented here.

## Primary reference context

[OSHA General machine guarding requirements](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.212). Read the reference within its stated scope. Company examples are not universal technical rules; regulatory applicability must be determined for the actual task and jurisdiction.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 - Choose the correct tool and machine
lessons.body:
Match equipment to the task, material and environment. An attachment that fits physically is not necessarily rated or approved for the machine. Confirm the manufacturer's intended configuration and the employer's method. Do not exceed ratings or invent a safe operating limit from experience with another tool.

Consider ignition, electrical, pressure, cutting and ejection hazards. A tool suitable in a dry shop may not be suitable in a wet or hazardous area. Only people with the applicable competence and authorization should operate the equipment.

If the correct equipment is unavailable, change or defer the task through the responsible role. Improvised extensions and altered attachments can change the force path and protective functions.

## Worked field example

A worker fits an unapproved cutting attachment because its shaft fits the available tool.

The safe decision is to hold use until the approved tool and attachment configuration is confirmed. Physical fit does not establish rated compatibility or suitability.

A useful field record is specific: A verified manufacturer-approved configuration and task-specific equipment selection. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

## Detailed field application

Tool selection should include the attachment and accessory as a system. Confirm the intended material, speed, mounting, guard and environmental suitability through the manufacturer's information and approved procedure. Do not make an adapter simply because it allows a part to be installed. A homemade extension can change leverage, reaction force and failure consequences.

Consider the workpiece too. A tool suitable for a secured part at a bench may not be suitable for an awkward in-place cut near other equipment. The supervisor should identify what the method assumes about position, restraint and access. If those assumptions are absent, the task needs review before use.

Workers should know how to obtain the correct tool without pressure to improvise. A stores system that issues whatever is available can undermine the approved method. Deferring the task for suitable equipment is a controlled response, not evidence that the worker should find a workaround.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 - Inspect guards and protective functions
lessons.body:
A guard protects against a defined hazard such as contact, entanglement or ejected material. Inspect the required guard, interlock and control condition through the approved procedure before use. A guard that is present but loose or unable to perform its function is not effective protection.

Do not bypass an interlock or remove a guard to improve production. Report repeated nuisance trips or jams as problems requiring competent review. The machine should not depend on the operator keeping a hand away from an accessible danger point.

Inspection and functional checks must themselves be safe. Do not reach into a moving machine to prove the guard is working. Follow the manufacturer's and employer's method and keep unqualified people out of technical testing.

## Worked field example

A machine interlock is taped closed so the guard can remain open during production.

The safe decision is to stop use and have the protective system restored and verified through competent maintenance. Bypassing the interlock defeats a designed protective function.

A useful field record is specific: A competent repair and safe functional verification of the guard/interlock arrangement. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

## Detailed field application

A guard check should address function and configuration. A cover fitted with missing fasteners or an interlock connected incorrectly may look complete. Users perform only the approved safe checks; competent personnel conduct technical inspection and testing where needed. Do not reach into a danger zone to demonstrate that the machine stops.

The reason for a guard complaint is useful information. Repeated removal may indicate poor access, visibility or material feeding, but that does not justify removal. The technical authority redesigns or corrects the method so the required protection remains effective.

Temporary defeat of a protective device is not authorized by this course. Any exceptional technical activity must follow the applicable controlled procedure and authority, with its own safety arrangements. Ordinary production should not continue around a missing safeguard because the operator has accepted personal risk or a supervisor has signed a note.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 - Keep people outside energy and ejection paths
lessons.body:
Position the work and secure it through the approved method so hands are not used as an improvised clamp. Consider the direction of cutting, recoil, rotation and ejected material. Protect nearby people as well as the operator.

Loose clothing, jewelry, hair and unsuitable gloves can create entanglement around rotating equipment. Follow the task-specific PPE and clothing requirements rather than assuming more material always provides more protection. Eye and face protection do not replace a missing guard.

Maintain a stable working position and clear access. A tool used from an overreach or unstable platform can escape control. Stop when the setup does not permit the approved method; do not rely on a coworker holding an unsafe position.

## Worked field example

A worker holds a small part by hand near a rotating tool because the fixture is missing.

The safe decision is to hold the task until the approved secure workholding and safe positioning are established. Hands used as a substitute fixture can enter the tool’s danger area.

A useful field record is specific: A verified fixture and observation of hands and bystanders outside the relevant danger paths. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

## Detailed field application

Map the likely energy and material paths before positioning people. A rotating part can grab loose material; a cutting wheel can eject fragments; a press can create a trapping zone; a hand tool can slip into another worker. The approved setup must address the relevant paths rather than only the point where work is performed.

Keep bystanders outside the affected area through the site method. A helper should not hold a part in a position the operator would not safely use themselves. Use suitable workholding and supports, and review what happens when the cut is complete or a load shifts.

The operator's stance and escape space matter. An obstructed floor, trailing lead or narrow access can defeat tool control. Clean and organize the area before starting, while preserving emergency and pedestrian routes. If the task forces an unstable position, redesign it rather than treating protective clothing as the solution.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 - Isolate before clearing or maintenance
lessons.body:
Stopping a machine at the control is not the same as isolating hazardous energy. A jam can store force, and automatic or remote restart can occur. The approved isolation process identifies energy sources, secures them and verifies the safe condition before the authorized intervention.

An operator must stay within their permitted role. If clearing a jam requires access to a danger area, obtain the authorized isolation and competent maintenance arrangement. Do not reach through an opening while another person holds the stop button.

Restart follows controlled handback: people clear, equipment restored, guards in place and the designated authority satisfied. A cleared jam is not enough if the original fault or protective defect remains.

## Worked field example

A conveyor jams and a worker proposes reaching inside while a coworker holds the stop button.

The safe decision is to use the approved isolation and verification process before authorized access to the danger area. A held stop button does not control every energy source or prevent unexpected movement.

A useful field record is specific: An authorized isolation record and verified safe condition for the specific intervention. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

## Detailed field application

A jam can retain tension, compression, gravity or other stored energy. The isolation plan identifies those sources and the method for securing or releasing them safely. A machine can be electrically isolated while a suspended or compressed component remains dangerous. Only authorized people perform the intervention within the reviewed method.

The person clearing the fault should verify the actual equipment identity. Similar adjacent machines and shared supplies can create mistakes. Follow the approved identification, isolation, securing and verification process rather than relying on someone saying the power is off.

Handback includes checking that tools and people are clear, guards and controls are restored and the machine is ready for authorized restart. Communicate any remaining limits. Do not remove another person's protection or energize the machine because a maintenance ticket shows the task complete. The applicable isolation procedure controls those actions.

lessons.title: Lesson 5 - Quarantine defects and maintain housekeeping
lessons.body:
Remove unsafe tools from service through a clear identification and segregation process. A note that falls off or a defective tool returned to the shared drawer can expose the next user. Competent repair and verified release are required before reuse.

Housekeeping protects routes, stable footing, access to controls and emergency equipment. Control hoses, leads, scrap, sharp offcuts and spills as work develops. Do not move a hazard from the bench into the pedestrian route simply to make the workstation look tidy.

Storage should prevent falling items and preserve safe access. Heavy or awkward items need suitable placement and handling. A clean floor does not compensate for unstable racking or a blocked emergency control.

## Worked field example

A damaged grinder is left in the common drawer with a loose paper note.

The safe decision is to segregate and identify it so it cannot be used until competent repair and release. A defect report is ineffective if another worker can unknowingly return the tool to service.

A useful field record is specific: A controlled quarantine record tied to the tool and verified repair status. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

## Detailed field application

Quarantine needs to prevent unintended use. Identify the item, defect and status through the approved process and place it in a controlled location where appropriate. If the equipment cannot be moved, maintain effective restriction and communication at the point of use. A shared drawer or ordinary tool rack does not provide that distinction.

Repair records should connect the competent action to the actual equipment. A generic invoice for several tools may need supporting identification before one item is released. Users still complete their required pre-use checks after repair.

Housekeeping is continuous. Plan where offcuts, packaging, hoses and waste go as work progresses. A cleanup that blocks an exit or hides a defect is not improvement. Review storage capacity and receiving practices where obstructions recur; repeated reminders cannot create space that the layout does not provide.

lessons.title: Lesson 6 - Verify competence and recurring faults
lessons.body:
A generic tool course does not authorize every machine. Record unassessed attachments, conditions and tasks rather than implying unlimited competence.

Review repeated jams, guard damage and workarounds with users and maintenance. The cause may involve unsuitable material, worn components, poor workholding or an unrealistic production method. A reminder to be careful does not resolve a recurring technical fault.

Observe the revised arrangement before closing an action. A maintenance ticket shows work was recorded; field verification establishes whether the protective function and task method are restored. Keep operation held if required safeguards remain uncertain.

## Worked field example

A supervisor closes repeated guard complaints after sending a reminder, without examining the machine.

The safe decision is to arrange competent investigation and verify the corrected protective function in the actual setup. Repeated protective failures need a verified technical and work-method response.

A useful field record is specific: A cause-specific repair or method change and safe observation of restored protection. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

## Detailed field application

Use a controlled representative task, not a deliberately defective machine or live jam. The assessor records coaching and unassessed operations.

If an operator identifies a guard failure, that is useful preventive behavior. The response should encourage prompt reporting and provide a safe alternative rather than reward the person who continues production. Management needs to resolve the technical cause and the work pressure together.

After correction, observe representative operation to verify the original problem has been addressed. A machine that no longer jams because workers feed it through an unsafe opening has not improved. Preserve previous findings, repair evidence and the limits of the field check. Future changes to attachments, materials or operating method require review of the affected competence and controls.

A tool returned from repair should be issued with clear identity and status. The user confirms the required pre-use checks and the approved attachment, while the competent repair record remains available through the authorized process. If the original fault recurs, stop and report it rather than assuming the previous repair guarantees continued safety. A recurring defect may require a deeper technical or work-method review. Record the new observation and preserve the earlier repair history so the next decision is based on the actual sequence rather than an isolated favorable entry.

lessons.title: Two applied scenarios and worked solutions
lessons.body:
## Scenario 1

A fictional shop machine jams repeatedly. An operator removes a guard to improve access and asks a coworker to hold the stop button during clearing. The production leader proposes continuing until the next maintenance day.

### Worked solution

Use stops and the authorized isolation arrangement is established before any permitted intervention. The held stop button and removed guard are not acceptable substitutes. Competent maintenance reviews the jam and protective system, while the supervisor reviews material and workholding. The machine is not released merely because the blockage is removed. Guards, interlocks and the complete operating configuration are safely verified, people are clear and the designated authority controls restart. The review records the fault, actual corrective action and limits of the check. Production pressure does not make bypassing a safeguard a valid temporary method.

## Scenario 2

A fictional crew cleans the shop for an inspection. Defective tools go back into drawers, hoses are piled against an exit and scrap is stacked beside an emergency control. The floor appears clear.

### Worked solution

The cleanup is not accepted as readiness. Unsafe tools are identified and segregated, exit and emergency-control access restored, and hoses and scrap placed in suitable storage. The responsible owner checks the complete routes and work areas rather than a photograph of the floor. Recurring storage pressure is reviewed so hazards are not simply moved during inspections. The final observation records the actual area and conditions; it does not certify machines whose technical condition was not assessed.

lessons.title: Final assessment - 20 questions
lessons.body: Answer each question without consulting an answer key. There are 20 final questions in addition to six lesson checks. Incorrect responses require reading and explicitly acknowledging the explanation. Both the first-attempt and remediated results must remain visible.

content.title: H24 — Specialist hazards: radiation, explosives, diving, marine and rail
content.description: Original guided company-program course with six lessons, six checks, two worked scenarios and 20 final questions. First and remediated scores remain separate.

explanations.H24_check1: Hold the specialist scope until the relevant technical authority, permissions, personnel and plan are verified. General safety learning does not establish specialist authorization or technical competence.
explanations.H24_check2: Remain outside the boundary and contact the authorized radiography representative. Absence of visible activity does not establish that the radiation hazard is absent.
explanations.H24_check3: Keep clear, restrict affected access and notify the explosives authority through the agreed process. An unknown explosive-related item requires specialist assessment rather than ordinary handling.
explanations.H24_check4: Hold the underwater task for the qualified commercial-diving authority and reviewed plan. Swimming ability does not control industrial diving hazards or establish team and rescue capability.
explanations.H24_check5: Use the rail authority’s approved access and movement-protection arrangement. Quiet or stationary rail equipment does not establish authorized safe access.
explanations.H24_check6: Return the changed scope to the radiation authority and verify revised interfaces before release. Approval for one specialist configuration does not automatically cover a changed configuration.

lessons.title: Start here: Specialist hazards: radiation, explosives, diving, marine and rail
lessons.body:
# Specialist hazards: radiation, explosives, diving, marine and rail

This original VNDRLY course teaches decisions within the company safety program. Work through six lessons, their six checks, two worked scenarios and a 20-question final. All cases are fictional. No equipment operation is required to complete the online learning.

Each of the 26 questions requires a recorded answer. Completion requires a correct answer or explicit acknowledgment of the explanation and corrected answer after an error. Preserve the first-attempt score separately from the remediated score; a correction never rewrites what was first understood. Read the explanation, return to the relevant lesson and resolve uncertainty with the responsible supervisor. The course does not substitute for a site assessment, permit or employer authorization.

The linked references support the subject and identify source context. Client procedures are examples of client requirements, not universal law or endorsement of this course. Apply the governing jurisdiction and actual site procedure; no numerical technical limits or universal renewal interval are invented here.

## Primary reference context

[OSHA Commercial diving — separate specialist scope](https://www.osha.gov/commercial-diving). Read the reference within its stated scope. Company examples are not universal technical rules; regulatory applicability must be determined for the actual task and jurisdiction.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 - Separate awareness from specialist qualification
lessons.body:
Radiation, explosives, diving, marine and rail work have different technical authorities, legal frameworks, equipment and emergency needs. Grouping them in a company register helps identify specialist scope; it does not make them one competence. This lesson teaches interface awareness for workers, supervisors and reviewers.

Identify the actual activity precisely. Industrial radiography differs from operating a non-ionizing device; a diver's underwater inspection differs from a worker standing on a quay. The scope determines the specialist requirements. Do not accept a certificate that merely contains the same broad word.

The qualified specialist and responsible employer must establish the technical method and personnel requirements. A general safety reviewer verifies that the appropriate evidence and decisions exist without pretending to approve technical parameters outside their competence.

## Worked field example

A vendor offers radiographic inspection with only a generic company safety certificate.

The safe decision is to hold the specialist scope until the relevant technical authority, permissions, personnel and plan are verified. General safety learning does not establish specialist authorization or technical competence.

A useful field record is specific: A scope-specific specialist package reviewed by the appropriate qualified authority. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

## Detailed specialist-interface application

A company service register can contain several specialist activities without every employee performing them. Map the actual role first: a scheduler arranging a radiography visit, a guard maintaining the site access boundary and a radiographer handling the device have different responsibilities. The scheduler and guard need interface awareness; neither becomes an authorized source operator from knowing the plan.

The evidence review should preserve that distinction. Verify the specialist organization and people for their actual technical scope, and verify the general workforce's understanding of boundaries and alarm routes. Do not issue a single specialist-qualified label to everyone who attended an awareness briefing.

Where a contract combines disciplines, name the separate authorities. A marine contractor may use commercial divers, rail transport and explosives subcontractors, but one company's broad experience does not establish every technical role. Confirm the relevant lower-tier arrangements and responsibilities before the affected activity begins.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 - Respect radiation boundaries and abnormal conditions
lessons.body:
Radiation work requires the relevant licensed or otherwise authorized organization and qualified personnel under the governing jurisdiction. The specialist establishes controlled areas, monitoring, access restrictions and abnormal-event arrangements for the particular operation. This course supplies no exposure limit or exclusion distance.

Workers near radiography must understand the announced restrictions and how to contact the specialist. Do not cross a barrier because no work is visibly happening. Radiation hazards may not be detectable by human senses. A quiet work area is not evidence that the source is secured.

If a source or device is suspected lost, damaged or not returned to its safe condition, keep clear and use the agreed alarm route. Do not retrieve or move it, adjust the boundary yourself or ask an unqualified guard to investigate. Only the appropriate specialist controls assessment and recovery.

## Worked field example

A radiography barrier blocks a shortcut and a worker sees no operator nearby.

The safe decision is to remain outside the boundary and contact the authorized radiography representative. Absence of visible activity does not establish that the radiation hazard is absent.

A useful field record is specific: A verified boundary briefing and communication route to the qualified radiation authority. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

## Detailed specialist-interface application

For a radiography interface, the specialist establishes the work restrictions and how other people will be notified. Site coordination then ensures pedestrian routes, deliveries and simultaneous work do not defeat those restrictions. The general supervisor should know whom to call, what area is held and how a changed condition is escalated.

A barrier is not an invitation for a general worker to determine whether the source is exposed. Workers remain outside and contact the qualified authority. Do not use a personal impression, silence or a lack of visible equipment as clearance. Technical monitoring and source status belong to the authorized personnel and method.

If an abnormal condition is reported, preserve the boundary and give reliable observations from safety. Do not touch an unfamiliar device or carry it to an office for identification. Source recovery and radiation emergency actions require specialist arrangements beyond this course.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 - Leave explosives decisions with the qualified authority
lessons.body:
Explosives and blasting-related operations require the applicable specialist permissions, secure arrangements and qualified personnel. Confirm the actual activity: transport, storage, preparation, use and abnormal-event response are not interchangeable duties. A worker authorized for one stage is not automatically authorized for another.

The specialist plan addresses interfaces such as access, other work, ignition or initiation hazards and emergency arrangements. General crews follow the stated restrictions. This awareness course deliberately does not teach initiation, charge preparation, magazine design or misfire handling.

Treat a suspected misfire, damaged item or unknown explosive-related object as an abnormal specialist event. Keep people clear and notify the designated authority. Do not touch, dismantle or attempt to make it safe. Schedule pressure and familiarity with ordinary tools do not create explosives competence.

## Worked field example

A worker finds an unfamiliar item after specialist blasting and offers to move it out of a vehicle route.

The safe decision is to keep clear, restrict affected access and notify the explosives authority through the agreed process. An unknown explosive-related item requires specialist assessment rather than ordinary handling.

A useful field record is specific: A specialist-controlled abnormal-event response and maintained access restriction. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

## Detailed specialist-interface application

Explosives controls begin before use and extend through storage, movement, preparation and abnormal-event response under the applicable authority. A person who is permitted to drive a vehicle does not automatically have permission to transport or handle its explosive cargo. The actual functions need separate verification.

General workers follow announced restrictions, stop conditions and communication rules from the specialist plan. They should report an unexpected object or changed activity without manipulating equipment or improvising protective measures. This course does not provide safe approach distances, initiation instructions or misfire waiting periods.

After the specialist work, release of an area follows the relevant technical authority and site process. The fact that a scheduled time has passed is not clearance. Workers should obtain the current instruction and report conflicting messages rather than choosing the one that allows work to continue fastest.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 - Do not turn swimming ability into diving competence
lessons.body:
Commercial diving needs a task-specific diving plan, qualified team, suitable equipment and emergency capability under applicable requirements. Water conditions, visibility, entanglement, energy sources and pressure differences can create severe hazards. A recreational qualification or good swimming ability does not establish competence for an industrial dive.

Coordinate the dive with operations. Pumps, intakes, discharges, vessel movement and adjacent work may affect the diver. The specialist authority identifies required isolations and controls and verifies them with the responsible operating roles. A general permit cannot replace that technical planning.

If a diver is in difficulty, activate the established diving emergency arrangements. Do not send a willing swimmer into the water. Rescue and treatment have specialist requirements, and an improvised second entry can create another casualty.

## Worked field example

A maintenance worker volunteers to inspect a submerged intake because they are a strong swimmer.

The safe decision is to hold the underwater task for the qualified commercial-diving authority and reviewed plan. Swimming ability does not control industrial diving hazards or establish team and rescue capability.

A useful field record is specific: A scope-specific diving plan with verified team, operational interfaces and emergency resources. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

## Detailed specialist-interface application

A diving interface assessment should identify the operational systems that can affect the underwater work. Pumps, intakes, outfalls, vessel propulsion and other energy sources can create hazards that are not visible from the surface. The qualified diving authority and operating roles coordinate the required controls and verification.

The shore team must understand its assigned role and how to activate the diving emergency arrangement. Watching bubbles or keeping a telephone nearby does not establish a qualified standby or rescue function. Recreational equipment and experience are not automatically suitable for the industrial task.

ROV operation is a different technical method and should not be described as a diver qualification. It still requires competent planning for equipment, cables, energy and marine interfaces. Confirm which method is actually contracted and preserve the qualification boundary rather than assuming all subsea labels mean the same workforce.

lessons.title: Lesson 5 - Coordinate marine and rail interfaces
lessons.body:
Marine and rail operations require their own qualified operating authority. A site worker should know the limits of the area, movement restrictions, communication and emergency route. Do not assume ordinary road-traffic habits apply to a rail corridor or that working beside water is the same as working on a vessel.

For marine work, the competent plan addresses access, vessel movement, water exposure, transfer, weather and rescue interfaces as applicable. General crews must not improvise boarding or transfer methods. For rail work, the responsible rail authority establishes the applicable access and movement protection; a parked wagon or quiet track is not clearance.

Coordinate overlapping work before it starts. A crane movement, a delivery or an inspection can affect the specialist operating area. Stop at an uncertain boundary and contact the appropriate authority instead of relying on a driver or bystander who may not control the operation.

## Worked field example

A contractor proposes crossing a quiet rail siding between parked wagons to reach a work area.

The safe decision is to use the rail authority’s approved access and movement-protection arrangement. Quiet or stationary rail equipment does not establish authorized safe access.

A useful field record is specific: A rail-authority access decision and briefing covering the actual crossing and movement controls. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

## Detailed specialist-interface application

Marine access and rail access each need their own current operating permission. A visitor inspecting a vessel may require an approved boarding arrangement and briefing without being a vessel operator. A consultant reviewing a rail yard drawing may remain entirely at a desk. Assign exposure-based learning to the actual activity rather than a keyword in the service name.

Where people enter an operating area, verify the relevant authority, route, movement restrictions and communication. A stationary ship, wagon or crane can change state. Do not rely on someone who is nearby but does not control that movement.

Emergency coordination also differs. A water rescue, vessel evacuation and rail incident can require specialist resources and access arrangements. General workers raise the alarm and follow their assigned safe actions; they do not improvise a crossover method because they hold an unrelated rescue or driving credential.

lessons.title: Lesson 6 - Review change without borrowing another discipline’s approval
lessons.body:
A change in location, equipment, personnel, material or surrounding operation can invalidate a specialist plan. Return it to the appropriate technical authority before relying on the original approval. Do not treat the most qualified person on site as qualified in every discipline.

Evidence should identify legal entity, specialist scope, applicable authority, personnel competence, equipment status, technical plan, interfaces and emergency capability. Verify authenticity and currency through the approved review process. Record exclusions and unresolved conditions rather than creating a broad specialist-ready label.

General workers can demonstrate boundary recognition, alarm and escalation in safe simulation. Technical operation, source recovery, explosives handling, diving, vessel duties and rail movement require separate specialist assessment and authorization. An awareness result can support interface readiness but must never be presented as those qualifications.

## Worked field example

A radiography crew changes equipment and location after its technical plan was reviewed.

The safe decision is to return the changed scope to the radiation authority and verify revised interfaces before release. Approval for one specialist configuration does not automatically cover a changed configuration.

A useful field record is specific: A specialist change review identifying equipment, location, boundaries and emergency arrangements. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

## Detailed specialist-interface application

A safe awareness evaluation can present a changed specialist boundary and ask the learner to identify the correct authority and hold. It should not expose them to a live source, explosive item, uncontrolled water entry or rail movement. The assessor records the demonstrated recognition and escalation, not technical operation.

The technical records remain separate. Where a specialist's licence, equipment, personnel or method changes, the appropriate authority determines what must be reviewed and verified. A general training renewal does not restore an expired technical permission.

The final handover should make restrictions clear to other employers and shifts. State what is approved, what remains held and who can authorize change. Preserve source references and original evidence, while protecting sensitive security details. A broad safety-program score must never be used to override a specialist hold or claim that online awareness has qualified radiation, explosives, diving, marine or rail operations.

lessons.title: Two applied scenarios and worked solutions
lessons.body:
## Scenario 1

At a fictional construction site, a vendor proposes radiographic inspection beside a busy pedestrian route. Its evidence pack contains a general safety certificate and a procedure from another location. A project supervisor offers to choose the boundary and asks gate staff to move the barrier whenever a delivery arrives. Explain the correct approval and interface sequence.

### Worked solution

The radiography activity is held. The responsible organization verifies the relevant jurisdictional authorization and appropriately qualified personnel and equipment. The radiation authority reviews the actual location and establishes the technical controls and abnormal-event arrangements. The site authority coordinates the pedestrian and delivery interfaces so access restrictions are maintained. Gate staff are briefed on the boundary, communication and hold process; they do not decide when radiation restrictions may be moved. A plan from another location is supporting background at most, not approval of this configuration. A safe interface exercise can confirm communication, but it does not replace specialist technical verification. The release record identifies the actual scope and the people responsible for the technical and site decisions.

## Scenario 2

A fictional water intake needs inspection near a rail-served terminal. A general contractor offers a recreational diver and proposes using a quiet rail siding as access. The manager says the combined specialist-awareness course should cover both activities.

### Worked solution

The underwater inspection and rail access are treated as separate specialist scopes. The commercial-diving authority evaluates the actual task, team, equipment, operational hazards and emergency capability. The rail authority establishes permitted access and movement protection. Neither is inferred from quiet conditions or broad course completion. The site coordinates any shared constraints and confirms that one activity cannot undermine the other’s controls. If either arrangement cannot be verified, that affected work remains held. The record preserves the distinction between awareness, specialist qualification and operational authorization. No one enters the water or track area merely to obtain missing information.

lessons.title: Final assessment - 20 questions
lessons.body: Answer each question without consulting an answer key. There are 20 final questions in addition to six lesson checks. Incorrect responses require reading and explicitly acknowledging the explanation. Both the first-attempt and remediated results must remain visible.
