lessons.title: Start here — Role/task competence matrix and authorization
lessons.body:
# C01: Role/task competence matrix and authorization

Tie capability to the actual tasks each worker may perform. This course teaches the decisions needed to implement that purpose in field operations. It covers role standards, prerequisites, assessment, authorization, renewal and suspension. The examples involve fictional oilfield crews and companies; none is a real incident record or evidence of a company's implementation.

Read six substantive lessons, answer each attached knowledge check, then study two applied cases and answer the twenty final questions. Every question has three choices and one correct answer. The course records the first answer separately from any correction. Completion requires all 26 answered correctly or acknowledged remediation, including reading the specific explanation for each correction. A remediated result must never replace the original score. There is no speed requirement: take the time needed to explain the decision in your own words.

The audience includes workers who recognize gaps, supervisors who coordinate work and program owners who maintain the system. Each has a different decision boundary. An observer may report an uncertain safeguard without personally being qualified to repair it. A supervisor may coordinate a hold without being the person authorized to clear a technical prerequisite. Learn both the action and the limit on that action.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Define tasks rather than job titles
lessons.body:
## Define tasks rather than job titles

A competence matrix connects people with specific work they may perform. Start with tasks, equipment, conditions and abnormal duties, not a broad title such as operator. Two people with the same title may have different limits. Include the task's prerequisites and who may authorize it. The matrix should help dispatch prevent an unsuitable assignment, rather than simply display a list of training dates.

### Deeper application

Break each role into verbs that can be assessed: inspect, operate, communicate, isolate within a defined role or stop on a defect. Attach the equipment and conditions that make those verbs meaningful. A matrix entry saying lifting does not distinguish operating from rigging or signaling. The person approving the matrix should understand those boundaries, while specialist task standards remain with the relevant technical owner.

### Worked oilfield example

The decision is to hold the unmatched assignment and verify task-specific competence and authorization.

A job title cannot establish the boundaries of assessed performance; the actual task and equipment must match. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A person-to-task matrix identifying assessed equipment, limitations and employer authorization. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the matrix lists only job titles and course dates. The appropriate correction is to add bounded task and equipment scope and verify the supporting assessment before relying on the matrix. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

An implementation record and a later effectiveness check answer different questions. The first shows whether the required action occurred within the stated scope. The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. In this example, the follow-up should return to the actual gap described above, rather than simply asking whether the file now looks complete. A genuine unknown must remain visible until resolved by appropriate evidence.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Map prerequisites and standards
lessons.body:
## Map prerequisites and standards

Separate mandatory prerequisites from desirable experience. A certificate may demonstrate a course result without covering the workplace task. Include abnormal decisions such as recognizing defects and stopping safely. Use the appropriate technical standard and competent assessor rather than writing an invented universal qualification rule.

### Deeper application

A prerequisite map is a chain, not a collection of interchangeable cards. State what each item demonstrates. A provider's assessment may support the employer's decision, but the employer still needs to define the assignment's permitted scope and conditions.

### Worked oilfield example

Knowledge and observed performance are different evidence; attendance does not establish the missing practical prerequisite. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A task standard and prerequisite map showing the practical evidence required for authorization. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the task standard omits abnormal-condition decisions. The appropriate correction is to have a competent owner revise the assessment scope to include relevant stop and abnormal decisions. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. In this example, the follow-up should return to the actual gap described above, rather than simply asking whether the file now looks complete. lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Verify authenticity and matching identity
lessons.body:
## Verify authenticity and matching identity

Check the issuing organization, worker identity, credential scope, restrictions and validity. Verification should use appropriate issuer channels and protect personal information. A clear photograph of a card is still only a submitted record until checked. Resolve name differences through a documented identity process, not assumptions. Do not publish sensitive identifiers in an unrestricted matrix when a verified status and controlled reference will suffice.

### Deeper application

Verify only the personal information necessary for identity and credential matching and keep sensitive identifiers in appropriate restricted records. The public-facing or dispatch matrix can show verified status and a controlled reference. When a mismatch is unresolved, record pending verification rather than guessing. An issuer's confirmation of authenticity answers a different question from whether the credential covers this worker's intended task.

### Worked oilfield example

A card has the right surname but a different person identifier and cannot be connected to the assigned worker. The decision is to resolve identity with appropriate verification before accepting the credential for that worker.

Evidence belongs to a particular person. An unresolved identity mismatch cannot support authorization. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A restricted verification record connecting the authentic credential to the assigned person's identity and scope. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the issuer confirms the credential is authentic but covers a narrower equipment class. The appropriate correction is to record the verified scope and restrict assignments to the supported class pending further assessment. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

An implementation record and a later effectiveness check answer different questions. The first shows whether the required action occurred within the stated scope. The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. In this example, the follow-up should return to the actual gap described above, rather than simply asking whether the file now looks complete. A genuine unknown must remain visible until resolved by appropriate evidence.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Make employer authorization explicit
lessons.body:
## Make employer authorization explicit

The employer decides what work a person may perform based on verified prerequisites and performance. State scope, supervision, equipment/site limits, authorizer and relevant dates. A training provider does not automatically issue the employer's operating authority. A site may add its own acceptance requirements. Dispatch needs the current usable decision, including restrictions, rather than access to a confusing folder of unrelated certificates.

### Deeper application

Authorization should be usable without reconstructing the whole training file. For example, specify the assessed task, relevant equipment scope and whether supervision is required. An authorization label must not broaden what the assessment supports. If the site adds familiarization or acceptance conditions, show those as pending readiness items rather than altering the authentic provider result. Record who made the employer decision.

### Worked oilfield example

A worker has a valid training certificate but no employer decision authorizing independent operation. The decision is to obtain a supported employer authorization before independent assignment.

The employer must make the assignment decision; a credential alone does not state that employer's operational limits. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A named employer authorization referencing verified evidence and stating independent or supervised task limits. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the signed authorization says equipment work without identifying equipment or restrictions. The appropriate correction is to clarify and approve bounded scope before dispatch relies on it. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

An implementation record and a later effectiveness check answer different questions. The first shows whether the required action occurred within the stated scope. The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. In this example, the follow-up should return to the actual gap described above, rather than simply asking whether the file now looks complete. lessons.title: Lesson 5 — Suspend and reassess affected scope
lessons.body:
## Suspend and reassess affected scope

Expiry, revocation, role change or a verified competence gap can require restriction. Restrict the affected scope promptly and communicate it to dispatch and site supervision. Preserve unaffected authorizations only where their basis remains valid. Create a reassessment route with feedback and appropriate practice. Do not treat a restriction as erasing historical training or assume an expired credential automatically means every unrelated task is prohibited.

### Deeper application

Restricting one task can leave other assignments valid when their evidence remains sound, but check interfaces before reallocating. A worker restricted from an attachment might still perform unrelated authorized work. Do not interpret that as permission to continue the unsupported operation through a renamed task. Give the worker specific feedback and a realistic route to reassessment, while ensuring dispatch cannot accidentally use the old scope.

### Worked oilfield example

A verified assessment gap is found for one attachment while the matrix still displays unrestricted authorization. The decision is to restrict the affected attachment task and arrange suitable reassessment with dispatch notified.

Authorization must reflect current evidence. The restriction should target the unsupported task and preserve the history. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A dated scope restriction, dispatch notification and reassessment plan linked to the finding. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the restriction was entered but the site still uses an exported old roster. The appropriate correction is to notify affected users and replace the stale operational roster with the current restriction status. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

An implementation record and a later effectiveness check answer different questions. The first shows whether the required action occurred within the stated scope. The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. In this example, the follow-up should return to the actual gap described above, rather than simply asking whether the file now looks complete. A genuine unknown must remain visible until resolved by appropriate evidence.

lessons.title: Lesson 6 — Sample the matrix against assignments
lessons.body:
## Sample the matrix against assignments

Assurance traces an actual job to the person, task standard, verified evidence and authorization in force at the time. Also sample people who were not assigned because prerequisites were missing. A matrix full of green cells is not enough if cells lack supporting records or use the wrong scope. Review after changed work and relevant performance findings, with renewal periods determined by applicable sources rather than a universal assumption.

### Deeper application

Audit at the time of the job. A credential renewed today does not prove it was valid last month's assignment. Trace evidence dates and authorization history without rewriting earlier decisions. Include rejected allocations in the sample: they show whether the matrix prevented unsupported work. Investigate inconsistencies between the matrix and dispatch as a system problem, not simply an administrative typo until the actual impact is known.

### Worked oilfield example

An audit finds every matrix cell green, but sampled dispatch records include a worker whose assessment was pending. The decision is to investigate the mismatch and correct assignment controls while preserving the original records.

Assurance tests whether the matrix controlled real assignments, not merely whether the display looked complete. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A traceable sample comparing assignment dates, supported task scopes and authorization decisions. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the sample checked only current credentials and ignored their status at the job date. The appropriate correction is to reconcile validity and authorization as they stood when the sampled work occurred. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

An implementation record and a later effectiveness check answer different questions. The first shows whether the required action occurred within the stated scope. The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. In this example, the follow-up should return to the actual gap described above, rather than simply asking whether the file now looks complete. A genuine unknown must remain visible until resolved by appropriate evidence.

lessons.title: Two applied scenarios and fully worked solutions
lessons.body:
## Applied scenario 1: an incomplete decision chain

At the handover, a second issue is identified: The task standard omits abnormal-condition decisions. The receiving supervisor has the earlier record but does not yet have evidence that the new issue was resolved. A colleague proposes the following shortcut: Accept the card because the surname matches. Work is due to begin on the next shift, so the supervisor needs a defensible decision that protects people and preserves a clear history.

### Worked solution — immediate decision

The first response is: Hold the unmatched assignment and verify task-specific competence and authorization. The reason is specific: A job title cannot establish the boundaries of assessed performance; the actual task and equipment must match. Determine which assignment depends on that unresolved condition. Tell the affected people the restriction and who is coordinating resolution. If there is an immediate exposure, move to a safe position and use the established warning or emergency route rather than completing records first. The supervisor must not use a favorable overall company score as a substitute for this missing decision.

### Worked solution — resolve the additional issue

For the handover finding, the next action is: Have a competent owner revise the assessment scope to include relevant stop and abnormal decisions. The supporting record should show: A task standard and prerequisite map showing the practical evidence required for authorization. This is important because knowledge and observed performance are different evidence; attendance does not establish the missing practical prerequisite. The receiving shift needs the actual status, not an assurance that someone intends to finish the check later. Identify the responsible role and obtain acknowledgment of the restriction. If the required authority or expertise is unavailable, the affected assignment remains unready; unrelated authorized work may be considered only after its interfaces are checked.

### Worked solution — reject the shortcut and verify the result

The proposed shortcut fails because evidence belongs to a particular person. An unresolved identity mismatch cannot support authorization. The suitable decision is: Resolve identity with appropriate verification before accepting the credential for that worker. Evidence for review would include: A restricted verification record connecting the authentic credential to the assigned person's identity and scope. Separate correction of the immediate problem from confirmation that the change works in later comparable conditions. A reviewer should check the actual control used and the scope represented by the evidence. If the same weakness recurs, reopen the issue and retain both the original decision and the new observation.

### What can be concluded

This solution establishes a bounded route from an identified gap to evidence and responsible acceptance. It does not establish that an assessment, clinical decision, technical test or employer authorization actually happened in a real company. The fictional case teaches how to decide and what to verify. Actual release remains with the designated employer/site authority after the applicable prerequisites are met.

## Applied scenario 2: an incomplete decision chain

A worker has a valid training certificate but no employer decision authorizing independent operation. At the handover, a second issue is identified: The restriction was entered but the site still uses an exported old roster. The receiving supervisor has the earlier record but does not yet have evidence that the new issue was resolved. A colleague proposes the following shortcut: Accept the green matrix as stronger evidence than actual dispatch. Work is due to begin on the next shift, so the supervisor needs a defensible decision that protects people and preserves a clear history.

### Worked solution — immediate decision

The first response is: Obtain a supported employer authorization before independent assignment. The reason is specific: The employer must make the assignment decision; a credential alone does not state that employer's operational limits. Determine which assignment depends on that unresolved condition. Tell the affected people the restriction and who is coordinating resolution. If there is an immediate exposure, move to a safe position and use the established warning or emergency route rather than completing records first. The supervisor must not use a favorable overall company score as a substitute for this missing decision.

### Worked solution — resolve the additional issue

For the handover finding, the next action is: Notify affected users and replace the stale operational roster with the current restriction status. The supporting record should show: A dated scope restriction, dispatch notification and reassessment plan linked to the finding. This is important because authorization must reflect current evidence. The restriction should target the unsupported task and preserve the history. The receiving shift needs the actual status, not an assurance that someone intends to finish the check later. Identify the responsible role and obtain acknowledgment of the restriction. If the required authority or expertise is unavailable, the affected assignment remains unready; unrelated authorized work may be considered only after its interfaces are checked.

### Worked solution — reject the shortcut and verify the result

The proposed shortcut fails because assurance tests whether the matrix controlled real assignments, not merely whether the display looked complete. The suitable decision is: Investigate the mismatch and correct assignment controls while preserving the original records. Evidence for review would include: A traceable sample comparing assignment dates, supported task scopes and authorization decisions. Separate correction of the immediate problem from confirmation that the change works in later comparable conditions. A reviewer should check the actual control used and the scope represented by the evidence. If the same weakness recurs, reopen the issue and retain both the original decision and the new observation.

### What can be concluded

This solution establishes a bounded route from an identified gap to evidence and responsible acceptance. It does not establish that an assessment, clinical decision, technical test or employer authorization actually happened in a real company. The fictional case teaches how to decide and what to verify. Actual release remains with the designated employer/site authority after the applicable prerequisites are met.

lessons.title: Final assessment — twenty questions
lessons.body: Answer each question individually. Apply the taught decisions to the facts given. Your first choices are retained. If an answer is wrong, read the specific explanation and explicitly acknowledge the corrected answer. A corrected score records learning after feedback; it does not overwrite the first-answer result. All twenty final questions and all six lesson checks must be completed.

lessons.title: Finish — separate practical qualification
lessons.body:
## Written completion and what it proves

Completion requires all 26 answered correctly or acknowledged remediation. Both first-answer and remediated scores remain separate. Completing the guided course is evidence that you worked through its knowledge and decision questions; it is not an observed practical performance result, a legal license, a provider certification or an employer authorization. Training evidence contributes to review within its scope and validity, rather than automatically establishing the whole company program.

## What needs separate assessment

The assessment should test recognition of an abnormal condition as well as routine performance. A person who can repeat a procedure but cannot identify when to stop has not demonstrated the whole task. Employer authorization should state the person, tasks, equipment or site limits, required supervision and the basis for the decision. Applicable legal, issuer, client and change-trigger requirements govern validity; this course invents no universal renewal period.

## Before actual work

Confirm current local instructions, reporting routes, emergency arrangements and the person who can resolve an operating hold. If assigned work exceeds your assessed scope, say so before accepting it. The Partner's job/site readiness decision remains separate from the company's evidence review. Preserve real records through the authorized process and protect personal information. The fictional examples in this course must never be submitted as evidence that your company performed the actions described.

## Legal requirements for the named work role
These apply only when you perform the work described below. They are not additional steps for completing this online course.

29 CFR 1910.178(l)(2), (4), (6) — Operators of powered industrial trucks covered by this standard: Formal instruction, practical training and workplace performance evaluation are required before independent operation, with employer certification and applicable refresher/evaluation duties. A trainer/evaluator needs the knowledge, training and experience specified in (l)(2)(iii); an outside assessor is not universally required. Source: https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.178

lessons.title: Start here — Induction, orientation and understandable communication
lessons.body:
# C02: Induction, orientation and understandable communication

Ensure workers understand hazards, reporting and emergency arrangements. This course teaches the decisions needed to implement that purpose in field operations. It covers initial/changed-role induction, language/accessibility checks and site bridging. The examples involve fictional oilfield crews and companies; none is a real incident record or evidence of a company's implementation.

Read six substantive lessons, answer each attached knowledge check, then study two applied cases and answer the twenty final questions. Every question has three choices and one correct answer. The course records the first answer separately from any correction. Completion requires all 26 answered correctly or acknowledged remediation, including reading the specific explanation for each correction. A remediated result must never replace the original score. There is no speed requirement: take the time needed to explain the decision in your own words.

The audience includes workers who recognize gaps, supervisors who coordinate work and program owners who maintain the system. Each has a different decision boundary. An observer may report an uncertain safeguard without personally being qualified to repair it. A supervisor may coordinate a hold without being the person authorized to clear a technical prerequisite. Learn both the action and the limit on that action.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Separate company induction from site readiness
lessons.body:
## Separate company induction from site readiness

Company induction introduces the employer's safety system, roles, reporting and general expectations. Site orientation explains the particular location's hazards, traffic, alarms and interfaces. One cannot silently replace the other. Before independent work, establish what has been completed and what remains required. A visitor or supervised access arrangement has its own boundaries; a badge is not automatic permission to perform work.

### Deeper application

A company induction should explain the employer's program and usable contacts; a site orientation should explain the location the worker is entering. A training coordinator can identify completion evidence, but cannot waive a site's operating prerequisites. Supervised access can be a bounded arrangement rather than independent readiness. Be precise about the worker's current status so a visitor badge or induction record does not become an unintended work authorization.

### Worked oilfield example

A newly hired mechanic has company induction but arrives at a production location without required site orientation. The decision is to complete the applicable site orientation and other readiness checks before independent site work.

Employer awareness does not establish knowledge of this site's hazards and emergency arrangements. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A record separating company induction scope from site-specific orientation and access conditions. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the site orientation record names a different location. The appropriate correction is to arrange the relevant location-specific orientation rather than extending the unrelated record. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

An implementation record and a later effectiveness check answer different questions. The first shows whether the required action occurred within the stated scope. The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. In this example, the follow-up should return to the actual gap described above, rather than simply asking whether the file now looks complete. A genuine unknown must remain visible until resolved by appropriate evidence.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Teach the actions people must take
lessons.body:
## Teach the actions people must take

Induction should prepare a worker to recognize limits, raise a concern, report an event and respond to an alarm. Use realistic examples tied to the worker's duties. Explain who controls the work and where to obtain current instructions. Avoid overwhelming learners with a list of policy titles without showing actions. The goal is usable understanding, not memorization of a lengthy manual's contents.

### Deeper application

Use a job-relevant sequence: recognize the condition, protect yourself, warn affected people and reach the responsible role. Explain the alternative route if the immediate supervisor is unavailable or part of the concern. Workers should know where current instructions are found. Avoid expecting novices to infer these actions from a policy title or an organization chart that lists names without explaining their responsibilities.

### Worked oilfield example

A gate worker can name the safety policies but cannot explain what to do when the vehicle route is blocked. The decision is to teach the relevant stop, warning and escalation actions and check the worker's explanation.

Induction must connect information to decisions the worker will make; title recall does not demonstrate that connection. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: An induction record mapping actual role hazards to taught responses and comprehension results. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the emergency section lists a telephone number but not alarm response or assembly arrangements. The appropriate correction is to teach the applicable alarm actions and local arrangements and verify understanding. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

An implementation record and a later effectiveness check answer different questions. The first shows whether the required action occurred within the stated scope. The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Use understood language and accessible delivery
lessons.body:
## Use understood language and accessible delivery

Determine how the worker can best understand the material, without confusing language needs with lack of ability. Use suitable translation, spoken explanation, clear diagrams or accessible formats as needed. Confirm technical meaning and give workers time to ask questions. Do not force someone to rely on guessing from pictures. If a translator is used, ensure the operational instructions and restrictions are communicated accurately.

### Deeper application

Accessible communication includes hearing, vision, literacy and the environment in which information is delivered. A noisy briefing beside operating equipment may defeat otherwise good instruction. Select a suitable setting and format, then test meaning through the learner's own explanation. Translation should include restrictions and emergency actions, not only the welcome message. Do not confuse difficulty with the delivery method with unwillingness to learn.

### Worked oilfield example

A worker signs an English induction but cannot explain the alarm instructions in an understood language. The decision is to provide suitable language support and verify the worker can explain the required alarm response.

A signature does not prove comprehension. The worker must understand the action they are expected to take. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A record of delivery language, support provided and the worker's own corrected explanation. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the translated material omits the alternative reporting route. The appropriate correction is to supply the missing safety meaning and verify that route is understood before release. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Check comprehension through relevant explanation
lessons.body:
## Check comprehension through relevant explanation

Ask learners to explain what they would do in a specific situation and why. A demonstration or teach-back reveals misunderstandings better than a yes-or-no question. Correct the misunderstanding, explain the reason and ask the learner to apply the correction to a fresh example. Retain the first response and learning correction.

### Deeper application

After a wrong answer, explain the actual error rather than announcing the correct letter. Then ask a fresh but related situation to check transfer. For example, if the worker assumes an unanswered message was received, discuss another safe warning route and acknowledgment. Retain the original and corrected response as different evidence. Copying an answer proves neither independent recall nor application of the reasoning.

### Worked oilfield example

During teach-back a worker says an unanswered radio warning means the warning was received. The decision is to explain acknowledgment and safe alternate warning routes, then recheck with another communication example.

Teach-back should test meaning and application. An unanswered warning leaves a communication gap that needs safe resolution. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: First-response and corrected-comprehension evidence for the specific communication decision. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the record marks understood although the learner's incorrect explanation was never corrected. The appropriate correction is to provide specific remediation and verify understanding before recording completion. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. lessons.title: Lesson 5 — Update induction when work changes
lessons.body:
## Update induction when work changes

Changed roles, sites, risks or instructions can make earlier induction incomplete for the new work. Review what changed and deliver the relevant additional content instead of automatically repeating everything. Identify the revision and affected population. A transfer from gate administration to field driving changes both task and site interfaces. Reuse only the existing learning that still matches, and separately verify any technical prerequisites.

### Deeper application

Changed-role induction should focus on differences while preserving valid earlier completion. A worker moving from an office to a field role needs exposure and interface instruction they did not previously require. The coordinator should identify which current content applies, deliver it and leave separate technical qualifications visible. Repeating an unchanged generic slideshow does not resolve a missing role-specific lesson.

### Worked oilfield example

An administrator moves into field dispatch and driving while the training record still reflects office-only induction. The decision is to provide relevant changed-role induction and verify separate driving prerequisites before assignment.

Experience in the company does not establish understanding or authorization for materially different work. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A change record identifying new duties, additional induction content and remaining qualification conditions. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the update covers driving hazards but omits the new site's emergency arrangements. The appropriate correction is to complete the missing site emergency content and check understanding before relevant work. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

An implementation record and a later effectiveness check answer different questions. The first shows whether the required action occurred within the stated scope. The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. lessons.title: Lesson 6 — Keep evidence usable and bounded
lessons.body:
## Keep evidence usable and bounded

Record learner identity, course and version, delivery method, trainer, comprehension outcome, date and scope. Keep a record of gaps and corrections rather than only a signature. Protect personal information and make current status available to the roles allocating work. Induction evidence supports readiness checks within its stated scope; it does not prove every company control is effective or qualify someone to perform a specialist task.

### Deeper application

A useful completion record lets another authorized person identify the worker, material and version, language or support, trainer and comprehension outcome. Keep unnecessary personal details out of a general roster. Where the original evidence is valid but the operational status is wrong, correct status from the authentic record rather than forcing duplicate learning. Where content cannot be established, label that uncertainty honestly.

### Worked oilfield example

A supervisor sees induction complete but cannot identify which version or role content the worker received. The decision is to verify the underlying content and scope and resolve missing learning before relying on the status.

An unbounded status cannot show whether the relevant current content was taught and understood. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A traceable completion record identifying actual version, role scope and comprehension outcome. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the original record is valid but dispatch exports a stale incomplete status. The appropriate correction is to correct the operational status from authentic records and notify affected users without repeating valid learning unnecessarily. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

An implementation record and a later effectiveness check answer different questions. The first shows whether the required action occurred within the stated scope. The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. In this example, the follow-up should return to the actual gap described above, rather than simply asking whether the file now looks complete. A genuine unknown must remain visible until resolved by appropriate evidence.

lessons.title: Two applied scenarios and fully worked solutions
lessons.body:
## Applied scenario 1: an incomplete decision chain

A newly hired mechanic has company induction but arrives at a production location without required site orientation. At the handover, a second issue is identified: The emergency section lists a telephone number but not alarm response or assembly arrangements. The receiving supervisor has the earlier record but does not yet have evidence that the new issue was resolved. A colleague proposes the following shortcut: Treat the signature as evidence the English content was understood. Work is due to begin on the next shift, so the supervisor needs a defensible decision that protects people and preserves a clear history.

### Worked solution — immediate decision

The first response is: Complete the applicable site orientation and other readiness checks before independent site work. The reason is specific: Employer awareness does not establish knowledge of this site's hazards and emergency arrangements. Determine which assignment depends on that unresolved condition. Tell the affected people the restriction and who is coordinating resolution. If there is an immediate exposure, move to a safe position and use the established warning or emergency route rather than completing records first. The supervisor must not use a favorable overall company score as a substitute for this missing decision.

### Worked solution — resolve the additional issue

For the handover finding, the next action is: Teach the applicable alarm actions and local arrangements and verify understanding. The supporting record should show: An induction record mapping actual role hazards to taught responses and comprehension results. This is important because induction must connect information to decisions the worker will make; title recall does not demonstrate that connection. The receiving shift needs the actual status, not an assurance that someone intends to finish the check later. Identify the responsible role and obtain acknowledgment of the restriction. If the required authority or expertise is unavailable, the affected assignment remains unready; unrelated authorized work may be considered only after its interfaces are checked.

### Worked solution — reject the shortcut and verify the result

The proposed shortcut fails because a signature does not prove comprehension. The worker must understand the action they are expected to take. The suitable decision is: Provide suitable language support and verify the worker can explain the required alarm response. Evidence for review would include: A record of delivery language, support provided and the worker's own corrected explanation. Separate correction of the immediate problem from confirmation that the change works in later comparable conditions. A reviewer should check the actual control used and the scope represented by the evidence. If the same weakness recurs, reopen the issue and retain both the original decision and the new observation.

### What can be concluded

This solution establishes a bounded route from an identified gap to evidence and responsible acceptance. It does not establish that an assessment, clinical decision, technical test or employer authorization actually happened in a real company. The fictional case teaches how to decide and what to verify. Actual release remains with the designated employer/site authority after the applicable prerequisites are met.

## Applied scenario 2: an incomplete decision chain

During teach-back a worker says an unanswered radio warning means the warning was received. At the handover, a second issue is identified: The update covers driving hazards but omits the new site's emergency arrangements. The receiving supervisor has the earlier record but does not yet have evidence that the new issue was resolved. A colleague proposes the following shortcut: Treat any completed status as proof of current all-role induction. Work is due to begin on the next shift, so the supervisor needs a defensible decision that protects people and preserves a clear history.

### Worked solution — immediate decision

The first response is: Explain acknowledgment and safe alternate warning routes, then recheck with another communication example. The reason is specific: Teach-back should test meaning and application. An unanswered warning leaves a communication gap that needs safe resolution. Determine which assignment depends on that unresolved condition. Tell the affected people the restriction and who is coordinating resolution. If there is an immediate exposure, move to a safe position and use the established warning or emergency route rather than completing records first. The supervisor must not use a favorable overall company score as a substitute for this missing decision.

### Worked solution — resolve the additional issue

For the handover finding, the next action is: Complete the missing site emergency content and check understanding before relevant work. The supporting record should show: A change record identifying new duties, additional induction content and remaining qualification conditions. This is important because experience in the company does not establish understanding or authorization for materially different work. The receiving shift needs the actual status, not an assurance that someone intends to finish the check later. Identify the responsible role and obtain acknowledgment of the restriction. If the required authority or expertise is unavailable, the affected assignment remains unready; unrelated authorized work may be considered only after its interfaces are checked.

### Worked solution — reject the shortcut and verify the result

The proposed shortcut fails because an unbounded status cannot show whether the relevant current content was taught and understood. The suitable decision is: Verify the underlying content and scope and resolve missing learning before relying on the status. Evidence for review would include: A traceable completion record identifying actual version, role scope and comprehension outcome. Separate correction of the immediate problem from confirmation that the change works in later comparable conditions. A reviewer should check the actual control used and the scope represented by the evidence. If the same weakness recurs, reopen the issue and retain both the original decision and the new observation.

### What can be concluded

This solution establishes a bounded route from an identified gap to evidence and responsible acceptance. It does not establish that an assessment, clinical decision, technical test or employer authorization actually happened in a real company. The fictional case teaches how to decide and what to verify. Actual release remains with the designated employer/site authority after the applicable prerequisites are met.

lessons.title: Final assessment — twenty questions
lessons.body: Answer each question individually. Apply the taught decisions to the facts given. Your first choices are retained. If an answer is wrong, read the specific explanation and explicitly acknowledge the corrected answer. A corrected score records learning after feedback; it does not overwrite the first-answer result. All twenty final questions and all six lesson checks must be completed.

lessons.title: Finish — separate practical qualification
lessons.body:
## Written completion and what it proves

Completion requires all 26 answered correctly or acknowledged remediation. Both first-answer and remediated scores remain separate. Completing the guided course is evidence that you worked through its knowledge and decision questions; it is not an observed practical performance result, a legal license, a provider certification or an employer authorization. Training evidence contributes to review within its scope and validity, rather than automatically establishing the whole company program.

## What needs separate assessment

The assessment should test recognition of an abnormal condition as well as routine performance. A person who can repeat a procedure but cannot identify when to stop has not demonstrated the whole task. Employer authorization should state the person, tasks, equipment or site limits, required supervision and the basis for the decision. Applicable legal, issuer, client and change-trigger requirements govern validity; this course invents no universal renewal period.

## Before actual work

Confirm current local instructions, reporting routes, emergency arrangements and the person who can resolve an operating hold. If assigned work exceeds your assessed scope, say so before accepting it. The Partner's job/site readiness decision remains separate from the company's evidence review. Preserve real records through the authorized process and protect personal information. The fictional examples in this course must never be submitted as evidence that your company performed the actions described.

lessons.title: Start here — Short-service workers and supervision
lessons.body:
# C03: Short-service workers and supervision

Control unfamiliarity with high-energy tasks and local conditions. This course teaches the decisions needed to implement that purpose in field operations. It covers identify support needs, assign mentor, restrict tasks and assess release from supervision. The examples involve fictional oilfield crews and companies; none is a real incident record or evidence of a company's implementation.

Read six substantive lessons, answer each attached knowledge check, then study two applied cases and answer the twenty final questions. Every question has three choices and one correct answer. The course records the first answer separately from any correction. Completion requires all 26 answered correctly or acknowledged remediation, including reading the specific explanation for each correction. A remediated result must never replace the original score. There is no speed requirement: take the time needed to explain the decision in your own words.

The audience includes workers who recognize gaps, supervisors who coordinate work and program owners who maintain the system. Each has a different decision boundary. An observer may report an uncertain safeguard without personally being qualified to repair it. A supervisor may coordinate a hold without being the person authorized to clear a technical prerequisite. Learn both the action and the limit on that action.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Recognize unfamiliarity rather than tenure alone
lessons.body:
## Recognize unfamiliarity rather than tenure alone

Short-service support addresses unfamiliar work and conditions, not simply a worker's age or calendar time. An experienced employee may be new to a role, attachment, site or team. Identify relevant prior experience and gaps before assignment. Avoid presenting any company's particular duration or marking system as universal. The support decision must correspond to the tasks and risks encountered now.

### Deeper application

Discuss relevant experience with the worker rather than relying solely on a hire date. Someone familiar with equipment may still be unfamiliar with a site's traffic, signals or emergency arrangements. Someone new to the company may have useful prior competence that can be verified. The support plan should explain the actual gaps and safeguards, avoiding a label that suggests every short-service worker has identical capabilities.

### Worked oilfield example

A long-serving mechanic transfers into an unfamiliar gate traffic-control role and is rostered alone. The decision is to assess the unfamiliar role and provide suitable supervision and restrictions before assignment.

Company tenure does not establish competence in a changed task or local conditions. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A role-specific experience review identifying unfamiliar tasks and the required support plan. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the review considers years employed but not the worker's new duties. The appropriate correction is to reassess relevant task familiarity and document the support actually needed. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

An implementation record and a later effectiveness check answer different questions. The first shows whether the required action occurred within the stated scope. The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. In this example, the follow-up should return to the actual gap described above, rather than simply asking whether the file now looks complete. A genuine unknown must remain visible until resolved by appropriate evidence.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Assign a capable available mentor
lessons.body:
## Assign a capable available mentor

A mentor needs relevant competence, time, communication ability and authority to intervene. Naming the most experienced person is insufficient if that person is simultaneously supervising incompatible work elsewhere. Define how supervision will occur and what the worker may do while the mentor is unavailable. The mentor coaches within their own assessed scope and escalates specialist decisions beyond it.

### Deeper application

Mentor workload is part of the plan. If one mentor covers several separated tasks, establish whether they can provide the supervision each needs. A worker should know what to do during a mentor's break or reassignment. Do not count availability by telephone as direct observation where direct supervision is required. Provide an explicit handover when another suitably competent person takes over.

### Worked oilfield example

A new equipment worker's named mentor is sent to a different crew during the planned supervised operation. The decision is to hold the dependent operation or provide another competent available supervisor.

Supervision is an active safeguard; a name on a roster cannot provide unavailable observation or intervention. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A mentor assignment showing competence, availability, supervision arrangement and handover coverage. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the replacement mentor has experience but no competence in the assigned equipment task. The appropriate correction is to provide a suitably competent mentor or restrict the assignment to supported work. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Make restrictions visible at allocation
lessons.body:
## Make restrictions visible at allocation

State task limits in terms dispatch and site supervision can use: permitted supervised activities, prohibited independent tasks and conditions requiring a stop. Share the necessary operational restriction without unnecessary personal labels. The worker should be able to explain these limits. A colored sticker or new-worker label may alert people, but it cannot replace explicit scope and supervision arrangements.

### Deeper application

Write restrictions in allocation terms: which tasks may be practiced with supervision, which remain prohibited and who must be present. The same information should reach the worker, dispatcher and site supervisor. A visible short-service identifier can support awareness, but it cannot tell a receiver whether the worker may operate a particular machine. Task-specific limits need an accessible authoritative record.

### Worked oilfield example

Dispatch allocates lone equipment operation even though the worker's plan permits supervised practice only. The decision is to stop the allocation and arrange the specified supervision or reassign to authorized work.

Restrictions protect only when the people allocating and performing work understand and apply them. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A current restriction record acknowledged by dispatch, site supervision and the worker. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the plan is correct but the night dispatcher has not received it. The appropriate correction is to communicate the restriction and confirm allocation controls cover the night shift. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Coach through demonstration and feedback
lessons.body:
## Coach through demonstration and feedback

Explain the task purpose and critical controls, demonstrate safely, let the worker practice under appropriate supervision and give specific feedback. Describe the observed action rather than labeling the person careless. Break complex work into manageable tasks and verify understanding before increasing independence. Never defeat a safeguard or create live exposure to test whether a novice reacts correctly. Use suitable simulation for abnormal decisions.

### Deeper application

Coaching is most useful when feedback describes an observed action and its consequence. Replace be more careful with the missed check, why it matters and how to perform it correctly. Let the worker explain the stop decision before further practice. Demonstration should use controlled conditions and a suitable mentor; never introduce a real uncontrolled hazard just to see whether the worker notices.

### Worked oilfield example

A trainee repeatedly misses the pre-use defect escalation step during supervised practice. The decision is to give specific feedback, practice the escalation and reassess before reducing supervision.

Missing a critical abnormal decision remains a competence gap even when routine performance is otherwise smooth. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: Observations identifying the missed escalation step, coaching provided and later demonstrated response. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the mentor records good attitude but no observed task performance. The appropriate correction is to record objective observations against task criteria and complete the missing assessment. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

lessons.title: Lesson 5 — Release supervision on evidence
lessons.body:
## Release supervision on evidence

Release is an authorized decision based on observed competence for defined work, not an automatic reward for time served. The assessor should review task performance, abnormal decisions and any unresolved restrictions. A mentor's recommendation may inform the decision but does not replace the employer's assigned authority. State what supervision remains and when changed work needs reassessment. Preserve the development history.

### Deeper application

A release recommendation should identify evidence and limits, not simply confidence in the person. The authorized employer role decides independence for the assessed scope. Record tasks not yet assessed and supervision still required. A customary support period can trigger a review, but cannot substitute for the result. If capability is not demonstrated, explain the next practice and assessment steps without pretending the calendar proves competence.

### Worked oilfield example

A worker reaches the company's usual support period but has not demonstrated the task's stop decision. The decision is to continue the relevant restriction and complete assessment before authorizing independent work.

Elapsed time is not evidence that the required performance standard has been met. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A documented release decision referencing observed performance, remaining limits and authorizer. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the release covers all site work although assessment covered one bounded task. The appropriate correction is to limit authorization to the demonstrated scope and assess additional tasks before expansion. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

An implementation record and a later effectiveness check answer different questions. The first shows whether the required action occurred within the stated scope. The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. In this example, the follow-up should return to the actual gap described above, rather than simply asking whether the file now looks complete. lessons.title: Lesson 6 — Monitor transfer and changing conditions
lessons.body:
## Monitor transfer and changing conditions

Independence for a defined task does not remove the need for reassessment when equipment, conditions or duties change. Watch for repeated errors, worker uncertainty or a support arrangement that no longer fits. Encourage early questions instead of treating a request for help as failure. Sample whether mentors have realistic workloads and whether restrictions survive shift handover. The support system should develop capability while controlling exposure.

### Deeper application

A worker requesting renewed help after a change is giving useful readiness information. Review the new condition instead of treating the earlier release as a permanent all-task pass. A return to supervised practice can be a proportionate protection for one changed task. Check that restrictions reach the next shift and are not overridden by an older roster or informal expectations based on tenure.

### Worked oilfield example

A newly released worker moves to unfamiliar equipment and says the earlier assessment does not cover its controls. The decision is to review the changed task and restore appropriate support pending relevant assessment.

An earlier release remains bounded by its assessed scope; changed work can require new support. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A changed-task review linking prior competence, new gaps and revised supervision conditions. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the revised plan is recorded but the previous unrestricted roster remains active. The appropriate correction is to update operational allocation status and confirm affected supervisors use the revised limits. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions.
