courses.title: E01 — Asset register and preventive maintenance
courses.purpose: Maintain traceable safety-critical equipment across fleets and shops.

content.title: E01 — Asset register and preventive maintenance
content.description: Complete guided E01 training: six taught lessons, two worked scenarios, six checks and a 20-question final. Separate first-answer and remediated scores; wrong answers require explicit correction acknowledgment.

explanations.E01_check1: Asset assurance depends on the actual physical item. Location and appearance cannot transfer maintenance evidence between similar equipment.
explanations.E01_final_1_1: The register must connect equipment to its safety and maintenance obligations. Financial inventory alone cannot support readiness decisions.
explanations.E01_final_1_2: Ownership does not eliminate exposure. The user and supplier must establish who controls maintenance, inspection, defects and release for the delivered item.
explanations.E01_final_1_3: Maintenance and pre-use checks serve different purposes. A current service record does not establish that transport or recent use caused no defect.
explanations.E01_check2: Standby assets can degrade or fail on demand. Required calendar, condition and functional checks remain governed by the maintenance basis.
explanations.E01_final_2_1: A low-cost component can protect against severe harm. Criticality must follow failure consequences rather than financial value alone.
explanations.E01_final_2_2: Intervals must be technically and legally supported for the equipment and use. Generic convenience cannot replace the required basis.
explanations.E01_final_2_3: Different deterioration mechanisms require different triggers. The program must identify which requirement becomes due and prevent one schedule from hiding another.
explanations.E01_check3: A booking does not establish equipment readiness. The restriction must remain effective until required work and acceptance are completed or a valid authorized disposition exists.
explanations.E01_final_3_1: Specific tasks allow competent execution and acceptance. Vague instructions can leave safety functions unchecked while the schedule appears complete.
explanations.E01_final_3_2: The control must affect actual use. Administrative reminders are useful only when linked to restrictions and accountable action.
explanations.E01_final_3_3: Changing dates can conceal unmet obligations. Any allowed deviation must have a defensible basis and cannot override requirements that do not permit it.
explanations.E01_check4: Commercial evidence and technical verification answer different questions. The release decision needs the actual required function check and its result.
explanations.E01_final_4_1: Traceability allows review of what was done and whether the required functions were verified for the actual item.
explanations.E01_final_4_2: Task competence must match the technical work. Administrative access does not establish repair or test capability.
explanations.E01_final_4_3: Planning milestones are not completed maintenance. The record must distinguish pending work from observed results.
explanations.E01_check5: Recurrence suggests the repair may not address the failure mechanism. The technical owner must examine service and system causes rather than treating each event as isolated.
explanations.E01_final_5_1: Different duty or environment can change degradation and protective requirements. The accepted basis must match actual service.
explanations.E01_final_5_2: History helps distinguish isolated defects from recurring mechanisms. Removing it can hide deterioration and weaken future decisions.
explanations.E01_final_5_3: Action completion is not proof of outcome. Follow-up should examine whether the failure mechanism and protective performance improved.
explanations.E01_check6: Conflicting status means readiness is uncertain. The owner must establish the actual accepted condition and align physical and administrative controls.
explanations.E01_final_6_1: Release depends on actual maintenance, verification and restrictions. Training knowledge or commercial demand cannot substitute for acceptance authority.
explanations.E01_final_6_2: Cross-checking actual equipment reveals mismatches that document counts can miss. Assurance must test whether records describe the item in use.
explanations.E01_final_6_3: Hands-on repair and technical acceptance require separately assessed competence and authority. The course supplies knowledge, not a machinery release.
explanations.E01_final_scenario1: Maintenance evidence is item-specific. Matching model and appearance do not transfer the original unit’s history or acceptance to another serial number.
explanations.E01_final_scenario2: Different functions require their own checks. A successful start cannot stand in for an unperformed safety-critical verification.

lessons.title: Start here: learning, scores and role boundaries
lessons.body:
# E01: Asset register and preventive maintenance

This original VNDRLY course teaches decisions for common asset screening; requirements by asset. Its purpose is to maintain traceable safety-critical equipment across fleets and shops. The six lessons explain the hazard, planning decisions, controls, checks, changing conditions and handback. Worked examples and two fictional scenarios show how those decisions fit together. Read the teaching before answering; no live hazardous activity is needed to complete this course.

There are six lesson knowledge checks and a 20-question final assessment. Submit each answer before viewing its feedback. Your first answer remains in the original score. If an answer is wrong, read the specific explanation and explicitly acknowledge the correction; acknowledged corrections contribute to a separate remediated score. Completion requires all sections and all 26 questions correct or explicitly acknowledged after remediation. A later corrected answer never erases the first-answer record.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Identify assets and assign ownership
lessons.body:
An asset register links a physical item to its identity, owner, service and required controls. Use a unique identifier suitable for the equipment and preserve manufacturer identity where relevant. A description such as “blue pump” is not enough when several similar units exist. Include hired or borrowed equipment in the applicable control arrangement, even if another company owns it.

Ownership means responsibility for the maintenance basis, status, records and release decision. The user still performs assigned pre-use checks. A rental company’s invoice does not prove that the item delivered matches a current accepted record.

Worked example: two identical pumps are exchanged between locations. Their maintenance histories must follow their identities, not the parking space or nickname.

### Applying the mechanism

Identity needs to survive ordinary equipment movement. A register should not depend solely on a location that changes every week or a nickname understood by one supervisor. Use an identifier suited to the asset and preserve any manufacturer serial or design information needed for technical decisions. When components are maintained separately, determine whether their histories must also be linked; replacing a pump drive or protective device can change the accepted assembly. Receipt is a useful control point: compare the delivered item against the order and technical requirements before it enters usable stock. If a rental substitution arrives, create or verify its own record rather than transferring another unit’s service date. This preserves the difference between model suitability and item readiness.

### Decision principles

The register must connect equipment to its safety and maintenance obligations. Financial inventory alone cannot support readiness decisions.

Ownership does not eliminate exposure. The user and supplier must establish who controls maintenance, inspection, defects and release for the delivered item.

Maintenance and pre-use checks serve different purposes. A current service record does not establish that transport or recent use caused no defect.

A changed component can also change the maintenance obligation. If a replacement protective device has different service instructions, the owner updates the asset basis rather than leaving the old schedule attached to a new configuration. The change record connects the accepted parts, required checks and user information so a future service technician does not unknowingly follow obsolete instructions.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Classify criticality and establish the maintenance basis
lessons.body:
Criticality considers what failure can do: harm people, release material, defeat a safeguard or disrupt essential response. It guides attention and escalation but does not permit neglect of lower-ranked equipment. Identify safety-critical functions such as braking, overload protection, guarding or alarm response for the actual asset.

Maintenance and inspection requirements come from applicable law, manufacturer information, technical assessment and service conditions. Calendar, usage and condition triggers can coexist. Do not invent a universal annual interval or extend a required interval because the item has not recently failed.

Worked example: a standby emergency unit has low operating hours but an important protective function. Low use does not eliminate age-related or readiness checks.

### Applying the mechanism

Failure consequences should be discussed in functional terms. A brake prevents uncontrolled movement; an alarm warns of an assessed condition; a guard separates people from machinery. The maintenance basis should identify how each relied-on function can fail and what work or test supports continued confidence. High utilization may accelerate wear, while standby service may create deterioration that appears only on demand. Environmental exposure can affect both. The owner therefore avoids a single convenience rule such as “service everything after the same number of hours.” Technical and legal requirements set the foundation, and a competent review considers actual duty. Operators contribute evidence by reporting changed use, harsh conditions and symptoms rather than silently continuing under an obsolete schedule.

### Decision principles

A low-cost component can protect against severe harm. Criticality must follow failure consequences rather than financial value alone.

Intervals must be technically and legally supported for the equipment and use. Generic convenience cannot replace the required basis.

Different deterioration mechanisms require different triggers. The program must identify which requirement becomes due and prevent one schedule from hiding another.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Plan work and prevent overdue dispatch
lessons.body:
Translate the maintenance basis into tasks, due triggers, required competence, parts and verification. The dispatch system must make relevant restrictions visible and prevent use when safety-critical work is overdue or status uncertain. A reminder email alone is not control if the item can still be sent to a job as ready.

Plan downtime and suitable substitutes rather than routinely extending dates under pressure. Any permitted deviation needs the applicable technical and authorization process; the planner cannot waive a legal or manufacturer requirement casually.

Worked example: a vehicle is booked for a remote job, but a required brake-related service is overdue. Dispatch holds it and arranges a suitable alternative instead of treating the booking as approval.

### Applying the mechanism

Scheduling has to connect to the moment of use. An asset can appear available in a booking system while its maintenance system shows an unresolved safety task. The program should define which status controls dispatch and how conflicts are resolved. The planner identifies upcoming work early enough to obtain parts, competent service and a suitable substitute. When a task becomes overdue, the restriction must follow the physical item even if someone changes its location or customer booking. A proposed deviation needs the proper technical basis and authority, with any temporary limits visible to users. Simply moving the due date removes a warning from the screen but does not perform maintenance or establish the asset’s actual condition.

### Decision principles

Specific tasks allow competent execution and acceptance. Vague instructions can leave safety functions unchecked while the schedule appears complete.

The control must affect actual use. Administrative reminders are useful only when linked to restrictions and accountable action.

Changing dates can conceal unmet obligations. Any allowed deviation must have a defensible basis and cannot override requirements that do not permit it.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Record competent maintenance and verify function
lessons.body:
Maintenance completion records identify the asset, work, findings, parts, measurements and responsible person. The required functional verification must show that the relevant safety functions work after maintenance. An invoice proves a transaction, not necessarily that the right task was performed on the right item.

Technical repairs and tests require suitably competent personnel. If a finding exceeds their scope, the item remains controlled until the appropriate specialist resolves it. Do not mark a task complete while a required test is still pending.

Worked example: a pump service invoice lists oil replacement but no evidence for the required protective shutdown check. The shutdown task remains unverified; it is not inferred from payment.

### Applying the mechanism

Maintenance evidence should distinguish observation, work and acceptance. “Seal leaking” is a finding; “seal replaced with identified part” is work; “required leak and protective-function checks passed under the specified method” supports acceptance. These are related but not interchangeable statements. A technician can finish replacing a part while a separate test remains pending. The owner must keep that pending status visible. Measurements should identify the method and item sufficiently for another competent person to understand their scope. Where a repair changes configuration, the technical change process determines any additional review. A receipt for a part does not prove it was installed correctly, and an invoice for general service does not prove every safety-critical function was tested.

### Decision principles

Traceability allows review of what was done and whether the required functions were verified for the actual item.

Task competence must match the technical work. Administrative access does not establish repair or test capability.

Planning milestones are not completed maintenance. The record must distinguish pending work from observed results.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Control changes and recurring defects
lessons.body:
A change in fluid, duty, environment, attachment or operating pattern can invalidate the maintenance basis. The technical owner reviews the new service and updates tasks, limits, parts and training as needed. Do not assume an asset suitable for one chemical or load remains suitable for another.

Recurring faults need cause analysis beyond repeated repair. Review installation, use, service conditions, parts, maintenance method and whether the chosen asset fits the duty. Preserve failures rather than resetting history with each work order.

Worked example: a hose on one unit repeatedly fails soon after replacement. The owner examines compatibility, routing, pressure behavior and component selection instead of simply shortening the replacement interval without understanding the mechanism.

### Applying the mechanism

Repeated failure often points to a system interaction. A coupling repeatedly loosening may involve alignment, installation, vibration or duty rather than a sequence of unrelated bad parts. A protective sensor repeatedly failing may be exposed to conditions outside its selected range. The technical review should preserve as-found observations and compare events across assets, locations and service conditions. Do not erase the history when a component is replaced, because that history may show whether the corrective action worked. Follow-up needs a relevant outcome: the targeted fault mechanism is controlled and the required function performs in the reviewed duty. A longer period without a reported failure is useful evidence, but its strength depends on actual use and observation.

### Decision principles

Different duty or environment can change degradation and protective requirements. The accepted basis must match actual service.

History helps distinguish isolated defects from recurring mechanisms. Removing it can hide deterioration and weaken future decisions.

Action completion is not proof of outcome. Follow-up should examine whether the failure mechanism and protective performance improved.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Release, audit and distinguish evidence from permission
lessons.body:
The designated owner accepts the asset after required work, verification and restrictions are resolved. Dispatch and users must see the same current status. Remove stale ready labels and prevent duplicate records from presenting one item as both available and quarantined.

Sample the register against physical equipment and maintenance evidence. Missing items, identity mismatches and overdue critical work require correction and review. Course completion can support the equipment program’s training evidence; it does not sign a maintenance release or certify machinery.

Worked example: the database says ready while a red tag remains on the unit. The contradiction is resolved with the responsible owner before dispatch; neither record is ignored merely because the other is convenient.

### Applying the mechanism

Physical sampling makes a register review concrete. Select an item shown as ready, locate it and compare its identity, configuration, visible restrictions and supporting work history. Then sample in the other direction: choose equipment in use and find the record that supports its status. The two directions can reveal missing assets, duplicate identities and stale release labels. Reviewers should state what they sampled rather than claim every asset is safe from a small check. An inconsistency requires a hold where readiness is uncertain and an accountable correction. If several inconsistencies share a cause, improve the receipt, maintenance or dispatch interface so the next asset does not inherit the same problem.

### Decision principles

Release depends on actual maintenance, verification and restrictions. Training knowledge or commercial demand cannot substitute for acceptance authority.

Cross-checking actual equipment reveals mismatches that document counts can miss. Assurance must test whether records describe the item in use.

The course supplies knowledge, not a machinery release.

lessons.title: Two applied scenarios and worked decisions
lessons.body:
## Applied scenarios: complete worked decisions

### Scenario 1: The rental swap

A rental supplier substitutes an identical-looking unit. The site has maintenance documents for the original serial number only.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** Dispatch or use is held until the delivered identity and required service and inspection status are established. The supplier and user clarify responsibilities and restrictions, and the asset record follows the actual unit. The old documents remain linked to the original asset; they are not relabeled to make the replacement appear accepted.

### Scenario 2: Overdue protective function

A low-use standby unit is booked for emergency support. Its required protective-function check is overdue, but the engine starts.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** The asset remains restricted while the responsible owner completes the required work and verification or establishes a valid permitted disposition. A suitable ready alternative is arranged. Starting the engine demonstrates only that response, not the overdue safety function or full readiness. The dispatch system is checked to ensure it cannot repeatedly bypass the restriction.

lessons.title: Final assessment: 20 individual decisions
lessons.body: Answer the 20 questions individually using the taught principles. Each submission preserves your first answer. Review feedback after submitting. When an answer is incorrect, explicitly acknowledge the correct decision and explanation before moving on. The result must show both the first-answer score and the remediated score across all 26 questions. Do not attempt a live hazardous task to obtain an answer; the assessment is a knowledge and judgment exercise.

lessons.title: Completion and separately assessed practical competence
lessons.body:
## What this completion means

The course is complete only after every section and all 26 questions have been accomplished, through correct responses or explicit acknowledgment of the supplied correction. Preserve the original and remediated results separately. Acknowledgment is a learning action, not evidence that the learner has performed the task safely in the field.

questions.prompt: Two identical pumps swap locations. What must follow each pump?

options.label: Its unique identity, status and maintenance history.
The history of the parking space.
Whichever record is most recent.

questions.prompt: What makes an asset register useful?

options.label: Only a purchase price list.
Only photographs without identifiers.
Traceable identity, ownership, service and applicable control requirements.

questions.prompt: Does hired equipment need a control arrangement?

options.label: Only if it is damaged.
Yes; responsibilities, identity and accepted status must be established.
No, the rental invoice covers everything.

questions.prompt: Who remains responsible for assigned pre-use checks?

options.label: The designated user or operator under the equipment system.
Only the asset accountant.
Nobody when scheduled maintenance is current.

questions.prompt: A standby emergency asset has low hours. Can maintenance be waived automatically?

options.label: Yes, low use means no deterioration.
Yes, if it started once last year.
No; the maintenance basis must address its critical function and applicable triggers.

questions.prompt: What does safety criticality consider?

options.label: Only how often equipment is used.
Consequences of failure and the function being protected.
Only purchase cost.

questions.prompt: Where do maintenance intervals come from?

options.label: Applicable requirements, manufacturer guidance and competent service assessment.
A universal period chosen by this course.
Only the supervisor’s preference.

questions.prompt: Can multiple maintenance triggers apply?

options.label: No, only the easiest trigger matters.
Only operating hours ever matter.
Yes, time, use and condition requirements can operate together.

questions.prompt: A booked asset has overdue safety-critical maintenance. What is the decision?

options.label: Change the due date to tomorrow.
Hold dispatch and resolve readiness through the responsible process.
Send it because the customer expects it.

questions.prompt: What should a maintenance task specify?

options.label: Work scope, due basis, competence, parts and required verification.
Only the phrase “service as needed.”
Only an invoice destination.

questions.prompt: What makes an overdue control effective?

options.label: It sends an email nobody acts on.
It hides the asset from reports.
It prevents inappropriate release or dispatch and identifies the responsible resolution.

questions.prompt: Can a planner casually extend a required interval?

options.label: Yes, if the asset looks clean.
No; applicable technical and legal limits and authorization govern any deviation.
Yes, if utilization is high.

questions.prompt: An invoice exists but a required safety-function test is missing. What is the status?

options.label: That required verification remains incomplete.
The asset is automatically fully accepted.
Payment proves every check passed.

questions.prompt: What should maintenance records identify?

options.label: Only the supplier’s logo.
Only a planned completion date.
Asset, actual work, findings, parts, tests and responsible personnel.

questions.prompt: Who performs specialist repair or testing?

options.label: The person entering the invoice.
Personnel competent and authorized for the specific work.
Any operator to avoid downtime.

questions.prompt: When can a maintenance task be marked complete?

options.label: After its required work and verification are actually completed and accepted.
When parts are ordered.
When the appointment is booked.

questions.prompt: The same fault recurs after several repairs. What additional action is needed?

options.label: Keep replacing parts without review.
Delete earlier work orders.
Review the underlying cause and asset suitability, then verify corrective effectiveness.

questions.prompt: What should a changed service trigger?

options.label: Only a new nickname.
Technical review of suitability and the maintenance basis.
Automatic use of the old schedule.

questions.prompt: Why preserve fault history?

options.label: Patterns can reveal unreliable controls or unsuitable equipment.
Only successful services matter.
Old failures are irrelevant once parts change.

questions.prompt: What demonstrates corrective effectiveness?

options.label: Only closing the work order.
Only buying a more expensive part.
Later evidence that the relevant function performs and recurrence is addressed within the reviewed scope.

questions.prompt: The register says ready but the physical item is tagged out. What happens?

options.label: Remove the tag without checking.
Hold release and resolve the conflicting status with the responsible owner.
Ignore the tag because the database is newer-looking.

questions.prompt: Who accepts equipment release?

options.label: The designated responsible owner through the required technical process.
Any person who completed this course.
The customer placing the order.

questions.prompt: What should an asset audit compare?

options.label: Only total purchase value.
Only the number of completed forms.
Physical identity and condition against register, due status and supporting records.

questions.prompt: What is not established by a written pass?

options.label: Understanding of record traceability.
Competent maintenance execution or equipment certification.
Awareness of overdue controls.

questions.prompt: What is missing after the rental swap?

options.label: Verified status for the actual delivered asset.
Only a new photograph for appearance.
Nothing because the model matches.

questions.prompt: Why is engine startup insufficient?

options.label: Any startup proves every component works.
Standby equipment does not need maintenance.
It does not verify the overdue protective function or complete readiness requirements.

explanations.E02_final_scenario1: A replacement is a different item with its own configuration and defects. Readiness must be established before reliance.

lessons.title: Start here: learning, scores and role boundaries
lessons.body:
# E02: Pre-use inspections, defects and out-of-service control

This original VNDRLY course teaches decisions for common where equipment is used. Its purpose is to prevent known defects from returning to work uncorrected. The six lessons explain the hazard, planning decisions, controls, checks, changing conditions and handback. Worked examples and two fictional scenarios show how those decisions fit together. Read the teaching before answering; no live hazardous activity is needed to complete this course.

There are six lesson knowledge checks and a 20-question final assessment. Submit each answer before viewing its feedback. Your first answer remains in the original score. If an answer is wrong, read the specific explanation and explicitly acknowledge the correction; acknowledged corrections contribute to a separate remediated score. Completion requires all sections and all 26 questions correct or explicitly acknowledged after remediation. A later corrected answer never erases the first-answer record.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Know what a pre-use inspection can establish
lessons.body:
A pre-use inspection checks whether the actual item is suitable for the intended task now. It can detect transport damage, missing protection, leaks, wear or a changed configuration since maintenance. It does not replace scheduled maintenance, statutory examination or specialist testing. The user needs the correct equipment identity and the manufacturer or approved task-specific criteria.

Inspect only from a safe state and position. Do not energize damaged equipment or reach past a guard to inspect it. Some checks need trained operators or technicians; a general user must recognize that limit and request the responsible person.

Worked example: a machine has a current maintenance sticker but a guard was damaged during delivery. The current defect controls the use decision; the sticker does not erase it.

### Applying the mechanism

An inspection is bounded by the task and equipment state. A visual check can reveal a missing guard but may not establish an internal protective function that requires a test. The checklist should make those distinctions clear so the user does not claim more than they actually checked. A worker who cannot safely access a required check reports the limitation and obtains the proper help. They do not crawl beneath an unsupported assembly or reach into a mechanism because the form requires an answer. Before inspecting, establish who controls movement and energy and use the approved safe arrangement. The inspection should reduce uncertainty without creating a new exposure for the checker.

### Decision principles

The check must support a real use decision. It is not a substitute for other required assurance and cannot be reduced to attendance or form completion.

Criteria must match the equipment and service. A generic list can miss model-specific protection or deterioration.

Inspection must not create the hazard it is meant to detect. Unsafe access or operation is not justified by the desire to complete a check.

The user must also recognize when inspection conditions themselves are unsuitable. Poor lighting, inaccessible components or uncontrolled movement can make a required check incomplete. Report that limitation and obtain a safe arrangement; do not record acceptance for a feature that was never actually examined.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Check systematically and identify the exact defect
lessons.body:
Use a systematic route that covers the relevant structure, guards, controls, connections, fluid systems, safety devices and identification for the actual item. Not every checklist applies to every machine. Record what was observed, including limitations or inaccessible checks, rather than marking an unperformed item as passed.

Describe defects so the owner can act: asset identity, location of the fault, observed condition, when found and any abnormal behavior. A photograph can help but may not capture function or hidden damage. Avoid unsupported diagnoses such as “safe crack” or “only cosmetic” unless a competent criterion establishes that conclusion.

Worked example: “hose bad” becomes “asset P-12, discharge hose outer cover cut near coupling, reinforcement condition unknown, found before use.” The report identifies the concern without pretending to certify its severity.

### Applying the mechanism

Describe the physical observation before offering a cause. “Fluid beneath the identified unit after shutdown” is a fact; “only a harmless old leak” is a conclusion requiring evidence. A good report tells the technician what happened, where and under what operating conditions. Include a photograph where safe and useful, but avoid placing a body near a hazard merely to get a better image. If equipment identity is unclear, preserve the location and identifying details and hold use until the owner resolves it. Specific reporting prevents repairs being applied to the wrong item and helps distinguish a new defect from an already controlled condition.

### Decision principles

A missing check is not evidence of acceptance. Its status must remain visible until the requirement is completed or a valid scoped disposition is made.

Photographs can document appearance but may miss hidden condition and function. The evidence must match the conclusion being claimed.

Some visible damage affects strength or protection. Classification must use defensible technical criteria rather than schedule pressure.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Stop use and establish physical and administrative control
lessons.body:
When a defect makes equipment unsafe or required readiness uncertain, stop reliance and follow the out-of-service process. Identify the item, communicate the restriction, and physically control access or operation as appropriate. The administrative status should prevent dispatch as ready. A tag alone can be ineffective if it is easily removed or ignored.

Do not create a new hazard while isolating the item. Electrical or pressure safe states require their own authorized methods. Move or store equipment only through a suitable controlled arrangement.

Worked example: a defective tool is returned to an open shelf with a note. Another worker could take it. The owner moves it to the designated controlled location and updates its status so physical and dispatch controls agree.

### Applying the mechanism

Quarantine must be effective across shifts and departments. A user may report a defect to a supervisor while dispatch, stores or another crew still sees the asset as available. The process connects those interfaces so the restriction follows the item. Physical control depends on the equipment and hazard: a portable tool may be segregated, while a large installed unit may need an authorized isolation and access arrangement. A tag communicates the reason and owner but should not be the only defense where someone can readily use the item. The owner confirms that the chosen control actually prevents inappropriate reliance, including informal borrowing and customer dispatch.

### Decision principles

Traceability prevents the wrong item being repaired or released and makes the restriction actionable.

Out-of-service control does not waive electrical, pressure or other specialist safeguards. The item must be controlled without creating another exposure.

Conflicting information means readiness is uncertain. The responsible owner must align the actual accepted state and both control systems.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Repair through competent methods and control changes
lessons.body:
Repair requires suitable competence, parts, instructions and a safe work arrangement. A user may perform only the tasks authorized within their training; a convenient improvised repair can defeat the equipment’s design or protection. Substituted parts and modifications need the applicable technical review.

The repair record identifies the defect addressed, work performed, parts and remaining limitations. If the observed condition suggests a broader failure, the technician escalates rather than closing only the visible symptom. A purchase receipt does not prove correct installation or restored function.

Worked example: a damaged guard is tied in place with wire. The item remains out of service unless the competent technical process establishes an approved repair; appearance of coverage is not proof of protective performance.

### Applying the mechanism

Repair planning should distinguish the user’s authorized adjustments from technical repair. Tightening a specified accessible fastener may be an assigned task on one item, while altering a guard, pressure connection or electrical circuit requires another competence. The boundary comes from the equipment program, not the worker’s confidence. The repairer also needs accurate service and contamination information. A component exposed to chemical or abnormal loading may require different disposition from ordinary wear. Substituting a part because it physically fits can change the safety function. The competent process establishes compatibility, approved installation and any tests before the repaired configuration can be accepted.

### Decision principles

Repair skill and authority depend on the equipment and hazard. Finding a defect does not itself qualify a person to fix it.

Fit alone does not establish strength, electrical rating or compatibility. The accepted repair must match technical requirements.

The release owner needs evidence of what was done, not merely ordered. Remaining limits must stay visible.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Verify the safety function before return
lessons.body:
A repaired item needs the required inspection and functional tests before release. The checks must address the defect and any affected safety functions. Testing itself follows a safe approved method, with separation and qualified personnel where needed. Do not use an unsuspecting operator as the first live test.

The designated release owner reviews the evidence and changes the physical and administrative status only after acceptance. An item is not ready merely because it has left the workshop. Where disposal is required, prevent rejected parts from returning to use.

Worked example: a brake repair is complete but the required performance verification is pending. The vehicle remains restricted; the driver does not discover brake adequacy during dispatch.

### Applying the mechanism

A post-repair test should be designed to reveal whether the relevant function was restored without exposing an unprepared user. The method identifies setup, safe positions, loads or conditions, instruments, acceptance criteria and stop actions as appropriate. A power-on test may show that an engine starts while leaving a brake, overload device or guard function unverified. The release owner checks the evidence against the original defect and required work rather than accepting the word “tested” without scope. If the test fails or is incomplete, the restriction remains. Correctly identifying a pending verification is a useful control outcome, not a reason to alter the record to make the repair appear finished.

### Decision principles

A limited response can leave the original protective function unverified. Tests must match the acceptance criteria and repair consequences.

Release is a controlled decision based on actual work and verification. Removing a label cannot create technical readiness.

Disposition must prevent accidental reuse. Rejected components can otherwise return through informal borrowing or parts recovery.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Review recurring findings and practical performance
lessons.body:
Inspection quality is measured by whether it finds and controls real defects, not by perfect pass rates. Repeated failures may reveal unsuitable equipment, transport damage, poor maintenance, unclear criteria or ineffective quarantine. Review patterns and verify that corrective actions reduce the problem.

The learner must inspect systematically, distinguish their limits, report accurately and establish the assigned control. Do not create live hazardous defects as a training challenge.

Worked example: several tools return to service with the same missing guard fastener. The owner reviews repair verification and release controls, rather than blaming inspectors for recording too many failures.

### Applying the mechanism

The learner should identify the item, follow its criteria, inspect in a safe order, record an actual observation and demonstrate the assigned hold and notification. The assessor also checks whether the learner recognizes a limitation and requests competent help. A worker who refuses to invent a rating or perform an unsafe live test demonstrates good judgment. Review later field findings against inspection records to see whether the learning transfers. Repeated missed defects may indicate unclear criteria, poor access, time pressure or weak supervision, while repeated recurrence after repair may indicate a technical cause that inspection alone cannot solve.

### Decision principles

Experience and written learning are supporting evidence, not substitutes.

Recurring defects can have system causes. A broad evidence-based review is more useful than assuming every event is an isolated user error.

Assessment must not create the dangerous event it teaches people to prevent. Safe representative conditions can test recognition and decisions.

lessons.title: Two applied scenarios and worked decisions
lessons.body:
## Applied scenarios: complete worked decisions

### Scenario 1: The borrowed replacement

A tagged-out grinder is replaced with a borrowed unit. Its guard is present, but the user does not know its rating, disc compatibility or condition.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** The user performs the applicable pre-use and suitability checks for the actual replacement and obtains any missing information from the responsible owner. The original restriction remains on the original item. Borrowing solves availability only if the replacement is verified suitable; it does not bypass inspection or operator training.

### Scenario 2: The workshop return

A repaired unit returns with an invoice but no required safety-function result. Dispatch removes the tag to meet a delivery slot.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** The release is held and the restriction restored. The owner obtains the missing competent verification and acceptance, then aligns workshop, physical and dispatch records. The review examines why schedule pressure could bypass the release gate. The invoice remains useful commercial evidence but is not relabeled as a test record.

## What this completion means

The course is complete only after every section and all 26 questions have been accomplished, through correct responses or explicit acknowledgment of the supplied correction. Preserve the original and remediated results separately. Acknowledgment is a learning action, not evidence that the learner has performed the task safely in the field.

## Legal requirements for the named work role
These apply only when you perform the work described below. They are not additional steps for completing this online course.

29 CFR 1910.178(l)(2), (4), (6) — Operators of powered industrial trucks covered by this standard: Formal instruction, practical training and workplace performance evaluation are required before independent operation, with employer certification and applicable refresher/evaluation duties. A trainer/evaluator needs the knowledge, training and experience specified in (l)(2)(iii); an outside assessor is not universally required. lessons.title: Start here: learning, scores and role boundaries
lessons.body:
# E03: Vehicles, trailers, load securement and recovery

This original VNDRLY course teaches decisions for service-specific: transport, hauling and mobile services. Its purpose is to control vehicle condition, shifting loads and unsafe recovery. The six lessons explain the hazard, planning decisions, controls, checks, changing conditions and handback. Worked examples and two fictional scenarios show how those decisions fit together. Read the teaching before answering; no live hazardous activity is needed to complete this course.

There are six lesson knowledge checks and a 20-question final assessment. Submit each answer before viewing its feedback. Your first answer remains in the original score. If an answer is wrong, read the specific explanation and explicitly acknowledge the correction; acknowledged corrections contribute to a separate remediated score. Completion requires all sections and all 26 questions correct or explicitly acknowledged after remediation. A later corrected answer never erases the first-answer record.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Match vehicle, trailer, driver and journey
lessons.body:
A safe transport assignment matches the vehicle and trailer capacities, condition and configuration to the load, route and driver qualifications. Consider coupling, braking, tires, lighting, dimensions, ground and weather, and applicable licensing and commercial transport rules. A vehicle that can physically pull a trailer is not automatically approved or rated for the combination.

Journey planning includes access restrictions, rest and fitness, communication and delivery conditions. Rental or contractor arrangements must identify who checks and accepts the actual combination.

Worked example: a heavier trailer is substituted on the morning of departure. The driver holds dispatch until the combination, coupling, braking, capacities and authorization are confirmed; the original booking does not cover every substitute.

### Applying the mechanism

Separate the capacity questions rather than treating them as one number. The tow vehicle, trailer, coupling and actual combination have their own limits, while weight distribution affects axles, steering and braking. Added tools, fuel, attachments and passengers can change the loaded condition. A trailer’s empty weight is not its loaded transport weight, and a vehicle’s ability to move it on level ground does not prove safe braking or legal operation. The responsible loading and transport roles obtain the actual rating and load information. If that information is unavailable, dispatch holds the combination or selects a verified alternative. A driver should not be asked to establish suitability by trial on the road, particularly on remote routes with poor stopping or recovery options.

### Decision principles

A powerful vehicle can still have inadequate combination or coupling capacity. All relevant ratings and configuration limits must be satisfied.

Different combinations and duties require specific competence and legal authorization. Written awareness cannot replace those requirements.

Transport includes arrival and unloading, not just highway travel. The chosen equipment must suit the full assignment.

Coupling and uncoupling are tasks with movement and crush hazards. Follow the equipment-specific method on suitable support, with people clear of closing gaps and uncontrolled vehicle movement. Do not place a body between units merely because both drivers believe the brakes are applied.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Inspect before dispatch and report changes
lessons.body:
Perform the applicable pre-trip checks and verify required documents and status. Examine safety-critical systems using the approved method: tires and wheels, brakes, steering, lights, coupling, safety connections and trailer equipment as applicable. Report defects with the actual vehicle or trailer identity. Do not crawl beneath unsupported equipment or perform tests beyond training.

Post-trip and en-route checks capture damage or changes discovered during use. A prior pass does not clear a new vibration, loose component or brake concern. Safety-critical defects hold dispatch through the equipment process.

Worked example: a driver notices a damaged tire after loading. The earlier pre-trip record remains history; the present condition must be assessed before travel.

### Applying the mechanism

A systematic walk-around follows the actual combination so coupling and trailer interfaces are not missed between two separate checklists. The approved method addresses mechanical engagement, required connections, braking and lighting arrangements, tires, wheels and load-related condition. Do not place yourself beneath an unsupported trailer or between vehicles that can move while checking it. Establish the safe state and communication with anyone controlling the vehicle. When a check cannot be completed, record the gap and its effect on dispatch instead of assuming that another person checked it. After a change in trailer or loading, revisit the affected checks. The earlier inspection remains valid history for the earlier arrangement, but it cannot verify a connection that was made later.

### Decision principles

Specific traceable observations allow the owner to control the right equipment and arrange competent repair.

Breakdown pressure does not establish repair skills or a safe work arrangement. The defect process must preserve task limits.

Later users may not know what occurred during the trip. Accurate handback prevents damaged equipment being presented as ready.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Understand cargo forces and securement selection
lessons.body:
Cargo can move forward, sideways, rearward or vertically during braking, turning and road inputs. The securement arrangement must suit the load’s mass, shape, center of gravity and tendency to roll or tip. Use the applicable rules, rated devices, anchor points and commodity-specific requirements. This course does not invent a universal strap count or working-load ratio.

Inspect tie-downs, connectors and anchors; protect against edges where required. Packaging or a tarp is not automatically load securement. A device’s rating applies within its specified use and condition.

Worked example: a round item is strapped but can still roll. The competent loading plan addresses rolling and movement in all required directions rather than counting straps alone.

### Applying the mechanism

Cargo restraint must address how a load behaves, not just its total mass. A tall narrow item may tend to tip, a cylinder may roll, and bundled material can settle or separate. Blocking, bracing and tie-downs perform different functions within a suitable arrangement. A tie-down’s rated performance depends on its actual use, including attachments, condition and the direction of force. The loading plan must also protect the cargo and restraints from damage that could loosen the system. A driver who sees an inaccessible anchor or a strap crossing a cutting edge should report the specific concern rather than accept a reassuring strap count. The applicable securement rules and competent load plan determine the accepted arrangement for that actual commodity.

### Decision principles

The system must resist the required forces and movement for that cargo. Convenience cannot establish adequacy.

A cover may contain small material or protect weather exposure but does not necessarily restrain the cargo under transport forces.

Rated performance depends on condition and proper use. Edge contact can defeat a device even when its label is suitable.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Verify loading and recheck during the journey
lessons.body:
The designated competent person verifies weight distribution, vehicle and axle limits, stability, securement and required clearances before departure. The driver must know their responsibilities even when another crew loads the vehicle. Do not accept an inaccessible or undocumented load merely because someone else says it is fine.

Rechecks follow applicable regulations and the load plan, including relevant changes, stops or observed movement. Stop at a safe location if the load shifts or a device loosens. Do not climb onto unstable cargo or adjust securement from a traffic-exposed position.

Worked example: after the first rough access road, a driver notices load movement. The journey pauses safely and the loading arrangement is reassessed, rather than simply pulling one strap tighter and assuming the original plan remains adequate.

### Applying the mechanism

A load can settle after departure as material compresses or road inputs change its position. Rechecks are intended to discover those changes before they progress, but the check itself must occur safely. Choose the approved stopping arrangement away from moving traffic and unstable ground, and do not climb on a shifted load to pull it back by hand. If the configuration has failed, the responsible loading or recovery roles establish a safe correction, which may require unloading or different equipment. Record the observed movement and action so the next stage is based on the corrected state. Tightening one device without assessing the whole load can leave another direction of movement or a damaged anchor uncontrolled.

### Decision principles

The loading interface must be coordinated. A third party’s work does not automatically waive the driver or carrier’s applicable responsibilities.

A load can meet total capacity yet overload an axle or remain unstable. The arrangement must satisfy all relevant requirements.

Legal and task-specific triggers govern rechecks. A universal guess can miss required checks or changed load conditions.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Plan recovery instead of improvising a pull
lessons.body:
Vehicle recovery can create tensioned-line recoil, component failure, rolling, crushing and traffic exposure. A competent recovery provider assesses the stuck vehicle, ground, slope, load, attachment points, equipment and exclusion area. A towing ball or convenient frame member is not automatically a recovery point.

Keep bystanders and unnecessary people out of the assessed danger area. Do not stand near a tensioned line or use a vehicle’s power to test unknown attachments. Recovery ratings and methods must match the actual forces and equipment.

Worked example: a loaded vehicle is bogged near a slope. The crew does not attach a random strap to the nearest hitch. They secure the situation and call the approved recovery capability.

### Applying the mechanism

Recovery is not ordinary towing performed with more enthusiasm. A bogged vehicle can resist movement through suction, grade, obstruction or a shifted load, and a moving recovery vehicle can introduce dynamic force. Failed hardware can become a projectile, and both vehicles may move unexpectedly when resistance changes. The competent plan considers whether to unload, stabilize, improve access or use specialist equipment before applying a pull. It also identifies people who must remain clear and who controls signals. Passengers and photographers do not stand near the line because they are not directly helping. A person must not step over or approach a tensioned assembly to inspect it. Stop and establish the approved safe state before any adjustment.

### Decision principles

Recovery requires assessment of forces, ground, vehicle stability and equipment. Owning a strap does not establish competence.

Tensioned systems and moving vehicles can fail violently. People must not be placed where recoil, hardware or vehicle movement can reach them.

Recovery can impose different dynamic loads and directions. Suitability must follow technical information and the competent plan.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Hand back equipment and assess practical driving skills
lessons.body:
After the journey, report defects, load events, coupling issues and recovery exposure so the next dispatch sees the actual condition. Equipment involved in abnormal forces may require competent inspection before further use. Preserve the event history rather than treating arrival without injury as proof of no damage.

Defensive driving, licensing and commercial requirements remain separate from this written course.

Worked example: a vehicle arrives after an improvised pull. The owner controls it for the required inspection of affected points and systems before the next booking.

### Applying the mechanism

A useful transport handback distinguishes vehicle condition, cargo condition and the journey outcome. “Delivered” does not mean the trailer remains roadworthy, and “no collision” does not mean a loose wheel or damaged attachment can be ignored. The driver records unusual vibration, handling, braking, load movement and any recovery, even if the symptoms later disappear. The owner uses competent inspection to decide readiness and communicates restrictions to dispatch. The assessor should not reward a completed journey that depended on bypassing those safeguards.

### Decision principles

Delivery success and equipment readiness are separate facts. Event information supports safe maintenance and later dispatch.

The actual combination and duties require demonstrated skills. Experience supports but does not replace assessment and legal requirements.

The course teaches awareness and judgment. Execution roles require their own qualifications and practical authorization.

lessons.title: Two applied scenarios and worked decisions
lessons.body:
## Applied scenarios: complete worked decisions

### Scenario 1: A covered but unstable load

A trailer carries a tall load under a tarp. The loader says the cover will keep it in place, but the driver cannot identify suitable restraint against tipping.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** Departure is held. The competent loading arrangement establishes weight, center of gravity, distribution, rated securement and required stability controls. The driver verifies their assigned responsibilities and obtains the needed information before acceptance. A weather cover does not prove restraint against transport forces.

### Scenario 2: The quick recovery

A loaded truck is stuck. A coworker offers a strap and proposes a running pull from an unverified hitch while others watch nearby.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** The improvised pull does not proceed. The area is secured through the site plan, people stay clear and a competent recovery provider assesses vehicle, load, ground, attachments, equipment and exclusion. The approved method is briefed before forces are applied. Any subsequent abnormal event is reported for equipment disposition.

courses.purpose: Avoid relying on unserviceable or unsuitable gas instruments.

content.title: E04 — Gas detectors and measurement assurance
content.description: Complete guided E04 training: six taught lessons, two worked scenarios, six checks and a 20-question final. Separate first-answer and remediated scores; wrong answers require explicit correction acknowledgment.

explanations.E04_check1: A reading only represents the instrument’s capabilities and method. A missing or unsuitable sensor cannot establish absence of an unmeasured contaminant.
explanations.E04_final_1_1: The program must match sensing capability and method to the actual decision. Channel count and price cannot establish suitability.
explanations.E04_final_1_2: Personal monitoring and technical atmosphere assessment have different demands. Instrument possession does not demonstrate sampling and interpretation skill.
explanations.E04_final_1_3: Electrical equipment can introduce ignition hazards. The actual equipment approval and use conditions must match the assessed location.
explanations.E04_check2: Assurance evidence must apply to the actual instrument. Similar appearance cannot transfer another device’s functional or calibration history.
explanations.E04_final_2_1: A functional challenge verifies a bounded instrument response. It does not replace calibration when required or establish workplace conditions.
explanations.E04_final_2_2: Electronic startup checks may not demonstrate sensor response to gas. Required challenge testing remains a separate safeguard.
explanations.E04_final_2_3: The reference mixture and delivery arrangement must support the specified check. An incorrect challenge can create false confidence in the instrument.
explanations.E04_check3: A sampling-system fault can prevent the target air reaching the sensors. The instrument display must be interpreted with the complete method and flow condition.
explanations.E04_final_3_1: The device must encounter air relevant to the wearer within its intended method. Obstruction or remote placement can defeat timely warning.
explanations.E04_final_3_2: Sensor technology has limitations beyond power supply. Users must understand the manufacturer’s interference and exposure instructions for the actual instrument.
explanations.E04_final_3_3: The complete sampling and sensing system must function. A readable display does not prove that the target atmosphere reaches a suitable working sensor.
explanations.E04_check4: Atmospheres can vary by location and process condition. A single point cannot be generalized beyond the method’s demonstrated coverage.
explanations.E04_final_4_1: Transport and sensor response affect when a representative result appears. The approved method defines the required timing for the actual setup.
explanations.E04_final_4_2: Traceability makes the result interpretable and prevents reuse for an unrelated place, time or configuration.
explanations.E04_final_4_3: Limits can have different scopes and averaging periods. Alarm settings trigger protective actions and cannot be casually converted into safe-work permission.
explanations.E04_check5: A fault does not establish safe atmosphere. Protective action comes first, and qualified investigation determines instrument and exposure conditions.
explanations.E04_final_5_1: Failed assurance means the detection safeguard is not established. The program must restore suitability before workers depend on it.
explanations.E04_final_5_2: Different placement, timing or condition can explain disagreement. A quiet device cannot casually cancel a protective alarm.
explanations.E04_final_5_3: A complete chronology supports diagnosis and control review. Later results do not erase earlier warnings or explain them automatically.
explanations.E04_check6: Service changes the measurement system. Required post-service verification must establish performance before reliance.
explanations.E04_final_6_1: Alarm settings are part of the protective system. Changes need a defined basis, authority and record rather than convenience.

lessons.title: Start here: learning, scores and role boundaries
lessons.body:
# E04: Gas detectors and measurement assurance

This original VNDRLY course teaches decisions for service-specific: gas testing and exposure detection. Its purpose is to avoid relying on unserviceable or unsuitable gas instruments. The six lessons explain the hazard, planning decisions, controls, checks, changing conditions and handback. Worked examples and two fictional scenarios show how those decisions fit together. Read the teaching before answering; no live hazardous activity is needed to complete this course.

There are six lesson knowledge checks and a 20-question final assessment. Submit each answer before viewing its feedback. Your first answer remains in the original score. If an answer is wrong, read the specific explanation and explicitly acknowledge the correction; acknowledged corrections contribute to a separate remediated score. Completion requires all sections and all 26 questions correct or explicitly acknowledged after remediation. A later corrected answer never erases the first-answer record.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Select the measurement for the hazard
lessons.body:
A gas detector is a measurement system with specific sensors, range, response and environmental limitations. Selection begins with the actual contaminants, oxygen and flammability hazards, task and sampling method. A four-channel display does not mean every chemical is detected. The qualified program determines personal, area or remote sampling arrangements and hazardous-location suitability.

The measurement purpose matters: warning a wearer, characterizing a space and documenting a technical test are different uses. A personal monitor does not automatically qualify its wearer to clear a vessel. Instrument selection must fit both the hazard and the decision being made.

Worked example: a solvent task uses a detector with an H2S sensor but no demonstrated capability for the relevant vapor. A zero H2S display cannot clear the solvent exposure.

### Applying the mechanism

Selection needs a clear statement of the decision. A personal monitor warns its wearer about selected hazards; an area instrument observes a defined location; a pumped sample system obtains air from another point. These uses are not automatically interchangeable. The qualified program considers target substances, range, response, environment and any ignition-safety approval. It also considers what the instrument cannot detect. A device with oxygen, flammable-gas and two toxic sensors still does not measure every vapor. If a task introduces another chemical, review capability rather than interpreting a familiar zero display as universal clearance. Document the selected function so users know the measurement’s scope and their own role limits.

### Decision principles

The program must match sensing capability and method to the actual decision. Channel count and price cannot establish suitability.

Personal monitoring and technical atmosphere assessment have different demands. Instrument possession does not demonstrate sampling and interpretation skill.

Electrical equipment can introduce ignition hazards. The actual equipment approval and use conditions must match the assessed location.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Maintain identity and understand assurance checks
lessons.body:
Identify each instrument and its sensors so tests, calibration, repairs and measurements can be traced to the actual device. Follow manufacturer and qualified program requirements for inspection, functional challenge, calibration and service. A startup self-test, fresh-air zero, bump test and calibration are different actions.

A bump test challenges response and alarms with known test gas under the specified method. Calibration checks or adjusts response against a reference as required. Neither a clean display nor a green battery icon proves sensor performance. Test gas, regulators, adapters and expiry or concentration information must suit the method.

Worked example: a shared monitor’s case number differs from the test log. The user resolves the identity before relying on the claimed test rather than assuming all devices in the cabinet were checked.

### Applying the mechanism

Assurance requires a suitable reference and delivery method as well as an instrument. Test gas concentration, mixture, condition and expiry information must support the manufacturer’s specified check. Regulators, adapters and tubing can affect delivery. A completed test on the wrong setup may not establish the intended response. The program distinguishes a functional challenge, calibration check, adjustment and service so users do not treat every dock event as the same evidence. Preserve the actual result, including a failed check. If calibration or repair is needed, the device remains restricted until the required work and verification are complete. Do not allow an attractive ready label to replace that sequence.

### Decision principles

A functional challenge verifies a bounded instrument response. It does not replace calibration when required or establish workplace conditions.

Electronic startup checks may not demonstrate sensor response to gas. Required challenge testing remains a separate safeguard.

The reference mixture and delivery arrangement must support the specified check. An incorrect challenge can create false confidence in the instrument.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Inspect and operate within manufacturer limits
lessons.body:
Before use, check physical condition, inlets, filters, pump or sampling line where fitted, battery, sensor identification, status and required assurance. Position personal monitors as instructed with sampling access unobstructed. A sealed pocket, contaminated filter or damaged line can delay or prevent representative sampling.

Environmental conditions and exposure to interfering substances can affect performance. Sensors can be poisoned, inhibited, overloaded or cross-sensitive depending on technology. The qualified user must know the actual model’s limitations and escalation instructions rather than interpreting every number as exact truth.

Worked example: a pumped sample line is kinked. The user does not accept the displayed value as representative of the remote point until the sampling system and required checks are restored.

### Applying the mechanism

The sensing path must remain open and appropriate. Dust, moisture, blocked filters, kinked lines or an obstructed inlet can prevent representative sampling. A pumped system’s flow indication is part of its method and must be understood for the actual instrument. A personal monitor hidden beneath impermeable clothing may encounter different air from the wearer’s breathing zone. Environmental limits and sensor interference also matter: a plausible-looking number is not a guarantee of accuracy under every condition. Users must follow the model-specific instructions and recognize fault or over-range responses. They should not invent an interpretation when the display is unfamiliar; the protective response and qualified help take priority.

### Decision principles

The device must encounter air relevant to the wearer within its intended method. Obstruction or remote placement can defeat timely warning.

Sensor technology has limitations beyond power supply. Users must understand the manufacturer’s interference and exposure instructions for the actual instrument.

The complete sampling and sensing system must function. A readable display does not prove that the target atmosphere reaches a suitable working sensor.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Plan sampling and interpret bounded results
lessons.body:
Qualified sampling considers where contaminants can occur, process configuration, layering or local sources, sample-line delay and sensor response, and the needed repeated or continuous measurements. Do not send an unprotected person into a hazard to carry the detector to a desired point. Use the approved safe sampling method.

Record location, time, task, conditions, device identity and responsible tester. A reading applies within those bounds. Exposure limits, alarm settings, entry criteria and emergency actions have different purposes and are interpreted through the approved program. This course supplies no universal safe number or sampling duration.

Worked example: an acceptable reading at a vessel opening does not automatically represent the bottom or an obstructed compartment. The qualified strategy must address the locations relevant to the planned work.

### Applying the mechanism

A sampling plan connects the physical atmosphere to the instrument. Where the air is drawn from, how it reaches the sensor, and how long the system takes to respond all affect the result. A long line can introduce delay, and some materials or contaminants can interact with sampling equipment. The qualified method addresses these issues for the actual setup. Locations may differ because of release sources, ventilation, geometry and changing operations. Record the measurement and relevant conditions so another competent reviewer can understand what it represents. Do not broaden a point result to an entire space, shift or process without the technical basis and required ongoing monitoring.

### Decision principles

Transport and sensor response affect when a representative result appears. The approved method defines the required timing for the actual setup.

Traceability makes the result interpretable and prevents reuse for an unrelated place, time or configuration.

Limits can have different scopes and averaging periods. Alarm settings trigger protective actions and cannot be casually converted into safe-work permission.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Respond to failed checks, faults and alarms
lessons.body:
A failed required check, unsuitable sensor, unexplained fault or overdue mandatory service removes the instrument from reliance. Obtain a suitable verified replacement and address any work that depended on the missing safeguard. Do not reset, silence or relabel the device to make it appear ready.

An exposure alarm triggers the site protective response. A suspected instrument fault is investigated under safe conditions by qualified personnel; it is not a reason for workers to remain in the affected area. Preserve event and fault data when available.

Worked example: a monitor alarms during a task and then displays an over-range or fault condition. The worker follows the emergency response and reports both indications rather than interpreting the fault as proof that no gas was present.

### Applying the mechanism

Disagreement between instruments is a reason for safe investigation, not a vote. Devices may be in different locations, have different sensors or response times, or have different faults. A worker follows the site alarm response rather than remaining in exposure until the cause is resolved. From safety, report the device identity, indication, location and sequence as accurately as possible. Preserve electronic logs when available through the program. An instrument fault after an alarm does not prove the earlier alarm was false; both observations need assessment. The responsible technical team establishes instrument condition and current atmosphere using a controlled method, and the site authority determines any authorized return.

### Decision principles

Failed assurance means the detection safeguard is not established. The program must restore suitability before workers depend on it.

Different placement, timing or condition can explain disagreement. A quiet device cannot casually cancel a protective alarm.

A complete chronology supports diagnosis and control review. Later results do not erase earlier warnings or explain them automatically.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Service, release and assess gas-testing competence
lessons.body:
Repair, sensor replacement and calibration must follow the manufacturer and qualified program requirements. After service, perform the required verification before release and update device and sensor records. Configuration changes, including alarm settings, need controlled authorization rather than casual adjustment by users.

A written pass does not demonstrate those skills. The equipment owner ensures users and dispatch see the correct ready or restricted status.

Worked example: a sensor is replaced but the required post-service checks are pending. The device remains restricted; a new sensor is not itself proof of a ready measurement system.

### Applying the mechanism

Competence should be scoped to the measurement task. A worker can learn to inspect and wear a personal monitor without being qualified to design a confined-space testing strategy. A technician can calibrate a model without being the person authorized to issue an entry permit. Record these distinctions in the role matrix and assess practical performance on the actual instrument and method. The learner should demonstrate preparation, safe sampling, response timing, interpretation, records and alarm actions within their scope. Do not introduce hazardous gas exposure to make the assessment realistic.

### Decision principles

Alarm settings are part of the protective system. Changes need a defined basis, authority and record rather than convenience.

Technical testing is a field skill with method-specific limits. Knowledge supports but does not replace observed performance and authorization.

Measurement assurance requires current traceable readiness, not just availability. Users must not receive a device whose technical status is unknown.

lessons.title: Two applied scenarios and worked decisions
lessons.body:
## Applied scenarios: complete worked decisions

### Scenario 1: A shared instrument cabinet

A worker selects a monitor from a cabinet. A nearby log shows a passed challenge for a different serial number, and the selected unit’s required status cannot be established.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** The selected unit is not relied on. The responsible equipment owner resolves identity and performs or documents the required assurance for that actual device, or provides a verified suitable replacement. The user confirms sensors, condition and task suitability. A shared storage location does not transfer one instrument’s test history to another.

### Scenario 2: A changed remote sample

A tester uses a longer sample line than planned and immediately records the displayed value as the remote atmosphere. The line and response timing have not been assessed.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** The result is not used for clearance. The qualified method is reviewed for the actual line, flow, compatibility and response delay, and the required instrument and sampling checks are performed. A representative measurement is then taken and recorded with its conditions. The earlier value remains identified as unverified rather than silently relabeled.

lessons.title: Final assessment: 20 individual decisions
lessons.body: Answer the 20 questions individually using the taught principles. Each submission preserves your first answer. Review feedback after submitting. When an answer is incorrect, explicitly acknowledge the correct decision and explanation before moving on. The result must show both the first-answer score and the remediated score across all 26 questions. Do not attempt a live hazardous task to obtain an answer; the assessment is a knowledge and judgment exercise.

lessons.title: Completion and separately assessed practical competence
lessons.body:
## What this completion means

The course is complete only after every section and all 26 questions have been accomplished, through correct responses or explicit acknowledgment of the supplied correction. Preserve the original and remediated results separately. Acknowledgment is a learning action, not evidence that the learner has performed the task safely in the field.

questions.prompt: A detector lacks a suitable sensor for the assessed contaminant. Can a zero display clear the task?

options.label: No; the measurement does not address that hazard.

options.label: The number of display channels alone.

options.label: Yes, after startup.

Yes, ownership grants testing authority.

options.label: The pump automatically corrects every blockage.
No reliable clearance until the sampling fault is resolved and the method verified.

options.label: In the approved position with sampling access unobstructed.
Inside a sealed bag.

Only whether a number appears.

Yes, all air is identical.

options.label: Readings are instantaneous everywhere.
Only battery charging creates delay.

Yes, every alarm is a legal work allowance.

explanations.E05_final_2_2: The same component can deteriorate differently in different duties. Inspection and retirement decisions must reflect the actual exposure history.

explanations.E05_final_3_2: Restraints can limit movement under defined conditions but do not restore hose integrity or compatibility.
explanations.E05_final_3_3: Installation conditions affect service life and failure risk. The approved routing must preserve the assembly’s limits and protect nearby people.

explanations.E05_final_6_2: Abnormal loads or exposure may impair components in ways requiring specific disposition. The next reviewer needs that context.
explanations.E05_final_6_3: Technical examination and certification require separately qualified personnel and applicable procedures. Written learning cannot substitute for them.
explanations.E05_final_scenario1: Copying identity would create false assurance and disconnect the item from its real design and history. The competent process must establish its own status.
