lessons.title: Start here: learning, scores and role boundaries
lessons.body:
# E05: Pressure equipment, hoses and relief devices

This original VNDRLY course teaches decisions for service-specific: pressure/production, compressed systems and testing. Its purpose is to match components and protection to actual pressure service. The six lessons explain the hazard, planning decisions, controls, checks, changing conditions and handback. Worked examples and two fictional scenarios show how those decisions fit together. Read the teaching before answering; no live hazardous activity is needed to complete this course.

There are six lesson knowledge checks and a 20-question final assessment. Submit each answer before viewing its feedback. Your first answer remains in the original score. If an answer is wrong, read the specific explanation and explicitly acknowledge the correction; acknowledged corrections contribute to a separate remediated score. Completion requires all sections and all 26 questions correct or explicitly acknowledged after remediation. A later corrected answer never erases the first-answer record.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Establish service suitability and traceability
lessons.body:
Pressure equipment includes assemblies and components whose failure can release stored energy or hazardous contents. Register or otherwise trace the items as required: vessels, hoses, connections, gauges and relief devices. Establish pressure, temperature, fluid, environmental and cyclic-service suitability using approved technical information. Size and appearance do not establish rating.

An assembly is only suitable when its components and configuration are compatible. A high-rated hose does not upgrade a lower-rated coupling. The competent technical owner controls selection and changes.

Worked example: an unmarked hose is found in usable stock. It is held from pressure service until identity and suitability are established through the equipment process, not assigned a rating from color.

### Applying the mechanism

Think of a hose assembly as several interfaces that must all remain suitable: the tube contacts the fluid, reinforcement carries load, the cover protects against the environment, and the end fittings transfer force into the connected system. A compatible tube does not prove an acceptable fitting, and an intact cover does not reveal every internal defect. The specification must describe the assembly rather than one attractive feature. For a vessel or receiver, identification similarly connects the item to its design conditions and accepted history. If a nameplate is unreadable, an operator cannot recreate the design basis from wall thickness by eye. The technical owner obtains defensible records or removes the item from the proposed duty. This is why procurement should preserve technical identity from receipt through storage and use.

### Decision principles

The component must perform in the actual service. A dimensional match can conceal unsuitable materials or limits.

The system can fail at an unsuitable component. Ratings must be assessed for the whole accepted configuration.

Selection affects integrity and protective functions. It requires suitable technical information and authority rather than convenience.

Service temperature can affect component limits even when pressure is unchanged. The technical owner must use the applicable combined pressure, temperature and material information rather than treating a room-temperature marking as universal. A worker reports a changed duty and holds use until suitability is resolved; they do not invent a new derated operating value.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Set inspection, examination and testing requirements
lessons.body:
Requirements come from applicable law, design basis, manufacturer information and competent assessment of service. Routine visual checks, periodic examination, proof or integrity testing and relief-device servicing have different purposes. Do not replace one with another merely because a form is available.

The program identifies due triggers, acceptance criteria, competent providers and records. Corrosion, fatigue, abrasion, temperature and chemical attack can require service-specific attention. A universal annual test interval is not invented here.

Worked example: a vessel’s external inspection is current, but a separate required examination is overdue. The external pass does not waive the overdue requirement; the owner resolves the actual status before release.

### Applying the mechanism

Inspection asks what deterioration could reasonably occur and what method can detect it. External abrasion may be visible while internal corrosion or fatigue needs another suitable examination. A pressure test answers a bounded integrity question under specified conditions; it does not automatically reveal every future failure mechanism. The program should distinguish an initial acceptance test, in-service examination and a user’s pre-use check so one record cannot accidentally close all three obligations. If a unit cycles frequently or changes to a corrosive fluid, the technical review considers whether the original assurance basis remains adequate. Users report those service changes even when they cannot interpret their engineering significance. Their responsibility is accurate information and respect for restrictions, not selecting a new test method.

### Decision principles

Deterioration and legal obligations vary by equipment and service. The maintenance basis must be technically supported.

The same component can deteriorate differently in different duties. Inspection and retirement decisions must reflect the actual exposure history.

Specialist assurance needs method-specific skills and equipment. Administrative handling does not establish examination competence.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Inspect hoses and connections before reliance
lessons.body:
Pre-use checks look for identification, damaged covers, exposed reinforcement, deformation, corrosion, coupling movement, leaks and other manufacturer-defined rejection conditions. Do not feel for pressure leaks with a hand or flex a suspect hose under pressure. Inspection must use a safe state and method.

Routing protects against sharp edges, excessive bending, heat, traffic and incompatible exposure as required. Restraints, where specified, must match the approved design and attachments; they do not make a failed hose acceptable.

Worked example: a hose has a cut near its end fitting and uncertain reinforcement condition. The user reports and quarantines it for competent disposition rather than wrapping the cover and returning it to pressure use.

### Applying the mechanism

A hose can be unsuitable even without visible damage when its installed shape exceeds the approved bend or loading conditions. Twisting during connection can introduce stress, and a fitting used as a handle can load an interface in an unintended direction. Routing across a vehicle path adds crushing and abrasion exposure. The task plan should provide a supported route that permits the intended movement without dragging, kinking or pulling on fittings. The user checks that the installed assembly matches that arrangement before pressure is applied. If a restraint is required, its attachments and geometry are checked separately; tying a random chain around a connection can create an unassessed assembly. Correct routing and restraint supplement suitable components rather than compensating for unknown ratings.

### Decision principles

A functioning flow path can still have impaired integrity. The check must address the components relied on to contain pressure.

Restraints can limit movement under defined conditions but do not restore hose integrity or compatibility.

Installation conditions affect service life and failure risk. The approved routing must preserve the assembly’s limits and protect nearby people.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Protect relief devices and verify their function
lessons.body:
Relief devices form part of an engineered protective system. Their selection, setting, capacity, installation and discharge destination must match the design and applicable requirements. Do not adjust, plug, bypass or isolate a required protective device casually. A leaking device is a defect needing competent assessment, not permission to defeat protection.

Maintain traceable servicing and test status. The presence of a seal or tag is useful only when linked to the correct device and current accepted condition. Discharge can create noise, temperature, pressure or chemical exposure and must be controlled.

Worked example: a relief outlet annoys workers with occasional discharge. The technical owner investigates the cause and safe arrangement; the outlet is not capped to stop the nuisance.

### Applying the mechanism

A relief device must be able to sense the protected condition and discharge as designed. An obstructed inlet, closed isolation path or blocked outlet can defeat that function even if the device itself was recently serviced. Backpressure and discharge routing can also affect performance and exposure, which is why installation changes belong to technical review. A user should be able to identify the required device and recognize unauthorized caps, disconnected sensing arrangements or other obvious changes, but should not adjust its setting to investigate. When a device repeatedly operates, ask the technical authority to examine both the system pressure behavior and device condition. Replacing the valve without understanding the initiating condition may leave the underlying overpressure problem unresolved.

### Decision principles

Relief performance depends on the complete protective design. A fitting match does not prove adequate capacity or correct function.

Protecting the vessel must not create uncontrolled exposure elsewhere. The outlet arrangement needs technical and site assessment.

Traceability establishes which protective item was serviced and accepted. Aggregate paperwork cannot verify an unidentified device.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Quarantine uncertain items and control repair
lessons.body:
Damaged, unidentified, overdue or unsuitable pressure components stay out of service until the responsible technical process resolves them. Use effective segregation and status control so they cannot be issued from stock. Do not recreate missing ratings from memory or treat an improvised pressure test as proof of unknown design.

Repair and testing require qualified methods, safe energy control and required acceptance. Some items must be retired rather than repaired. The applicable criteria determine disposition, not the desire to recover purchase cost.

Worked example: a coupling is deformed after an abnormal event. It is controlled with its history and assessed by the competent owner; straightening it in the field does not establish restored rating.

### Applying the mechanism

Quarantine should preserve the item and its history for diagnosis. Record the service, observed defect and any abnormal event before separating it from ready stock. Do not clean away evidence or dismantle a failed component casually if an investigation or technical assessment needs the as-found condition. Where contamination creates its own hazard, the qualified plan controls handling and identifies what preparation occurred. A repair provider needs the real service information to judge material compatibility and applicable methods. A return labeled simply “repaired” should not be accepted when the work scope, tests or limitations are unknown. The owner must know whether the provider repaired the original defect, replaced the item or rejected it, and what must happen before reuse.

### Decision principles

Unknown integrity or suitability is not a safe operating basis. The item must not circulate as ready stock.

A test result is bounded by its method and conditions. It cannot create missing design information or certify every service condition.

Some damage or service history requires retirement. Economic preference cannot override technical rejection criteria.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Release the accepted configuration and retain history
lessons.body:
Return to service requires traceable technical acceptance of the actual item and assembly, required tests and resolved restrictions. Keep inspection, repair, test and abnormal-event history linked to identity. If service or configuration changes, review suitability and refresh affected evidence.

The owner checks that physical tags, stock and dispatch systems agree. Review recurring defects to address compatibility, routing, operating transients or maintenance weaknesses. A written course pass supports awareness only; it does not certify a pressure vessel or relief valve.

Worked example: an accepted hose is transferred to a hotter chemical service. The technical review occurs before transfer because prior acceptance was bounded to different conditions.

### Applying the mechanism

Release should answer a practical question: can the next user identify this exact component, understand its permitted duty and see any restriction without having attended the repair discussion? If the answer depends on memory, the handback is fragile. An assembly record may need to link its components and configuration so later substitution is visible. When a fitting is replaced, retain the earlier history but establish the new accepted configuration and required tests. During follow-up, compare failures by service and installation as well as by supplier. Several different hoses failing at the same hot edge may indicate a routing problem; one model failing across different sites may suggest selection or manufacture. Either pattern requires evidence-based technical review, not an unsupported blame assignment.

### Decision principles

Readiness must be supported by technical evidence for the item being used. Commercial completion is not integrity acceptance.

Abnormal loads or exposure may impair components in ways requiring specific disposition. The next reviewer needs that context.

Technical examination and certification require separately qualified personnel and applicable procedures. Written learning cannot substitute for them.

lessons.title: Two applied scenarios and worked decisions
lessons.body:
## Applied scenarios: complete worked decisions

### Scenario 1: Mixed stock

A store contains rated hoses and an identical-looking unmarked hose. Dispatch wants the unmarked one because it is longest.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** The unmarked item remains held. The owner establishes identity, service suitability and required inspection status or replaces it with verified equipment. No one copies another label or invents a lower pressure rating. The stock-control review checks how uncertain equipment entered usable storage.

### Scenario 2: Nuisance relief discharge

A relief device repeatedly opens. A crew proposes isolating it while production continues and checking it after the shift.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** The required protection is not defeated. The operating and technical authorities follow the approved response, establish a safe condition and investigate the pressure behavior and device. Any repair, replacement or operating change receives required verification and acceptance. Repeated discharge can signal a system problem as well as a device issue.

lessons.title: Final assessment: 20 individual decisions
lessons.body: Answer the 20 questions individually using the taught principles. Each submission preserves your first answer. Review feedback after submitting. When an answer is incorrect, explicitly acknowledge the correct decision and explanation before moving on. The result must show both the first-answer score and the remediated score across all 26 questions. Do not attempt a live hazardous task to obtain an answer; the assessment is a knowledge and judgment exercise.

lessons.title: Start here: learning, scores and role boundaries
lessons.body:
# E06: Lifting gear, access equipment and fall protection inspection

This original VNDRLY course teaches decisions for service-specific: lifting and elevated work. Its purpose is to ensure critical load-bearing equipment is fit and traceable. The six lessons explain the hazard, planning decisions, controls, checks, changing conditions and handback. Worked examples and two fictional scenarios show how those decisions fit together. Read the teaching before answering; no live hazardous activity is needed to complete this course.

There are six lesson knowledge checks and a 20-question final assessment. Submit each answer before viewing its feedback. Your first answer remains in the original score. If an answer is wrong, read the specific explanation and explicitly acknowledge the correction; acknowledged corrections contribute to a separate remediated score. Completion requires all sections and all 26 questions correct or explicitly acknowledged after remediation. A later corrected answer never erases the first-answer record.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Separate equipment classes and protective functions
lessons.body:
Lifting gear, access equipment and fall protection share a need for traceable assurance, but they perform different functions. A sling supports a load, a scaffold or ladder provides access, and a harness system protects a person under a defined arrangement. A rating or inspection for one purpose does not establish suitability for another.

Identify the actual item, intended use, manufacturer limitations and required competent inspection or examination. Never use a cargo tie-down as a lifting sling or a convenient handrail as an unverified fall-protection anchor. Similar appearance is not technical equivalence.

Worked example: a worker proposes using a lifting sling to secure a person because it is strong. Human fall protection requires its own approved complete system, compatibility and technical basis; strength alone does not establish that use.

### Applying the mechanism

A user should first ask what the item is designed to support or prevent. Lifting gear carries a material load through an approved configuration. Access equipment supports a person while reaching the work. A personal fall-protection system manages a specific fall exposure and requires the correct connectors, anchors, clearance and rescue. These functions can involve different directions and types of loading even when the material looks similar. A catalog rating only applies within its defined use. The safe selection process therefore checks intended function before comparing capacity. This prevents a common mistake: choosing the strongest-looking available item and inventing a use that its manufacturer and technical assessment never approved.

### Decision principles

Suitability follows intended performance and use conditions. Visual similarity or convenience cannot establish a safe substitute.

Cargo restraint and lifting impose different requirements and use conditions. A device must be approved and rated for the actual function.

A handrail’s purpose and capacity may not support fall-protection loads. Appearance cannot establish an approved anchorage system.

An item’s storage location is not its identity. When equipment moves between crews, the accepted records and restrictions must still follow the actual item. A borrowing arrangement should include the required condition and suitability check; informal transfer does not turn another crew’s recent successful use into proof for a different task.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Maintain identity, ratings and required status
lessons.body:
Traceability connects an item to its rating, inspection, examination, repairs and retirement criteria. Preserve manufacturer markings and assigned identifiers where required. Color coding can communicate a local status but does not replace the underlying item-specific evidence or a current pre-use check.

Set inspection and examination requirements from applicable rules, manufacturer information and competent assessment. There is no universal interval for every sling, ladder and harness. Rental equipment needs clear responsibilities and accepted status for the actual delivered items.

Worked example: a sling has a current-looking color mark but its identification is unreadable. The user holds it for competent resolution rather than assuming the color establishes capacity.

### Applying the mechanism

An inspection record has value only when the user can connect it to the item in hand. A batch certificate may support manufacture, while periodic examination and event history may be item-specific. The equipment program defines how those records fit together. A replacement tag must follow an authorized traceability process; a user cannot copy the rating from a similar item because the original tag was lost. Likewise, a local color mark may show that a review period was addressed without stating every limitation. Before selecting equipment, read the actual identity and required status, then perform the pre-use check. If either technical identity or current condition cannot be established, hold reliance rather than combining two uncertain clues into a pass.

### Decision principles

Assurance evidence must follow the item being used. Without that link, another item’s records can be mistaken for proof of suitability.

Equipment functions and deterioration differ. The program must establish the correct requirement for each class and service.

The delivered equipment can have damage or mismatched identity. The user must establish accepted status and perform assigned checks before reliance.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Inspect lifting gear against its own criteria
lessons.body:
Lifting gear checks cover the actual type and manufacturer criteria: identification, wear, cuts, deformation, corrosion, heat or chemical damage, stitching, hooks, latches and connectors as relevant. Do not apply one rejection rule blindly to every material. A competent examiner handles technical disposition beyond the user’s scope.

Inspect in a safe unloaded arrangement. Never proof-test questionable gear by lifting a valuable load or placing people nearby. Configuration, hitch, angle and edge conditions still affect suitability even when an item passes its condition check.

Worked example: an intact sling is selected for a sharp-edged load without suitable protection. The inspection pass does not establish that this configuration is acceptable; the lift plan must address the edge and geometry.

### Applying the mechanism

Configuration changes the forces carried by lifting gear. Sling legs, hitches and attachment directions must match the competent lift plan and applicable rated information. An item can be undamaged yet overloaded in an unsuitable geometry. Edges can cut or concentrate load, and heat or chemicals can degrade materials that look acceptable from a distance. The user’s inspection should therefore include the proposed contact points and environment as well as the loose item on the rack. If the lift requires a configuration the user does not understand, the correct response is the qualified rigger or planner, not a rough calculation made beside a suspended load. Condition inspection supports selection; it does not replace lifting engineering.

### Decision principles

Different materials and components have different deterioration and rejection conditions. The check must use the relevant criteria.

An improvised trial can fail violently and does not establish technical rating. Testing requires its own safe qualified method.

Technical disposition needs suitable expertise and evidence. Schedule pressure cannot classify uncertain load-bearing damage as acceptable.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Inspect access equipment and fall protection distinctly
lessons.body:
Access checks examine the relevant structure, feet, rungs, connections, platform, support and protective components. Scaffold inspection and authorization follow the competent system; ordinary users do not alter or certify it. Portable access must match the task and support conditions.

Fall-protection checks examine the specific harness, lanyard, connectors and other system parts under manufacturer criteria. Cuts, damaged stitching, corrosion, deformation or an arrest event may require removal and competent disposition. A harness pass does not prove anchorage, clearance or rescue adequacy.

Worked example: a harness is undamaged but the proposed anchor is unverified. Work remains held until the complete system is technically established; the equipment inspection does not certify the installation.

### Applying the mechanism

For access equipment, inspect the features that keep the worker supported and separated from a fall: the structure, connections, feet or base, platform and required protective components. For personal fall protection, inspect the actual webbing or other material, stitching, connectors and event indicators where provided under the manufacturer’s criteria. Neither class should be judged only by cleanliness. A clean ladder can have a damaged structural member, and a clean harness can have chemical degradation. Users must know which findings they can classify and which require competent disposition. Where equipment is already installed, its setup and support also need acceptance. A sound portable item placed on unsuitable support remains an unsafe access arrangement.

### Decision principles

Scaffold changes can affect stability and protection. User awareness does not grant erection, alteration or competent inspection authority.

Arrest forces can impair equipment beyond visible damage. Manufacturer and program requirements determine inspection or retirement.

An intact ladder or platform can still be wrong for the task. Selection and setup must fit actual use conditions.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Quarantine, store and retire without recirculation
lessons.body:
Control damaged, unidentified, overdue or rejected equipment physically and administratively. A common storage bin must not mix ready and held items. Protect accepted equipment from moisture, chemicals, sunlight, heat, abrasion and other conditions relevant to its material and manufacturer instructions.

Repairs require the approved qualified method; some items cannot be field repaired. Retired equipment must be disposed of so it cannot be mistaken for usable gear. Do not cut identifiers off and then return an item as an anonymous spare.

Worked example: a rejected sling is left near usable stock for later disposal. The owner secures its disposition and status immediately, preventing a worker from borrowing it during a busy shift.

### Applying the mechanism

Storage should be designed around how people issue and return equipment. A clearly controlled rejected area prevents a busy worker from taking an item whose defect was reported on a different shift. Ready stock should be protected from sharp surfaces, incompatible chemicals, excessive heat and other identified degradation sources. Returned gear needs a defined check before it becomes ready again; placing it back on the hook is not an inspection. If an item was exposed to an abnormal event, preserve that information even when no visible damage is found. Retirement should make the decision durable through the approved disposal process. Leaving a rejected item available as an unofficial emergency spare defeats the reason it was rejected.

### Decision principles

Storage can degrade protective and load-bearing equipment. The program must preserve condition, not merely inventory count.

Unapproved repairs can change strength or protective performance. Some equipment requires retirement rather than repair.

A retired item must not become a hidden fallback. Its final disposition must preserve the rejection decision and prevent inadvertent use.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Release with evidence and qualify the assigned role
lessons.body:
The responsible owner releases an item only after required inspection, examination, repair and acceptance are complete. The record identifies the actual item, criteria, findings, examiner and limitations. Current status must agree across the item, storage and issue system.

Review recurring findings to improve selection, handling, storage and maintenance. A written awareness score cannot establish all those roles.

Worked example: several harnesses show similar chemical damage. The owner controls affected equipment and reviews the exposure and storage arrangement, rather than repeatedly replacing harnesses without addressing the cause.

### Applying the mechanism

Assessors should distinguish recognition from technical examination. A user may correctly identify a cut sling and remove it from service without being qualified to measure remaining strength or approve repair. An examiner may assess one equipment class without authority to design a fall-protection installation. A scaffold user may recognize a missing rail without authority to rebuild the scaffold. Record these role boundaries in the competence matrix so a broad training title is not mistaken for unlimited authority. Do not require hazardous loading to prove that the learner can recognize an uncertain item.

### Decision principles

Item-specific evidence supports a defensible status. Aggregate counts cannot establish that the selected item was examined and accepted.

Technical examination requires demonstrated skill for the class and method. Ownership and written awareness are not substitutes.

An item can be in good condition yet unsuitable for the load or task. Selection and site readiness need their own decisions.

lessons.title: Two applied scenarios and worked decisions
lessons.body:
## Applied scenarios: complete worked decisions

### Scenario 1: A color-coded sling

A sling has the current local color but its rating is unreadable and it has been stored beside chemicals. The crew needs a quick lift.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** The sling is not used. The owner resolves identity and condition through the competent process or supplies verified suitable gear. The lift plan still checks the actual configuration and edge conditions. The color is preserved as one status cue but is not treated as evidence of rating or chemical integrity.

### Scenario 2: The undamaged harness

A harness passes inspection. A worker proposes attaching it to a nearby rail without a clearance or rescue review.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** The work remains held. A qualified person establishes the complete fall-protection arrangement, including suitable anchorage, connectors, geometry, clearance and feasible rescue. The harness inspection remains valid evidence of that component’s checked condition, not a certificate for the whole installation.

lessons.body: Answer the 20 questions individually using the taught principles. Each submission preserves your first answer. Review feedback after submitting. When an answer is incorrect, explicitly acknowledge the correct decision and explanation before moving on. The result must show both the first-answer score and the remediated score across all 26 questions. Do not attempt a live hazardous task to obtain an answer; the assessment is a knowledge and judgment exercise.

courses.title: E07 — PPE assessment, issue and care
courses.purpose: Make protection fit the exposure and worker.

content.title: E07 — PPE assessment, issue and care
content.description: Complete guided E07 training: six taught lessons, two worked scenarios, six checks and a 20-question final. Separate first-answer and remediated scores; wrong answers require explicit correction acknowledgment.

explanations.E07_check1: Glove protection depends on material, chemical and use conditions. Generic issue or layering does not establish resistance to the actual exposure.
explanations.E07_final_1_1: Protective performance must match the harm mechanism. Brand familiarity cannot establish chemical, impact or thermal suitability.
explanations.E07_final_1_2: A baseline addresses common conditions. Specialized work can introduce hazards beyond that baseline and needs its own assessment.
explanations.E07_final_1_3: PPE has limitations and depends on correct selection and use. It does not remove stored energy, releases or the source of exposure.
explanations.E07_check2: Protection must work as a combined system. Interference can defeat a seal or coverage even when each item is individually suitable.
explanations.E07_final_2_1: Different glove materials and constructions protect against different exposures. Thickness and marketing terms cannot establish the required performance.
explanations.E07_final_2_2: The protective function must persist in use. Static comfort alone does not prove that coverage or compatibility remains adequate during work.
explanations.E07_final_2_3: Unapproved modification can alter protection and fit. The responsible program should provide a suitable alternative rather than requiring an improvised compromise.
explanations.E07_check3: Issue and training are different evidence. Correct use and any additional program requirements must be demonstrated and verified separately.
explanations.E07_final_3_1: Workers need to know how the item protects and when it no longer does. A slogan cannot guide safe inspection or replacement.
explanations.E07_final_3_2: Respiratory protection has specialized selection and user prerequisites. General awareness and ownership do not establish those conditions.
explanations.E07_final_3_3: Demonstration can reveal fitting and use errors that attendance records miss. Language and delivery must allow the worker to understand the actual instruction.

lessons.title: Start here: learning, scores and role boundaries
lessons.body:
# E07: PPE assessment, issue and care

This original VNDRLY course teaches decisions for common needs assessment; specialist ppe conditional. Its purpose is to make protection fit the exposure and worker. The six lessons explain the hazard, planning decisions, controls, checks, changing conditions and handback. Worked examples and two fictional scenarios show how those decisions fit together. Read the teaching before answering; no live hazardous activity is needed to complete this course.

There are six lesson knowledge checks and a 20-question final assessment. Submit each answer before viewing its feedback. Your first answer remains in the original score. If an answer is wrong, read the specific explanation and explicitly acknowledge the correction; acknowledged corrections contribute to a separate remediated score. Completion requires all sections and all 26 questions correct or explicitly acknowledged after remediation. A later corrected answer never erases the first-answer record.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Assess the exposure before choosing equipment
lessons.body:
PPE protects a person against defined hazards within its performance limits. Selection starts with the task and exposure: impact, splash, heat, noise, airborne contaminants, electrical energy or other hazards. First consider eliminating or controlling the hazard through safer methods and engineering; PPE can remain essential but does not remove the source.

The assessment identifies the body areas exposed, severity, duration and conditions, then selects suitable protective performance. A standard site minimum is a baseline, not proof that every task-specific need is met. A brand or familiar color does not establish suitability.

Worked example: a worker handling a corrosive product receives ordinary work gloves because they are stocked. The competent assessment must establish chemical and task suitability; issue from a cabinet is not a hazard assessment.

### Applying the mechanism

Name the harm mechanism before selecting the item. A splash can reach skin or eyes, a flying particle can strike, heat can burn and airborne contaminants can be inhaled. Each mechanism calls for particular performance rather than the generic word “protection.” The assessment also considers whether the task can be changed to reduce exposure at the source. For example, a suitable closed transfer may reduce splash and vapor while PPE addresses the remaining risk. Workers must not redesign the process themselves, but they can report when the method forces repeated exposure. The competent owner then reviews both stronger controls and the protective equipment instead of treating PPE issue as the end of the assessment.

### Decision principles

Protective performance must match the harm mechanism. Brand familiarity cannot establish chemical, impact or thermal suitability.

A baseline addresses common conditions. Specialized work can introduce hazards beyond that baseline and needs its own assessment.

PPE has limitations and depends on correct selection and use. It does not remove stored energy, releases or the source of exposure.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Match performance, compatibility and fit
lessons.body:
Different PPE classes protect against different hazards. Impact eyewear may not supply the needed splash protection; a face shield may need compatible eye protection beneath it. Gloves differ in chemical resistance, cut protection, heat performance and dexterity. The competent assessment and manufacturer information establish the correct combination.

Fit must allow the protective function while the worker performs the task. Combined equipment can interfere: eyewear, hearing protection, headgear and respirators may affect each other’s seal, position or field of view. Do not modify equipment informally to make an incompatible combination fit.

Worked example: new eyewear disrupts the seal of another protective device. The combination is reassessed and replaced or adjusted through the approved method before exposure, rather than accepting one protection at the expense of another.

### Applying the mechanism

Compatibility should be checked as the worker will actually use the equipment. Headgear, eyewear, hearing protection and respirators can compete for space or change a seal. Clothing and gloves can affect dexterity, snagging and access to controls. A protective combination that works while standing still may shift when reaching, kneeling or turning. If the worker cannot perform the task while preserving coverage and fit, reassess the combination or work method. Removing one required item or cutting a strap informally can defeat protection. A suitable alternative must preserve the relevant functions together.

### Decision principles

Different glove materials and constructions protect against different exposures. Thickness and marketing terms cannot establish the required performance.

The protective function must persist in use. Static comfort alone does not prove that coverage or compatibility remains adequate during work.

Unapproved modification can alter protection and fit. The responsible program should provide a suitable alternative rather than requiring an improvised compromise.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Issue equipment and teach correct use
lessons.body:
Issue the correct type and size with understandable instruction. Training covers when protection is needed, how to put it on and remove it, adjustment, limitations, inspection, cleaning, storage and replacement. The worker demonstrates the required use; a receipt establishes delivery, not competence.

Some equipment requires additional program prerequisites. Respirators can require medical evaluation, fit testing and specific training under the applicable respiratory program. Electrical, fall-protection and specialist PPE also have task-specific assessment needs. This course does not replace those programs.

Worked example: a worker signs for a respirator but has not completed the required respiratory prerequisites. The signature does not authorize exposure; the respiratory program must establish readiness separately.

### Applying the mechanism

Instruction should explain limitations with concrete examples. A chemical glove can protect against an assessed substance without resisting every solvent; impact eyewear may not provide the same coverage as a splash arrangement; a filtering facepiece does not supply oxygen. The worker needs to know what not to assume when the task changes. Demonstration then establishes fitting, adjustment, inspection, use and removal for the assigned item. A trainer should correct specific errors and observe the corrected action rather than merely repeat the explanation. Where a specialist program requires medical, fit or technical prerequisites, keep them as separate recorded decisions. A general PPE receipt or quiz must never be relabeled as those results.

### Decision principles

Workers need to know how the item protects and when it no longer does. A slogan cannot guide safe inspection or replacement.

Respiratory protection has specialized selection and user prerequisites. General awareness and ownership do not establish those conditions.

Demonstration can reveal fitting and use errors that attendance records miss. Language and delivery must allow the worker to understand the actual instruction.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Inspect before use and recognize loss of protection
lessons.body:
Check PPE using the relevant manufacturer and program criteria. Look for damage, contamination, wear, missing parts, degraded materials and status or expiry requirements where applicable. Do not use damaged protection because the task will be short. Some failures are not obvious, so follow event-based and service-life rules as well as visual checks.

The inspection must fit the item. A scratch on eyewear, cut glove, cracked shell or damaged connector can have different disposition criteria. When the user cannot establish acceptance, hold exposure and obtain the competent responsible decision.

Worked example: chemical gloves appear intact after contact but their safe use period or contamination status is uncertain. The worker follows the chemical-specific program rather than assuming no visible hole means continued protection.

### Applying the mechanism

Inspection criteria can include condition that is not obvious from a quick look. Chemical contact, heat, age, an impact or another abnormal event may require replacement or specialist disposition even if the item remains intact. Follow the applicable manufacturer and program requirements rather than waiting for a visible hole or crack. Users should understand any event that requires immediate removal from reliance and how to obtain a suitable replacement. If identifying information or required status is missing, the owner resolves it through the approved process. Do not guess a protection class from color or assume that more layers make an unknown item suitable for a different hazard.

### Decision principles

Different protection fails in different ways. Criteria must match the material, design and hazard rather than a generic appearance check.

Hazard consequences do not depend on the worker’s intended duration. A brief event can occur immediately, so required protection must be effective at the start.

Uncertainty must remain visible. The user should not create a technical acceptance decision they are not qualified to make.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Clean, store and replace without transferring exposure
lessons.body:
Care preserves protection and prevents contamination reaching the worker, other people or clean areas. Follow the manufacturer and hazard-specific cleaning method; an unsuitable cleaner can damage materials. Store equipment away from the conditions that degrade it and separate contaminated or rejected items from ready stock.

Doffing can expose skin or clothing to contamination. Use the taught method and disposal or decontamination arrangements for the actual hazard. Do not take contaminated equipment home casually or share items without the required hygiene and fit controls.

Worked example: a worker removes contaminated gloves and touches their face with the outer surface.

### Applying the mechanism

Care begins when the worker leaves the exposure area. Contaminated outer surfaces can transfer material during removal, transport or storage. The task-specific method establishes where doffing occurs, how contaminated items are contained and whether they are cleaned, decontaminated or disposed of. A worker should not take potentially contaminated gear home for ordinary laundry without an approved arrangement. Cleaning products and drying conditions can also damage protective materials, so use the specified method. Ready equipment needs protected storage separate from rejected or contaminated items. If shared equipment is allowed, the program addresses hygiene, fitting and condition for the next user rather than assuming that wiping the surface restores every requirement.

### Decision principles

Cleaning can degrade materials or spread contamination. The method must suit the equipment and substance.

Protection can be defeated during handling after the task. Practical removal and hygiene steps must match the actual contamination.

Ordering equipment does not protect a worker now. Work must remain controlled until a suitable effective item and its prerequisites are available.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Reassess problems and preserve qualification boundaries
lessons.body:
Reassess when tasks, products, equipment, environment or worker needs change, and when discomfort or interference prevents correct use. Do not treat a reported problem as refusal without examining whether the selected equipment fits and protects. Involve the worker and competent program owner in finding a suitable arrangement.

Records should link the hazard assessment, selected equipment, issue, training and observed use, while protecting any medical information in the proper program. Review whether PPE is worn correctly and whether stronger controls could reduce reliance. A general written pass is not a respirator fit test, electrical qualification or fall-protection demonstration.

Worked example: several workers remove eye protection because it fogs and obscures the task. The owner addresses compatibility and conditions rather than merely collecting new signatures.

### Applying the mechanism

A reported fit or usability problem is information about control performance. Fogging, slipping, restricted movement or conflicting equipment can cause workers to use protection incorrectly or create another hazard. The supervisor should establish a safe interim arrangement and obtain competent review, involving the worker in checking the proposed solution. Observation after the change asks whether the item now protects during the actual task, not just whether a replacement was issued. The program should also examine whether stronger controls can reduce dependence on PPE.

### Decision principles

Selection is bounded by assumptions. Changed exposure or fit can invalidate the prior assessment before any incident occurs.

Delivery and attendance do not establish effective use. Observation checks whether the selected protection works in the actual task.

A written general PPE course cannot substitute for them.

lessons.title: Two applied scenarios and worked decisions
lessons.body:
## Applied scenarios: complete worked decisions

### Scenario 1: A new cleaning product

A shop changes cleaning chemical but keeps issuing the same gloves. The worker notices softening and is told all gloves are chemical gloves.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** Affected handling is held while the competent assessment uses the actual product and manufacturer information to select suitable protection and stronger controls where appropriate. Damaged or contaminated gloves are controlled and replaced. Workers receive instruction in the new limitations, inspection, removal and care. The old issue record does not establish compatibility with the new chemical.

### Scenario 2: The signed respirator receipt

A worker has signed for a tight-fitting respirator and passed this PPE course. The required respiratory program prerequisites and fit evaluation have not been established.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** The worker is not assigned exposure requiring that respirator. The respiratory program establishes the appropriate hazard assessment, selection, medical and fit prerequisites where required, training and practical use. The general course and issue receipt remain learning and delivery evidence only. They are not relabeled as a medical clearance or fit-test result.

lessons.title: Final assessment: 20 individual decisions
lessons.body: Answer the 20 questions individually using the taught principles. Each submission preserves your first answer. Review feedback after submitting. When an answer is incorrect, explicitly acknowledge the correct decision and explanation before moving on. The result must show both the first-answer score and the remediated score across all 26 questions. Do not attempt a live hazardous task to obtain an answer; the assessment is a knowledge and judgment exercise.

lessons.title: Completion and separately assessed practical competence
lessons.body:
## What this completion means

The course is complete only after every section and all 26 questions have been accomplished, through correct responses or explicit acknowledgment of the supplied correction. Preserve the original and remediated results separately. Acknowledgment is a learning action, not evidence that the learner has performed the task safely in the field.

options.label: Hazard-based selection using the actual product and task information.
Use them because gloves are mandatory.

lessons.title: Start here: Shop and facility readiness
lessons.body:
# Shop and facility readiness

This original VNDRLY course teaches decisions within the company safety program. Work through six lessons, their six checks, two worked scenarios and a 20-question final. All cases are fictional. No equipment operation is required to complete the online learning.

Each of the 26 questions requires a recorded answer. Completion requires a correct answer or explicit acknowledgment of the explanation and corrected answer after an error. Preserve the first-attempt score separately from the remediated score; a correction never rewrites what was first understood. Read the explanation, return to the relevant lesson and resolve uncertainty with the responsible supervisor. The course does not substitute for a site assessment, permit or employer authorization.

The linked references support the subject and identify source context. Client procedures are examples of client requirements, not universal law or endorsement of this course. Apply the governing jurisdiction and actual site procedure; no numerical technical limits or universal renewal interval are invented here.

## Primary reference context

[OSHA Machine guarding — technical inspection remains separate](https://www.osha.gov/machine-guarding). Read the reference within its stated scope. Company examples are not universal technical rules; regulatory applicability must be determined for the actual task and jurisdiction.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 - Inspect by area and task
lessons.body:
A facility walk-through should follow the work: receiving, storage, machine areas, chemical use, maintenance, pedestrian routes, welfare and emergency access. Identify who uses each area and how conditions change between shifts. A daytime office inspection cannot represent an operating night yard.

Separate what a general inspector can observe from what requires technical examination. Visible cable damage can be reported, but a general walk-through does not certify an electrical installation. Use competent specialists for the relevant systems.

Record the actual location, condition and affected activity. 'Shop needs attention' is too vague to drive correction. Link each finding to a specific risk and owner without claiming an entire facility safe from a narrow sample.

## Worked field example

A manager declares the whole yard ready after inspecting only the office corridor.

The safe decision is to inspect the relevant operating areas and state the limits of the completed sample. A narrow walk-through cannot establish readiness of unobserved tasks and areas.

A useful field record is specific: An area/task inspection record identifying coverage and unassessed locations. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

## Detailed field application

A facility inspection should have an understandable route and scope. Identify the areas in use, the activities occurring, the shifts represented and any location that cannot be accessed safely. Do not enter a restricted technical area merely to complete the checklist. Arrange the appropriate competent inspection and state the gap.

Look beyond a static photograph. Receiving, maintenance and shift change can create different conditions from a quiet office visit. Workers can explain where queues form, stock accumulates or emergency access becomes difficult. Include their information while separating reported concerns from direct observations.

An inspector should describe what they actually checked. A general walk-through may confirm a visible route was clear at that time; it does not establish structural rack capacity, electrical integrity or fire-system performance. Those need their own appropriate examinations. Keeping the distinction visible makes the final conclusion more useful and prevents a broad readiness label from concealing unassessed systems.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 - Keep fire and emergency access usable
lessons.body:
Check exits, escape routes, alarms, emergency equipment and responder access through the facility plan. Access must remain usable during operations, not just while the inspector is present. Stored materials in front of an exit create an immediate issue requiring correction and control.

Do not move stock into another emergency route to clear the first one. Review where material should be received and stored so the obstruction does not recur. The responsible owner should verify the route remains clear during busy periods.

A general inspection can identify an obstructed extinguisher or damaged sign, but technical fire-system testing and design belong to qualified people. Do not mark systems tested when only their external appearance was checked.

## Worked field example

Pallets block an emergency exit and are repeatedly returned there after inspections.

The safe decision is to clear and maintain the exit and change the storage arrangement to prevent recurrence. A temporarily cleared route is not an effective control if normal storage recreates the obstruction.

A useful field record is specific: A verified clear route and sustainable assigned storage arrangement checked during operations. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

## Detailed field application

Fire and emergency access must remain usable when the facility is busy. Review the path from occupied areas to the designated exit and the approach for responders, considering doors, gates, stored items and vehicle queues. A clear doorway with an obstructed approach is not complete access.

If an exit is blocked, correct the immediate condition through safe handling and prevent its return. The supervisor should identify the storage decision that created the obstruction. A temporary overflow area may be needed through a reviewed layout; moving stock to another critical route is not an acceptable closure.

Emergency equipment should be accessible and its required technical status verified through the proper system. A general inspector can note a damaged item, missing sign or blocked cabinet. They must not mark an alarm system functionally tested merely because a light is illuminated or a service label is visible.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 - Control storage and cylinders
lessons.body:
Review storage for stability, compatibility, access and handling. Check racking and restraints through the approved system, and report damage rather than guessing remaining capacity. Avoid overloading or unstable stacking and keep people clear of falling-object paths.

Cylinders require suitable identification, securing, protection and segregation under the applicable product and facility requirements. Do not treat all cylinders as interchangeable because they share a shape. Confirm the contents and appropriate handling method.

Technical design, inspection and repair of pressure or storage systems require the appropriate competent authority. A general worker can recognize a damaged or unsecured item and stop exposure without pretending to certify it.

## Worked field example

An unidentified cylinder is standing unsecured beside a busy workshop route.

The safe decision is to restrict the immediate exposure and obtain the approved identification and secure-storage arrangement. Unknown contents and unstable placement cannot be cleared by a general visual check.

A useful field record is specific: A verified cylinder identity and suitable secured storage checked by the responsible role. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

## Detailed field application

Storage review considers the item, support and handling sequence. Look for unstable stacks, damaged racks, projecting material and loads that require unsafe access. Do not climb an improvised stack to read a label or estimate capacity. The responsible specialist evaluates damaged structural storage where needed.

Cylinder handling requires the approved method for the actual contents and package. A cap, valve or securing device should not be used in an unapproved way to move the cylinder. Keep identification and storage arrangements reliable so a new shift does not confuse gases or assume a returned cylinder is empty.

Where materials are incompatible or require special conditions, the facility owner obtains the relevant product and technical guidance. Alphabetical storage or available floor space alone is not a compatibility assessment. The inspection record identifies the observed condition, immediate protection and competent decision needed.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 - Recognize electrical and equipment defects
lessons.body:
Inspect visible condition through the safe checklist: damaged leads, covers, plugs, exposed parts, compromised guards or blocked controls. Do not open electrical enclosures or defeat guards to complete a general inspection. Report and isolate through authorized roles when a serious defect is found.

Wet conditions and temporary supplies can change suitability. A device used safely at a dry bench may be unsuitable in another location. Follow the approved equipment and electrical process rather than improvising protective arrangements.

Repairs and technical testing require the applicable competence. A repair invoice or a newly attached label does not prove that the actual defective item is serviceable. Verify equipment identity and release status before use.

## Worked field example

A damaged extension lead is still powering equipment in a wet workshop area.

The safe decision is to stop reliance on the defective supply through the authorized process and obtain competent correction. Visible damage and changed conditions require action rather than a favorable checklist mark.

A useful field record is specific: A defect record linked to the actual lead and verified competent repair or replacement. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

## Detailed field application

Visible defects can require action before a technical examination is complete. A damaged lead, exposed part or compromised guard should be reported and controlled through the authorized process. A worker does not need to prove an electrical fault by touching or opening equipment.

Identify the actual item and location so maintenance cannot repair a similar unit while the defective one remains in use. Mark or segregate equipment as the procedure requires and communicate any fixed-area restriction to the operating shift. A work-order number does not itself establish that exposure is controlled.

After repair or replacement, verify identity, service status and the required release through the competent authority. The general inspector checks the field arrangement and relevant evidence without claiming to have conducted technical tests they did not perform. The user still completes applicable pre-use checks before work.

lessons.title: Lesson 5 - Prioritize and own corrective action
lessons.body:
High-consequence hazards need immediate control, such as stopping affected use or restricting access, while correction is arranged. Other findings still need an owner, due date, interim controls and a clear verification method. A color on a spreadsheet does not itself protect workers.

Describe the expected outcome, not merely an activity. 'Purchase a shelf' is an action; 'store the items stably without blocking access' is the result to verify. Track dependencies so a delayed contractor repair does not silently remove interim protection.

Escalate overdue or ineffective controls through the accountable manager. Do not close a finding because the responsible person is on leave or the issue has existed for years.

## Worked field example

An inspection finding remains overdue while its temporary barrier has been removed.

The safe decision is to restore suitable interim protection and escalate the unresolved correction to the accountable owner. An overdue task and lost interim control leave the original exposure unmanaged.

A useful field record is specific: An updated action record and field verification of effective interim protection. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

## Detailed field application

Corrective action should have a clear protective outcome. For a damaged barrier, the objective is not merely to order parts; it is to restore effective separation for the relevant route. The owner needs resources, authority and a method to verify the result. Interim controls remain until the intended safeguard is actually available.

Prioritization should consider consequence and exposure rather than the ease of closing a task. A simple housekeeping item may be easy to complete, but that does not make an unresolved critical electrical or fire-access issue acceptable. Escalate the serious condition through the appropriate operating role.

If a deadline passes, review the actual site state. A revised date must not quietly remove a restriction or imply that the condition improved. Record why the action remains open, who accepts the interim arrangement and when further escalation is required under the organization's process.

lessons.title: Lesson 6 - Verify sustained readiness
lessons.body:
After a correction, check the real area during representative work. A clear exit during shutdown may become blocked during receiving. A new rack may change vehicle routes or handling exposure. Involve the workers who use the arrangement and review new interactions.

Look for recurrence across areas and shifts. Repeated housekeeping findings may reflect poor storage capacity, unclear ownership or a receiving process that overloads space. Address the system rather than repeatedly instructing people to tidy up.

Keep conclusions bounded. An inspection is evidence of what was checked under recorded conditions, not a guarantee of all future safety. Separate technical examination records from the general walk-through and maintain their applicable status.

## Worked field example

A new storage rack clears an exit but blocks the forklift turning route during deliveries.

The safe decision is to review the changed layout and verify both emergency access and operating traffic controls. A correction can transfer risk into another part of the facility.

A useful field record is specific: A representative delivery observation and layout review showing both functions remain usable. It records observed conditions and the decision, rather than treating a signature as proof that the safeguard existed.

## Detailed field application

Follow-up should reproduce the conditions that generated the finding where safe and practicable. If deliveries block a route each Monday, a Friday shutdown photograph is weak effectiveness evidence. Observe receiving flow and ask the people doing the work whether the new storage method is usable.

A change can create a second problem. Adding a rack may reduce floor storage while narrowing a vehicle route or increasing difficult lifts. Review the changed layout as a whole, with competent technical input for any affected specialist system.

The final report should separate corrected conditions, verified effective changes, remaining restrictions and unassessed items. Preserve the original finding and supporting evidence. A clean inspection result under one set of conditions is bounded evidence, not a promise that every future shift is safe. Workers must continue to report defects and changes after the inspection is closed.

A useful shift handover identifies live facility restrictions, equipment out of service, temporary routes and outstanding technical inspections. The receiving supervisor confirms responsibility for maintaining interim controls. An unread action log does not establish that the next shift understands which area is restricted. If a barrier or alternative route cannot be maintained, the affected operation returns to the responsible authority for a safe decision.

Workers should have a practical reporting route between scheduled inspections. A newly blocked exit or damaged cable needs action when discovered, not at the next walk-through. Record the current condition, immediate response and owner. The inspection program then uses those reports to improve its sampling and prevention without pretending that the earlier favorable visit described all later conditions.

## Further application

Keep all remaining restrictions visible.

lessons.title: Two applied scenarios and worked solutions
lessons.body:
## Scenario 1

A fictional yard is preparing for a client visit. Workers move pallets away from an exit into a forklift turning area. An unsecured cylinder and damaged cable remain beside a bench. The inspection form has already been signed as satisfactory.

### Worked solution

The signed form is corrected to reflect the actual findings. Exit access is protected without transferring the storage into the traffic path. The cylinder and electrical defect are controlled through the responsible competent processes; a general inspector does not certify either by sight. The manager assigns owners and interim controls and checks the revised layout during real receiving work. Specialist technical records are obtained where required. The readiness conclusion states the inspected scope and unresolved restrictions. A client visit or a completed form does not authorize continued exposure to the observed defects.

## Scenario 2

A fictional facility clears the same emergency route every Friday, but deliveries block it again on Monday. The action log shows repeated completed housekeeping tasks with no layout change.

### Worked solution

The immediate obstruction is removed and the route kept available. Management then reviews storage capacity, receiving flow and ownership with the workers. A sustainable arrangement identifies where deliveries may wait and who prevents overflow into the route. Verification occurs during the period when obstruction normally recurs, not only after cleanup. The action remains open if the route is blocked again. The evidence distinguishes repeated activity from effective prevention. No technical approval is claimed for unassessed systems simply because the housekeeping result improves.

lessons.title: Final assessment - 20 questions
lessons.body: Answer each question without consulting an answer key. There are 20 final questions in addition to six lesson checks. Incorrect responses require reading and explicitly acknowledging the explanation. Both the first-attempt and remediated results must remain visible.

lessons.title: Finish - Practical evaluation and work authorization
