lessons.title: Start here — Corrective actions and effectiveness verification
lessons.body:
# I03: Corrective actions and effectiveness verification

Distinguish completing a task from fixing a safety weakness. This course teaches the decisions needed to implement that purpose in field operations. It covers cause-linked action, accountable owner, deadlines, interim controls and effectiveness review. The examples involve fictional oilfield crews and companies; none is a real incident record or evidence of a company's implementation.

Read six substantive lessons, answer each attached knowledge check, then study two applied cases and answer the twenty final questions. Every question has three choices and one correct answer. The course records the first answer separately from any correction. Completion requires all 26 answered correctly or acknowledged remediation, including reading the specific explanation for each correction. A remediated result must never replace the original score. There is no speed requirement: take the time needed to explain the decision in your own words.

The audience includes workers who recognize gaps, supervisors who coordinate work and program owners who maintain the system. Each has a different decision boundary. An observer may report an uncertain safeguard without personally being qualified to repair it. A supervisor may coordinate a hold without being the person authorized to clear a technical prerequisite. Learn both the action and the limit on that action.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Connect action to the failed control
lessons.body:
## Connect action to the failed control

Start with a clear finding: what protection was missing or ineffective, who was exposed and what evidence supports that conclusion. The corrective action must change that weakness. An attractive purchase or training session is not automatically relevant. Prefer effective control improvements over vague reminders where practicable, with competent technical review for methods and equipment changes. Keep the causal link visible so later reviewers can test whether the action did what was intended.

### Deeper application

State the failure narrowly enough to design a response but broadly enough to address its supported cause. Replace pedestrian conflict with the actual missing or ineffective separation arrangement and the conditions that allowed it. A technical solution may need competent design review. A procedural solution may need changes to allocation or supervision. Training can support a control, but should not be selected automatically when equipment or planning is the principal weakness.

### Worked oilfield example

A gate conflict finding identifies missing pedestrian separation, but the proposed action purchases unrelated office supplies. The decision is to define a reviewed action that addresses pedestrian separation and the process that left it uncontrolled.

Spending is not corrective effectiveness. The action must address the failed protection identified by evidence. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the action merely says improve safety without describing a control or outcome. The appropriate correction is to specify the actual control change and measurable intended protection before accepting the action. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. In this example, the follow-up should return to the actual gap described above, rather than simply asking whether the file now looks complete. A genuine unknown must remain visible until resolved by appropriate evidence.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Assign ownership deadlines and interim protection
lessons.body:
## Assign ownership deadlines and interim protection

Name one accountable owner with authority and resources, a justified due date and the restriction or temporary control protecting people meanwhile. Support roles can contribute without obscuring accountability. Escalate inability to meet the date before exposure is left uncontrolled. A due date is not permission to continue unsafe work until that date. Critical gaps may require immediate suspension of dependent activity.

### Deeper application

Ownership means the person can coordinate resources and escalate constraints, not that they personally perform every task. Assign supporting roles explicitly where needed. A temporary control should have a defined scope and review conditions. If it becomes unsuitable or cannot be maintained, stop dependent work or implement another approved arrangement. Moving a deadline without reexamining exposure leaves the original safety question unanswered.

### Worked oilfield example

Permanent route changes will take time, but workers continue crossing uncontrolled traffic while the action waits. The decision is to establish suitable interim protection or suspend dependent movement while the permanent correction is developed.

A future correction does not protect current work. Interim measures must address the actual exposure. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: An owned action with due date, resources, interim traffic arrangement and escalation conditions. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the named owner lacks authority to secure the required site change. The appropriate correction is to escalate ownership and resources while maintaining the protective restriction. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

An implementation record and a later effectiveness check answer different questions. The first shows whether the required action occurred within the stated scope. The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. In this example, the follow-up should return to the actual gap described above, rather than simply asking whether the file now looks complete. A genuine unknown must remain visible until resolved by appropriate evidence.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Define completion evidence before doing the work
lessons.body:
## Define completion evidence before doing the work

Specify what will show the action was implemented: installed control, approved instruction, verified allocation or observed performance as appropriate. A purchase order or invoice proves a transaction, not installation or usability. Decide who will check completion and the scope of that check. This helps prevent a checkbox being closed on the wrong evidence. Keep technical acceptance with the appropriately qualified person.

### Deeper application

Define completion in terms of the promised output. For a revised procedure, that may include approval, issue and withdrawal of obsolete operational copies. For an installed route, it may include appropriate installation and readiness review. The exact technical acceptance comes from the responsible competent source. Purchasing materials and scheduling a contractor can be progress milestones without being misrepresented as completion of the protective change.

### Worked oilfield example

An action to install a protected pedestrian route is marked complete when paint is purchased. The decision is to keep implementation open until the approved route is installed and its required readiness checks are complete.

Purchased materials are inputs. Completion evidence must show the specified control was actually implemented. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. ### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: An actual installation and readiness check linked to the approved route and remaining restrictions. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the route is painted but conflicts with an active reversing area. The appropriate correction is to obtain competent interface review and resolve the conflict before accepting the route for use. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Test effectiveness separately from completion
lessons.body:
## Test effectiveness separately from completion

Effectiveness asks whether the control achieves its purpose during relevant later work. Define the observation, sample or test before closure, including conditions where failure is plausible. A route installed today may need checking under night traffic or delivery peaks. Use suitable expertise and do not create exposure to test it. A favorable observation supports only its bounded scope, not every job in the company.

### Deeper application

An effectiveness question should be specific enough to fail. Are pedestrians using the separated route during busy night deliveries is testable; is everyone safer is too vague. Choose a representative safe observation or other appropriate method and state its limits. Lack of recurrence in a small sample is not universal proof, especially where reporting coverage is weak. Use worker feedback to identify practical difficulties that a tidy installation photograph hides.

### Worked oilfield example

A new walkway is installed, but nobody has checked whether arriving drivers actually use it during busy deliveries. The decision is to observe relevant later work safely and test whether separation works under representative conditions.

Implementation establishes that a change exists; effectiveness examines whether it protects people in real use. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A later representative traffic observation recording route use, conflicts and worker feedback. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the effectiveness sample includes only quiet daytime conditions despite a night-glare concern. The appropriate correction is to test under relevant night conditions with suitable protection before concluding the glare-related action works. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. In this example, the follow-up should return to the actual gap described above, rather than simply asking whether the file now looks complete. A genuine unknown must remain visible until resolved by appropriate evidence.

lessons.title: Lesson 5 — Verify with suitable challenge and records
lessons.body:
## Verify with suitable challenge and records

A verifier should have competence matching the judgment and enough separation to challenge unsupported closure. Record what was checked, when, by whom and with what limitations. Do not call a self-check independent. Separate completion status from effectiveness status so a manager can see work installed but follow-up pending. Preserve evidence and original findings; correction should add traceability rather than erase the problem.

### Deeper application

Verification should state which evidence was examined and what conclusion it supports. A reviewer can accept installation while leaving effectiveness pending. That is more accurate than forcing a single closed label to represent both. Where independence is required or claimed, explain the reviewer's actual relationship to the work. A technical acceptance should not be signed by someone whose role is only administrative file completion.

### Worked oilfield example

The action owner marks their own work independently verified without another suitable review. The decision is to describe the self-check accurately and obtain the required suitable verification before claiming that state.

Verification claims must reflect what occurred. A self-check cannot be represented as independent review. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. lessons.title: Lesson 6 — Reopen recurrence and escalate overdue risk
lessons.body:
## Reopen recurrence and escalate overdue risk

A failed effectiveness test or recurring weakness requires renewed control of exposure and reconsideration of the action. Preserve the closed record and link a reopening reason or new action as appropriate. Investigate whether the design, implementation or operating conditions differed from assumptions. Overdue actions need risk-based escalation, not silent date changes. Learning from recurrence should improve the system without automatically treating the incident count as the maturity score.

### Deeper application

Reopening does not mean the original work was never done. It means new evidence shows the intended protection remains unsupported or ineffective. Link the recurrence to the earlier finding, establish immediate protection and examine whether assumptions, design or implementation failed. Preserve previous decisions to learn from them. For overdue actions, escalate remaining risk and needed resources instead of merely changing dates to remove an overdue indicator.

### Worked oilfield example

A closed gate action is followed by the same pedestrian conflict under normal deliveries. The decision is to reopen the issue, protect the exposure and review why the correction failed.

A timely completed action can still be ineffective; recurrence is evidence requiring reassessment, not deletion. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A linked recurrence review with protective response, revised control and new effectiveness test. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the owner repeatedly extends dates without reviewing remaining exposure. The appropriate correction is to escalate the unresolved risk and verify interim protection with an accountable decision-maker. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. lessons.title: Two applied scenarios and fully worked solutions
lessons.body:
## Applied scenario 1: an incomplete decision chain

A gate conflict finding identifies missing pedestrian separation, but the proposed action purchases unrelated office supplies. At the handover, a second issue is identified: The named owner lacks authority to secure the required site change. The receiving supervisor has the earlier record but does not yet have evidence that the new issue was resolved. A colleague proposes the following shortcut: Accept the invoice as proof the route exists. Work is due to begin on the next shift, so the supervisor needs a defensible decision that protects people and preserves a clear history.

### Worked solution — immediate decision

The first response is: Define a reviewed action that addresses pedestrian separation and the process that left it uncontrolled. The reason is specific: Spending is not corrective effectiveness. The action must address the failed protection identified by evidence. Determine which assignment depends on that unresolved condition. Tell the affected people the restriction and who is coordinating resolution. If there is an immediate exposure, move to a safe position and use the established warning or emergency route rather than completing records first. The supervisor must not use a favorable overall company score as a substitute for this missing decision.

### Worked solution — resolve the additional issue

For the handover finding, the next action is: Escalate ownership and resources while maintaining the protective restriction. The supporting record should show: An owned action with due date, resources, interim traffic arrangement and escalation conditions. This is important because a future correction does not protect current work. Interim measures must address the actual exposure. The receiving shift needs the actual status, not an assurance that someone intends to finish the check later. Identify the responsible role and obtain acknowledgment of the restriction. If the required authority or expertise is unavailable, the affected assignment remains unready; unrelated authorized work may be considered only after its interfaces are checked.

### Worked solution — reject the shortcut and verify the result

The proposed shortcut fails because purchased materials are inputs. Completion evidence must show the specified control was actually implemented. The suitable decision is: Keep implementation open until the approved route is installed and its required readiness checks are complete. Evidence for review would include: An actual installation and readiness check linked to the approved route and remaining restrictions. Separate correction of the immediate problem from confirmation that the change works in later comparable conditions. A reviewer should check the actual control used and the scope represented by the evidence. If the same weakness recurs, reopen the issue and retain both the original decision and the new observation.

### What can be concluded

This solution establishes a bounded route from an identified gap to evidence and responsible acceptance. It does not establish that an assessment, clinical decision, technical test or employer authorization actually happened in a real company. The fictional case teaches how to decide and what to verify. Actual release remains with the designated employer/site authority after the applicable prerequisites are met.

Evidence for review would include: A linked recurrence review with protective response, revised control and new effectiveness test. A reviewer should check the actual control used and the scope represented by the evidence. If the same weakness recurs, reopen the issue and retain both the original decision and the new observation.

This solution establishes a bounded route from an identified gap to evidence and responsible acceptance. It does not establish that an assessment, clinical decision, technical test or employer authorization actually happened in a real company. The fictional case teaches how to decide and what to verify. Actual release remains with the designated employer/site authority after the applicable prerequisites are met.

lessons.title: Final assessment — twenty questions
lessons.body: Answer each question individually. Apply the taught decisions to the facts given. Your first choices are retained. If an answer is wrong, read the specific explanation and explicitly acknowledge the corrected answer. A corrected score records learning after feedback; it does not overwrite the first-answer result. All twenty final questions and all six lesson checks must be completed.

lessons.title: Finish — separate practical qualification
lessons.body:
## Written completion and what it proves

Completion requires all 26 answered correctly or acknowledged remediation. Both first-answer and remediated scores remain separate. Completing the guided course is evidence that you worked through its knowledge and decision questions; it is not an observed practical performance result, a legal license, a provider certification or an employer authorization. Training evidence contributes to review within its scope and validity, rather than automatically establishing the whole company program.

## What needs separate assessment

The assessment should test recognition of an abnormal condition as well as routine performance. A person who can repeat a procedure but cannot identify when to stop has not demonstrated the whole task. Employer authorization should state the person, tasks, equipment or site limits, required supervision and the basis for the decision. Applicable legal, issuer, client and change-trigger requirements govern validity; this course invents no universal renewal period.

## Before actual work

Confirm current local instructions, reporting routes, emergency arrangements and the person who can resolve an operating hold. If assigned work exceeds your assessed scope, say so before accepting it. The Partner's job/site readiness decision remains separate from the company's evidence review. Preserve real records through the authorized process and protect personal information. The fictional examples in this course must never be submitted as evidence that your company performed the actions described.

lessons.title: Start here — Learning alerts and post-job review
lessons.body:
# I04: Learning alerts and post-job review

Transfer learning between crews and repeat work. This course teaches the decisions needed to implement that purpose in field operations. It covers debrief, validate lesson, distribute, update controls and check understanding. The examples involve fictional oilfield crews and companies; none is a real incident record or evidence of a company's implementation.

Read six substantive lessons, answer each attached knowledge check, then study two applied cases and answer the twenty final questions. Every question has three choices and one correct answer. The course records the first answer separately from any correction. Completion requires all 26 answered correctly or acknowledged remediation, including reading the specific explanation for each correction. A remediated result must never replace the original score. There is no speed requirement: take the time needed to explain the decision in your own words.

The audience includes workers who recognize gaps, supervisors who coordinate work and program owners who maintain the system. Each has a different decision boundary. An observer may report an uncertain safeguard without personally being qualified to repair it. A supervisor may coordinate a hold without being the person authorized to clear a technical prerequisite. Learn both the action and the limit on that action.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Debrief the work people actually performed
lessons.body:
## Debrief the work people actually performed

A post-job review compares the intended plan with actual conditions, changes and results. Include the people doing the work and relevant interfaces, not only managers. Discuss what helped as well as what failed so effective safeguards can be preserved. Use factual examples and avoid turning the review into a blame session. A quiet job can still reveal weak controls or useful adaptations worth evaluating before repetition.

### Deeper application

Ask what the plan expected, what actually happened, why differences arose and what should be preserved or changed. Include useful adaptations, but assess them before turning them into standard practice. A worker workaround can reveal an impractical plan while also introducing new exposure. Review that tension with the relevant technical owner instead of automatically praising improvisation or blaming the worker for deviating from an unworkable method.

### Worked oilfield example

A maintenance job finishes without injury, but workers describe an unplanned access change that repeatedly placed them near vehicle movement. The decision is to record and review the access change and its exposure before repeating the job.

Successful outcome does not prove the method was adequately controlled; workers' observations reveal what actually occurred. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A factual debrief identifying the planned route, actual change, exposure and agreed next steps. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the debrief includes supervisors but excludes the crew who used the changed route. The appropriate correction is to obtain relevant worker accounts and update the review with their actual experience. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

An implementation record and a later effectiveness check answer different questions. The first shows whether the required action occurred within the stated scope. The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Validate the lesson before distributing it
lessons.body:
## Validate the lesson before distributing it

A lesson should identify the relevant condition, control and supported change. Distinguish established facts from possible causes and avoid publishing an early theory as a proven conclusion. Seek technical review when the proposed lesson affects a specialist method. Deidentify unnecessary personal information. A dramatic story can attract attention without providing accurate guidance; relevance and evidence matter more than impact.

### Deeper application

An alert should identify its evidence status. A preliminary message can warn of a known exposure while stating that causes remain under investigation. Later corrections should be traceable and redistributed to affected users. Avoid naming individuals or sharing medical details unless the authorized process genuinely requires it. The lesson should teach a relevant control decision, not rely on dramatic or stigmatizing descriptions to gain attention.

### Worked oilfield example

A draft alert says a detector failed, but the investigation has established only that no usable test record was available. The decision is to describe the verified evidence gap and qualify unresolved technical conclusions before distribution.

Learning must not turn missing evidence into an unsupported technical conclusion; inaccurate alerts can create new errors. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A reviewed alert separating verified facts, uncertainty and approved interim guidance. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that a specialist method change is included without competent technical review. The appropriate correction is to obtain the required technical review before issuing that change as operating guidance. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

An implementation record and a later effectiveness check answer different questions. The first shows whether the required action occurred within the stated scope. The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. In this example, the follow-up should return to the actual gap described above, rather than simply asking whether the file now looks complete. lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Translate learning into a specific change
lessons.body:
## Translate learning into a specific change

Information becomes operational learning when it changes planning, equipment, procedures, training or another relevant control. Identify who owns the change and which work packs or systems must be updated. An alert saying take care is weaker than a clear approved change responding to the failed control. Maintain temporary protection while permanent revisions are reviewed and issued. Do not let an alert become an uncontrolled substitute procedure.

### Deeper application

Assign the operational change to the owner of the system it affects. Planning lessons belong in work-pack preparation; equipment lessons may require technical modification; communication lessons may require a changed handover. One alert can trigger several linked actions without itself completing them. Preserve interim restrictions while the permanent revision is pending. The worker should not be left choosing between an email and an unchanged approved procedure.

### Worked oilfield example

A near-miss email recommends a new route, but the next work pack still directs traffic through the old crossing. The decision is to update and approve the applicable work pack and brief affected people before the next relevant movement.

A lesson must reach the instructions actually used; an email cannot resolve conflicting operational documents by itself. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A controlled work-pack revision linked to the alert and its approved traffic-control decision. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the revision is approved but obsolete field copies remain in the active binder. The appropriate correction is to withdraw obsolete operational copies and verify the current instructions are available to users. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Distribute to relevant people and check understanding
lessons.body:
## Distribute to relevant people and check understanding

Identify crews, shifts, subcontractors and planners whose work shares the exposure. Tailor the message to their decisions and communicate through usable understood channels. Ask recipients to explain the change and stop conditions, rather than relying only on a read receipt. Avoid flooding everyone with unrelated alerts; excessive distribution can hide relevant actions.

### Deeper application

Map recipients by exposure rather than seniority. A planner at another site may need the lesson if they prepare the same work, while an unrelated office group may not. Use understood communication and confirm what recipients will do differently. A read receipt can support delivery evidence but not comprehension.

### Worked oilfield example

Only day-shift employees receive an alert about delivery routing that also affects night subcontract drivers. The decision is to reach the affected night and subcontract drivers and check their understanding before the changed task.

Distribution must follow the exposure and actual users, not only the company's convenient mailing list. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A relevant recipient map with shift coverage, communication method and comprehension check. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that recipients acknowledge receipt but explain the old route during teach-back. The appropriate correction is to correct the misunderstanding and verify the actual new decision before relying on acknowledgment. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

An implementation record and a later effectiveness check answer different questions. The first shows whether the required action occurred within the stated scope. The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. lessons.title: Lesson 5 — Verify transfer into later work
lessons.body:
## Verify transfer into later work

Follow-up asks whether the next relevant job uses the change and whether it works in the intended conditions. Inspect planning records and safely observe implementation where appropriate. A learning alert count or signature total is not evidence of transfer. If the change creates new difficulties, feed those facts back into competent review rather than blaming workers for not adopting an impractical method. Bound the conclusion to the sample checked.

### Deeper application

Transfer is demonstrated when a later comparable job incorporates the accepted change and people can apply it. Trace the revised plan to actual setup and behavior using a suitable safe method. If the change is not used, examine availability, clarity and practicality before assuming resistance. A lesson that creates another conflict needs further competent review. Keep the follow-up conclusion bounded by the conditions actually sampled.

### Worked oilfield example

An alert is closed after distribution, but the next crew repeats the unchanged setup and the same access conflict. The decision is to reopen the learning action and correct the implementation gap before further affected work.

Learning requires changed practice and appropriate follow-up; distribution alone cannot establish transfer. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A later job sample linking the approved change to actual setup, worker explanation and observed result. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the follow-up verifies the new document but never checks the setup it describes. The appropriate correction is to add suitable observation or equivalent evidence of actual implementation before concluding transfer occurred. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

An implementation record and a later effectiveness check answer different questions. The first shows whether the required action occurred within the stated scope. The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. In this example, the follow-up should return to the actual gap described above, rather than simply asking whether the file now looks complete. lessons.title: Lesson 6 — Maintain a traceable learning system
lessons.body:
## Maintain a traceable learning system

Preserve the source event, reviewed lesson, controlled changes, recipients and later results as a connected history. Update or withdraw superseded alerts from operational use while retaining archival records. A correction should say what changed and why. Protect confidential details and distinguish fictional training cases from real company evidence. Review whether similar work elsewhere needs the lesson, but do not claim an alert proves every site's effectiveness.

### Deeper application

A learning record should connect source, approved message, controlled changes, recipients and later results. Superseded operational guidance must be withdrawn while historical versions remain available for audit. If the original conclusion changes, explain why and who is affected. Do not overwrite the event record or quietly leave two competing instructions active. Deidentified learning can travel between crews without exposing unnecessary personal information.

### Worked oilfield example

An alert's technical guidance is corrected, but an earlier copy remains pinned in the workshop as current instruction. The decision is to withdraw the superseded operational alert and communicate the correction to affected users.

Traceability preserves learning while preventing obsolete guidance from continuing to direct work. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A versioned alert history showing the correction, operational withdrawal and confirmed redistribution. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the correction was archived but never sent to a contractor who received the first alert. The appropriate correction is to notify that affected contractor and verify the current applicable message is understood. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. In this example, the follow-up should return to the actual gap described above, rather than simply asking whether the file now looks complete. lessons.title: Two applied scenarios and fully worked solutions
lessons.body:
## Applied scenario 1: an incomplete decision chain

A maintenance job finishes without injury, but workers describe an unplanned access change that repeatedly placed them near vehicle movement. At the handover, a second issue is identified: A specialist method change is included without competent technical review. The receiving supervisor has the earlier record but does not yet have evidence that the new issue was resolved. A colleague proposes the following shortcut: Treat the email as proof the operational change is complete. Work is due to begin on the next shift, so the supervisor needs a defensible decision that protects people and preserves a clear history.

### Worked solution — immediate decision

The first response is: Record and review the access change and its exposure before repeating the job. The reason is specific: Successful outcome does not prove the method was adequately controlled; workers' observations reveal what actually occurred. Determine which assignment depends on that unresolved condition. Tell the affected people the restriction and who is coordinating resolution. If there is an immediate exposure, move to a safe position and use the established warning or emergency route rather than completing records first. The supervisor must not use a favorable overall company score as a substitute for this missing decision.

### Worked solution — resolve the additional issue

For the handover finding, the next action is: Obtain the required technical review before issuing that change as operating guidance. The supporting record should show: A reviewed alert separating verified facts, uncertainty and approved interim guidance. This is important because learning must not turn missing evidence into an unsupported technical conclusion; inaccurate alerts can create new errors. The receiving shift needs the actual status, not an assurance that someone intends to finish the check later. Identify the responsible role and obtain acknowledgment of the restriction. If the required authority or expertise is unavailable, the affected assignment remains unready; unrelated authorized work may be considered only after its interfaces are checked.

### Worked solution — reject the shortcut and verify the result

The proposed shortcut fails because a lesson must reach the instructions actually used; an email cannot resolve conflicting operational documents by itself. The suitable decision is: Update and approve the applicable work pack and brief affected people before the next relevant movement. Evidence for review would include: A controlled work-pack revision linked to the alert and its approved traffic-control decision. Separate correction of the immediate problem from confirmation that the change works in later comparable conditions. A reviewer should check the actual control used and the scope represented by the evidence. If the same weakness recurs, reopen the issue and retain both the original decision and the new observation.

### What can be concluded

This solution establishes a bounded route from an identified gap to evidence and responsible acceptance. It does not establish that an assessment, clinical decision, technical test or employer authorization actually happened in a real company. The fictional case teaches how to decide and what to verify. Actual release remains with the designated employer/site authority after the applicable prerequisites are met.

## Applied scenario 2: an incomplete decision chain

Only day-shift employees receive an alert about delivery routing that also affects night subcontract drivers. At the handover, a second issue is identified: The follow-up verifies the new document but never checks the setup it describes. The receiving supervisor has the earlier record but does not yet have evidence that the new issue was resolved. A colleague proposes the following shortcut: Delete the source event so nobody notices the changed advice. Work is due to begin on the next shift, so the supervisor needs a defensible decision that protects people and preserves a clear history.

### Worked solution — immediate decision

The first response is: Reach the affected night and subcontract drivers and check their understanding before the changed task. The reason is specific: Distribution must follow the exposure and actual users, not only the company's convenient mailing list. Determine which assignment depends on that unresolved condition. Tell the affected people the restriction and who is coordinating resolution. If there is an immediate exposure, move to a safe position and use the established warning or emergency route rather than completing records first. ### Worked solution — resolve the additional issue

For the handover finding, the next action is: Add suitable observation or equivalent evidence of actual implementation before concluding transfer occurred. The supporting record should show: A later job sample linking the approved change to actual setup, worker explanation and observed result. This is important because learning requires changed practice and appropriate follow-up; distribution alone cannot establish transfer. The receiving shift needs the actual status, not an assurance that someone intends to finish the check later. Identify the responsible role and obtain acknowledgment of the restriction. ### Worked solution — reject the shortcut and verify the result

The proposed shortcut fails because traceability preserves learning while preventing obsolete guidance from continuing to direct work. The suitable decision is: Withdraw the superseded operational alert and communicate the correction to affected users. Evidence for review would include: A versioned alert history showing the correction, operational withdrawal and confirmed redistribution. Separate correction of the immediate problem from confirmation that the change works in later comparable conditions. A reviewer should check the actual control used and the scope represented by the evidence. If the same weakness recurs, reopen the issue and retain both the original decision and the new observation.

### What can be concluded

This solution establishes a bounded route from an identified gap to evidence and responsible acceptance. It does not establish that an assessment, clinical decision, technical test or employer authorization actually happened in a real company. The fictional case teaches how to decide and what to verify. Actual release remains with the designated employer/site authority after the applicable prerequisites are met.

lessons.title: Final assessment — twenty questions
lessons.body: Answer each question individually. Apply the taught decisions to the facts given. Your first choices are retained. If an answer is wrong, read the specific explanation and explicitly acknowledge the corrected answer. A corrected score records learning after feedback; it does not overwrite the first-answer result. All twenty final questions and all six lesson checks must be completed.

lessons.title: Finish — separate practical qualification
lessons.body:
## Written completion and what it proves

Completion requires all 26 answered correctly or acknowledged remediation. Both first-answer and remediated scores remain separate. Completing the guided course is evidence that you worked through its knowledge and decision questions; it is not an observed practical performance result, a legal license, a provider certification or an employer authorization. Training evidence contributes to review within its scope and validity, rather than automatically establishing the whole company program.

## What needs separate assessment

The assessment should test recognition of an abnormal condition as well as routine performance. A person who can repeat a procedure but cannot identify when to stop has not demonstrated the whole task. Employer authorization should state the person, tasks, equipment or site limits, required supervision and the basis for the decision. Applicable legal, issuer, client and change-trigger requirements govern validity; this course invents no universal renewal period.

## Before actual work

Confirm current local instructions, reporting routes, emergency arrangements and the person who can resolve an operating hold. If assigned work exceeds your assessed scope, say so before accepting it. The Partner's job/site readiness decision remains separate from the company's evidence review. Preserve real records through the authorized process and protect personal information. The fictional examples in this course must never be submitted as evidence that your company performed the actions described.

lessons.title: Start here — Incident history and exposure-data integrity
lessons.body:
# I05: Incident history and exposure-data integrity

Keep transparent event context without treating zero reports as maturity. This course teaches the decisions needed to implement that purpose in field operations. It covers consistent definitions, hours/population, period, corrections and privacy controls. The examples involve fictional oilfield crews and companies; none is a real incident record or evidence of a company's implementation.

Read six substantive lessons, answer each attached knowledge check, then study two applied cases and answer the twenty final questions. Every question has three choices and one correct answer. The course records the first answer separately from any correction. Completion requires all 26 answered correctly or acknowledged remediation, including reading the specific explanation for each correction. A remediated result must never replace the original score. There is no speed requirement: take the time needed to explain the decision in your own words.

The audience includes workers who recognize gaps, supervisors who coordinate work and program owners who maintain the system. Each has a different decision boundary. An observer may report an uncertain safeguard without personally being qualified to repair it. A supervisor may coordinate a hold without being the person authorized to clear a technical prerequisite. Learn both the action and the limit on that action.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Define the population period and measures
lessons.body:
## Define the population period and measures

An incident summary needs a defined time period, workforce and event definitions. State whether employees, subcontractors or both are included and how hours are attributed. A company-wide count cannot be compared with a single-site denominator. Separate actual events from reporting activity and maturity review. A favorable outcome history is not proof that the underlying safety practices are implemented or effective.

### Deeper application

Write a measure definition before entering numbers. Identify the event category, time period, included workforce and exposure units. Distinguish employee hours from contractor hours and site-specific work from the whole business. A statement such as no events may be valid for one bounded population but misleading when displayed as all-company history. Keep the scope alongside the figure so it survives export and presentation.

### Worked oilfield example

A vendor combines subcontractor incidents with employee-only hours and presents the resulting rate as company-wide. The decision is to reconcile a consistent event and exposure population before calculating or comparing the measure.

A rate requires compatible numerator and denominator scope; real numbers can still produce a misleading comparison. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A period and population definition linking included event categories to matching exposure sources. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the report says year-to-date but includes hours from a different cutoff date. The appropriate correction is to align the event and exposure period and disclose the correction before using the measure. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

An implementation record and a later effectiveness check answer different questions. The first shows whether the required action occurred within the stated scope. The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. In this example, the follow-up should return to the actual gap described above, rather than simply asking whether the file now looks complete. A genuine unknown must remain visible until resolved by appropriate evidence.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Reconcile exposure data to traceable sources
lessons.body:
## Reconcile exposure data to traceable sources

Identify where hours or other exposure measures come from and what they represent. Payroll, timekeeping and subcontractor submissions may use different cutoffs or include nonworking categories. Reconcile differences rather than choosing the largest denominator. Keep source references and review notes so another suitable reviewer can reproduce the summary. Do not invent missing hours or assume a standard number for each worker without an approved valid basis.

### Deeper application

Reconciliation explains differences rather than concealing them. One source may include leave, another only productive hours, and a subcontractor may submit on a different cutoff. Determine which values match the defined exposure and document justified adjustments. Two accurate source totals can legitimately differ because they measure different things. Do not resolve that difference by selecting whichever denominator gives the most favorable rate.

### Worked oilfield example

Timekeeping and payroll show different hours, and the preparer selects the higher figure because it lowers the reported rate. The decision is to investigate the scope and cutoff differences and use a supported consistent exposure total.

The denominator must represent the defined exposure. Choosing a convenient number distorts the measure. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A reconciliation documenting source definitions, differences, adjustments and accepted exposure total. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the reconciliation includes office hours while the stated measure covers only a field contract. The appropriate correction is to correct the exposure scope and retain the adjustment trail and calculation basis. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

An implementation record and a later effectiveness check answer different questions. The first shows whether the required action occurred within the stated scope. The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. In this example, the follow-up should return to the actual gap described above, rather than simply asking whether the file now looks complete. A genuine unknown must remain visible until resolved by appropriate evidence.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Distinguish verified zero from missing coverage
lessons.body:
## Distinguish verified zero from missing coverage

No reports received, verified zero events and unknown reporting coverage are different states. A zero requires a defined covered population and appropriate source checks. If subcontractors did not submit information, label the gap instead of assuming zero. A blank field should not become a favorable number. Explain what is known and what evidence is still needed before presenting a complete history.

### Deeper application

A verified zero needs a defined coverage statement and appropriate checks of relevant sources. No email received is evidence only about that inbox, not the whole workforce. Mark missing submissions and unknown periods separately. Where part of the population is verified, report that bounded result without extending it to the unverified part. A blank or unavailable measure must not appear as a green zero in a dashboard.

### Worked oilfield example

A vendor reports zero incidents but cannot confirm whether any subcontractor supplied event information. The decision is to show subcontractor coverage as unknown and reconcile it before claiming a complete zero.

Missing information is not evidence of absence. A zero must be bounded by verified reporting coverage. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A coverage declaration identifying checked sources, confirmed zero scope and outstanding gaps. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that employee coverage is verified but the summary labels the whole company zero. The appropriate correction is to limit the claim to the verified population and disclose the unresolved coverage separately. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

An implementation record and a later effectiveness check answer different questions. The first shows whether the required action occurred within the stated scope. The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. In this example, the follow-up should return to the actual gap described above, rather than simply asking whether the file now looks complete. lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Calculate only supported comparisons
lessons.body:
## Calculate only supported comparisons

Before calculating a rate, verify event definitions, exposure units, population, period and any normalization basis required by the intended measure. This course does not invent a universal formula or compare unrelated rates. Small denominators can make changes unstable; explain limits rather than treating a rank as a precise measure of competence. For a fictional count, two qualifying events over a defined exposure are meaningful only once the relevant measure's basis is established.

### Deeper application

Use the specified normalization and category rules for the intended measure, with an authoritative basis where needed. This course deliberately does not provide one rate formula for every comparison. Explain small exposure and incompatible definitions rather than ranking numbers without context. A measure can be unavailable while the underlying event count is known; do not invent exposure data to force every cell into a numeric format.

### Worked oilfield example

A customer asks for a rate comparison, but the vendors use different event definitions and one lacks verified hours. The decision is to mark the comparison unsupported and explain the missing compatible definitions and exposure evidence.

A numerical comparison is only meaningful when its inputs and definitions are compatible and known. This is a decision about the described conditions, rather than a conclusion that every related activity is unsafe. Identify which people and assignments depend on the unresolved point. Maintain the relevant restriction while the responsible person checks the facts; avoid spreading an unsupported approval to another crew or task.

### What the record must show

Useful evidence would be: A measure specification and compatibility review showing why a calculation or comparison is supported or unavailable. Record what was actually checked and the scope of that check. Distinguish the observation from an opinion about it. A record of the decision should allow the next responsible person to tell what is accepted, what remains unresolved and whose authority is needed. If a check has not occurred, state that it is pending. Do not convert a planned check into a completed result.

### A later challenge to the decision

During follow-up, the reviewer finds that the underlying data is valid but the displayed rate uses an undocumented normalization factor. The appropriate correction is to establish and disclose the applicable measure basis and recalculate transparently if needed. This additional fact changes what can be relied on. Preserve the earlier record and add the correction with its reason; quietly rewriting history would hide how the gap arose. Confirm that anyone relying on the earlier status receives the changed restriction before the next affected assignment.

### Applying the distinction

An implementation record and a later effectiveness check answer different questions. The first shows whether the required action occurred within the stated scope. The second examines whether its intended protection works during relevant later work. Neither an unrelated credential nor a completed form answers both questions. In this example, the follow-up should return to the actual gap described above, rather than simply asking whether the file now looks complete.
