Training and demonstrated capability must match the function. Familiarity with a site is useful information; it is not a substitute for role qualification.

Before an incident, understand the actions expected of you. If your employer’s emergency plan directs evacuation and notification, follow that plan. Do not convert yourself into a responder because a customer requests help or because a spill kit is visible. If you are part of a response team, confirm the actual role, equipment, procedures, team organization and current training. A certificate with a broad title does not explain which duties the employer has assessed and authorized.

Defensive work does not automatically mean zero exposure or unlimited authority. Protecting an unaffected area can still require suitable equipment, competent direction and a safe position. Approaching a leaking valve to tighten it is source-control work; calling it “just a quick turn” does not remove its hazards. Do not cross a protective boundary or change roles without the incident organization’s approval and the required capability.

An online quiz cannot simulate all of the decisions and physical demands of response. Workers also need any required medical fitness and employer arrangements. For your own record, identify the exact training completed and any supervised experience or evaluation still required. Never convert this foundation’s completion into a specialist response endorsement or erase a practical requirement because the learner achieved a corrected score of 100%.

lessons.title: Understand zones, accountability and decontamination
lessons.body:
Response zones control who enters, what work occurs and how contamination is managed. Their location depends on the incident assessment and must be adjusted as conditions change. Treat a boundary as an operating control. A person without the required assignment, equipment and permission must not enter simply because the work area appears quiet. An apparently unaffected worker or tool may still carry contamination.

Check in and out through the designated accountability process. Team leaders must know who is inside, the duties being performed and whether communications and backup arrangements are working. If your assignment changes, make that change visible through the incident organization. Walking to another sector without telling anyone can turn a manageable interruption into a missing-person emergency. If a check-in or communication control fails, follow the stop/withdrawal instructions rather than continuing on assumptions.

Decontamination is part of the work plan, not an afterthought at the parking lot. The method must suit the substance, protective equipment and potential exposure. Do not invent a rinse or mix cleaning agents to deal with unknown contamination. An improvised wash can spread contamination, react with a chemical or damage protective equipment. Qualified personnel must establish the method and manage contaminated water, clothing, tools and waste.

Keep clean and potentially contaminated items separated through the designated process. Do not place gloves, sampling tools or work clothing on vehicle seats, lunch tables or shared desks. A worker who leaves the scene should not carry an unresolved exposure into a medical waiting area without notifying the emergency/medical team. Emergency care must not be delayed, but responders and clinicians need accurate information so they can protect everyone involved.

For nonresponders, understanding the system means respecting the boundaries and reporting a breach. It does not mean setting zones or operating decontamination yourself. If you see a contaminated person moving into a clean area, alert the incident organization from a safe position and follow its instructions; do not create an additional exposure by grabbing the person or their equipment.

lessons.title: Communicate exposure and rescue information without creating another casualty
lessons.body:
An incident can expose a worker through breathing, skin or eye contact, ingestion from contamination or a physical injury associated with the response. Symptoms and visible contamination do not always tell you the full exposure. Report a suspected exposure promptly through the emergency and medical process. Give the actual observations, the task, known substances and relevant equipment information. Do not make a diagnosis or declare someone safe because they say they feel better.

If someone becomes unresponsive in a hazardous area, call for the designated rescue response and provide the last known location. Do not rush into an unknown atmosphere. An unprotected rescuer can become another casualty and complicate access for the trained team. The response plan must establish rescue capability suitable for the hazard and work; a generic emergency telephone number does not demonstrate that a team can carry out the required rescue.

Use the agreed communication method and keep messages concise enough to act on. State who you are, where you are, what happened, who may be affected and what help is needed. If a fact is unknown, say so. Avoid speculative messages that might cause someone to use the wrong route, protective equipment or treatment information. Keep sensitive health details within the people who need them for care and incident management.

Equipment alarms or monitoring results have defined limits. A normal reading from an unsuitable instrument cannot prove that an area is safe. Do not use your personal detector to clear an area unless you hold the specific gas-testing assignment and have suitable equipment, methods and authorization. Give responders the reading and its context when requested: the device, location, time and what it was capable of measuring. The incident organization must interpret it alongside the other information.

After reporting, follow the instruction for your role. Workers directed to evacuate should account for themselves and communicate relevant observations from the assembly location. Returning to retrieve a phone, sample or tool is still a re-entry and needs authorization; personal property does not justify exposure.

lessons.title: Control the handoff from emergency response to cleanup
lessons.body:
Stopping an active release and cleaning up afterward are different phases. The end of visible leaking does not establish that the site is ready for ordinary work. Residues, contaminated soil, damaged equipment, pressure, vapors or unstable containers can remain. The responsible organization must define the handoff: what has been stabilized, what hazards remain, which controls continue and who has authority over the next operation.

Workers joining later must receive the information needed for their actual cleanup duties. Do not treat them as covered by the briefing given to the initial response team. A separate cleanup crew may need a different training program, site plan, medical arrangements, equipment and supervised experience. The employer must determine the applicable requirements. A previous responder’s presence or a contractor’s logo does not establish that every new worker is ready.

Inspect the work authorization against the current phase. A waste-haul driver may be authorized to collect characterized, packaged material from a designated clean transfer point without being assigned to enter the contaminated work zone. A cleanup technician may have authority to handle waste within a defined method while lacking authority to repair the damaged process. Keep these boundaries visible in the handoff and stop when the next request goes beyond them.

Preserve trustworthy training and task evidence. A record of attendance is not a demonstration of every response skill. A completion certificate must not be renamed to imply hours, field experience or endorsements that were not provided.

Before re-entry or restart, obtain the designated authorization after the required checks are complete. If the cleanup reveals another unidentified container, unexpected atmosphere or a damaged isolation, the earlier release decision may no longer cover the task. Stop the affected work and return the new facts to the responsible people. The safe outcome is an explicit, verified handoff, not a clean-looking photograph with unresolved hazards outside the frame.

lessons.title: Two worked scenarios and decisions
lessons.body:
Scenario 1 — “Just absorb it.” A yard worker assigned to receive sealed waste containers finds a damaged package with an unfamiliar liquid spreading toward a drain. A customer says it is only a small amount and points to the spill kit. Another worker reports eye irritation.

The correct first decision is to stop the receiving task and move clear without entering the liquid or vapor area. The package condition and symptoms do not match a controlled sealed-container receipt. The worker reports the location, the damaged package, the apparent drain direction and the affected person. The worker does not identify the chemical by smell or repeat the customer’s guess as a confirmed fact. The designated response organization evaluates the conditions and controls access. Only appropriately assigned people take response action under the applicable arrangements.

Why not put absorbent down immediately? The worker does not know the substance, whether the absorbent is suitable, whether approach is safe or whether the task exceeds the assigned response level. A small puddle can coexist with a significant inhalation hazard. Why not walk to the drain for a closer look? That would add an exposure without resolving the missing competence. A safe-position report of the possible migration gives responders useful information without pretending that the observation is a complete assessment.

Before receiving resumes, the responsible people must establish what was released, what controls and cleanup remain, whether the affected worker needs care and which parts of the operation are authorized. A customer’s statement that the incident is over cannot replace that handoff.

Scenario 2 — A second crew after stabilization. A qualified response team stops a release from process equipment. Later, a waste-haul driver and a separate cleanup crew arrive. The supervisor suggests that everyone use the response team’s clearance and begin removing material. A cleanup worker notices an unlabelled container outside the original assessed area.

The correct decision is to define the next phase and each role. The driver’s job may be receiving characterized, correctly packaged material at a designated transfer point; it does not necessarily include entry into the contaminated area. The cleanup crew needs the applicable qualification, site briefing, protective arrangements, decontamination method and task authorization. The unlabelled container is new information that the original response decision did not resolve.

The cleanup worker stops the affected task and reports the container from a safe position. The organization assesses and characterizes the new issue before expanding the work. It does not ask the driver to sample it merely because the driver has a waste-training record. It also preserves the distinction between emergency response qualification and the training required for the new cleanup duties.

The correct closeout records the actual stabilized condition, residual restrictions, transferred responsibilities and remaining work. A photograph of a dry floor or a copied certificate would not establish these facts. Restart and return to ordinary work require the designated verified authorization.

lessons.title: Final assessment
lessons.body: Answer each final decision using the taught role boundaries and handoff process. A wrong first answer remains recorded and must be explicitly remediated. No final answer grants a response role.

lessons.title: Finish the knowledge course; preserve the open requirements
lessons.body:
After all checks, scenarios and final questions are accomplished, this foundation knowledge course is complete. Retain both scores. Do not record this course as a 24-hour, 40-hour, response-level or annual refresher program.

If your next work request exceeds the scope established for you, state the specific missing qualification or authorization and notify the responsible supervisor. A software completion status is useful evidence of this teaching; it cannot resolve an unidentified substance, provide field experience or make an unsupported entry safe.

## Legal requirements for the named work role
These apply only when you perform the work described below. They are not additional steps for completing this online course.

29 CFR 1910.134(e), (f), (k)(1) — Required respirator users; tight-fitting facepieces require the applicable fit test: Complete the required medical evaluation before fit testing or use, the applicable fit test, and training that enables demonstration of the listed knowledge and respirator-use skills. These duties apply to the actual respirator assignment, not everyone taking awareness training. Source: https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.134

29 CFR 1910.120(e)(3), (e)(4), (q)(6) — Workers whose actual hazardous-waste or emergency-response duties fall within the cited provisions: Apply the training and supervised field-experience or response-role competence requirements specified for that actual assignment. Do not assign the hazardous-waste field-experience requirement to ordinary waste handling or awareness-only roles. Source: https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.120

questions.prompt: A routine sealed-container pickup reveals leaking drums and an unidentified vapor. What should the pickup worker do?

options.label: Continue because the order says routine disposal.
Stop the dependent task from a safe location and report the changed conditions.
Open a drum to identify the material.

questions.prompt: Which fact alone is enough to label an unfamiliar release incidental?

options.label: It looks like less than one bucket.
It is near a spill kit.
Neither fact establishes that available people and controls can safely manage it.

questions.prompt: Your assigned role is evacuation and notification. A customer asks you to enter a restricted area and tighten a leaking valve. What is correct?

options.label: Remain outside your role boundary and request the designated qualified response.
Enter if the task should take less than a minute.
Put on available gloves and proceed.

questions.prompt: A response worker wants to place potentially contaminated gloves in a clean crew vehicle. What is the appropriate action?

options.label: Allow it if the gloves look dry.
Keep them in the controlled contamination/decontamination process and notify the responsible team.
Rinse them with any available cleaning chemical.

questions.prompt: A person is down inside an unidentified vapor area. You have no assigned rescue qualification. What should you do?

options.label: Enter while holding your breath.
Use a normal personal-detector reading as clearance.
Stay clear, activate the designated rescue response and report the location and known facts.

questions.prompt: After the leak is stopped, a separate crew arrives for cleanup. What must be established?

options.label: That the new crew has the applicable training, briefing, equipment, controls and authorization for its actual cleanup duties.
That any initial response certificate covers everyone.
That visible dryness proves the area is safe.

questions.prompt: Does a waste-disposal service label establish HAZWOPER coverage?

options.label: No; the actual operation, exposure and applicable provisions must be assessed.
Yes, for every worker in the company.
No safety requirements can apply to routine waste.

questions.prompt: What can change a routine pickup into an unresolved hazard?

options.label: A customer changing the invoice address.
Finding leaking containers and an unknown vapor.
A vehicle having clean tires.

questions.prompt: Which observation proves an unknown spill is incidental?

options.label: Small visible volume.
A spill kit in the vicinity.
Neither observation alone.

questions.prompt: Who should determine the response arrangements?

options.label: The responsible organization using competent assessment and applicable requirements.
Whichever worker first sees the leak.
The customer based only on schedule.

questions.prompt: What is a notification-only worker expected to do?

options.label: Approach to stop the source.
Recognize, report and follow the evacuation/notification plan.
Choose a response suit for entry.

questions.prompt: Does a prior general certificate authorize every response duty?

options.label: Yes, if it contains the word hazardous.
Yes, when the worker is experienced at the site.
No; the training and assessed capability must match the function.

questions.prompt: What is source-control work?

options.label: Approaching a leak to stop its release.
Reporting from an unaffected assembly point.
Checking yourself into evacuation accountability.

questions.prompt: What does a protective-zone boundary mean for unassigned people?

options.label: It is advisory if the scene looks quiet.
They must not enter without the required assignment and controls.
They may enter to take photographs.

questions.prompt: Why must workers check in and out?

options.label: To replace medical evaluation.
To avoid wearing protective equipment.
So the response organization can account for people and their assignments.

questions.prompt: Who establishes decontamination methods?

options.label: Appropriately qualified personnel using the substance, equipment and exposure assessment.
Any worker with water and soap.
The first person to leave the site.

questions.prompt: What should happen to potentially contaminated tools?

options.label: Place them in the lunch area until transport arrives.
Keep them within the controlled segregation/decontamination process.
Wipe them once and assume they are clean.

questions.prompt: What information should you give medical/response personnel?

options.label: A guessed diagnosis.
A guarantee that a worker is safe if symptoms fade.
Observed exposure facts, known substances, task and relevant equipment information.

questions.prompt: A worker collapses in an unknown atmosphere. What should a nonrescuer do?

options.label: Activate the designated rescue response from a safe location.
Enter quickly without breathing.
Follow another untrained worker inside.

questions.prompt: Can a normal personal-detector reading clear every chemical hazard?

options.label: Yes, if the battery is charged.
No; instruments measure only their supported hazards under defined conditions.
Yes, if no odor is present.

questions.prompt: What should happen if the planned evacuation route is affected?

options.label: Use it anyway to follow the original map.
Return to collect personal property first.
Use the safe alternative in the emergency arrangements and notify the designated contact.

questions.prompt: What does stopped visible leakage establish?

options.label: Only part of the incident condition; residual hazards and handoff still need assessment.
Unrestricted return to work.
That all containers are now correctly characterized.

questions.prompt: What must a separate cleanup crew receive?

options.label: Only the initial team’s attendance sheet.
The applicable qualification, site information, controls and authorization for its actual duties.
A verbal statement that everything is routine.

questions.prompt: What does this VNDRLY foundation course provide?

options.label: A 40-hour qualification regardless of actual duration.
Authority to command an emergency.
Knowledge instruction and an assessment of the decisions it teaches.

questions.prompt: A cleanup reveals an unidentified container. What is correct?

options.label: Stop the affected task and have the new hazard assessed before continuing.
Open it to complete the manifest quickly.
Assume the old briefing covers it.

questions.prompt: Which training record is truthful?

options.label: A renamed certificate claiming skills never assessed.
The actual course/version, scores and separately verified qualifications or outstanding requirements.
A perfect corrected score with the original result removed.

courses.title: G03 — Process safety and operating-procedure competence
courses.purpose: Recognize loss-of-control pathways and support disciplined procedure, safeguard, change and handback decisions.

content.title: G03 — Process safety and operating-procedure competence
content.description: Complete original G03 guided knowledge course: six taught lessons, two fully worked cases and 26 individually explained questions. Practical qualification and employer-specific implementation remain separate.

explanations.G03_check1: Uncertain identity undermines the work boundary. Resolve it through the proper operating/technical route without introducing an exposure or improvising a test.
explanations.G03_check2: Procedure scope includes phase and configuration. A normal checklist or obsolete revision cannot establish the new startup prerequisites.
explanations.G03_check3: Conflicting evidence creates uncertainty; an average or convenient reading does not verify the real process state. The actual procedure and authorized roles govern the response.
explanations.G03_check4: Disabling a safeguard changes protection. This course gives no bypass permission; the proper controlled route must address the actual conflict and prerequisites.
explanations.G03_check5: Connection compatibility does not establish suitability for the process service. The technical owner determines specification match and whether change control is required.
explanations.G03_check6: Actual state and outstanding prerequisites must transfer. Shift change does not clear a hold, and repaired cannot be equated with ready without its required evidence.
explanations.G03_final1: Applicability follows actual operations and governing criteria. Useful principles do not justify claiming the same legal coverage for every service.
explanations.G03_final2: Personal protection and process-event prevention have different functions. Good results in one area do not verify the controls needed in the other.
explanations.G03_final3: The information must match the real system. An obsolete connection can mislead safe work; resolve the discrepancy without unauthorized physical manipulation.
explanations.G03_final4: A technical basis needs relevant current information. Document volume and experience do not establish actual hazards, boundaries or equipment design.
explanations.G03_final5: Foundation knowledge does not establish assessed performance or employer/site authority for a real operating role.
explanations.G03_final6: An expected prerequisite cannot be represented as verified when evidence is absent. Follow the actual procedure and authority rather than backfilling completion.
explanations.G03_final7: A private revision can create incompatible instructions. Route the difficulty through the proper procedure/change owner and communicate an approved resolution.
explanations.G03_final8: An alarm may alert while a trip may act. Understand the real design rather than inferring automatic protection from a label.
explanations.G03_final9: Limits come from the relevant technical basis and controlled decisions. A deadline cannot turn an unsupported deviation into safe operation.
explanations.G03_final10: A listed safeguard may be ineffective if condition or configuration prevents its function. Verify the actual relevant readiness through competent methods.
explanations.G03_final11: Repair completion and plant release are distinct. The responsible operating system coordinates all applicable prerequisites before startup.
explanations.G03_final12: Affected operators need the real protection state and restrictions. A private note cannot serve as a reliable operating handover.
explanations.G03_final13: Replacement-in-kind is a supported technical determination, not a purchasing description or visual assumption.
explanations.G03_final14: An approved change must reach operational users. Preserving history and issuing usable current instructions are different from leaving obsolete guidance active.
explanations.G03_final15: A review must examine real prerequisites. A label or meeting does not make unfinished checks complete or replace the evidence they require.
explanations.G03_final16: Repeated abnormal events can reveal degraded controls. Lack of injury does not establish that the condition is harmless or justify suppression.
explanations.G03_final17: A shift boundary is not technical release evidence. Transfer the restriction and actual clearance responsibility explicitly.
explanations.G03_final18: Effectiveness concerns use in relevant work, not document appearance or purchasing. Observe whether the intended communication actually occurs.
explanations.G03_final19: Independent prerequisites cannot be averaged away by administrative completion. Keep the dependent restart held until its actual requirements are met.
explanations.G03_final20: A later finding may explain an indication without establishing the full earlier process state. Preserve evidence and uncertainty rather than rewriting history.

lessons.title: Start here — prevent a loss of process control
lessons.body:
# G03 — Process safety and operating-procedure competence

A production facility can have an excellent personal-injury record while a wrong valve lineup, degraded safeguard or unmanaged change creates potential for a major release. Process safety focuses on preventing and limiting releases, fires, explosions and other severe process events. It asks whether the operating system remains within a justified safe envelope, not simply whether people are wearing PPE or avoiding slips.

This course is a foundation for operators, maintenance workers, service contractors, supervisors and technical reviewers. Six lessons explain process information, procedure use, operating limits, safeguards, change and disciplined handback. Two fictional cases work through the decisions. Six lesson checks and twenty final questions retain your first choices and any acknowledged corrections. Completion requires all 26 answered correctly or acknowledged remediation; the original result remains distinct from the remediated result.

OSHA's U.S. process safety management standard, 1910.119, has specific coverage criteria and exceptions. The presence of hydrocarbons or an oilfield service label alone does not establish that a particular operation is legally covered. A competent employer review must determine applicability. Principles taught here can support safe judgment beyond a covered process without pretending that every facility has the same legal duties.

The course supplies no operating limits, startup sequence, isolation method, bypass permission or plant qualification. Those must come from the actual process design basis, approved operating procedures, competent technical decisions and employer/site authorization. You can learn the decisions here without manipulating a live process. A knowledge pass cannot release equipment or authorize an unassessed person to operate it.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — understand the process and its hazard pathways
lessons.body:
## Start with what can be released and why

A process hazard can involve toxic material, flammable inventory, reactive chemistry, pressure, temperature or an incompatible combination. The event may develop through several linked failures: an unsuitable material, a blocked path, a faulty indication and a misunderstood response. Think beyond the final person touching a control. Ask which conditions could allow a release and which protections are intended to prevent or limit it.

Process safety information provides the basis for decisions. Relevant information includes chemical hazards, process technology and equipment design. In practice this can involve the identified material, a process flow description, safe operating boundaries, equipment information and the basis for protective functions. The information must match the actual installation. A drawing with the right title but an obsolete line connection can mislead a maintenance crew as badly as no drawing at all.

## Read equipment identity and interfaces together

Use the site's identification system to distinguish the exact equipment, line, operating area and connected systems. A familiar-looking valve is not enough. Check whether the task can affect upstream supply, downstream pressure, shared utilities, relief paths, drains, vents or another crew. The responsible technical people determine the real interfaces; a worker should report uncertainty rather than invent a process explanation from appearance.

Personal protection and process protection have different roles. A hard hat does not prevent overpressure. A sound relief arrangement does not prevent every slip. Both may matter, but a strong result in one area cannot compensate for a missing safeguard in the other. A low incident count likewise does not prove the system's protective functions are intact.

## Worked example: an apparently identical branch

Ravi is assigned to service one branch of a fluid system. The field identification does not agree with the current work pack. A colleague says the branches are interchangeable. Ravi stops the affected intervention and asks the responsible operations/technical roles to resolve identity and connectivity. He does not trace the line by opening a drain or moving a valve. The decision preserves protection while the information gap is resolved through an authorized method.

The eventual record should distinguish the actual installation from the corrected documentation. Updating a drawing is necessary where appropriate, but does not by itself verify that isolation, maintenance or restart prerequisites have been met. Each operating decision still needs its own valid basis.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — use the correct procedure for the actual operating phase
lessons.body:
## Procedure identity matters as much as availability

An operating procedure turns technical intent into an executable sequence for a defined process and phase. Normal operation, initial startup, temporary operation, emergency shutdown, normal shutdown and restart after interruption can have different prerequisites and risks. A normal-running checklist is not automatically a startup instruction. The current revision must match the equipment and operating state being handled.

Before acting, understand the task's purpose, entry conditions, responsibilities, sequence, limits and expected indications. Identify the points at which a result is checked before the next step. A check is not complete merely because the operator intends to perform it later. If an expected indication is missing or conflicting, use the procedure's abnormal route and obtain clarification; do not skip ahead to make the sequence appear complete.

## A procedure is not permission for everyone to perform it

An experienced mechanic may understand equipment but lack authority to operate a process. A qualified operator may still need site-specific instruction for an unfamiliar unit. Contractors need the relevant process hazards and interface information without being assigned operating decisions outside their scope.

Readbacks, checklists and peer checks can support reliable execution when specified. Their purpose is to confirm a critical action or state, not add decorative signatures. Record actual completion and communicate any restriction. If a procedure cannot be executed as written, stop the affected sequence and have the proper owner resolve it. Do not create a private field revision that others cannot see.

## Worked example: the wrong startup checklist

Lena receives a checklist used before a modification. Its equipment identifiers look familiar, but the updated system now has a different monitored prerequisite. She does not assume the missing step is optional. She checks the applicable controlled startup procedure with operations and the technical owner and maintains the hold on dependent actions.

The correction should address both the current work and distribution of obsolete instructions. The team must not backfill a signature claiming the prerequisite was checked before it actually was. A later genuine check can support a later release decision while the original gap remains part of the traceable history.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — distinguish operating limits, alarms and protective actions
lessons.body:
## Know the safe envelope and the response boundary

Operating limits describe the conditions within which the process is intended to operate safely. The applicable procedure should explain the consequence of deviation and the steps required to correct or respond. Limits may involve pressure, temperature, flow, inventory, composition or another relevant parameter. This course intentionally gives none of their values: a number valid for one system can be dangerous on another.

An alarm alerts someone to a condition; a trip or interlock may perform a protective action. They are not interchangeable, and their relationship depends on the actual design. Do not assume that the absence of an alarm proves a process variable is safe or that one protective layer makes every other check unnecessary. A faulty sensor can affect more than one displayed function, so apparent agreement is not automatically independent confirmation.

## Respond to uncertainty without inventing a control move

If an indication conflicts with another or the expected response does not occur, use the approved abnormal or emergency procedure and contact the responsible operating role. A worker who is not authorized to control the process should raise the concern and keep clear rather than moving unfamiliar controls. A trained operator follows the plant-specific response, including shutdown where required. This course does not specify which valve to move or which device to reset.

Schedule pressure is not an operating parameter. A customer deadline cannot redefine a limit, extend an unapproved temporary condition or make an unreliable indicator trustworthy. Likewise, a successful previous run does not prove today's indication or safeguard is sound.

## Worked example: two readings disagree

A panel display shows the expected pressure while a local indication differs materially. A supervisor suggests choosing the favorable reading to finish a transfer. The operator does not average the readings or select the convenient one. The actual approved response to uncertain process state governs. The team identifies the affected operation, communicates the restriction and obtains competent evaluation of the instruments and process before relying on the disputed condition.

Afterward, distinguish the faulty instrument from the process state during the event. Finding an instrument defect later does not prove every earlier condition was acceptable. Preserve the uncertainty and evaluate its implications using the actual evidence.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — preserve safeguards and mechanical integrity
lessons.body:
## A safeguard must be suitable and available

Safeguards can include design features, containment, protective instrument functions, relief arrangements, detection, operating procedures and emergency provisions. Each has a function and conditions needed to work. A relief device recorded on an asset list cannot protect the process if its required path is improperly blocked. A detector with an unresolved fault cannot be treated as ready merely because a dashboard icon remains green.

Mechanical integrity addresses the condition of relevant equipment through appropriate inspection, testing, maintenance and correction of deficiencies. The technical requirements must match the equipment and service. Maintenance completion and operating readiness are related but different: fitting a replacement does not necessarily complete required checks, restore every protective function or authorize return to service.

## Bypasses and temporary arrangements need real control

A disabled or bypassed safeguard changes the protection available. Do not silence, defeat or reset a protection just to stop an inconvenience or complete a test. The actual site's authorized process determines whether a temporary arrangement is permissible, what technical review is needed, what alternative protection applies and how the condition is tracked and restored. This course grants no bypass permission.

Temporary conditions should be visible at the point of operation and through handover. A note in a private maintenance diary is inadequate when operators rely on the safeguard. Check duration, scope, responsible role and restoration criteria through the applicable procedure. An authorized temporary decision is not proof that the permanent protection has been repaired.

## Worked example: the maintenance shortcut

A service technician discovers that a protective function prevents the planned test. Someone proposes disconnecting the input briefly and reconnecting it before shift end. The technician stops the unsupported action and routes the conflict through the responsible operating and technical authorities. The test plan and protective requirements must be reconciled without improvisation.

When the approved work is complete, the team verifies the actual restored configuration and any required functional evidence. A statement that it should be back to normal is not the same as confirmation. If restoration cannot be verified, the remaining condition and its operating restrictions must be handed over explicitly rather than hidden by closing the maintenance ticket.

lessons.title: Lesson 5 — manage changes before they alter the hazard
lessons.body:
## Similar appearance does not prove replacement in kind

A change can involve equipment, material, software, process conditions, operating procedure or an organizational arrangement that affects safe execution. The site's management-of-change process establishes what requires review. Replacement in kind is a bounded determination that the replacement satisfies the existing design specification; a supplier describing an item as equivalent does not make that technical decision.

Review what changes, why it is proposed, the technical basis, safety implications, operating-procedure effects, required authorization and necessary duration if temporary. Include affected workers and interfaces. A change can introduce a new hazard or weaken an existing protective function even when its immediate purpose is reliability or efficiency. Do not treat a lower purchase price or identical connection as evidence of compatibility with the process service.

## Carry the change into real readiness

Accepted technical review must reach drawings, equipment information, procedures, training and the people performing the work. An approved change file in the office is not enough if the next shift still uses the old startup sequence. Some changes need a pre-startup safety review under applicable requirements and the site's system. That review checks readiness; it is not simply a celebration that construction is complete.

Contractors should communicate proposed deviations from the accepted scope rather than making them silently. If a change is discovered during a task, preserve the safe condition and obtain the required review before continuing dependent work. A risk-assessment signature for the old method does not automatically accept the new one.

## Worked example: a different replacement component

The specified component is unavailable, and procurement offers one with the same fittings but a different material and operating characteristic. The installer cannot approve process compatibility from the fitting size. The technical owner evaluates the actual specification, hazards and affected procedure. Pending that decision, the component is not represented as an accepted replacement in kind.

If the change is accepted, complete the required updates and readiness checks before restart. Keep original and revised records traceable. A later discovery that the replacement was unsuitable requires prompt protective action and review of affected equipment, not editing the specification to make the installed item appear compliant.

lessons.title: Lesson 6 — hand over, return to service and learn from weak signals
lessons.body:
## Transfer the actual state, not a reassuring summary

A handover should tell the receiving role what system is affected, operating state, open permits or holds, unavailable safeguards, temporary arrangements, abnormal indications and outstanding actions. Identify who has authority to clear each restriction. Confirm receipt and understanding where the procedure requires it. Shift change does not expire an operating hold, and an incoming operator should not have to infer a plant's state from its sound or appearance.

Return to service depends on the actual maintenance, operating and technical prerequisites. Work completion, permit handback, restoration of isolations and safeguards, current procedures and necessary training may have separate owners. The responsible authority coordinates them under the applicable process. A contractor's statement that the repair is finished does not alone authorize startup of the plant.

## Treat abnormal events as information

Repeated trips, unexplained leaks, unreliable indications or recurring temporary arrangements can signal a deeper weakness. Record and escalate them through the relevant process rather than normalizing them because no major event occurred. Incident and near-miss review should examine failed controls and contributing system conditions. A reminder to operators may be insufficient when the process information, equipment or plan is wrong.

Use follow-up that tests the intended correction in relevant conditions. A closed action proves a workflow state, not necessarily a reliable safeguard. Preserve event history and changed decisions. Share deidentified useful learning with affected crews, and update the actual work instructions where necessary.

## Worked example: an unfinished restoration at night

At the end of maintenance, one required safeguard-restoration check remains pending. The outgoing supervisor describes the equipment as repaired. The incoming operator asks for the actual status and keeps the dependent start on hold. The handover is corrected to identify the pending check, responsible role and release authority.

When the check is genuinely completed and the authorized readiness decision is made, the next shift can act on a supported basis. The earlier handover gap should still be reviewed: why did repaired become ready in the message? Improving the communication system and observing later handovers is more useful than asking everyone to sign a form saying they will be careful.

lessons.title: Two applied process-safety cases with worked solutions
lessons.body:
## Case 1: a substitute part and a rushed restart

A maintenance contractor replaces a component on a process system. The approved specification is unavailable locally, so a visually similar item with different material information is installed. Procurement calls it equivalent. The old operating checklist remains in the work pack, and a safeguard restoration check is still pending. The customer asks the night shift to restart immediately because the repair ticket is marked complete.

### Worked solution: identify the independent gaps

There are at least three unresolved prerequisites: technical suitability of the replacement, applicability of the operating procedure and completion of the safeguard restoration. A completed repair ticket proves none of them by itself. The responsible operating role keeps the dependent restart on hold and communicates the actual state to affected people. The contractor does not move process controls to demonstrate that the part seems to work.

The technical owner checks the specification and determines whether the proposed replacement is in kind or a change requiring the site's management-of-change process. Matching fittings are not the technical basis. If a change is accepted, its consequences for equipment information, operating steps, limits, inspection and training must be addressed. Do not revise the drawing retrospectively to claim the original installation was already approved.

### Worked solution: establish real release evidence

Operations obtains the applicable controlled procedure for the actual configuration and phase. The responsible qualified personnel complete the required restoration and readiness checks. Any required pre-startup review and authorizations are completed under the actual system. The incoming shift receives the supported status, remaining restrictions and who authorized the release. If one condition remains unresolved, the other completed checks do not average it away.

The later review should examine how procurement, installation and ticket status became disconnected. Useful actions might improve specification verification, change notification and handback language, subject to competent review. Effectiveness needs later evidence that replacement decisions and restart handovers follow the corrected process. An invoice for the proper part or a new form alone is not proof that the system works.

## Case 2: a recurring alarm becomes normal practice

During a transfer, operators receive a recurring abnormal indication. A colleague says it happens frequently and suggests suppressing the input to finish the transfer. A local indication disagrees with the panel display. A temporary arrangement mentioned last week has no clear current status in the shift log. The next crew expects an ordinary handover and has not been told a safeguard may be unavailable.

### Worked solution: do not normalize uncertain protection

Frequent occurrence does not prove the condition is benign. The disagreement and unclear temporary status mean the process state or protection basis cannot be assumed from the favorable display. The authorized operator follows the actual abnormal/emergency procedure and coordinates with the responsible operations and technical roles. This case deliberately supplies no valve movement or shutdown sequence; inventing one would exceed a foundation course.

Do not suppress the input through an improvised workaround. The site's formal route governs any proposed temporary protection change, including technical review, authority, suitable alternative measures and restoration. A past temporary decision is not necessarily current, and an undocumented memory is not a valid release basis. Record and communicate the actual restriction to the incoming crew rather than reporting normal operation.

### Worked solution: correct the cause and test the follow-through

Competent personnel examine the process and instruments using appropriate safe methods. Finding a faulty sensor later can explain an indication but does not automatically prove that all earlier conditions stayed within limits. Preserve what was known and uncertain at the time. Investigate recurring signals, temporary arrangements and operating pressure as supported factors rather than blaming the last operator alone.

Before renewed reliance, complete the applicable technical restoration and operating release. Hand over actual evidence and any remaining limits. Later assurance should check that the corrected indication and safeguard perform as intended and that crews no longer rely on an informal suppression habit. A stable-looking dashboard immediately after reset is not a complete effectiveness conclusion.

lessons.title: Final assessment — twenty process decisions
lessons.body: Answer each question using the process phase, authority and evidence given. First answers remain recorded. For an incorrect answer, read and explicitly acknowledge the specific correction. All six checks and twenty final questions require a correct answer or acknowledged remediation; the remediated result does not overwrite the original score.

lessons.title: Finish — plant-specific competence remains separate
lessons.body:
## What this knowledge result means

Completion requires all 26 answered correctly or acknowledged remediation, retaining first-answer and remediated scores separately. You have studied process-safety decisions and fictional examples. You have not demonstrated the ability to operate a real unit, interpret all its hazards, test a safeguard or authorize restart.

## What the employer must establish

The employer and competent technical authorities determine legal applicability, process hazards, design information, operating limits, approved procedures, safeguards and change/release responsibilities. OSHA 1910.119 has specific coverage and exceptions; a service name does not settle that determination. Current plant information and accessible procedures must be available to the people relying on them. Contractor interfaces must identify the actual work and the limits of each party's authority.

An appropriate assessor should test routine execution, phase identification, abnormal recognition, safe stop/escalation decisions and handover using suitable controlled methods. Do not defeat a live safeguard or create a process upset to make training realistic. Record unassessed items and retain restrictions until the required capability and authority are established.

This course issues no operator license, bypass permit, change approval, isolation authorization or technical certification. A written pass cannot replace a pre-startup review or clear a site hold. If the governing procedure, responsible role or required condition cannot be identified, keep that uncertainty visible and resolve it through the actual operating system before relying on the affected work.

questions.prompt: The field equipment identity conflicts with the work pack. What should the worker do?

options.label: Hold the affected intervention and obtain authorized resolution of identity and connectivity.
Open a drain to see which branch is live.
Assume similar-looking branches are interchangeable.

questions.prompt: A normal-operation checklist is offered for startup after a modification. What is appropriate?

options.label: Use it because it has the correct company logo.
Verify the current procedure for the actual configuration and operating phase before dependent actions.
Skip unfamiliar prerequisites to preserve the old sequence.

questions.prompt: Two process readings disagree. Which response is sound?

options.label: Average the readings and continue automatically.
Choose the reading that meets the delivery target.
Use the approved abnormal-response route and competent evaluation rather than choosing the favorable reading.

questions.prompt: A safeguard obstructs a planned test. Can the technician disconnect it briefly on personal initiative?

options.label: No; resolve the test/protection conflict through the authorized operating and technical process.
Yes; any short bypass is automatically acceptable.
Yes; reconnecting it later erases the need for review.

questions.prompt: A replacement has matching fittings but different material information. What is needed?

options.label: Approval based only on appearance.
A competent specification and change review before treating it as an accepted replacement.
A supplier invoice declaring it equivalent.

questions.prompt: One required restoration check remains pending at shift change. What should handover say?

options.label: Call the system ready because maintenance is mostly complete.
Let the incoming shift infer status from the equipment sound.
State the pending condition, restriction, responsible role and release authority explicitly.

questions.prompt: Does an oilfield service label alone establish OSHA PSM coverage?

options.label: No; competent review must apply actual coverage criteria and exceptions.
Yes; every hydrocarbon task is legally identical.
No safety practice applies unless the company chooses a label.

questions.prompt: What is a key distinction between personal and process safety?

options.label: A hard hat prevents every loss of containment.
Process safety addresses severe process-event pathways and cannot be inferred solely from a good personal-injury record.
A low injury count proves protective systems function.

questions.prompt: A correct-looking drawing shows an obsolete connection. What matters?

options.label: Its title alone makes it reliable.
A worker should move valves until the drawing appears correct.
Resolve the mismatch with actual installation information before relying on the work boundary.

questions.prompt: Which information supports process decisions?

options.label: Relevant chemical hazards, process technology and equipment design information matching the installation.
Only the number of pages in a manual.
Only a statement that the crew is experienced.

questions.prompt: A mechanic has equipment experience. Does reading this course authorize plant operation?

options.label: Yes; all maintenance experience transfers automatically.
No; plant- and role-specific competence and authorization remain separate.
Yes; a written pass is a startup permit.

questions.prompt: An expected indication is missing during a procedure. What should happen?

options.label: Sign the check now and perform it later.
Skip ahead to make the sequence look complete.
Use the applicable abnormal route and resolve the uncertainty before unsupported dependent steps.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with privately editing a field procedure to make the job possible?

options.label: It bypasses the required competent review and controlled communication to affected users.
Nothing if only one worker uses it.
The edit automatically changes the design basis.

questions.prompt: Are alarms and trips interchangeable?

options.label: Yes; either one proves every protective layer works.
No; their functions and relationship depend on the actual design.
Yes; an alarm always shuts the plant down automatically.

questions.prompt: Can a delivery deadline redefine a process operating limit?

options.label: Yes; customer urgency is a safety parameter.
Yes; a manager can erase any limit verbally.
No; schedule pressure does not supply technical justification or authority.

questions.prompt: A relief device is on the asset list. What else matters?

options.label: Its actual suitable condition and required functional path/configuration.
Nothing; listing alone proves protection.
Only whether its photograph is recent.

questions.prompt: Maintenance is complete. Does that alone authorize startup?

options.label: Yes; a closed ticket replaces every operating check.
No; required restoration, operating readiness and release conditions must also be satisfied.
Yes; the contractor decides all plant operating authority.

questions.prompt: A temporary protection arrangement is mentioned only in a private diary. What is missing?

options.label: A larger diary.
Proof that temporary arrangements never matter.
Visible controlled status and communication to the people relying on that protection.

questions.prompt: Who determines whether a proposed replacement is in kind?

options.label: The appropriate technical/authorized process using the actual specification and service.
Any buyer who sees matching fittings.
The installer based only on appearance.

questions.prompt: A change is approved in the office but workers retain the old startup instructions. What is needed?

options.label: Nothing because the approval signature exists.
Complete applicable procedure/information updates, communication and training before dependent work.
Delete the old job record to conceal the mismatch.

questions.prompt: What does a pre-startup readiness review not represent?

options.label: A process for examining readiness where required.
A point for checking necessary updates and preparation.
A substitute for actually satisfying the applicable safety prerequisites.

questions.prompt: A recurring trip causes no injury. What is appropriate?

options.label: Report and examine it as a possible weak signal using the relevant process.
Normalize it and suppress it informally.
Delete it from history because consequences were small.

questions.prompt: A new shift begins with an open operating hold. Does the hold expire?

options.label: Yes; every shift starts with a clean slate.
No; actual clearance must follow the designated authority and prerequisites.
Yes; the incoming worker can infer clearance from silence.

questions.prompt: What best tests a handover correction?

options.label: The new form has more fields.
The training invoice was paid.
Later representative handovers accurately carry actual state, restrictions and clearance responsibility.

questions.prompt: In Case 1, which unresolved point can the completed repair ticket offset?

options.label: None; suitability, procedure and restoration prerequisites each need their actual supported resolution.
Any missing technical condition if the score is high.
Every operating condition once a contractor signs.

questions.prompt: In Case 2, a faulty sensor is found later. What follows about earlier process conditions?

options.label: All previous uncertainty automatically disappears.
Evaluate the actual evidence; the defect alone does not prove every earlier condition was safe.
Every earlier reading can be rewritten as normal.

courses.title: G04 — Bloodborne pathogens and occupational exposure controls
courses.purpose: Prevent occupational contact with human blood and other potentially infectious material and support prompt confidential response when exposure may occur.
courses.practicalBoundary:
29 CFR 1910.132(f)(2), (g) — Employees using the eye/face, head, foot, hand or personal fall protection covered by paragraph (g): Before that work, demonstrate understanding of the PPE training and ability to use the PPE properly. This is not a separate independent certification requirement. Respirators and electrical protective equipment follow their own standards rather than paragraph (f). Source: https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.132
29 CFR 1910.134(e), (f), (k)(1) — Required respirator users; tight-fitting facepieces require the applicable fit test: Complete the required medical evaluation before fit testing or use, the applicable fit test, and training that enables demonstration of the listed knowledge and respirator-use skills. These duties apply to the actual respirator assignment, not everyone taking awareness training. Source: https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.134

content.title: G04 — Bloodborne pathogens and occupational exposure controls
content.description: Original guided knowledge course: six taught lessons, two fully worked field/service cases, six lesson checks and twenty final decisions. Employer-specific implementation, interactive questions, practical assessment and clinical decisions remain separate.

explanations.G04_check1: Infection status cannot be judged from appearance. Plan precautions around the material, contact route and task rather than assumptions about the person.
explanations.G04_check2: The changed material and handling duties can change anticipated exposure. Review and provide suitable arrangements before accepting the changed task as ready.
explanations.G04_check3: An improvised container does not establish suitable sharps protection. Maintain a safe boundary and obtain the prepared personnel and equipment rather than personally improvising handling.
explanations.G04_check4: Contaminated gloves can transfer material to clean surfaces. Gloves do not make a shared phone clean; follow the appropriate task-exit or clean-assistance arrangement.
explanations.G04_check5: The disposal system must remain suitable. Do not compress or manually rearrange sharps to defeat the replacement condition; obtain the approved replacement safely.
explanations.G04_check6: A small wound or lack of symptoms cannot establish absence of risk. Prompt reporting and professional evaluation are needed; supervisors and this course do not diagnose or prescribe.
explanations.G04_final1: The eye is a mucous-membrane route. A splash needs the immediate response and prompt evaluation process; merely viewing a record or clean package is not that contact.
explanations.G04_final2: Different hazards require their own controls. An oil leak can be dangerous without being a bloodborne exposure; identify the source and uncertainty instead of ignoring or misclassifying it.
explanations.G04_final3: Exposure determination follows actual tasks. Shared employment does not make duties identical, and normal PPE use is not a reason to disregard the underlying anticipated contact.
explanations.G04_final4: A quiz can present cases and record answers. It cannot supply the real plan, local arrangements or meaningful answers to every employer-specific question; those elements remain separate.
explanations.G04_final5: Missing procedures or suitable controls leave the task unready. Prevent contact while the responsible role resolves the gap rather than asking an unprepared person to improvise.
explanations.G04_final6: An appropriate physical disposal system can reduce contact with sharps. A warning communicates information but does not itself provide the physical containment or establish its readiness.
explanations.G04_final7: Visible cleanliness does not establish completion of the applicable decontamination method. Verify actual approved actions and handling, while keeping technical product requirements with the proper procedure.
explanations.G04_final8: Products and methods have relevant instructions and compatibility limits. This course intentionally supplies no improvised recipe or universal time, so obtain the applicable authorized method.
explanations.G04_final9: Gloves have limits and do not eliminate hidden sharps. Prevent blind contact through the planned handling method rather than treating PPE as permission for an unsafe practice.
explanations.G04_final10: Written knowledge does not establish observed skill. A suitable practical assessment can test safe removal and hygiene without using infectious material, while recording gaps and limitations.
explanations.G04_final11: Bloodborne and airborne routes are different. Respiratory hazards can exist in a particular task, but selection and required program elements must follow actual assessment rather than a universal assumption.
explanations.G04_final12: The observer can recognize and report the hazard without handling it. Pocket transport and unnecessary contact create new exposure and do not demonstrate safe control.
explanations.G04_final13: Containment must function in practice. A label communicates status but cannot stop leakage; obtain the approved suitable handling arrangement and do not move workplace contamination into a home.
explanations.G04_final14: Use the taught hygiene response and prompt professional evaluation. Harsh surface chemicals are not wound treatment, and administrative convenience cannot justify delaying the response.
explanations.G04_final15: Clinical decisions require qualified professional assessment. Supervisors coordinate safe work and referral, while this knowledge course does not prescribe drugs, interpret tests or declare immunity.
explanations.G04_final16: Factual exposure information supports evaluation and prevention. Guessing a diagnosis or identifying blame does not describe the route and circumstances needed for an appropriate response.
explanations.G04_final17: Vaccination information is relevant to professional evaluation, but the course cannot establish individual protection or waive response. The clinician reviews the appropriate facts and follow-up.
explanations.G04_final18: Prevention learning can describe a failed container or handling method without disclosing diagnoses. Clinical information stays appropriately restricted, and unsupported source allegations should not be distributed.
explanations.G04_final19: The task requires a prepared suitable worker and controls. Protect access and obtain the proper arrangement; queue pressure does not create competence, and the spill still needs controlled handling.
explanations.G04_final20: Effectiveness concerns whether the changed system prevents the relevant handling exposure during later work. Payment is not field evidence, and medical evaluation does not erase the event history.

lessons.title: Start here — bloodborne exposure is a task question
lessons.body:
# G04 — Bloodborne pathogens and occupational exposure controls

A gate first aider approaches a worker with a bleeding hand. At another site, a housekeeping worker finds a discarded needle in a washroom. A laundry worker receives a bag of blood-soiled clothing. These jobs have different immediate tasks, but each can create a pathway between blood or other potentially infectious material and another person's body. A job title, clean-looking uniform or familiar coworker does not tell you whether that pathway is controlled.

This course teaches recognition, prevention, safe role boundaries and prompt response. You will learn how anticipated duties connect to an employer's exposure-control arrangements; how engineering controls, work practices and personal protective equipment work together; and how to report an exposure while protecting medical privacy. It supplies no diagnosis, medication regimen, clinical credential or permission to perform medical procedures.

Work through six taught lessons, each with a knowledge check, then two fictional cases with fully written solutions and twenty final questions. All 26 questions must be answered correctly or completed through acknowledged remediation. Your first-answer and remediated results remain separate. Reading the explanation after an error is part of learning; it must not rewrite your first result.

The examples are original fictional training cases, not actual company evidence. An employer must determine which duties create reasonably anticipated occupational exposure and implement the applicable local requirements. A written course cannot supply the employer-specific exposure-control plan, equipment practice, vaccination arrangements, medical follow-up or the opportunity for interactive questions with a knowledgeable trainer. Resolve those elements separately before treating a worker as prepared for assigned exposure duties.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — recognize a transmission pathway
lessons.body:
## Material, route and task

Bloodborne pathogens are disease-causing microorganisms that can be present in human blood. Important examples include hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus and HIV. You cannot determine infection status from a person's appearance, job, reputation or symptoms. Treat blood and relevant potentially infectious materials with the precautions required by the task rather than deciding that one coworker looks safe.

The practical question is whether material can reach a susceptible route of contact. A contaminated needle or broken sharp can puncture skin. Blood can splash into eyes, nose or mouth. Contact with damaged skin, such as a cut or abrasion, can also matter. An exposure does not mean infection is certain, but it warrants prompt appropriate evaluation rather than reassurance based on appearance.

Other potentially infectious material is a defined term in the applicable program, not a label for every unpleasant substance. Certain human fluids and tissues fall within it, and visible blood changes the handling decision. Where body fluids cannot be differentiated, do not guess that the material is harmless. Conversely, an oil spill is not automatically a human bloodborne-pathogen event; it can require chemical controls under a different hazard program. Identify the actual material and uncertainty, then use the appropriate response.

## Worked example: two different stains

Nora sees a red liquid on the floor beside a worker whose hand is bleeding. She does not touch the liquid to identify it. She keeps people from tracking it through the room and alerts the designated responder. The material is treated as potentially contaminated in the planned cleanup process. In a separate location, red hydraulic fluid leaks from a machine with no evidence of human blood. That requires machinery and chemical controls; calling everything blood would obscure the actual source and response.

## Why routes matter

A contaminated glove touching a phone can transfer contamination to another surface even if the wearer was not punctured. A cleaner reaching into a waste bag may encounter a hidden sharp they cannot see. Plan the task to interrupt those pathways before contact occurs. Gloves do not make blind reaching safe, and a known worker's negative-looking health status does not justify omitting precautions.

Recognize the potential exposure, stop the unplanned contact and obtain the designated help. You do not need to diagnose the source person to report a hazard, and you should not seek their private medical history before taking protective action.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — connect duties to the employer exposure-control plan
lessons.body:
## The plan must describe the real work

The employer's exposure determination examines duties where contact can reasonably be anticipated. Examples can include assigned first aid, handling blood-soiled laundry, cleaning contaminated facilities or handling human remains. The service name alone is insufficient: an office administrator booking laundry transport has different contact from a worker sorting contaminated linen. An exposure determination should not assume the hazard disappears because gloves are normally worn; prevention measures are selected after recognizing the exposure.

The written exposure-control plan is the employer's operational arrangement, not this generic lesson. Workers need to know where it is available, which tasks and roles it covers, who owns it and how its procedures apply to their assignment. It should connect prevention, suitable supplies, housekeeping and waste arrangements with reporting and confidential post-exposure care. Applicable requirements govern review and training. Completing this course does not demonstrate that those employer arrangements exist or are current.

## A usable pre-task discussion

Before a cleanup assignment, the supervisor and assigned worker should establish what material is known, what remains uncertain, the approved method, suitable equipment, segregation of the area and the escalation route. They should identify who is trained and authorized for the task. If the worker cannot obtain the applicable instruction or suitable supplies, hold the cleanup and prevent others entering the affected area. Do not allocate it to whichever person is nearest.

## Worked example: laundry scope changes

A company previously handled ordinary uniforms. A new contract adds visibly blood-soiled garments from a treatment room. The owner cannot simply extend the ordinary laundry checklist. The changed duty needs an exposure review and suitable arrangements for collection, containment, handling, worker preparation and response. The office booking clerk does not automatically become a contaminated-laundry handler, but the actual handlers need the relevant preparation before receiving the changed material.

## Questions are part of readiness

Workers must have a meaningful opportunity to ask a knowledgeable person about unclear instructions. An automated quiz cannot inspect the site, explain an employer's particular sharps system or answer every job-specific question. Ask where to report after hours, which supplies are authorized and who arranges immediate evaluation. A manager's instruction to just finish the job is not a substitute for resolving a missing exposure-control arrangement.

When duties change, communicate revised restrictions to supervisors, dispatch and affected workers. Preserve the earlier scope and the new decision so a later reviewer can understand why additional preparation was needed.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — prevent contact through engineering and work practices
lessons.body:
## Change the pathway before relying on a barrier

Engineering controls reduce contact through equipment or physical design, such as an appropriate sharps container or a suitable safer device used by trained personnel. Work practices change how tasks are performed: keeping hands out of waste containers, segregating contaminated items, avoiding actions that spread material and using designated handling methods. PPE adds protection for remaining exposure. These layers should work together; choosing gloves does not excuse an absent suitable disposal arrangement.

The person planning a task should identify how contamination could travel. Could a waste bag conceal a needle? Could a splash reach the face? Could a worker touch a radio with contaminated gloves? Could laundry leak onto a vehicle seat? A control addressing one pathway may leave another open. Review the full task, including preparing equipment, moving material, cleaning the area and leaving the work zone.

## Worked example: the available container is wrong

Mason is asked to collect a discarded sharp. The only receptacle offered is a thin plastic drink bottle. He does not accept the substitution merely because its cap closes. He keeps people away and contacts the person responsible for the approved collection and disposal method. The correct decision requires suitable equipment and a prepared worker. This course does not authorize Mason to handle the sharp; it teaches why an improvised receptacle does not establish safe readiness.

## Keep clean and contaminated tasks distinct

Plan where clean supplies remain, where contaminated items go and how a worker avoids carrying contamination across the boundary. If a cleaner's gloved hand touches the door, the door may become another transfer surface. A colleague can manage clean communications or access where the approved procedure provides for it. Do not solve the problem by removing a glove mid-task without a safe sequence; use the trained method and adequate supplies.

Hand hygiene and decontamination are different actions. Gloves do not replace hand cleaning after their removal. A surface becoming visually clean does not establish that the approved decontamination method was completed. Select products and methods through the employer's competent procedure and follow applicable instructions, including compatibility and handling precautions. This course supplies no improvised disinfectant mixture or universal contact time.

Report missing facilities, damaged containers or methods that force workers into avoidable contact. A good report identifies the pathway and the needed decision rather than merely asking staff to be more careful.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — use appropriate PPE without transferring contamination
lessons.body:
## Match the barrier to anticipated contact

PPE selection follows the task's expected exposure. Hand protection may be needed for contact, while anticipated splashes can require protection for eyes, face and clothing. Ordinary work gloves are not automatically suitable biological-exposure protection, and gloves that resist one chemical may not be suitable for another task. Use the employer's assessed PPE and trained method. If the correct items are unavailable or damaged, do not treat a makeshift substitute as equivalent.

PPE protects only the areas and conditions for which it is suitable. A glove cannot prevent every sharp from penetrating it and does not justify placing a hand into concealed waste. Face protection does not make a worker qualified to provide medical care. Respiratory hazards require their own assessment and program; this course does not prescribe a respirator for every blood cleanup or equate bloodborne transmission with airborne exposure.

## A clean exit is part of the task

Prepare supplies and an appropriate disposal or handling arrangement before starting. During work, avoid touching the face, phone, steering wheel or other clean surfaces with contaminated PPE. If PPE becomes compromised, stop the affected task and use the taught safe response. Removal needs practice so contaminated outer surfaces do not contact skin or clothing. Follow the employer's trained sequence, discard or segregate items appropriately and perform hand hygiene.

## Worked example: the radio call

Elena finishes a planned cleanup while wearing the assigned gloves. Dispatch calls her handheld radio. She notices the temptation to answer with the same gloves used on contaminated material. Instead, she maintains the clean/contaminated boundary and follows the trained method for leaving the task or obtaining clean assistance. The key decision is not silence versus service; it is preventing an avoidable transfer while maintaining communication through a safe arrangement.

## What a practical observer should see

An observer can check selection against the task, condition checks, avoidance of clean-surface contact, safe removal and hand hygiene in an appropriate simulation. They should record errors and provide further practice. Reading these words or choosing a correct quiz answer does not establish that the worker can perform removal without contaminating themselves. Do not use actual infectious material to make the assessment realistic; a suitable safe simulation can demonstrate the relevant handling behavior.

lessons.title: Lesson 5 — control sharps, laundry and contaminated waste
lessons.body:
## A hidden sharp changes the task

A sharp can puncture skin and carry contamination beneath the normal barrier. Needles are not the only example: broken contaminated glass and other sharp objects can create the same concern. Never reach blindly into a waste bag or compress it by hand to make room. Keep people clear of an unexpected sharp and contact the designated trained personnel. Do not bring it to a supervisor by carrying it loose or placing it in ordinary pockets.

Sharps disposal requires suitable containers and handling arrangements. A container should be used within the applicable instructions and not forced beyond its intended fill condition. Do not reach inside, push contents down or transfer them manually into another receptacle. Healthcare device handling, including any exceptional recapping technique permitted by a specific procedure, requires its own qualified training; an oilfield cleanup worker should not improvise such a practice.

## Worked example: full container at shift end

Omar notices that a sharps container has reached its specified replacement condition. A colleague proposes pushing the contents down with a tool so the last item fits. Omar does not accept that workaround. He prevents further unsafe use and arranges the approved replacement through the responsible role. The solution is a ready disposal system, not asking the next shift to inherit a concealed overfilled hazard.

## Laundry and waste have transfer pathways too

Blood-soiled clothing can expose people during collection, sorting, transport or laundering. Use the employer's designated containment and handling method, minimizing unnecessary disturbance and segregating the material as required. A bag that leaks is not an adequate boundary merely because someone wrote contaminated on it. Do not take potentially contaminated work items home to solve a workplace shortage; route them through the approved system.

Waste classification and disposal requirements depend on the actual material and governing arrangements.
