No one leans in because the original task was almost complete, and no one stops a protective purge casually to make the permit description easier to satisfy.

lessons.title: Lesson 6 — escape, summon qualified help and control re-entry
lessons.body:
## Respond before investigating

On an atmosphere alarm, suspected release, unexplained collapse or other defined stop trigger, follow the site's protective response promptly. Stop the affected activity only as the trained response allows without delaying escape or creating exposure. Move to the designated safe area and use the emergency communication and accountability system. Do not delay to finish a connection, collect tools or compare detectors. From safety, give the location, equipment or gas if known, observed alarm or symptoms, potentially affected people and last known casualty position. Distinguish facts from assumptions: report an oxygen alarm rather than inventing an oxygen concentration.

An ordinary worker's most important rescue action can be preventing another unprotected entry. Do not enter a vessel, enclosure or release area to retrieve someone while holding your breath. Do not assume a dust mask, filter respirator, escape-only unit or personal monitor provides the capability to perform rescue. Raise the designated response and keep others clear where this can be done safely. Only the trained, equipped and authorized rescue organization uses its approved method. A coworker's collapse is not permission to ignore the hazards that may have caused it.

## An emergency response is a planned capability

The site must establish the response arrangements before exposure, including access, communications, accountability and a feasible rescue for any authorized entry task. A telephone number alone does not demonstrate that responders have the right equipment or can reach the casualty. Support workers need to know their safe reporting and access-control actions without being assigned hazardous entry. Clinical treatment, respiratory use and first aid have their own training and scene-safety prerequisites. Never expose a second person in order to move the first casualty into a safer place; the qualified response must first control the rescue exposure.

The CSB's Foundation Food Group investigation found that a liquid-nitrogen release created an oxygen-deficient atmosphere and that inadequate preparedness contributed to additional people entering to investigate or help. Use that event to test the local plan's assumptions: do nearby workers know the gas hazard, recognize the alarm and know where to summon the correct capability? The lesson is not that every nearby person should learn a rescue technique online. It is that effective prevention, warning and a qualified response must be established before a release creates an urgent emotional decision.

## Re-entry is a separate decision

Silence after an alarm, disappearance of a cloud, a closed supply valve or a worker feeling better does not authorize re-entry. The designated operating/site authority coordinates qualified assessment of the atmosphere, equipment and cause, verifies required safeguards and communicates any permitted return. If the original task or configuration changed, reassess that work as well. Preserve the alarm and the later measurements as separate observations with their times and conditions. Handback identifies continuing restrictions and the responsible next role. A completed knowledge course can help a worker recognize this boundary; it cannot supply atmospheric clearance or make an unsafe job ready.

lessons.title: Two applied cases — complete worked decisions
lessons.body:
## Case 1: the external pipe job and the dropped socket

At fictional Birch Unit, a catalyst contractor hands a reactor back for external pipe reconnection. The loading task is finished, but the approved process arrangement still requires a nitrogen purge. A top opening remains available for the planned connection. The maintenance permit says external work and lists lifting and hand-tool controls. It does not address nitrogen near the opening. A helper drops a socket inside and offers to reach in with a hook while another worker watches. The supervisor has an H2S-only monitor and says its zero display shows that the air is good.

**Step 1 — identify the conflicting assumptions.** Loading completion is not confirmation that the purge stopped. External work does not establish safe air at the opening. The H2S-only measurement does not establish oxygen concentration. Reaching through the opening can change the entry and exposure scope. A watcher does not provide an entry system or rescue capability.

**Step 2 — control the immediate exposure.** Hold the affected approach and retrieval, keep the crew at the designated safe location and notify operations and the responsible supervisor. Nobody leans over the opening to inspect the socket, uses smell as a test or takes the monitor into the vessel to obtain a better result. The helper describes the dropped item and last known position without converting it into an emergency requiring personal entry.

**Step 3 — obtain the right technical handoff.** Operations and the competent catalyst/entry authorities establish the actual purge, material and equipment state. They determine the approved atmosphere and monitoring method, separation and permit requirements for the external task. The team does not stop the purge or add air casually, because the purge may control a material hazard. Any retrieval method receives its own assessment, including whether it can be done through an approved non-entry method without exposure.

**Step 4 — verify before authorized restart.** The designated roles verify actual safeguards and communicate the accepted task limits. The crew is rebriefed about the nitrogen source, opening, safe positions and stop response. If entry is necessary, the qualified entry and rescue program establishes its prerequisites separately; this written foundation supplies none of those permissions. The record preserves the initial mismatch, corrective decisions and actual authorization rather than backdating a permit as if nitrogen had already been addressed.

## Case 2: a cold cloud during a temporary nitrogen supply

At fictional Cedar Yard, a nitrogen supplier supports a temporary service. A delivery coordinator sees unexpected discharge and a white cloud near the connection. The coordinator is trained to control deliveries, not operate the nitrogen equipment. A nearby worker says the cloud is only water and proposes walking through it to reach a shutoff. Someone else brings a filter respirator. The fixed oxygen alarm activates. A subcontractor then reports that one person may still be near the work area.

**Step 1 — act on the protective signal.** The coordinator follows the site stop and evacuation procedure, warns others from safety and uses the emergency/accountability system. The white appearance cannot establish the cloud's full hazard boundary, and the oxygen alarm must not be dismissed because nitrogen is nonflammable. The coordinator does not walk toward the source or delay while deciding whether the instrument is faulty.

**Step 2 — reject inadequate protection and improvised intervention.** A filter respirator does not supply oxygen. The coordinator does not assign an untrained worker to close a valve through the release. Only the designated operator or emergency team acts under the approved safe response. Pressure and cold hazards remain relevant as well as atmosphere; tightening the connection, capping a vent or touching frost-covered equipment is not an awareness-level troubleshooting method.

**Step 3 — provide useful rescue information without entering.** Report the person's name if known, last known location, the alarm, gas supply involved and safe responder access point. State clearly that the person's current location is unconfirmed. Do not lead a group back to search. The designated response establishes its own safe access and rescue capability, while muster staff continue accounting for people.

**Step 4 — require verified clearance and handback.** When the cloud disappears and the alarm later stops, the crew remains at the designated safe area. The site authority obtains qualified atmosphere and equipment assessment, resolves the fault and verifies required controls before communicating a return. The record keeps the first alarm and later findings distinct. Arrival of a replacement connection or a favorable later reading alone does not establish that the complete temporary arrangement is ready for the next task.

lessons.title: Final assessment — twenty decisions about nitrogen and inert-gas interfaces
lessons.body: Answer each final question individually using the hazard pathway, actual role and stated conditions. First answers remain recorded. An incorrect answer requires reading and explicitly acknowledging the specific correction before completion. The six lesson checks and twenty final questions all require a correct response or acknowledged remediation. Your remediated result records learning after feedback and does not replace the original score. No assessment answer authorizes a live test, entry, catalyst intervention or rescue.

lessons.title: Finish — knowledge completion and the remaining qualified work
lessons.body:
## What this result establishes

Complete every section and all 26 questions correctly or through acknowledged remediation. Keep original and remediated scores separate. The result supports recognition of oxygen displacement, instrument and respiratory limits, cold/pressure hazards, catalyst interfaces and safe stop/handoff decisions. It is not evidence that you have operated a real nitrogen unit or performed hazardous work safely.

## What the employer and technical owner must establish

Determine the actual service and each person's duties: desk engineering, equipment supply, transport, operation, catalyst handling, work near an opening, technical testing, entry or emergency response. Use the actual products, material history, equipment information, approved procedures and applicable jurisdiction to establish controls and training. The source service labels do not make every alternative activity part of the contract. OSHA entry and respiratory standards have defined scopes; the employer must determine the applicable requirements rather than applying a catalog label as law.

Respiratory use requires its applicable program prerequisites, including medical and fit requirements where applicable. Inert entry and atmospheric rescue require their own specialist team, equipment, method and feasible emergency capability. A breathing apparatus or course certificate alone does not establish any of those roles.

Record the role, method, equipment, conditions, assessor, observed criteria, limitations and any unassessed steps. Do not create a live gas release, oxygen-deficient environment, cryogenic splash or process upset to test a learner. Use controlled simulation and qualified training arrangements. Keep restrictions in place until the actual competence and employer/site authorization are established. This course does not clear an alarm, approve a purge change, certify breathing air or authorize return to service.

questions.prompt: A nitrogen-purged reactor is nonflammable. What does that establish about air at its opening?

options.label: It does not establish a breathable atmosphere; the actual exposure needs qualified assessment.
It proves the air is safe because nitrogen is familiar.
It clears external work as long as nobody fully enters.

questions.prompt: A hose connector fits an available nitrogen line. May it be used as a breathing-air supply?

options.label: Yes, if the line looks like the previous breathing-air line.
Yes, after someone briefly tries breathing from it.
No; gas identity, quality and approved breathing-air arrangements must be established by the qualified program.

questions.prompt: An H2S-only detector reads zero beside a nitrogen vent. What has been established about oxygen?

options.label: The area is safe until the H2S instrument alarms.
Nothing; the measurement does not address oxygen concentration.
The atmosphere contains enough oxygen.

questions.prompt: A liquid-nitrogen cloud disappears after a release. What is the appropriate conclusion?

options.label: Atmospheric safety is still unestablished; remain clear until authorized qualified assessment.
The nitrogen has completely vanished.
Any nearby worker may now inspect the leak.

questions.prompt: External maintenance near a catalyst reactor now requires retrieving an item through an opening. What is required?

options.label: Treat it as covered because the original permit is still valid.
Stop the purge informally so the helper can reach in.
Hold the changed task and obtain the appropriate scope, atmosphere and entry assessment.

questions.prompt: A coworker collapses in a suspected oxygen-deficient area. What is the awareness-level response?

options.label: Enter with a filter respirator and a monitor.
Raise the designated emergency response from safety and prevent further unprotected entry where safe.
Enter immediately while holding your breath.

questions.prompt: Why can concentrated nitrogen cause asphyxiation?

options.label: It can displace oxygen needed for human breathing.
Its nonflammability supplies oxygen.
Its normal presence in air makes every concentration harmless.

questions.prompt: Which sensory observation can establish acceptable oxygen?

options.label: No unusual smell.
Clear air without a visible cloud.
None of smell, appearance or lack of irritation can establish it.

questions.prompt: Can a person outside a vessel still be exposed to its nitrogen purge?

options.label: Only after the person climbs fully inside.
Yes; gas near openings or discharge points can affect external work.
No; a vessel wall contains every atmosphere hazard.

questions.prompt: A source label says nitrogen-unit engineering. What should determine an individual’s training and authorization?

options.label: The actual assigned desk, supply or field duties and applicable scope.
Every engineer should automatically operate the unit.
The service title alone grants all nitrogen qualifications.

questions.prompt: How should an unknown gas line be identified?

options.label: By cylinder or hose color alone.
By using a connector that happens to fit.
Through controlled product/system information and the responsible qualified process before use.

questions.prompt: Does an acceptable oxygen reading rule out every toxic or flammable hazard?

options.label: Yes; inert service cannot contain other hazards.
No; the actual substances may require other measurements and controls.
Yes; oxygen measures all contaminants indirectly.

questions.prompt: What should happen if another crew changes the vent path after a supporting atmosphere test?

options.label: Pause affected work and obtain reassessment of the changed conditions.
Use the old reading for the remaining shift.
Copy the reading to the new position without testing.

questions.prompt: What does an instrument powering up prove?

options.label: Every sensor is accurate for every gas.
Calibration and functional challenge are no longer needed.
Only the functions established by that startup; required sensor/alarm assurance remains separate.

questions.prompt: Who performs technical atmosphere testing or clearance?

options.label: Any worker who owns a multi-gas instrument.
Personnel qualified and authorized for the actual sampling and interpretation task.
Any graduate of this awareness foundation.

questions.prompt: Why can liquid nitrogen create an overpressure hazard?

options.label: It can convert to gas and build pressure if expansion is trapped in unsuitable equipment.
Cold liquid removes the need for pressure protection.
Only flammable liquids can create pressure hazards.

questions.prompt: A required vent or relief path is discharging. What should an awareness worker do?

options.label: Cap it until the shift ends.
Move its outlet toward another crew without review.
Follow the approved reporting/protective response and obtain qualified disposition; do not cap it.

questions.prompt: What should PPE selection for cold/splash exposure establish?

options.label: That a face shield qualifies the wearer for nitrogen entry.
Suitability for the actual task, compatibility and taught use; it does not establish breathable air.
That thick gloves provide oxygen protection.

questions.prompt: Can a dust mask or air-purifying respirator supply missing oxygen?

options.label: No.
Yes, if it has a new filter.
Yes, when used only briefly.

questions.prompt: Why must a proposed purge shutdown during catalyst work receive technical review?

options.label: All catalysts become safe as soon as nitrogen stops.
Only the maintenance schedule matters.
The purge may control a material/process hazard that changes when air is introduced.

questions.prompt: Does suitable breathing equipment by itself control catalyst burial or falling material?

options.label: Yes; an inert atmosphere stabilizes catalyst.
No; mechanical, material-movement and engulfment hazards need separate controls.
Yes; breathing protection prevents all entry injury.

questions.prompt: What should a catalyst-to-maintenance handover communicate?

options.label: Actual purge/supply state, openings, restrictions, material hazards and responsible next-stage authority.
Only that catalyst loading is finished.
Only the number of workers leaving.

questions.prompt: What is useful to report from safety after an atmosphere alarm?

options.label: A guessed oxygen number.
An unsupported claim that the monitor is faulty.
Actual location, equipment/gas if known, alarm or symptoms, affected people and uncertainties.

questions.prompt: Who may authorize re-entry after an alarm ends?

options.label: Anyone who resets the display.
The designated site/operating authority through required qualified assessment and verified conditions.
The first worker who notices silence.

questions.prompt: In the Birch Unit case, what is the best response to the dropped socket?

options.label: Hold retrieval and resolve the changed scope through the qualified operating/entry process.
Reach in with a hook while another worker watches.
Use the H2S-only zero as oxygen clearance.

questions.prompt: In the Cedar Yard case, what should happen when a person’s location is uncertain?

options.label: Send several coworkers back through the cloud.
Assume the person left because the cloud is fading.
Give the last known location through emergency/accountability channels from safety; do not launch an unprotected search.

courses.title: G22 — Facility support, water hygiene and biological task safety
courses.purpose: Address TG31 foundation knowledge by distinguishing actual facility/water/biological duties and preventing contamination through suitable systems, hygiene and handoff decisions.

content.title: G22 — Facility support, water hygiene and biological task safety
content.description: Complete original G22 guided knowledge course: six taught lessons, two fully worked cases and 26 individually explained questions. Practical qualification and employer-specific implementation remain separate.

explanations.G22_check1: Broad service categories do not establish actual exposure or authority. Decompose the work and assign preparation to the real task and role.
explanations.G22_check2: Appearance and taste cannot establish microbiological safety or connection suitability. Use the actual approved supply and release process.
explanations.G22_check3: Low use and system conditions can differ. The actual facility team must evaluate and release the affected system under its program.
explanations.G22_check4: The proposed method can create spread, runoff or aerosol exposure. Resolve source control, handling and disposal through suitable competent arrangements.
explanations.G22_check5: Carts, tools and gloves can transfer contamination. Address the actual pathways, not only visible room cleanliness.
explanations.G22_check6: A physical repair and supported water-use release are different decisions. Preserve the restriction until its actual prerequisites and authority are established.
explanations.G22_final1: Contact pathways depend on actual handling. Contaminated hands can transfer material to ingestion routes; administrative association alone does not establish that exposure.
explanations.G22_final2: Bloodborne, sewage, food and building-water hazards have distinct scope and controls. Overlap does not make one foundation a universal qualification.
explanations.G22_final3: Nonpotable identity must be respected. Appearance cannot turn it into an approved supply for drinking or other protected uses.
explanations.G22_final4: A connection can permit backflow under changed conditions. Competent assessment determines suitable protection; present flow does not prove permanent safety.
explanations.G22_final5: External cleanliness and matching fittings do not establish hygienic suitability or backflow protection. Obtain the actual approved arrangement.
explanations.G22_final6: Different advisories and contaminants require different responses. This course does not supply a universal treatment remedy.
explanations.G22_final7: Downstream systems can change conditions after supply entry. The relevant management program must consider the actual installation and use.
explanations.G22_final8: The actual system and aerosol route matter. Do not reduce every water-associated hazard to ingestion or infer a diagnosis from appearance.
explanations.G22_final9: System methods can create scalding, chemical and aerosol risks. They need actual technical instructions and suitable capability; the foundation supplies no operating recipe.
explanations.G22_final10: A result supports the scope actually checked. Competent interpretation and the relevant release criteria remain necessary for the affected system.
explanations.G22_final11: Biological hygiene does not resolve confined-space, atmosphere or energy hazards. Keep clear and obtain the proper competent arrangement.
explanations.G22_final12: Control continues when leaving the task. Soiled hands, clothing and equipment can spread material to food, vehicles and other people.
explanations.G22_final13: PPE has limits. Use the actual handling method and do not assume a glove eliminates hidden sharp or contact hazards.
explanations.G22_final14: The actions and required conditions differ. Apply the actual facility/product procedure instead of equating visual cleanliness or odor with a completed control.
explanations.G22_final15: Product suitability and conditions matter. Improvised mixing can create chemical hazards and may not control the intended organism.
explanations.G22_final16: CDC distinguishes norovirus control from relying on sanitizer alone. Use suitable handwashing and the actual program rather than a universal product assumption.
explanations.G22_final17: Material and handling changes can introduce different exposure. Establish a suitable prepared arrangement and keep contamination out of clean/home spaces.
explanations.G22_final18: Prompt factual escalation supports professional assessment. Workers should neither make unsupported diagnoses nor delay response because the cause is uncertain.
explanations.G22_final19: Commercial and visual facts do not establish the annex's water-management or connection prerequisites. Obtain the relevant competent evidence and release.
explanations.G22_final20: Effectiveness concerns the operational pathways and handoff. Purchasing or knowledge completion alone does not prove the facility response and hygiene controls work.

lessons.title: Start here — identify the actual water and biological duty
lessons.body:
# G22 — Facility support, water hygiene and biological task safety

A housing provider, a warehouse clerk, a plumber and a wastewater worker can all appear within a broad facility-support service category. They do not automatically share the same exposure or qualification. A lease does not prove the supplier treats drinking water, and a maintenance role does not automatically include contaminated laundry, sewage entry or clinical care. This course begins by identifying the actual duty and the route by which people could be exposed.

G22 addresses the water-hygiene and broader communicable-exposure foundation identified by TG31. It complements food hygiene G05 and bloodborne-pathogen G04; neither course alone covers every water or facility biological hazard. You will study six taught lessons with six checks, two fully worked fictional cases and twenty final questions. Completion requires all 26 answered correctly or acknowledged remediation. First-answer and remediated scores remain separate.

The course teaches recognition, prevention, safe handoff and escalation. It supplies no drinking-water release certificate, treatment-operator license, plumbing/backflow qualification, laboratory authority, clinical training or medical advice. Requirements depend on the work and jurisdiction; no universal treatment dose, flushing duration, disinfectant recipe or water-system operating limit is invented here.

All examples are original fiction. They demonstrate decisions without operating a water system or exposing anyone to contaminated material. The employer and responsible water/facility authorities must establish what applies to the actual people, system and task before assigning work.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — recognize sources, routes and distinct responsibilities
lessons.body:
## A biological concern is not a single hazard category

Biological hazards can involve microorganisms in contaminated water, human waste, bodily material or the environment. Exposure can occur by swallowing contamination from hands or food, splashes to eyes or mouth, contact with damaged skin, or inhaling relevant aerosols. Different tasks create different pathways. A person recording a water-delivery invoice does not necessarily have the same contact as the person connecting a hose or cleaning a sewage-contaminated drain.

Distinguish potable-water hygiene, wastewater/sewage work, building-water systems, ordinary housekeeping, contaminated laundry and personal/clinical care. There can be overlap, but one label does not replace another's assessment. A bloodborne-pathogen program addresses specified blood and other potentially infectious material; it does not automatically control every sewage organism or building-water aerosol. Food hygiene likewise does not qualify someone to repair a potable-water connection.

## Trace what the worker actually touches or changes

Identify the material/system, task, people affected and potential route. Ask whether work could contaminate a clean supply, create splashes, disturb soiled items or expose another crew through a shared space. The absence of odor or visible dirt cannot demonstrate microbiological safety. Conversely, every wet surface is not proof of a particular infection. Preserve the distinction between a suspected exposure pathway and a confirmed diagnosis or laboratory finding.

Use the service definition as a starting point, then confirm the person's actual duties. Broad property, accommodation, storage or support contracts need decomposition. Select additional training only where the role and exposure are established; do not assign clinical care or sewage-handling qualification merely because a company rents housing.

## Worked example: the camp office and the drain crew

Talia handles room bookings. A separate contractor clears a backed-up sanitary drain. Talia needs to know the restricted area, reporting and access arrangements, but the booking role does not authorize drain clearing. The drain crew needs an actual contamination and physical-hazard assessment, suitable method and prepared personnel. A supervisor who asks Talia to mop the overflow has changed her duty and must resolve readiness before she handles contaminated material.

A sound record states what is known and what remains uncertain. Do not write a guessed disease name to make the concern seem serious. Describe the overflow, affected surfaces, contact routes and protective restriction so the appropriate facility or health authority can make the next decision.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — protect drinking-water identity and connections
lessons.body:
## Clear appearance does not establish potability

Drinking water must come through an appropriate approved supply and handling arrangement. Rainwater, process water, fire-system water and wastewater are not automatically suitable for drinking, food work or personal washing. Water can be clear while unsuitable. The responsible authority determines applicable water-quality requirements and restrictions; a worker must not make a release decision from taste, odor or a photograph.

Maintain the identity and separation of potable and nonpotable supplies. Use suitable designated containers, hoses, fittings and connection procedures. A hose previously used in a contaminated service does not become drinking-water equipment just because the outside is washed. Keep outlets and containers protected from contamination, and prevent users confusing nonpotable outlets with the drinking supply. Shared dipping utensils or an open pail can introduce contamination into otherwise suitable water.

## Recognize a cross-connection

A cross-connection is an actual or potential link between a potable system and another source that could contaminate it. Backflow can occur when pressure relationships change. For example, immersing a supply hose in a contaminated tank can create a potential pathway back toward the clean system under adverse conditions. Do not assume current forward flow proves the arrangement remains safe.

The correct protection depends on the actual installation and governing requirements. A competent plumbing/water authority determines suitable separation or backflow protection and any testing needed. This course does not tell an unqualified worker which assembly to install or certify. If the connection cannot be verified, hold the affected use and obtain authorized resolution rather than rely on a convenient adapter.

## Worked example: the borrowed fill hose

A camp needs additional water quickly. Someone proposes filling its drinking-water storage using a hose previously used for drain cleaning and a connection whose protection is unknown. The receiver declines the unsupported arrangement and contacts the responsible supply/facility role. They obtain a suitable approved alternative or keep the affected supply restricted. Buying fresh bottled water for immediate needs can be considered through the approved contingency, but it does not by itself correct the connection hazard.

For a water advisory, follow the actual issuer's instructions and employer response. Boiling is not a universal remedy for every chemical or biological concern, and this course supplies no substitute treatment procedure. Communicate which uses are restricted, what alternative is authorized and who can clear the restriction.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — understand building-water stagnation and aerosol concerns
lessons.body:
## Water quality can change inside a building

An approved incoming supply does not guarantee every downstream outlet remains controlled indefinitely. Storage, low use, building shutdown, equipment changes and poor maintenance can alter the conditions in a water system. A long-closed camp wing, an infrequently used outlet or a cooling-water system may need attention under the applicable management program before normal use resumes.

Legionella is an example of a water-associated hazard requiring a suitable management approach. Building systems can support growth and spread under certain conditions, and exposure can involve inhalation of contaminated water aerosols. This is different from treating every water concern as a bloodborne event or assuming the only route is drinking. The actual system and use determine what needs competent review.

## Follow the water-management program rather than improvise

A suitable program identifies the system, hazards, control measures, monitoring, corrective responses and verification responsibilities. The facility's technical team determines relevant operating conditions and methods. A general cleaner or receptionist should not change hot-water settings, dose chemicals or perform an improvised system flush. Such actions can introduce scalding, chemical, aerosol or other exposures and may not address the underlying system.

Monitoring values must be interpreted within the actual program. A single result at one outlet is not automatically proof that every branch, tank or device is suitable. Distinguish a planned inspection, an actual check and the responsible release decision. If a required condition is unknown or a control fails, restrict the affected use through the appropriate authority and investigate the specific system.

## Worked example: reopening an unused annex

A housing manager reopens an annex after a long closure. The main camp remained occupied, so someone assumes the annex water needs no separate review. The manager checks the actual reopening and water-management arrangements with the responsible facility team before dependent use. The team evaluates the annex's real conditions and required controls instead of borrowing the main building's status.

The completion record should describe what was assessed, corrected and verified and which uses are released. A statement that a tap ran clear does not establish microbiological safety or competent system commissioning. Communicate remaining restrictions to cleaners, maintenance staff and occupants. G22 supports recognizing this readiness gap; it does not qualify Legionella system assessment, water treatment or specialist sampling.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — handle sewage, drains and wastewater without creating exposure
lessons.body:
## Recognize both biological and physical hazards

Human waste and sewage can contain organisms capable of causing illness. Exposure can occur during splashing, handling contaminated tools or touching the face with soiled hands. A worker can transfer material to food, a vehicle or a clean room after leaving the immediate task. Wastewater treatment or dilution does not justify assuming all biological hazards have disappeared.

Sewage-related work can also involve hazardous atmospheres, oxygen deficiency, moving equipment, pressure, electricity, unstable surfaces or concealed sharps. A drain, sump, tank or pit may need confined-space assessment. Do not enter, lean into an unassessed opening or attempt a rescue on the basis of this hygiene course. Odor cannot verify atmospheric safety, and a general face covering cannot supply respiratory or rescue qualification.

## Establish the handling and hygiene arrangement first

Use a task assessment and suitable controlled method. Protect bystanders, arrange appropriate equipment, minimize avoidable splashing and maintain clean/contaminated boundaries. Select protective clothing, gloves, footwear and splash protection from the actual exposure and other hazards. Workers need to know how to use and remove their assigned PPE without transferring contamination.

Provide appropriate handwashing and clean welfare arrangements. Wash hands with soap and safe water after the relevant handling and after PPE removal, and before eating or drinking. Keep soiled equipment and workwear from clean cabins and food areas through the designated handling route. Do not eat, smoke or handle a phone with contaminated hands. PPE is not a reason to reach blindly into waste or compress a bag that could contain a sharp.

## Worked example: a backed-up sump near the break area

An overflow reaches a walkway beside a break cabin. A worker proposes pushing it toward a storm drain with a pressure hose. The supervisor stops the unsupported method, controls access and obtains the appropriate facility/environmental response. The assessment must address source control, contamination, runoff and any aerosol generation; relocating waste into another drainage system is not automatically a safe correction.

The team identifies the prepared personnel and approved disposal/decontamination arrangements. If a sharp or unknown material is found, the task is reassessed rather than handled by guesswork. Clinical advice about immunization or health conditions belongs with appropriate professionals; this course does not prescribe vaccines or decide individual fitness for sewage duties.

lessons.title: Lesson 5 — control facility cleaning, laundry and shared-contact pathways
lessons.body:
## Cleaning and disinfecting are different actions

Cleaning removes soil and reduces contamination. Disinfection uses an appropriate product and method against relevant microorganisms on suitable surfaces. A visibly tidy room is not proof that the required infection-control process was completed. Conversely, indiscriminate disinfectant use is not always the appropriate response to every ordinary surface. Follow the facility's actual risk-based procedure and any specific setting requirements.

Read the product instructions, including intended use, material compatibility, protective measures and required application conditions. Do not mix cleaning chemicals or invent a stronger concentration. A product appropriate for one surface or organism may not be appropriate for another. Keep food, clean laundry and personal items protected from cleaning chemicals. Healthcare and specialized care settings can require controls beyond ordinary community-building guidance.

## Prevent transfer across the clean boundary

Plan handling so tools, cloths, carts and PPE do not carry contamination from toilets or affected rooms into clean areas. Gloves can contaminate door handles and radios; they do not make every touched object clean. Use suitable task transitions and hand hygiene. For some communicable illnesses, hand sanitizer alone is not a substitute for soap-and-water washing; norovirus is an important example. The employer's actual procedure must address relevant exposure rather than rely on one universal hygiene product.

Handle soiled laundry under the designated method, avoiding unnecessary disturbance and keeping its identity and containment intact. A routine linen service is different from handling blood-soiled items or material associated with a suspected infectious event. Refer bloodborne exposures to the G04/employer program and food-handling issues to the G05/food program where relevant. Do not treat those overlaps as clinical qualification.

## Worked example: shared cleaning equipment

A cleaner uses a cart and cloths in an area affected by vomiting, then prepares to clean dining-room tables without the required transition. A colleague stops the transfer and the responsible person applies the appropriate cleaning, disinfection, equipment and affected-surface response. Replacing the cloth alone may leave the cart, gloves or touched handles unresolved. The team checks actual pathways rather than simply adding a completed-room tick.

Report relevant symptoms or contamination concerns through the designated route. Management should arrange safe work and suitable coverage without asking staff to hide illness. Only appropriate clinical/public-health roles determine diagnoses and any individual medical decisions; an administrator should not circulate a person's health details as a cleaning instruction.

lessons.title: Lesson 6 — coordinate safe release, exposure response and public-health interfaces
lessons.body:
## Transfer a usable operating status

A facility handoff should identify the affected system or area, known concern, immediate restriction, work performed, pending verification and the responsible release authority. A maintenance invoice, a closed cleaning task or a photograph of clear water is not enough. The receiver needs to know which uses are permitted and which remain restricted, especially across night shifts, contractors and occupant changes.

Separate correction of a physical defect from verification of water or biological control. Repairing a broken pipe may not establish that the affected supply is ready for drinking. Removing visible sewage may leave contaminated surfaces or an unresolved drainage source. Appropriate competent personnel determine what checks and release conditions apply. A worker should not waive a missing condition because occupants are arriving or another crew needs the room.

## Respond promptly without diagnosing

For possible exposure or illness, use the established care/emergency route and appropriate immediate instructions. Give responders factual information: location, task, material or system known/uncertain, contact route and actions taken. Protect other people from the same hazard through safe authorized measures. Do not delay care to identify an organism or complete a routine report, and do not enter an unsafe space to retrieve a sample.

A suspected cluster of illness or water-quality concern may require public-health, water-authority or environmental coordination. The responsible organization determines applicable notifications and manages the response. Workers should report accurate observations without claiming an outbreak is confirmed or attributing disease to a person. Preserve relevant supply, maintenance, room/use and event records through the authorized process. Medical and identifying information needs appropriately restricted handling.

## Worked example: a repair without a release

Maintenance repairs a water-system defect before shift end and sends a message saying fixed. The receiving supervisor still has an active restriction on drinking use and no verification from the designated authority. They maintain the restriction, arrange the approved alternative and obtain the actual status. They do not treat the repair message as a water-quality certificate.

After a supported release, communicate it to affected users and preserve its basis. Later follow-up should examine whether the control works and the handoff remains reliable. Counting maintenance tickets or noting that nobody complained cannot prove the water-management or hygiene program is effective in the relevant conditions.

lessons.title: Two facility-support cases and fully worked solutions
lessons.body:
## Case 1: reopened housing and the borrowed hose

A camp reopens a long-unused housing annex. The main camp's water service has remained in use, and management assumes this covers the annex. Additional water is needed, so a worker proposes a hose previously used for drain work. The hose's connection to the potable system has not been assessed. A tap in the annex runs clear. Occupants are due to arrive that evening, and the property supplier says its rental contract means every water-system duty is already accepted.

### Worked solution: separate the contract from the tasks

A property rental does not establish who operates, maintains or verifies the water system. Identify the actual facility owner/operator and competent water-management roles, plus what the supplier has contracted to provide. The person coordinating rooms should not become a treatment operator or backflow tester by assumption. Keep dependent uses restricted while the specific readiness questions are resolved through those responsible roles.

The main camp's operating history does not by itself verify an annex after extended low use. The facility team applies the actual reopening and water-management arrangements to the annex. Clear appearance is not microbiological release evidence. G22 supplies no flushing duration, disinfectant dose or temperature setting; competent system-specific instruction must determine the actual method and its safety controls.

### Worked solution: protect the supply connection

Do not use the drain-service hose or unverified connection as the drinking-water arrangement. Contamination can enter through equipment condition or a cross-connection/backflow pathway. Obtain suitable designated supply equipment and the appropriate technical review. Current forward flow or a convenient adapter does not prove protection under changed pressure conditions. An unqualified worker does not certify an assembly or improvise its design.

Use the approved contingency for drinking and other affected needs while the system is unready. Communicate the actual restricted uses to occupants and cleaners; do not issue a generic boil instruction for an unknown concern. The eventual release should identify the system/uses, checks and responsible authority. A rental invoice, repair receipt or photograph of a clear tap cannot replace that decision.

### Later follow-up

Review whether annex reopening is recognized in planning, whether clean supply equipment remains segregated and whether responsibility is explicit in the contract and shift handoff. Observe a later representative delivery or reopening check where appropriate. A new hose purchase is useful progress but does not prove the full connection and water-management system works.

## Case 2: sewage overflow and a shared laundry route

A sanitary drain backs up beside a laundry room. A worker tries to move soiled linen across the wet area, while another proposes washing the overflow into a nearby surface-water drain. Cleaning staff have ordinary housekeeping instruction but no established contaminated-cleanup method for this event. A nearby sump cover is open, and a supervisor suggests looking inside to find the blockage. Several occupants report stomach symptoms, but no diagnosis is established.

### Worked solution: stop the exposure pathways

Control access to the affected area, protect the clean laundry route and notify the responsible facility/environmental roles. Do not flush sewage into another drainage system or create uncontrolled splashing. Do not inspect an unassessed sump by entry or unsafe approach; biological hygiene knowledge does not resolve atmosphere, confined-space or physical hazards. Obtain a suitable assessed method and prepared personnel for source control and cleanup.

Separate ordinary laundry from material whose handling conditions have changed. Keep soiled items appropriately contained and use the designated route so carts, gloves and footwear do not spread contamination into clean storage or dining areas. A label saying dirty is not proof that a leaking bag is adequate containment. If blood, sharps or another special hazard is found, reassess and invoke the applicable program rather than assume one general procedure covers everything.

### Worked solution: support care and accurate reporting

Arrange appropriate care/referral for reported symptoms and provide factual information through the authorized route. Do not diagnose norovirus or another illness from the pattern alone, and do not dismiss the reports because workers cannot identify an organism. The responsible health/public-water/environmental roles determine what investigation and notifications apply. Keep personal clinical details restricted while sharing necessary area and task restrictions with operational staff.

### Worked solution: verify release and lasting control

The competent response addresses the drainage source, contaminated area, equipment/linen pathways and any affected water or welfare use. The area is not ready merely because visible water is gone. Obtain the required completion and release evidence and communicate it to the next shift. Record what remains uncertain rather than writing an unsupported all-clear.

Review the failed drainage, access planning and missing event-specific worker preparation. Later follow-up should examine the actual collection/handling route and response arrangement, not simply count cleaning supplies ordered. Preserve the original event and decisions so recurrent problems remain visible. A completed G22 quiz helps knowledge; it does not establish that the facility system has been corrected or that anyone is qualified for entry, treatment or clinical work.

lessons.title: Final assessment — twenty water and biological decisions
lessons.body: Answer all twenty final questions individually using the actual task, exposure route and authority described. First responses remain recorded. For an incorrect answer, read and explicitly acknowledge the specific correction. All six checks and twenty final questions require correct answers or acknowledged remediation; the remediated score does not overwrite the original score.

lessons.title: Finish — retain the employer, operator and clinical boundaries
lessons.body:
## What guided completion shows

Completion requires all 26 answered correctly or acknowledged remediation, with first-answer and remediated scores retained separately. You have studied task recognition and safe judgment for water and facility biological concerns. The fictional cases are not real company implementation evidence or records of a practical observation.

## What the employer must supply

Confirm actual duties and exposure for the particular people rather than assigning every TG31 service the union of water, sewage, laundry and care duties. Establish the applicable system procedures, clean/contaminated boundaries, protective equipment, suitable supplies, emergency arrangements and release roles. Food safety G05 and bloodborne G04 apply to their actual task overlaps; they do not replace water-management or broader biological controls.

Use appropriately qualified personnel for drinking-water treatment, sampling interpretation, plumbing/backflow decisions, confined-space work and specialist cleanup. Legal licensing or credentials depend on the actual duty and jurisdiction, and this course grants none. Clinical assessment, vaccination advice, treatment and public-health conclusions remain with qualified professionals. G22 is not medical advice or a licensed-operator qualification.

## Separate practical preparation

An appropriate assessor should observe relevant safe skills using controlled tasks or suitable simulation: identifying potable/nonpotable equipment, recognizing an uncertain connection, preventing contaminated-to-clean transfer, using assigned PPE and hygiene methods, and communicating a hold and release accurately. Do not intentionally contaminate water, create a sewage exposure or enter an unsafe space to test a learner. Record unassessed capabilities and arrange further instruction before expanding duties.

Technical water limits, flushing/treatment methods, disinfectant conditions and testing/release criteria must come from the actual competent program. Unknown conditions remain unverified until properly resolved. A course pass, a busy camp or a favorable company score cannot authorize an unsupported drinking-water or facility all-clear.

questions.prompt: A company rents housing. Does that alone establish that its staff handle sewage or provide clinical care?

options.label: No; identify the actual contracted duties, people and exposures.
Yes; every facility-support service includes every biological task.
Yes; the category replaces practical qualification.

questions.prompt: A clear-looking water supply has uncertain source and connection protection. What is appropriate?

options.label: Approve it because it looks clear.
Restrict the affected use and obtain competent verification through the water/facility process.
Taste it to establish safety.

questions.prompt: A long-unused annex is reopening. Can the main building's normal operation automatically clear its water use?

options.label: Yes; all connected outlets remain verified forever.
Yes; any clear tap is a certificate.
No; apply the actual reopening and water-management review to the annex.

questions.prompt: Sewage has overflowed near a break area. Is hosing it into a storm drain an automatic safe correction?

options.label: No; control access and obtain the assessed facility/environmental response.
Yes; moving it out of sight completes control.
Yes; pressure washing removes every other hazard.

questions.prompt: A contaminated cleaning cart is about to enter a clean dining area. What is appropriate?

options.label: Change only the room label.
Stop the transfer and apply the required equipment/PPE/hygiene transition.
Assume gloves make all touched objects clean.

questions.prompt: A water repair message says fixed, but a drinking-use restriction has not been cleared. What should the receiver do?

options.label: Treat the repair message as a water-quality certificate.
Let arriving occupants decide.
Maintain the restriction and obtain the actual authorized release status.

questions.prompt: Which is a possible biological exposure route during waste handling?

options.label: Transfer from contaminated hands to the mouth or food.
Only reading a room-booking record.
Only seeing a sealed clean supply.

questions.prompt: Does bloodborne-pathogen awareness control every sewage or building-water hazard?

options.label: Yes; all biological hazards are identical.
No; the actual sources, routes and programs can differ.
Yes; it automatically grants treatment-operator authority.

questions.prompt: A label says nonpotable water. What should a worker avoid?

options.label: Maintaining its identity and separation.
Asking the responsible authority about permitted uses.
Assuming it is suitable for drinking or personal washing because it is clear.

questions.prompt: What is a cross-connection concern?

options.label: A potential path from another source into a potable system under adverse flow/pressure conditions.
Only a visibly dirty faucet handle.
A guarantee that normal forward flow can never change.

questions.prompt: May a drain-cleaning hose automatically be used to fill drinking-water storage after an external rinse?

options.label: Yes; a rinse proves its entire history and condition.
No; use a suitable designated supply and verified connection arrangement.
Yes; matching fittings establish potability.

questions.prompt: Is boiling a universal response to any water advisory?

options.label: Yes; it fixes every chemical and biological problem.
Yes; it replaces competent release of the system.
No; follow the actual issuer's restrictions and approved contingency.

questions.prompt: What can change water conditions inside a facility?

options.label: Storage, low use, shutdown or changes in system operation and maintenance.
Only the supplier's invoice format.
Nothing after an approved source is connected.

questions.prompt: Why can Legionella require a different exposure assessment from a simple drinking-water assumption?

options.label: It is always the same as a bloodborne puncture.
Relevant exposure can involve water aerosols and particular building systems.
It can be diagnosed from water color.

questions.prompt: Who should determine a building-water treatment or flushing method?

options.label: Any receptionist who has read G22.
The person who guesses the strongest chemical dose.
The appropriately competent facility/water-management process.

questions.prompt: Does one favorable check at one outlet automatically verify every tank and branch?

options.label: No; evidence must be interpreted within its actual system and sampling scope.
Yes; any passing value is universal.
Yes; no program review is needed afterward.

questions.prompt: A sump is open beside sewage work. Does hygiene training authorize inspection by entry?

options.label: Yes; a face covering qualifies entry.
No; space, atmosphere and physical hazards need their own assessment and authorization.
Yes; lack of odor proves a safe atmosphere.

questions.prompt: What helps interrupt contamination transfer after sewage handling?

options.label: Eating with the same contaminated gloves.
Using the work cab as a contaminated-clothing store by default.
Appropriate PPE removal, handwashing and separation from clean welfare areas.

questions.prompt: Is a glove permission to reach blindly into a waste bag?

options.label: No; a concealed sharp or other hazard remains possible.
Yes; every glove is puncture-proof.
Yes; the bag's contents no longer matter.

questions.prompt: How do cleaning and disinfection differ?

options.label: A tidy appearance proves both are complete.
Cleaning removes soil; appropriate disinfection addresses relevant remaining microorganisms under product conditions.
Using the strongest-smelling chemical replaces both.

questions.prompt: What should a worker do about disinfectant mixing and concentration?

options.label: Combine cleaners to make them stronger.
Borrow a recipe from an unrelated surface or organism.
Follow the actual suitable product instructions and facility procedure; do not improvise mixtures.

questions.prompt: For norovirus prevention, is hand sanitizer alone a substitute for soap-and-water handwashing?

options.label: No; follow the appropriate handwashing and task hygiene arrangements.
Yes; one sanitizer controls every organism in every setting.
Yes; gloves also remove all need for handwashing.

questions.prompt: A routine linen contract receives newly contaminated material. What is appropriate?

options.label: Assume every linen task is unchanged.
Review the changed exposure, containment and handling method before unsupported duties.
Send it home with a worker to avoid a delay.

questions.prompt: Several occupants report stomach symptoms. What should operational staff do?

options.label: Declare a specific outbreak from the reports alone.
Dismiss the concern until workers identify an organism.
Arrange appropriate care/reporting and provide facts without diagnosing or disclosing unnecessary clinical details.

questions.prompt: In Case 1, which fact independently clears drinking use of the annex?

options.label: None of the rental invoice, main-camp history or clear tap substitutes for the actual authorized release.
The rental invoice alone.
A photograph of clear water alone.

questions.prompt: In Case 2, what best tests lasting correction?

options.label: Only the number of cleaning supplies ordered.
Later real handling/access arrangements prevent spread and communicate actual restrictions and release.
Only whether a worker passed the quiz.

courses.title: G23 — OT/cyber operational safety: defensive work boundaries and safe change
courses.purpose: Recognize when digital work can affect physical safeguards and preserve authorized, coordinated defensive behavior without claiming technical operation or engineering competence.

content.title: G23 — OT/cyber operational safety: defensive work boundaries and safe change
content.description: Original TG32 knowledge foundation: six fully taught lessons, two worked cases and twenty-six explained decisions on authorized access, physical safety, controlled change, incident reporting, recovery and handover.

explanations.G23_check1: The worker must understand what the task can affect before changing it. Appearance, account access and an exploratory interruption do not establish a safe operating boundary.
explanations.G23_check2: An alternative support route can change exposure and access. A familiar caller and a successful login do not replace the approved purpose, privileges and operational coordination.
explanations.G23_check3: A display may influence decisions in a hazardous operation. The team must establish what is affected and how the change will be safely verified; production is not an uncontrolled training environment.
explanations.G23_check4: Report facts and protect the operation within the assigned role. A cyber suspicion does not give a general worker authority to investigate or shut down systems indiscriminately.
explanations.G23_check5: Screen behavior is one observation. Recovery must establish the relevant configuration, dependencies and safety functions through the authorized technical and operating processes.
explanations.G23_check6: Understanding, practical performance and authorization are separate. A handover must preserve the actual limitation instead of converting an administrative acknowledgment into demonstrated capability.
explanations.G23_final1: OT scope follows the function and dependencies of the system. Appearance and device shape do not determine whether a support action can affect physical safety.
explanations.G23_final2: Access credentials are not a practical qualification or an unrestricted work permission. The task, system and approval boundary still apply.
explanations.G23_final3: A usable scope check connects the requested work to the actual system and authority. Familiarity and schedule do not describe physical consequences.
explanations.G23_final4: Knowledge of site details does not establish identity or permission. The verified access process protects both the digital boundary and the affected operation.
explanations.G23_final5: An unfamiliar device should not be used as an exploratory diagnostic. The approved process determines how it is handled without introducing an unreviewed connection.
explanations.G23_final6: Temporary access needs ownership and controlled closure or reviewed continuation. Convenience does not establish a permanent approved route.
explanations.G23_final7: A test result is bounded by its configuration and conditions. The relevant authority determines what evidence supports use on the actual operational system.
explanations.G23_final8: This course teaches defensive recognition and coordination. It grants no permission for live probing, exploitation, configuration experiments or technical testing.
explanations.G23_final9: Stable output does not establish continued authorization or adequate protection. Temporary measures must follow their actual approval and review conditions.
explanations.G23_final10: A factual report helps both operational and cyber responders. Unsupported certainty can misdirect the response, while uncertainty should be made explicit.
explanations.G23_final11: The designated response coordinates physical safety and containment. The lesson is to follow the approved safe response, not to preserve all connections or disconnect indiscriminately.
explanations.G23_final12: An uncertain digital indication does not transfer operating authority to a general support worker. The actual role and procedure govern the safe state.
explanations.G23_final13: Recovery requires a trustworthy source for the actual approved state. A name or past success does not establish suitability for this configuration and incident.
explanations.G23_final14: Recovery concerns the whole required operating function. A single restored component does not automatically verify its dependencies.
explanations.G23_final15: Technical work completion and operating release are different decisions. The assigned authority needs evidence for the actual readiness conditions.
explanations.G23_final16: The incoming role needs actionable state and limitations. A reassuring summary cannot replace the information needed to manage the next shift safely.
explanations.G23_final17: The investigation illustrates readiness and human-system interfaces. The course does not attribute the accident to cyberattack or teach operational bypass methods.
explanations.G23_final18: Safe simulation can assess the learner’s assigned recognition and communication. Live uncontrolled exposure or technical interference is not justified as a teaching method.
explanations.G23_final19: The issue is the unreviewed access and work boundary, not the vendor’s identity alone. Operational pressure does not supply the missing approval or verification.
explanations.G23_final20: The case contains separate recovery, verification and competence gaps. Each relevant prerequisite must be addressed through its responsible role before the operating release.

lessons.title: Start here — digital support has a physical safety boundary
lessons.body:
# G23 — OT/cyber operational safety foundation

A service name such as software support, telecommunications or automation does not identify every employee’s duty. This course applies when the actual assigned work has a confirmed interface with an operational system or its safety-related information, access, change or recovery arrangements. Desk-only work unrelated to those functions is a different scope.

Work through six taught lessons and their six knowledge checks, two fully worked fictional cases and twenty final questions. All twenty-six questions need a recorded response. Completion requires correct responses or explicitly acknowledged remediation after reviewing the specific explanation. Preserve the original response and first-attempt score alongside the remediated result. A correction never rewrites what was first understood.

The cases are fictional and require no live system access. Do not connect devices, conduct tests or change equipment to complete them. The references provide defensive guidance and an investigation context, not automatic local legal requirements, approval of a system design or endorsement of this course. NIST’s cited Revision 3 is final guidance; the existence of a later draft does not turn draft material into an operating instruction.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Recognize when a digital task can change physical safety
lessons.body:
Operational technology includes programmable equipment that monitors or influences a physical activity. A terminal loading system, building access controller, pump control display, gas-monitoring link or protective instrument interface can have consequences beyond the computer screen. Ordinary business software can also connect to these systems through reporting, identity, communications or shared support services. The important question is what the actual task can affect.

Start by identifying the asset, location, operating function, owner and boundaries of your assignment. A request saying “fix the network” does not tell you whether the affected connection carries office email, loading authorization, an alarm or a control function. Ask the responsible operations and technical contacts before changing it. A helpdesk account or engineering title establishes neither permission to operate equipment nor authority to alter a protective function.

Keep information and control functions distinct. A dashboard may show a process value without being the approved operating interface. A drawing or three-dimensional visualization may be planning information rather than the current configuration. Conversely, a device that looks like an ordinary workstation can provide commands to physical equipment. Appearance and convenience are poor ways to decide the boundary.

For this course, identify three responsibilities in every affected job: the person accountable for the physical operation, the person responsible for the digital work, and the authority approving changes that may affect safeguards. One person may hold more than one responsibility only when the employer has explicitly assigned it and the person has the appropriate competence. Do not infer those duties from membership-admin access.

In a fictional yard, a technician is asked to move an access-control connection while a fuel delivery is arriving. The technician first establishes whether the connection controls only an office door or also a gate interlock used by the loading arrangement. They coordinate the affected admission and operating state with the site. They do not unplug the device to see what stops.

[NIST SP 800-82 Revision 3](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/82/r3/final) supplies OT security guidance that explicitly considers performance, reliability and safety. Apply the employer’s actual architecture and procedures; this foundation supplies no approved network design or operating method.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Use authorized access without creating an informal bypass
lessons.body:
Access should be connected to an identified person, an approved purpose and the minimum duties needed for the task. Use the employer’s authorized access route and the privileges approved for your assignment. A password that works, an account saved on a contractor laptop or an invitation from a familiar colleague is not by itself an authorization decision.

Before a support session, confirm the system, person requesting work, permitted actions, responsible local contact and the period or conditions of access. Use the agreed verification channel when a request is unexpected. Do not approve a new connection or disclose credentials because a caller knows equipment names or says production will stop. Escalate pressure to the accountable contact while maintaining the safe operating arrangement.

Remote access needs coordinated boundaries. Operations must know when a support session could affect the physical system, who is supervising the work and how the session will be ended. A temporary connection should not become an undocumented permanent path. Do not create a private workaround around the approved access arrangement, even when the official route is inconvenient.

Use assigned accounts and approved authentication. Do not share a colleague’s identity to avoid waiting for access, and do not accept an unsolicited authentication request as a routine maintenance step. Report unexpected prompts through the established security route. The employer’s specialists determine the appropriate technical controls and exceptions; this lesson does not prescribe commands for changing authentication or network settings.

Equipment and removable media need their own approved handling process. An unfamiliar USB device or personal laptop should not be connected to an operational asset to “check what is on it.” Keep it unconnected and contact the responsible role. A file can be legitimate while the device or connection is outside the reviewed arrangement.

In a fictional monitoring job, a vendor offers an alternative remote-support tool after its approved account fails. The local technician holds the new connection and contacts the designated operations and security owners. They verify the proposed route and task through the change process rather than accepting a successful login as proof of safety.

[CISA’s primary OT mitigations](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-05/fact-sheet-primary-mitigations-to-reduce-cyber-threats-to-operational-technology-508c.pdf) support reducing unnecessary exposure and controlling necessary remote access. Exact access design and implementation require the authorized specialists.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Control configuration, software and maintenance changes
lessons.body:
A digital change can alter a physical process without moving a pipe or machine. Software, firmware, network connections, user rights, alarm displays, data scaling and configuration files can affect how people see or control equipment. A small-looking edit can therefore require more than a routine office support ticket.

Describe the proposed change precisely. Identify the affected asset and version, the reason for work, the expected behavior, the people and systems affected, and the authority required. Ask whether the task touches an operating limit, protective function, alarm, permissive, interlock, safety-related communication or recovery capability. Refer technical uncertainty to the appropriate engineer or system owner; do not guess a safe setting.

The approved process should establish preparation, suitable testing, operational coordination, verification and a safe contingency. Testing on an office machine does not prove compatibility with the actual operational environment. Equally, a vendor saying a package is current does not establish that it is appropriate for this installed configuration. The responsible authority determines the needed evidence and conditions.

Do not perform intrusive investigation, active scanning, unscheduled rebooting or exploratory configuration changes on production equipment as an awareness exercise. Activities acceptable in a separate approved test environment can disturb an operational system. This course gives no permission to probe, exploit, bypass or test live defenses. Report the concern and obtain the specific authorized technical method.

Temporary measures need an owner and a defined path to restoration or reviewed continuation. A disabled feature, temporary account or alternate route must not remain simply because production appears stable. Record the actual state and the limits of the approval. A work order waiting in a queue does not extend an expired authorization.

In a fictional tank-farm update, a programmer proposes changing an alarm display during loading because the change is “only visual.” The responsible team checks how operators interpret that display, what information is relied upon and what verification and instruction are required. If those questions remain unresolved, the affected change is held. They do not use live loading to discover whether the operator understands the new display.

A safe change record links the actual configuration to the decision, verification, affected-person briefing and handback. Completion of a download is an activity; accepted safe operation is a separate decision.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Respond to suspicious behavior and uncertain indications safely
lessons.body:
A cyber-related concern may appear as unexpected remote activity, unexplained account prompts, changed configuration, repeated communication failure or an indication that does not match other available information. These observations can also have nonmalicious causes. The worker’s first job is to report the facts and protect the operation through the assigned procedure, rather than prove an attack.

Use the established operations and security reporting routes together where physical behavior could be affected. Give the asset, location, time, observed message or behavior, current work and known consequences. Distinguish what you saw from what someone suggested. Do not delay an urgent operational alarm while collecting a complete technical diagnosis.

If an indication is uncertain, do not assume either that it is trustworthy because it looks normal or that it can be ignored because a computer may be compromised. The qualified operating role determines the required safe response using the actual process information and procedures. Do not improvise manual operation, defeat an alarm or continue hazardous work on an unverified assumption.

Preserve useful information through the approved incident process. Record what can be captured safely within your role, such as an observed message and time. Do not install an unapproved investigation tool, run experiments on the live asset or remove equipment needed for safe control. Technical responders decide what evidence collection, containment or disconnection is appropriate.

Avoid an automatic “unplug everything” reaction. An abrupt loss of communications or power can itself affect a physical operation. The designated operations and cyber responders coordinate the safe response, including any approved isolation. A general worker who recognizes a concern does not acquire technical shutdown or network-isolation authority.

In a fictional loading area, the display freezes while a remote-access notification appears. The attendant reports both observations and the actual loading state to the assigned coordinator. They follow the operating instruction for loss of reliable indication and keep people clear as directed. They do not click through the remote prompt, reboot the controller or diagnose the event from a personal phone.

The same discipline applies when the event appears minor. A support worker should not quietly clear logs or close a ticket simply because the display recovers. The responsible roles need to know the uncertainty, actions and resulting condition before deciding whether work can continue.

lessons.title: Lesson 5 — Recover deliberately and verify the whole safety function
lessons.body:
Recovery means more than making a screen respond again. The operation may depend on the correct configuration, trustworthy data, required communications, protective functions and people who understand the restored state. A successful login or a green status indicator cannot independently establish all of those conditions.

A backup is useful only within a managed recovery arrangement. The responsible team identifies what was saved, which configuration and time it represents, how it is protected and whether restoration has been tested under suitable conditions. A file named “latest” is not reliable evidence that it matches the approved installed state. Do not restore a device from a convenient copy found on a personal drive.

Changes and backups should be coordinated so the recovery team understands what state it may return to. A backup taken before an authorized modification may omit a required correction. One taken after a suspected compromise may not be an appropriate recovery source. Qualified technical and operational roles determine the source and verification; the awareness learner reports the available information without choosing independently.

Recovery planning also considers dependencies. Restoring one server may not restore its field communications, alarm path, time reference, user access or related equipment. The team verifies the actual functions needed for the work and any limitations that remain. Do not release an entire facility from a successful test of one display.

The responsible authority controls return to service. Confirm the required technical checks, operational state, personnel briefing and safe handback. Where a function cannot be verified, maintain the appropriate restriction and communicate it to the next shift. A contractor finishing a repair is not automatically the person authorized to restart the process.

In a fictional gate-and-loading system, the support team restores an approved configuration after an incident. The gate display works, but the loading operator has not received confirmation that the required interface and protective behavior were checked. The gate remains under the approved restricted arrangement while the responsible people complete the verification and handover. The ticket is not closed as “fully operational” based only on the gate screen.

[NIST’s OT Backup Quick Start Guide](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/1339/final) connects backups with change management, testing and recovery exercises. This foundation does not teach live restoration or certify a recovery design.

lessons.title: Lesson 6 — Make handover, competence and improvement evidence usable
lessons.body:
A handover should describe the current state, not a reassuring summary. Identify work completed, changes still pending, active support sessions, temporary arrangements, defects, restrictions and the people who own the next decisions. The receiving role confirms responsibility and access to the information before the outgoing role leaves.

Communicate changes in the way people perform the task. Sending release notes is not the same as verifying that an operator understands the relevant change. The employer determines the appropriate controlled exercise and technical training for the actual role.

The U.S. Chemical Safety Board’s Bayer CropScience investigation described incomplete training on a new computer control system and weaknesses in startup and safeguards. Its [investigation record](https://www.csb.gov/bayer-cropscience-pesticide-waste-tank-explosion/) provides a process-safety lesson about readiness and human-system interfaces. This course does not characterize that event as a cyberattack. The relevant connection is that software-related change can affect a hazardous operation even when equipment appears ready.
